_note: September section stamps that pass 1 of the corpus run did not pin to a clause: 'general' (the section's drift) or 'disputed' (Flash judged it wrong for the section, with its reason). Built by tools/clause_tags.py.

reason: The section is a genealogy from Adam to Abraham; no clause in it mentions a covenant, and 1Chr 1:1 is only the name 'Adam' (1Ch.1.1#cl0). The stamp is being pinned to the verse merely because Adam appears in it.
Noah appears only as a name in a genealogy line ('Noah Shem Ham and Japheth', 1Ch.1.4#cl0) and in the Berean text 'The sons of Noah'. No clause speaks of a covenant, flood, ark or its sign.
Abram/Abraham appears only in the closing identification clause ('Abram he [is].Abraham', 1Ch.1.27#cl0, and the nested 1Ch.1.27#cl1). Nothing in the section says covenant, promise or land.
1Chr 1:10 speaks of Nimrod as a 'mighty one' (1Ch.1.10#cl1: 'he he.began to be a.mighty.[man] on the earth'), not as a king; no clause of this section names a king or reign.
The Hebrew for Nimrod behind 1Ch.1.10#cl1 is 'began to be a mighty man' — no fighting, warfare or battle is stated in the clause or anywhere in the section.

The genealogy's movement from Adam to Abraham may be read as evidence of God's carrying forward of his purpose, but no clause states a promise, oath, or act of faithfulness; the stamp is general drift only.

The section as a whole distinguishes lines descending from Noah's sons, and 1Chr 1:4 ('Noah Shem Ham and Japheth', 1Ch.1.4#cl0) and 1Chr 1:17 ('the.sons of.Shem', 1Ch.1.17#cl0) head the line that leads to Abraham, but no clause states that any group is God's people; general only.
1Chr 1:10 ('he he.began to be a.mighty.[man] on the earth', 1Ch.1.10#cl1) contains no blessing, commission, or divine speech; nothing in the section does.

The only candidate is Peleg ('in days his it.was.divided the earth', 1Ch.1.19#cl2), but that clause states a division of the earth in his days, not a divine judgment; no clause in the section speaks of judgment.
The section is a genealogy heading ("The sons of Abraham were Isaac and Ishmael"), not a covenant scene; nothing is said of covenant, promise or its terms.

The section's drift is the line of Abraham and Isaac from which Israel comes, but no clause singles out a people belonging to God; the chosen-line distinction is not drawn here and Ishmael and Esau are listed alongside.
The section never contrasts younger with elder: it lists Nebaioth as firstborn before Kedar, and Esau and Israel in that order with no reversal; Jacob and Esau are not mentioned as such here.
A bare genealogical list of Esau's sons; no clause states or alludes to a promise or to God's faithfulness, and no clause rests on words carrying that idea.
The clauses are names only (sons of Eliphaz, and Timna/Amalek); no clause speaks of sin, exile or death.

These clauses list Seir, Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, Dishan and their sons as named individuals in a genealogy; nothing in the section presents them as nations acting, speaking or being addressed as characters.
No clause here states, recalls or echoes a divine promise or its fulfilment; the section is a bare list of Edomite/Seirite names with no reference to God, covenant or promise.

The names given (Seir, Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, Dishan and their sons) are the line of Seir/Edom outside the people of God; no clause speaks of Israel or of a people belonging to God.

Nothing in the section states or refers to a promise or to God's faithfulness. The nearest phrase is 'before any king reigned over the Israelites' (1Ch.1.43#cl0/cl1/cl2), which is a chronological formula about the Israelite monarchy (cf. Gen.36.31), not a statement of promise; no divine speech, oath or fulfilment language appears in any clause.

The cited verse (1Chr 1:46) contains only Hadad's defeat of Midian. Defeat of an enemy in war is not, in this text, presented as an act of divine judgment: no verdict, no judge, no ground for judgment, no consequence for sin is stated in any clause of the section.
The section narrates Saul's defeat and death, but no clause names or states an act of judgment (no sentencing, no verdict, no stated cause).
Same as judgment_ev: the death of Saul reads as judgment to a reader who knows the larger story, but no clause here says so.
The cited verse has the LORD giving victory (1Ch.11.14#cl3), but no procession, triumphant march, or ritual entry occurs anywhere in the section.
1Ch.11.10#cl3 says David was made king 'according to the word of the LORD', but no anointing act or anointing language appears; the Hebrew verb here is not a 'mashach' anointing.
1Chr 11:19 has David's exclamation 'Far be it from me, my God', which is not an oath formula, and no swearing or oath-taking occurs in the section.

David 'poured it out to the LORD' (1Ch.11.18#cl7) is a drink offering in imagery, but the text presents it as David refusing to drink water earned at risk of life; no altar, no priest, no sacrificial ritual is narrated. Whether the ontology counts this as a sacrifice event is the deciding question.
Jonathan does not appear in 1Chr 11:10-47, and 1Chr 11:18 concerns three unnamed men of the Thirty, not Jonathan; the named covenant is not present.
1Chr 11:21 says Abishai was 'doubly honored above the Three' and did not come into the Three (1Ch.11.21#cl2), but there is no prior humiliation or reversal of fortune narrated, only rank ordering.
1Chr 11:25 describes Benaiah as honored and appointed over David's guard, but no exile, captivity, or return precedes it in the section.

1Chr 11:39 names Zelek the Ammonite and 1Chr 11:41 Uriah the Hittite in the roster, but no clause says they believed, converted, or confessed anything; a foreign name is not faith, and 1Ch.11.39#cl0 is a bare genealogy-style name list.
1Chr 11:25 has Benaiah honored among the Thirty while not becoming one of the Three; this is a ranking statement, not a reversal in which the last is made first.
1Chr 11:7 records David taking up residence in the fortress and the city being named after him; there is no procession, parade or celebratory entry in the section.
The section's closing note that the LORD of Hosts was with David reflects the general drift of divine faithfulness, but no clause states a promise or its fulfilment.
The Jebusites' taunt is answered by David's capture of the stronghold; the section shows a strong attacker prevailing, not a weak party defeating a strong one.
David takes up residence in the fortress and it is named the City of David; there is no exile or return from exile in the section.
Joab went up first and became chief; the section rewards the first, which is the reverse of the last being first.
The Jebusites are the opposing inhabitants who are conquered; no outsider comes to faith in the section.
The text says David was 'kept back/banished from the presence of Saul' (a political exclusion, cl2), not deported into exile; no exile event is narrated in this section
no anointing or anointing language anywhere in the chapter; the stamp can only be background to David's kingship
Jonathan is not mentioned anywhere in this section; the friendship/covenant with Jonathan is not in view
no promise is given or recalled in this section; the steady day-after-day coming is the general drift only

The section narrates the muster at Hebron and the making of David king; no covenant, oath or covenant formula is made with David. 'according to.the.mouth of.Yahweh' (1Ch.12.24#cl3) is a word-fulfilment note, not a covenant ceremony.

No oath, swearing, or vow appears anywhere in the section's clauses. The closest ideas - 'all relatives their were on mouth their' (1Ch.12.33#cl0) and 'a heart complete/one' (1Ch.12.39#cl0/cl2) - express unity and undivided allegiance, not an oath.
The section's drift is David accepted by all Israel after Saul's rejection; but no clause states mercy, forgiveness, or restoration - it is the general historical shape, not a clause.
No fighting is mentioned: the commanders of hundreds and thousands (1Ch.13.1#cl0) are consulted about moving the ark, not battle; 1Chr 13 is the ark procession, not a war narrative.
The section has no covenant making or covenant formula; David's actions are consultative and liturgical (summoning Israel, retrieving the ark), with no promise, oath or covenant language.
No clause uses servant language (no 'ebed' or service idiom) for David, the leaders or the priests here.
1Chr 13:5 says David assembled all Israel from Shihor of Egypt to Lebo-hamath for the ark's journey; the whole body of Israel is assembled as participants, not as witnesses testifying to anything.

The movement here is David's assembly coming up to Baalah/Kiriath-jearim to fetch the ark (1Ch.13.5#cl0, 1Ch.13.6#cl0), not worshippers journeying to a sanctuary; no feast or pilgrimage language is present.
1Chr 13:7 has Uzzah and Ahio guiding the cart and the ark being carried on a new cart; no warrior, weapon or fighting role appears in the section.

No appearance or visible manifestation of God is narrated: the LORD's anger burns and He strikes Uzzah down (1Ch.13.10#cl0-1) and the ark is handled (1Ch.13.9#cl1), but nothing in this section describes God appearing, being seen, or descending.
The section speaks of Yahweh establishing/exalting David as king, but no covenant promise (2 Sam 7) is stated or cited in these clauses.
A palace for David is built, not a temple or place of divine presence.

The section has a victory and a naming of the place (Baal-perazim, 1Ch.14.11#cl4), but no procession — no movement of David or the ark in triumph with accompanying crowd, music or route; the reader's cited verse 1Chr 14:11 speaks only of the rout and the naming.

The section reports a military defeat of the Philistines (1Ch.14.16#cl2) and no judicial verdict, sentence or condemnation; God's word here is guidance for battle, not judgment, so the reader's cited verse does not carry the idea.

Nothing in the section marks David's force as weak or the Philistines as the strong side; the text has God breaking out and giving them into David's hand (1Ch.14.10#cl6, 1Ch.14.11#cl3), an outright rout, not a reversal by a weaker party.
The gods are abandoned in the field at Baal-perazim and burned there (1Ch.14.12#cl0, 1Ch.14.12#cl2); no holy place, temple or sanctuary appears in the section.
No clause in 15:1-13 states, recalls or alludes to a covenant with David; the ark's move to Jerusalem is not the covenant.
Nothing in 1Chr 15:1-13 is sworn, vowed or promised; 15:2 is David's instruction about the Levites, not an oath.

The section is about the ark's transport to Jerusalem; no clause says 'presence', 'dwell', or 'temple'. The ark itself and 'before the ark of God' are the closest language, but the stamp as worded is not asserted by any clause.
No clause names Israel/the people as God's people; only 'the God of Israel' (cl.15.14#cl0) and named individuals. General drift only.

This section shows the ark being brought up and carried, and God helping the Levites who carried it, but nothing about the ark being preserved, kept safe, or rescued — the idea 'preservation' is not in any clause of 1Chr.15.25–28.

The Hebrew of 1Chr.15.27 says Levites and singers, and 'Kenaniah the leader the.lifting up the singers' — no word for priest (kohen) occurs in this section. The ephod is worn by David, not a priest here. The stamp is about priests; these clauses do not say it.

The only 'covenant' in this section is 'the ark of the covenant of the LORD' — the ark, not a covenant made with David. The passage is David bringing up the ark; it makes no statement of a covenant with David.

The only covenant named is the ark of the covenant of the LORD (cl0); nothing in the clause names or alludes to a covenant with David — the ark covenant is the Sinai/Mosaic covenant, not the dynastic promise to David.

Michal's contempt (cl5) is the humiliation pole, but the clause records no reversal to vindication within this verse; the stamp is only the section's general drift, not carried by any clause in particular.

The section's drift is the ark's installation at Jerusalem, but no clause speaks of preserving the ark; the bringing and placing are a procession and an installation, not a preservation (contrast passages where the ark is kept, hidden or guarded).

Nothing in the section speaks of a servant or of serving; the only related wording is 'serve' nowhere present, and 16:35 asks God to save/gather/deliver the speaker — no servanthood is predicated of anyone.
No clause mentions peace or a peace covenant; 1Chr 16:34's 'loving devotion endures forever' does not identify a named covenant.
Nothing in the section speaks of a new covenant or its provisions; 1Chr 16:34 is a thanksgiving refrain, not new-covenant language.
No oath or promise to the patriarchs is stated or alluded to in any clause.
The cited verse 1Chr 16:30 ('The world is firmly established; it cannot be moved') attests the world's stability, but no clause evokes a covenant with creation.
No flood, Noah, or Noachic covenant language appears in the section.
No Abraham, seed, land-promise or covenant-with-Abraham language appears.
No Sinai, law-giving, or mountain covenant language appears.
No Phinehas, priesthood-zeal, or perpetual-priesthood language appears.
No Shechem or renewal-at-Shechem language appears.
No salt or salt-covenant language appears.
No marriage, husband/wife, or betrothal language appears.
No circumcision language appears.
No Jonathan, David-friendship, or personal-covenant language appears in this section.
No cutting of animals, blood, or covenant-ratification rite appears.
No oath, swearing, or vow formula (no 'as the LORD lives', no raising of hand) appears.
No accusation, indictment, or covenant-lawsuit speech appears; the section is praise and petition.
The only cultic act is 'bring an offering' (1Ch.16.29#cl1), which is a gift-presentation, not a covenant meal shared between parties; no eating or table language appears.

cl2 of v34 says חֶ֫סֶד "loving devotion/covenant loyalty" endures forever, but the text names no covenant and no new one; the only covenant-ish noun is the abstract loyalty, and nothing in the section announces or inaugurates a covenant. The reader cited v34 for the wrong stamp.

Nothing in the section mentions David, his house, his throne, or a covenant made with him; v34's חֶ֫סֶד is covenant loyalty language but attaches to no named covenant and no Davidic promise. Being set in 1 Chronicles 16 (the ark procession) does not make a clause speak to it.
No clause speaks of peace, of a covenant of peace, or of shalom; the nearest items are "loving devotion" (v34) and "deliver us" (v35), neither of which is a peace covenant.

Cited verse 17 is Jacob/Israel ('He confirmed it to Jacob as a decree, to Israel as an everlasting covenant'), not David; the whole section's covenant language (vv.15-18) is the Abrahamic oath, and David appears only as the one who appointed the song in v.7.
Verse 8 has 'call upon His name; make known His deeds among the nations' — proclamation, not witness-bearing; no clause has a witnessing act, testimony given, or a witness role.
Verse 13 says 'O offspring of His servant Israel, O sons of Jacob' — 'sons of Jacob' is the designation of the people/nation, not a father-son relationship or a son as character.

Verse 13 names Israel/Jacob as a whole ('O offspring of His servant Israel, O sons of Jacob, His chosen ones'); 'few in number' in v.19 describes the patriarchs sojourning, not a remnant surviving judgment.
Verse 22 names 'My prophets' as persons to be spared, and the only spoken oracle in the section is God's own word in vv.18/22; no clause is a prophetic utterance or a prophet speaking.
The speech is introduced as 'this is what the LORD says' and its promises rest on divine declaration, not on any oath or swearing; no clause in the section contains an oath formula or sworn vow.
No clause names a nation or nations acting as a character; the nearest are enemies and 'the sons of wickedness', which are not identified with any people.
No clause mentions anointing, oil, or the anointing of David; his rise is told as being taken from the pasture, not as an anointing.

No crowning or installation rite is described; David's rule is referred to as already given ('to be the ruler over My people Israel'), and the throne language in 17:12,14 is about a future dynasty, not a coronation ceremony.
No clause speaks of a temple or house being destroyed; the house in question is not yet built ('You are not the one to build Me a house', 17:4#cl3).

Nothing in 1Chr 17:1-15 concerns an offering or sacrifice; the nearest ideas are David's palace, the ark under tent curtains (1Ch.17.1#cl4-5), a house/temple, and dynastic promise. No Hebrew term for sacrifice appears.
No clause has a watchman, guard or warning role; Nathan is a prophet relaying words, not a watchman.

No clause in this section presents a witness, testimony, or act of witnessing; 17:20's 'we have heard with our own ears' is the speaker's own report, not a witness role. The stamp describes the section's drift at best and no clause in particular.
No clause in this section speaks of a kingdom, reign, or royal rule as such; 'King' in 17:16#cl0 is a title for David, and 'house of David' is dynastic, not kingdom language. General drift at best.

No clause in this section mentions a temple, dwelling place, or divine presence in a place; 17:25's 'house' is David's dynasty, not a temple, and the 'house' of 17:25#cl2 is what God will build for David. General drift only, and arguably wrong here.
The section reports repeated victories (1Chr 18:6, 13) but no procession, parade, or triumphal march is described in any clause here.

No covenant (Hebrew בְּרִית) is mentioned or enacted anywhere in this section; 1Chr 18:13 only says the LORD made David victorious and the Edomites became his subjects. The Davidic covenant is 2 Samuel 7 / 1 Chronicles 17, not this chapter.
No promise of God and no reference to its fulfilment is articulated in any clause of this section; only the summary 'the LORD made David victorious' (1Chr 18:6, 13).

No clause presents a weaker party overcoming a stronger one; David is the stronger party throughout (thousands of chariots and foot soldiers captured from Hadadezer, 1Chr 18:4), and the only agent named for the victories is the LORD (1Chr 18:6, 13).
No exile and no return from exile appears in this section; it concerns military campaigns, tribute and booty, not deportation or restoration.
No clause of this section talks of sin, exile or death; it is only the drift of the wider story that leads into war, not an idea any clause here carries.
Jarha is an Egyptian slave, but the genealogies speak of no resident alien or sojourner; the only foreigner named is called a slave, not a stranger.
1Chr 2:23 reports a city captured, not people taken into captivity or exile.
David appears only as the seventh son of Jesse (1Chr 2:15); nothing in this section speaks of a covenant with him.

The section narrates a siege, the seizure of the Ammonite king's crown and plunder, and forced labour; the Hebrew never presents these as a verdict pronounced on Ammon. Adjudication belongs to the reader, not the section's own clauses.
No clause names a kingdom: the clauses that fit are Joab's army, David's throne-city and the conquered Ammonite cities, which describe military action rather than rule or realm.

Nothing in the section shows a procession or celebratory march; the closest material is the summary of the enemies' defeat in 20:8 ("they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants"), which is a defeat notice, not a procession. The reader cited 1Chr 20:8, but 1Ch.20.8#cl0-cl1 carry only the enemies' origin and their fall.

Israel is named only as the object of the giant's taunt (1Ch.20.7#cl0); no clause speaks of Israel as God's people, and the killers are named as individuals (Sibbecai, Elhanan, Jonathan) and as David's servants.
No clause in 1Chr 21:1-6 states or performs a judgment; Joab's "guilt" (1Ch.21.3#cl5) names the sin, not its sentence, which comes after v6.
Nothing in these clauses pronounces or depicts judgment; Joab's word is guilt (1Ch.21.3#cl5), and the judgment follows in vv.7-17.
No clause has a prophet or a divine word through him; Joab's speech (1Ch.21.3#cl1-cl5) is objection, not prophecy, and the section is narrated with no prophetic speech.

The section has no servant of the LORD who suffers vicariously for others; David offers himself as the guilty party, not as an innocent servant bearing the people's suffering, so the stamp's distinctive idea is absent.
No clause in this section mentions a covenant, its promises, David's dynasty or the word 'covenant' at all; the chapter concerns the altar and the plague, not the Davidic covenant.
David offers sacrifices and builds an altar (21:26), a priestly-type act, but no clause calls anyone a priest or names priestly duty; the stamp fits the drift rather than any clause.
The section is about building the house and preparing materials for it; nothing in it speaks of destruction of the temple.
Nothing in this section speaks of a temple being destroyed; the house for the LORD is still to be built (1Chr 22:11, 19), and the only negative note is that David was not to build it (22:8).
The priests are named as a group gathered (1Chr 23:2) but no clause of this section speaks of a priest as such or of priestly work; the stamp is true only of the section's general setting.
The only cultic acts named are consecrating the most holy things, burning incense, ministering and blessing; no offering, slaughter or altar is mentioned anywhere in the section.
Shebuel is called 'the first' (the chief), not a firstborn; the Hebrew here is a headship term, and no birth-order claim is made.
Rehabiah is called 'the first' (the chief); the verse even says Eliezer had no other sons, so 'first' marks headship, not firstborn status.
Shelomith is called 'the first' (the chief); no firstborn language in the clause.
Jeriah is called 'the first' and the brothers are numbered second, third, fourth — a list order, not firstborn status.
Micah is called 'the first' (the chief) and Isshiah 'the second'; no firstborn claim.

No clause in this section names a priestly role or any priestly act: the clauses are only genealogies (1Ch.23.21#cl0, 1Ch.23.21#cl1, 1Ch.23.23#cl0), a death (1Ch.23.22#cl0), childlessness (1Ch.23.22#cl1, 1Ch.23.22#cl2) and a levirate-type marriage (1Ch.23.22#cl3). The word 'priest' does not occur in the Berean text of these verses; the cited verse 23:21 speaks only of Merari's and Mahli's sons.

No clause mentions a firstborn or birth order. Eleazar's lack of sons is stated as 'not they.belonged to him sons' (1Ch.23.22#cl1) with 'daughters' (1Ch.23.22#cl2), which concerns having no sons at all, not the firstborn.

The section as a whole shows the Levite line continuing (1Chr 23:23 'three in all'), which a reader may take as evidence of God's promise to Levi being kept, but no clause states or alludes to a promise or to God's faithfulness; it is only the general drift.

The only mention of the tabernacle is that the Levites no longer need to carry the tabernacle or its articles for its service (1Ch.23.26#cl0/cl1) — its furnishings are denied as a present duty, not in view; 23:28-29 lists courts, chambers, showbread and offerings, not furnishings.
1Ch.23.25 (the cited verse) says the LORD has given rest and has come to dwell in Jerusalem forever — the opposite of destruction.
The section orders worship by ordinance and prescribed numbers but contains no explicit law or wisdom word; it grounds the regulation rather than speaks it.

The section is a genealogical/census list of Levite clans (Gershonites, sons of Ladan and Shimei); no clause in it speaks of Israel as God's people or of belonging to God. The stamp, if it belongs here at all, describes the general drift — this being part of the Levites set apart for the LORD's work — not any particular clause. No clause in the section carries the idea.
No clause in 1Chr 24:1-19 mentions an offering, slaughter or altar; 24:5 speaks only of officials of the sanctuary, and the division by lot, not of any sacrifice performed.

The section names no furnishing, vessel or object of the sanctuary; the nearest terms are 'officials of holiness' (24:5#cl1) and 'the house of the LORD' (24:19#cl0), which are persons and a building, not furnishings.

Phinehas is not named in this section (the descendants are traced to Aaron, Eleazar and Ithamar, 24:1, 24:19), and no covenant is mentioned; 24:19 speaks of 'the regulations prescribed for them by their forefather Aaron', which is a command, not a covenant with Phinehas.

The section records the orderly continuation of Aaron's priestly line and its service, which is the outcome of earlier divine promises, but no clause states a promise or an act of faithfulness; 24:19#cl0 comes nearest in 'as the LORD, the God of Israel, had commanded him', and even that is command, not promise.
1Chr 25:5 speaks only of Heman the king's seer, his sons and daughters; no priest, priesthood role or priestly act appears in the clause.
1Chr 25:6 has cymbals, harps and lyres for the service of the house of God — music for temple service, not a sacrifice; no offering, altar or slaughter is mentioned.
1Chr 25:7 speaks of relatives trained and skillful in the songs of the LORD, numbering 288; no witnessing, testimony or witness role is expressed.
1Chr 25:9 gives the first lot falling to Joseph; 'first' is the order of the lot, not birthright or firstborn status. No firstborn language appears anywhere in the section.
1Chr 25:31 closes the lot list with the twenty-fourth lot for Romamti-ezer; a numbered allotment list has nothing to do with a remnant.
1Chr 25:1 names David, the commanders, Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun; these are levitical singers and the king's men, not priests, and no priestly duty is stated.

1Chr 26:12/26.12#cl1-cl2 describe Levitical gatekeepers serving in the house of the LORD, not priests; the text never calls these men priests (they are Korahites/Merarites, Levites), so priest is the wrong role for this section.
1Chr 26:13 (26.13#cl0) only records casting lots for the gates; no king, reign or royal act appears in this section.

The section concerns Levitical gatekeeping divisions (Korahites and Merarites) rather than the priesthood itself; no clause states priestly duty or status, so the theme is only the section's general Levitical-cult drift.
1Chr 26:5 says 'God had blessed Obed-edom' (26.5#cl3); that is a blessing, not a statement of promise or covenant faithfulness, and no other clause in the section speaks of promise.

1Chr 26:13 (26.13#cl0) is only the casting of lots; the section contains no law, instruction or wisdom saying. The nearest item, 'a wise counselor' (26.14#cl1), is a personal epithet for Zechariah, not law or wisdom teaching.
No clause names priests or priestly service; the Levites here are storehouse officials, officers, judges and overseers of work, not priests offering sacrifice.
No clause mentions gates, doorways or guarding; this section concerns treasuries, outside duties, judges and regional oversight (the gatekeepers belong to the preceding 26.1-19).
Nothing in the section speaks of a covenant with David; David appears only as king dedicating treasuries, appointing officials and in the fortieth year of his reign.
No oath, promise or reference to the fathers/patriarchs is spoken of; 'the heads of the fathers' are family heads, not the patriarchs sworn to.
The section is about Levites as treasurers, officers, judges and overseers; no clause concerns priestly office or its duties.
The section records administrative arrangements and a census in David's fortieth year; no promise is made or appealed to and no covenant faithfulness is spoken of.
The section is about the organisation of a standing army on rotating monthly duty; no fighting, campaign or clash is narrated in any clause.
No clause states, teaches or applies a command, statute, proverb or piece of wisdom; the section is a roster of military divisions and their commanders.

Nothing military is said: the section lists tribal officers and a census. The reader cited 27:23, which is about not counting men under twenty because the LORD had promised descendants like the stars — no warrior, fighting or army.

The section has no sin-offence committed by name, no exile, and no death (no slaughter is reported here; only 'wrath came upon Israel'). The census is called the cause of wrath, but the stamp's three elements are absent.
No clause describes building, construction or a built object; the 'storehouses' (cl0/cl1 of v25, cl2 of v28) are places of storage, not things being built, and no clause speaks of construction.
These men are royal officials 'in charge of' David's property, not slaves or bondservants; no clause uses language of slavery or bondage.
No clause speaks of Israel as God's people, covenant or worship; the section concerns David's administrators and property only.
The stamp describes the section's general drift (ordered, wise administration) but no clause states law or wisdom.
The section names Joab as commander of the army (1Ch.27.34#cl1) but no clause speaks of a warrior, fighting, or any martial act; the stamp is not carried by these clauses.
The section is about the king's court and officials, with no clause naming Israel, the assembly, or God's people.

No clause in this section speaks of priestly office or duties; the only cultic references are to building the house/ark (28:2, 6, 10), and the leaders, commanders and court officials of 28:1 are civil, not priestly.
Nothing in the section describes a prophet: the speech is David the king addressing the assembly, with God's words quoted in 28:3 and 28:6, and no clause presents any speaker as a prophet.

No clause refers to judging, judges, or judicial activity; the roles named in 28:1 are leaders, commanders and officials, and 28:7's 'commandments and ordinances' are YHWH's statutes, not human judging.
No nations other than Israel appear in the section: the assembly is 'all Israel' (28:1, 28:8) and the land is Israel's inheritance (28:8); no foreign nation acts or is addressed.
There is no clause about a surviving remainder of Israel; the section speaks of 'all Israel' as a whole and of the dynasty and land, not of a remnant.
No clause uses 'firstborn' or any firstborn idea; the father-son language of 28:6 is adoption of Solomon, and 28:5 speaks only of many sons.
No clause presents a new or second David; the Davidic promises of 28:4, 28:6-7 are spoken by David about himself and about Solomon, and Solomon is nowhere called David.
No clause casts Solomon, David or the assembly as a new Moses; 28:8's commands are 'the commandments of the LORD your God' given to the people, not a Mosaic office.
No clause speaks of a renewed or reconstituted Israel; the references to 'all Israel' (28:1, 28:4, 28:5, 28:8) are the existing people and kingdom.
No clause mentions anointing, oil, or the anointing of a king or object; the choosing language of 28:4-6 is divine election, not an anointing rite.

Nothing is sworn and no oath formula appears in 28:8; the verse is an exhortation with the assembly and God as witnesses ('in the sight of all Israel ... in the hearing of our God'), not an oath taken.

No clause brings a charge, indictment or lawsuit against Israel: 28:8-9 are positive exhortation and warning (keep the commandments, seek Him, do not forsake Him), without the accusation form of a covenant lawsuit.

Nothing in 1Chr 28:1-10 speaks of the temple being destroyed; the temple/house is only spoken of as something to be built (1Chr 28:2 '#cl4/#cl5', 1Chr 28:6 '#cl2', 1Chr 28:10 '#cl1/#cl2'). The verse cited (28:2) is David's intention to build, the opposite of destruction.

The section's exhortations to keep and seek the LORD's commandments, to know and serve Him and to seek Him (28:8-9) are the general drift of the stamp, but no clause names repentance or a reviving; 28:9 '#cl7' only warns of forsaking.

No curse is pronounced or described in these verses. The nearest negative note is 'if you forsake Him, He will reject you forever' (1Chr 28:9 '#cl7', '#cl8'), which is a warning to Solomon, not a curse on the section.
No exile is spoken of. 28:8 speaks only of possessing and inheriting the land, which is the opposite of being carried out of it.
No return from exile appears; 28:8 (the cited verse) concerns keeping the commandments so as to possess the land and leave it to descendants, not a return to it.

Nothing in the section speaks of destruction of the temple; David hands over plans for building it (1Chr.28.11#cl0 'the pattern of the porch...'), and the only 'end' language is completion of the work (1Chr.28.20#cl9/cl10), not ruin.

No clause names a priest or priestly act; the only cultic wording is 'consecrate himself to the LORD' (1Ch.29.5#cl2), which is the freewill dedication of donors, and David calls the temple 'not for man, but for the LORD God' (1Ch.29.1#cl4-#cl5) with no priestly role anywhere in the section.
No clause reports a sacrifice, an altar or an offering victim; the giving vocabulary is freewill contribution (1Ch.29.6#cl0, 1Ch.29.7#cl0, 1Ch.29.9#cl2), not sacrifice.
The section is David's provision for building the temple; nothing in it speaks of destruction.
There is no turning from sin in the section; the people's response is a willing contribution (1Ch.29.6#cl0, 1Ch.29.9#cl2) and rejoicing (1Ch.29.9#cl0, #cl3).
No clause speaks of mercy, deliverance or restoration; at most it is the general drift of a wholehearted return to the LORD's house.
No clause names a priest, Aaron, Levi, or priestly service; David blesses, gives thanks and the assembly bows, none of which is a priestly act in the text.
The section never names mercy or restoration; the closest it comes is asking God to exalt and strengthen, and it stresses mortality and helplessness rather than mercy shown.
Zadok is named as priest at the anointing; this section says nothing about the priesthood as an institution, its duties or its line
no clause mentions a promise, oath or God's faithfulness; it is at best the drift of the whole succession scene
no clause speaks of mercy, forgiveness or restoration; the section is prosperity and exaltation, not restoration after failure

The section narrates David's reign, death and the written record of his acts; no clause mentions a covenant, promise, oath, or its terms to David. The stamp may belong to 1Chr 29 as a larger unit (and to the cited verse only as the record of David's acts), but no clause here carries the idea.

No clause states a promise or God's faithfulness; the nearest material is the bare total of forty years of reign (1Ch.29.27#cl0), which is a summary of duration, not a statement of promise or faithfulness.
Nothing in the section is a judgment: 29:30 names the times that 'came upon' (passed over) David, Israel and the kingdoms, which is circumstance, not a judicial verdict, sentence or punishment.
No clause mentions a covenant, an oath, or God's promise to David; the section is a bare list of births and names.
David's sons are listed genealogically; nothing here presents a successor as a new David or invokes the Davidic promise.
The cited verse (3:4) reports David's reign lengths in Hebron and Jerusalem only; no promise, oath or divine faithfulness is stated in any clause.
The unbroken Davidic line could be read as the promise to David holding, but no clause in this bare genealogy states a promise or God's faithfulness.
The section is a list of Judah's kings ('Solomon's son was Rehoboam'...), so kingship/kingdom is its general drift, but no clause speaks of the kingdom itself.
The Judean royal line stands for the covenant people, but no clause mentions the people; it is general drift only.
3:16 names Jeconiah and Zedekiah, who were taken into exile, but the clause itself says only 'Jeconiah his son, and Zedekiah' - no sin, no exile, no death is stated anywhere in the section.
Nothing in these clauses pronounces or narrates judgment; the genealogy simply lists sons down to Jeconiah and Zedekiah.

The section names Jeconiah as 'the captive' (1Ch.3.17#cl0) but says nothing of a return; it is a genealogy running from the captivity to the sixth generation, with no clause asserting restoration or return.
No clause in this section calls anyone a king or names a throne; Jeconiah's royal status is background to the genealogy, not stated in any clause here.
Nothing in the section marks a firstborn: the lists give sons and descendants in order but no clause says 'firstborn' or singles out an eldest.
The section is a bare genealogy with no clause about a promise, an oath, or God's faithfulness; at most a reader could read the unbroken line as the general drift.
No clause calls these men God's people or names Israel/the assembly; the stamp is the section's general drift as a list of the house of David.
Only the captivity is named (1Ch.3.17#cl0); no clause speaks of exaltation, restoration, or a rise from the exile, so the reversal the stamp names is not in this section.

No clause in 1Chr 4:1-8 names a king or kingship; the cited verse 1Chr 4:1 introduces only Perez, Hezron, Carmi, Hur and Shobal, with no royal title. (Note: if 'king' is meant as the genealogical line of Judah's royal house, it is still not stated in any clause here.)

No clause states a promise or God's faithfulness; the stamp could only apply as the general drift of the Judah genealogy (Judah being the line of the promise), and 1Chr 4:4, the cited verse, contains no promise language.

No clause speaks of a promise or of covenant faithfulness; the cited verse 22 has only Jokim, the men of Cozeba, Joash and Saraph who ruled in Moab, and the note that the names are from ancient records
No clause states or presupposes a promise or its fulfilment; v.33 only records settlements and enrolment
1Chr 4:43 records defeat of Amalek and Simeonite occupation, not mercy or restoration

Nothing in the section is a promise or an act of covenant faithfulness: Jabez asks, and God grants (cl7). 'Granted' is a response to a request, not the keeping of a word given. No clause carries promise or faithfulness.

The reader cited 1Chr 4:9, but the only speech there is the mother's explanation of the name she gave (cl1, cl3), which is a naming word, not a prophetic utterance. No clause in the section is a divine oracle or prophecy.

No clause states a promise or divine faithfulness; the verses speak of the birthright passing to Joseph and of genealogical records, not of a promise kept. If pressed, 1Ch.5.2#cl2 ('the birthright belonged to Joseph') is the nearest, but the text gives no promise language, so I mark it general rather than pin a clause.
The section narrates a battle and its spoil (1Ch 5:19-22) but nothing in it describes a procession, triumphal or otherwise; no clause carries the idea.

1Chr 5:17 concerns enrolment in genealogies during the reigns of Jotham and Jeroboam—a record of reckoning, with no statement of a promise or of faithfulness (divine or human) anywhere in the section.

God's answering the cry (1Ch 5:20) is help and deliverance in battle, not mercy shown to the guilty or restoration; the section ends with occupation of the land only until the exile (1Ch 5:22), the opposite of restoration.
1Chr 5:19 is an earthly war between the Reubenites/Gadites/half-tribe of Manasseh and the Hagrites, Jetur, Naphish and Nodab; no heaven, angelic or cosmic combat appears in the section.

The clause speaks of the LORD sending Judah and Jerusalem into exile, an act of judgement, not of faithfulness to a promise; no clause in the section states or implies God's faithfulness to a promise.

The sections' genealogies of Levi, the Levites and their clans and the service of song at the house of Yahweh describe the community of Israel as God's people as a whole, but no single clause states the idea 'people of God'. The clause closest to it, 1Ch.6.4#cl1 ('these are the clans of the Levites'), only names Levitical clans.

1Chr 7:27 names Nun and Joshua, but this section says nothing of Egypt, slavery, exodus or exaltation; the genealogy contains no reversal from humiliation to honour.

The section is a genealogy of Benjamin's descendants (sons, heads of families, counts of warriors) and names no king or kingship anywhere in these verses.

The section's drift—the multiplication of Israelite clans recorded in genealogies—can be read as fulfilment of the promise to Abraham, but no clause in this section states or refers to a promise or to God's faithfulness.
A genealogical/geographical list closing with 'they lived in Jerusalem'; no clause asserts a divine promise or its keeping. General at best, and arguably not present in the section at all.
The section reports an exile to Manahath with no return or elevation anywhere in the section; the reversal idea is not present.
Exile is mentioned but no sin and no death are stated in the section; only one-third of the stamp's chain appears, so the stamp as a whole is not carried by these clauses.
The section is a genealogy plus the note about Ulam's archers (1Chr 8:33-40); no clause states or alludes to a promise or to God's faithfulness, so the stamp does not belong to this section
1Chr 9:20 names Phinehas son of Eleazar as having been in charge of the gatekeepers and that the LORD was with him; nothing in the section mentions a covenant, its terms, or its permanence.

1Chr 9:22 says David and Samuel had appointed them to their positions of trust—a human appointment described as faithful; the section contains no divine promise.

Saul is named as fathered in 1Ch.9.39#cl1 and listed as ancestor in 1Ch.9.39#cl2, but no clause here says he is or was king; the kingship is background knowledge from elsewhere, not asserted in this section.

No clause uses 'son'; Christ Jesus is named in 1Co.1.1#cl0, 1Co.1.2#cl1, 1Co.1.2#cl2 and 1Co.1.3#cl0, but never as 'Son' of the Father — 'Christ' is a title, not this stamp.
'Lord' (1Co.1.3#cl0, 1Co.1.2#cl2) is lordship, not kingship; no clause calls Christ king or speaks of a reign.

No clause in the section speaks of redemption, ransom, purchase or deliverance; 1Co.1.2#cl1 has sanctification (set apart) and 1Co.1.3#cl0 has grace and peace, but neither is a redemption saying — possibly the reader took 'sanctified in Christ' broadly, which the Greek does not state.
Only the cross of Christ (1Co.1.17#cl4, 1:17) touches redemption, and it is named for the gospel's power, not for redemption; the stamp names the section's drift rather than any clause.
No clause speaks of sin, exile or death: 1:11 names "quarrels" and 1:13-17 name baptism, crucifixion and preaching.
Nothing in the section speaks of a covenant, its parties, or its institution; 1:18 speaks of the message of the cross and power of God, not covenant.
No slave/servant figure or service language appears; being 'called' (1:24) is not servanthood.
No kingship, rule or royal title is mentioned anywhere in 1:18-25.
The wise, scribe and debater (1:20) are not prophets, and the citation of Isaiah is not attributed to a prophet here.
No priest, temple or cultic mediation language occurs; the cross is spoken of as message and power, not sacrifice or priesthood.
Christ is 'crucified' (1:23), but no servant figure, vicarious suffering or Servant language from Isaiah is present; the crucifixion here is a stumbling block and foolishness.
The section contrasts perishing with being saved (1:18) and speaks of the cross as message and power, but nowhere says death yields life.
The stumbling block of 1:23 is the crucified Christ as offence to Jews, not the rejected stone becoming the cornerstone; no Psalm 118 language appears.

1Cor 1:30 speaks of being 'in Christ Jesus' and of wisdom, righteousness, holiness and redemption given by God, but no clause here mentions a covenant, its making, its parties or its promises; the covenant idea is not carried by any clause of this section.
No clause describes anyone as a servant, slave, or as serving; 'boast' (1Co.1.29#cl0, 1Co.1.31#cl1-2) concerns boasting, not service, so the role is absent from this section.
Christ is named in 1Co.1.30#cl0 ('you are in Christ Jesus'), but the clause says nothing of kingship, rule, throne or kingdom; the stamp is not spoken of here.
No clause mentions a priest, priesthood, sacrifice, altar or mediation; 'redemption' in 1Co.1.30#cl1 does not by itself make a priest, so the role is not carried here.
1Cor 1:31 is a citation of Scripture ('as it is written', 'Let him who boasts boast in the Lord') — a quotation, not anyone bearing witness or testifying; no clause here describes witnessing.
No covenant language here: 1Co.1.9#cl0/cl1 speak of God's call into fellowship with His Son and of His faithfulness, not of a covenant made or renewed; the Greek diatheke does not appear.
The section speaks of grace given 'in Christ Jesus' and enrichment in Him, but no clause states redemption, ransom or deliverance; the idea is the drift rather than any clause's content.
The Spirit is nowhere named in 1Co.1.4-9; 1Cor 1:7 reads 'spiritual gift' (charisma), an adjective, not the Holy Spirit, and the clause names no third person of the Trinity.
1Cor 1:8 speaks of being sustained blameless at the end, not of new creation, new birth or renewal; no clause mentions creation, rebirth or making new.
The section speaks of baptism 'into Moses' but no clause portrays Christ as a new Moses; the role is not carried by any clause here.
The section calls the events 'examples' and 'warnings' but has no wisdom-instruction clause; the stamp is at best the general drift of the exhortation.
The section warns against idolatry (1Co.10.7#cl0) but has no clause about an idol set in a holy place; that image does not occur here.

No clause in 10:14-22 speaks of tempting or being tempted: 10:22 asks whether 'we' provoke the Lord to jealousy, which is not temptation, and 10:13 (the temptation verse) is outside this section. If the stamp means testing/provoking generally, 10:22#cl0 is the only candidate.

The section mentions food sacrificed to idols (10:19) and the table/cup of demons (10:21) in contrast with the Lord's table, but nothing about an idol set up in a holy place; the apocalyptic motif (Dan 12:11; Matt 24:15) is absent.

No clause pronounces or describes a judgment: 10:15 asks the readers to judge/discern what Paul says, and 10:22 asks about provoking the Lord to jealousy and being stronger than He; neither is a judgment.

The cited verse (10:33) speaks of pleasing everyone and seeking the good of many 'that they may be saved' — salvation as the goal of self-denial in a dispute about food offered to idols. Nothing in this section speaks of mercy shown, or of restoration after failure or loss; 'may be saved' is the saving of others, not the restoring of the lapsed. The stamp is not this section's idea.

The cited verse's 'that they may be saved' (1Co.10.33#cl2) is the only salvation language here, and it is stated as the aim of Paul's self-denying conduct, with no mention of Christ, his death, purchase, or redemption. This is a chapter on idol-food and freedom of conscience; 'redemption in Christ' is not spoken of in any clause of the section.

Nothing in the section presents the woman as a wisdom figure or as wisdom personified; v.7 'the woman is the glory of man' is about glory/headship, not wisdom. The stamp looks misapplied to this section.
No bridal or marriage imagery appears; the woman/man language concerns head covering, glory and origins, not a bride or bridegroom.
The cited v.16 speaks of dispute, custom and the churches of God, not of testimony or witness; no clause in the section carries the idea of witness.
v.16 mentions 'the churches of God', which is the church, not the nations/Gentiles as a character; no clause speaks of nations.
Nothing law- or wisdom-related is argued in v.3; the headship statement 'the head of every man is Christ ...' is neither Torah nor wisdom. The stamp does not fit this section.
v.4 speaks of any man praying or prophesying with a covered head, not of priests or priestly service; no clause carries the idea of priesthood.
v.10 ('authority to have on the head, on account of the angels') concerns head covering and the angels, not the temple or God's presence dwelling in a place; no clause carries the idea.

1Cor 11:30 'fallen asleep' is a euphemism for death; the section speaks of judgment and discipline, not of anyone being raised. The only future coming named is the Lord's coming (1Co.11.26#cl3), which is not a resurrection event.

No clause in the section states that believers are in Christ or share his life; the body and blood are spoken of as his and as received in the supper, and 'in remembrance of Me' (1Co.11.24#cl4, 1Co.11.25#cl4) is remembrance, not union.

The servant of Isaiah who suffers for others is not in view; the body 'for you' (1Co.11.24#cl3) and the betrayal (1Co.11.23#cl3) give the death for others but no clause describes a servant who suffers.

No clause in the section speaks of new creation, new birth or a new heaven and earth. The 'new covenant' of 1Co.11.25#cl3 is the nearest phrase, but the section presents it as the covenant in Jesus' blood, not as a re-creation.

1Cor 12:3 names the Spirit of God and the Holy Spirit as the source of confessing Jesus as Lord, but nothing here speaks of the Pentecost event (tongues of fire, the day of Pentecost, Acts 2): the Spirit is cited as the criterion of confession, not as the poured-out gift of that event.

The section speaks of one Spirit, one Lord, one God working all things in all people (1Cor 12:4-6, 12:11), which is the general drift the stamp names, but no clause in this section uses kingdom language or speaks of the kingdom itself.

This section (12:12-26) never names gifts (charismata) or their distribution; it speaks only of the Spirit as the agent of baptism and of the body and its members. The stamp is wrong for this section.

Christ is named only as 'Christ' at the end of 12:12; no sonship, Father-Son relation, or 'Son' term occurs in the section.
The body imagery here is a body with many members (12:12, 14, 20), not a bride or spouse; no bridal language appears.
Nothing in these clauses names redemption, ransom, blood, cross, or purchase; the section has the Spirit's baptism into one body but not redemption.
The body-and-members imagery in 12:25 concerns mutual concern within Christ's body, not humanity as God's image; no image/eikōn language occurs.
No reign, king, kingdom, or rule is mentioned in 12:26 or anywhere in the section.
The suffering in 12:26 is shared bodily sympathy among members, not the Servant of Isaiah who bears and suffers for others.
Nothing in this section speaks of sending or being sent; apostles are named as a role/office in the church, not as ones sent, and no sending verb or act appears in any clause.
No clause speaks of witnessing, testimony, or bearing witness; the section concerns church roles and gifts, not witness.
The section names the church (ekklesia), not the kingdom; no clause speaks of God's reign, kingship, or kingdom.
The cited verse's 'most excellent way' is the way of love (1 Cor 12:31-13:13), not redemption; no clause mentions Christ's redeeming work in this section.

1Cor 13:12 speaks of knowing and being known ("Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known"), not of testifying or bearing witness to anything; no clause in the section carries the idea of witness.
No clause in the section mentions covenant, its making, parties, or its newness; 13:13 rests only on the three that remain, faith, hope and love.
The section names love, faith, hope, knowledge and prophecy; it speaks of being "fully known" (13:12) but never of being in Christ or joined to him.
13:10 speaks of "the perfect" coming and the partial passing away, which is not described as a new creation or a making of anything new in the section.
The "we" of the section is the first-person speaker of the argument ("If I speak", "we know in part"); no clause speaks of a people belonging to God.
The word "spirit" or the Holy Spirit is never mentioned in this section; 13:1 "tongues of men and of angels" and 13:2's gifts do not name the Spirit.
13:13 names "faith" and "love" as abiding, but no clause states a promise or God's faithfulness to one; "love never fails" (13:8) is about love's own endurance.
13:7's "bears all things... hopes all things" describes love's conduct, not God's mercy or a restoration; no clause carries either idea.
The section never mentions a kingdom, king, or reign; 13:12's "then" refers to the coming of "the perfect" without naming it.
13:4 describes love's character ("Love is patient, love is kind"), not law or wisdom; no clause speaks of instruction, commandment or wisdom.
Nothing in the section speaks of being made in God's image or likeness; 13:4's list of love's qualities is not such a statement.
No clause mentions Christ, purchase, ransom or redemption; 13:12's "then I shall know fully" is about knowledge, not redemption.

13:8's "they will cease... be restrained... be dismissed" is the passing away of prophecies, tongues and knowledge, not rescue or deliverance.
13:6's "takes no pleasure in evil, but rejoices in the truth" concerns love's disposition, not a judgment or verdict rendered by God.
13:11's child and man, "I set aside childish ways", is a metaphor for the partial passing away (13:10), not a statement about sin, exile or death.
No clause speaks of God making, creating or the created order; 13:12's "through a glass in obscurity" is about present knowledge.
13:7's "bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things" describes love, not a blessing given or a commission to go.
