The oath appealed to in 1Ki.1.13#cl4 and 1Ki.1.17#cl2 is David's sworn promise that Solomon will reign and sit on his throne, not the Nathan covenant of 2 Samuel 7 (an eternal dynasty/seed, not a named successor). Since the stamp is not defined for me here, I read it as naming the 2 Samuel 7 covenant, which no clause of this section states; Nathan's own reference to it (1Ki.1.24#cl2) is likewise only about Adonijah reigning.

Nathan is titled prophet (1Ki.1.22#cl2; 1Ki.1.23#cl3), but in this section he speaks his own counsel and questions to David about Adonijah's self-coronation and did not invite your servant Solomon (1Ki.1.24#cl2, 1Ki.1.25, 1Ki.1.26#cl0) - no clause here carries a word from the LORD. Nothing in the section is prophetic speech.

Unsure whether this stamp is meant to cover sworn-promise/oath material generally or a named covenant (see covenant_with_david). The only candidate clauses here are the oath clauses 1Ki.1.13#cl4 and 1Ki.1.17#cl2, which say "swore"/"swore ... by the LORD your God" and never the word covenant; I did not pin them for lack of a definition.
No covenant-making, covenant formula or covenant parties appear in these clauses; the section's oath and succession promise are the general drift the stamp would rest on, not any particular clause.
1Ki.1.29#cl2/#cl3 speak of the LORD ransoming David's life from trouble, but nothing in the section speaks of Christ or of redemption in him.

Solomon is set above David's other sons and is made king in David's place (1Ki.1.35#cl2, #cl4), but the section names no elder brother or rival son, so nothing here marks it as younger over elder—the contrast the stamp needs is absent.
Seizing the horns of the altar is a plea for asylum, not an offering or slaughter; the clause names no victim, altar rite or offering.
No clause here is a prophetic utterance or its fulfilment; Nathan is named only through his office, while the speeches are David's, Jonathan's, Adonijah's and Solomon's.

The section names no enemy or adversary: Adonijah's opponents are Zadok, Benaiah, Nathan, Shimei, Rei and the mighty men, who simply 'would not join Adonijah'; opposition is to a self-exalting royal bid, not the stamp's idea, and no clause states enmity.

The section's cast is Israel's king's household, priests, prophet and 'the men of Judah who were servants of the king', but no clause carries the theme itself; it is the section's setting rather than any clause's content.
The section speaks of the LORD's eternal love for Israel (10:9) but no clause in this section presents mercy or restoration as an event.
Nothing in this section concerns exile or a return from it; the queen of Sheba's journey is a visit, not an exile, and the only exaltation is Solomon's throne, which is not the reversal of exile.
The section's general drift (Solomon's surpassing wealth/wisdom) echoes David's successor, but no clause in this section invokes David or the dynastic promise.
Solomon's wealth may be read as fulfilment, but no clause states a promise or God's faithfulness.

The section's subject matter is Solomon's marriages and intermarriage (1Ki.11.1#cl0, 1Ki.11.2#cl0-cl4, 1Ki.11.3#cl0), which is the drift the stamp points at, but no clause states or treats the marriages as a covenant (there is no covenant word, oath or party language anywhere in these clauses); so it is general, not pinned.

No clause presents Solomon (or anyone else) as a prophet or as speaking in God's name, falsely or otherwise; the cited verse 11:4 speaks of his wives turning his heart after other gods, which is apostasy by a king, not false prophecy. Closest candidates 1Ki.11.4#cl1 and 1Ki.11.4#cl2 do not carry the role.

The sin half of the theme is present ('did the evil', heart turned after other gods), but no clause in 1Kgs 11:1-8 speaks of the sentence carried out - no exile, no death, no removal, no consequence. The cited verse 11:4 supplies only the sin, so the theme lives here only as drift.

'In the sight of the LORD' and 'did evil' establish culpability in a court-like frame, but no clause of 11:1-8 pronounces or executes a judgment (cf. the announced consequence in 11:11ff, outside this section). The stamp belongs to the section's drift but not to a specific act of judging in these clauses.

Nothing in 11:1-8 speaks of a broken/crushed staff, a rod, or the concrete image of a trampled support (cf. the staff motif in Zech 11); the cited verse 11:3 gives 'his wives turned his heart away', which is apostasy, not the staff image. No clause carries it.
No clause in the section names a promise or the LORD's faithfulness to it; the stamp is not carried by any specific clause here.
Hadad is an Edomite outsider and receives royal favor, but nothing in the section says he believes or comes to faith; the stamp is about belief, which no clause expresses.
the section speaks of external adversaries raised against Solomon, not of the division of the kingdom into Israel and Judah; no clause carries a divided kingdom
no clause speaks of sin, exile or death; the section is the general drift of trouble for Solomon, so it is at most general
Israel/the tribes are spoken of as the LORD's people throughout, but no single clause carries the idea

The section names David only as the city's namesake and Solomon's father (1Ki.11.43#cl1 "the city of David his father"); no covenant, oath, or promise to David is stated or implied by any clause here. This is a citation of a burial place, not an act of covenant.

Rehoboam's accession (1Ki.11.43#cl2 "he became king Rehoboam his son in his place") is a smooth succession, not a division; the text here names no rival, no split, no northern tribes. The division comes later (1Kgs 12), not in this section.

No clause here states, recalls, or evokes a divine promise or its fulfillment; the forty years (1Ki.11.42#cl0) and the succession (1Ki.11.43#cl2) are reported as chronicle facts, with no mention of God, oath, or promise.
The section pronounces a specific judgment (tearing away the kingdom) on Solomon; no clause states a curse formula or calls down a curse.

Wrong for this section: Shechem appears only as the place Rehoboam went to be made king (1Ki.12.1#cl0); nothing here makes a covenant there, and no covenant language ('cut a covenant', 'before the LORD') occurs in these clauses.

No clause in this section speaks of sin, exile or death; the nearest is Jeroboam in Egypt (1Ki.12.2#cl3, cl5), which is flight and residence, not exile, and Egypt is where he already was, not a place of exile named here.

Wrong for this section as worded: there is no covenant language in these clauses (no covenant made, broken or appealed to). What the section has is a royal assembly, advice rejected and the LORD's turn of events in 1Ki.12.15, none of which is a covenant crisis in the text.
No armed engagement occurs in these clauses: Israel stones Adoram (12:18 cl2/cl3) and the king flees (12:18 cl4-cl6); there is no battle between armies.
The oracle in v.24 is a prohibition and command ('You are not to go up...return home'), not a promise; nothing here promises anything.
No clause pronounces or executes judgment; the section's divine word forbids fighting and sends the men home, and the outcome is obedience, not judgment.

Jeroboam is a king who makes idols, appoints non-Levite priests and institutes a rival feast; the section never presents him as a prophet or as speaking in God's name — the language of false prophecy (claiming to speak for Yahweh) is absent.
no clause mentions an idol, image, or worship of another god; the clauses name 'priests of the high places' and 'sin', not idolatry as such, so this stamp is not carried here as worded
the section is set in the divided kingdom (Judah/Bethel, Jeroboam), but no clause states the division itself
the section concerns 'the man of God' and the house of Jeroboam, but no clause speaks of God's people as a body

Nothing in this section enthrones an idol; the idols are "made" (1Ki.14.9#cl4) and the Asherah poles are "made" (1Ki.14.15#cl6). The language is making/provoking, not enthroning, so the stamp as stated is not carried by any clause here.

The scattering here is of Israel as people (1Ki.14.15#cl4 "He will scatter them beyond the Euphrates"), not of sheep; the only sheep-like image is unrelated. The stamp's specific image is not present.

The divided monarchy is the setting (Jeroboam over Israel, Nadab succeeding him) but no clause states the division itself; the only explicit kingdom word is 'Kings of Israel' in the Book title, which names a source, not the division.
No clause here states or implies divine judgment: it is a formulaic regnal summary, and 'he rested with his fathers' is the standard death notice, not a judgment.
Nothing in these clauses speaks of a promise or of God's faithfulness; the section is a chronicle notice, and no divine speech or promise appears.
Clauses mention only Jeroboam, Nadab and the source scroll; no clause refers to God's people as such.

The section (1Kgs 14:21–24) records offence only — building high places and imitating the nations' abominations; the punishment (Shishak's invasion) comes in 14:25–28, outside this section. No clause here states a judgment event.

The high places, pillars and Asherah poles are built on "every high hill and under every green tree" (1Ki.14.23#cl0), not in the chosen city or its temple, which the text names only as the place of the LORD's Name (1Ki.14.21#cl4/cl5). Idolatry is present in the land, but no clause puts an idol in the holy place.
"Abominations" appears (1Ki.14.24#cl1), but as the nations' cultic practices imitated in Judah, not as a desolating or destructive abomination; nothing here speaks of desolation.
Only the offence is narrated (1Ki.14.22#cl0/cl1); the section contains no clause stating judgment, verdict or punishment — that follows in 14:25ff.

No clause depicts anyone as a warrior or as bearing arms: the 'runners/commanders' of 27#cl1-2 carry shields and guard a doorway (a guard detail), and Shishak's action in 25#cl1 is an attack on the city, not combat. The section has a war notice (30#cl0) but no warrior figure.

Nothing here invokes the promise to David: 31#cl1 names the City of David only as the burial place, and 31#cl3 records an ordinary succession of a son. The connection to the covenant is the section's implication from its place in the books, not something any clause says.
The section concerns the two houses/kings of Israel and Judah, but no clause names or addresses the people of God as such.

The covenant named in the text is the treaty between Asa and Ben-hadad and 'my father and your father' (1Ki.15.19#cl0, cl4) — a political treaty between Judah/Aram, not the divine covenant with David; nothing in these clauses speaks of David's covenant.

No clause here speaks of sin, exile or death; the section concerns war, a treaty bought with temple treasure, and building — the nearest thing to a loss (silver and gold taken from the treasuries of the house of the LORD) is not exile or death.

The section shows the outworking of conflict (Baasha's blockade broken, his building works dismantled) but no clause announces or executes a divine judgment; it is the general drift of the narrative rather than any particular clause.
cl4 says the opposite: Asa 'became diseased in his feet' (he became sick), with no healing stated or implied anywhere in the section; the stamp cannot be pinned to these clauses.
The section records Asa's death, burial in the city of David and the succession of his son; nothing states or presupposes a divine promise or God's faithfulness.
Judah/the kings of Judah and the ancestors are in view, but no clause speaks of Israel as God's people.

The section speaks of Jeroboam's sin and of provoking the LORD to anger (1Ki.15.30#cl0, #cl3), but no clause names idols, other gods, or the golden calves; the reader's verse (1Kgs 15:30) has no idolatry wording.
The text names only 'the evil' and 'the way of Jeroboam and in his sin'; no idol, image, altar or worship of another god is mentioned in either verse.
Only sin is present; no exile and no death is spoken of in these two verses.

The verse says Baasha did evil and walked in Jeroboam's sin, but states no verdict, sentence or act of judgment; the clause 'he did the evil in the eyes of Yahweh' is the evaluation of his conduct, not a judgment event.
No sacrifice is performed here: the dedicated silver, gold and articles are brought into the temple as gifts (1Ki.15.15#cl0), not offered as a sacrifice.
The opposite occurs: articles are brought into the house of the LORD (1Ki.15.15#cl0); the only burning/destruction is of the Asherah pole in the Kidron Valley (1Ki.15.13#cl4-5), not the temple.
No covenant, no parties summoned, no accusation/witness/verdict structure: the section is a word of the LORD against Baasha's house, not a lawsuit speech.
Nothing is promised or kept here; the section is accusation and sentence. The only 'made you ruler' in 16:2 cl2 is recalled as past giving, not a promise to Baasha.
No clause names an idol, image, altar or false god; 'walking in the way of Jeroboam' and 'doing evil' (16.19#cl2, cl3) are the nearest language but the text here does not itself say idolatry.
No prophet, prophecy or divine word occurs in this section; 1Ki.16.27#cl3 refers only to the written chronicles of the kings of Israel.

The section records the rebuilding of Jericho and the deaths of Abiram and Segub as the cost, but nothing here performs or pronounces the judgment: it is presented as the fulfilment of the word spoken through Joshua. The idea is present only as the general drift of the section's closing note, not carried by a clause of this section.
No false prophet appears in this section. 1Kgs 16:31 speaks of Ahab's marriage to Jezebel and his serving Baal; Jezebel is not called a prophetess here, and the verse cited does not carry the stamp.

The word cited in 1Kgs 16:34 is the word the LORD spoke through Joshua son of Nun, i.e. the oath sworn to the fathers at the entry to the land (Josh. 6:26). But that oath is not quoted or referred to in this section: only Joshua's word is named, with no mention of the fathers or of an oath.

Nothing in the section is a battle: no armies, engagement or combat vocabulary. 16:9 is a palace conspiracy ('conspired against him'), 16:10-#cl1/#cl2 a surprise strike and killing, 16:11 a purge of a household. I mark this not 'wrong' outright only because the stamp is vague, but no clause speaks to it; if 'battle' means armed engagement, the stamp is wrong for 1Kgs 16:8-14.

No clause in this section states or recalls a promise of God and its fulfilment. The nearest is 17:22#cl0 ('the LORD listened to the voice of Elijah'), which is answer to prayer, not promise-keeping; and a general theme is not a clause in particular.

The widow's words are an oath by 'the LORD your God lives' (12#cl1) and she acts on Elijah's word (15#cl1), but the section never states that she comes to believe or confesses the LORD as her God; she remains 'your God', and her obedience is not narrated as faith. Low confidence would be dishonest scoring; the idea is not carried by any clause here.

The end of the drought answers the promise of 1Kgs 18:1, but no clause in this section states a promise or covenant; the rain and the servant's report only narrate fulfilment. The stamp fits the section's drift (Yahweh's word to Elijah coming true) without any clause saying so.
The heavy rain is the restoration of the land after drought, but the clauses say only 'rain great' (1Ki.18.45#cl2); no clause speaks of mercy or restoration. General drift.
The section ends the drought, which is deliverance from famine, but no clause here names a rescue or a delivered party - it is rain, a ride and a run. General drift only, and weakly so.

No appearance of God occurs in 1Kgs 19:1–8: the angel of the LORD touches Elijah (1Ki.19.5#cl3, 1Ki.19.7#cl0–cl1) and God is addressed and named in the oath formula and in Elijah's prayer (1Ki.19.2#cl2, 1Ki.19.4#cl7), but the mountain is only reached at the end; the theophany of wind, earthquake and fire is 19:9–18, outside this section.

No prophetic speech or oracle appears in this section: Elijah's only words are 'Go on back, for what have I done to you?' (1Ki.19.20#cl5-cl8), a personal reply, and nothing here is presented as a word from God.

Nothing in the section describes humiliation followed by vindication; it narrates call, farewell and departure to serve, and the reader's cited verse (19:21) shows no reversal from low estate to vindication.
The LORD's presence on the mountain is a presence scene, but no temple or temple-presence clause exists here.
The Spirit is not mentioned; the wind, earthquake, fire and whisper are not called the Spirit.

The section reports David's death, reign length and Solomon's succession; it contains no divine promise, oath or covenant speech to David (nothing like 2 Sam 7 or Ps 89). Merely calling David 'my father David' at 1Ki.2.12#cl0 does not state the covenant.
No oath is sworn or invoked anywhere in the section; Joab is not even allowed to speak beyond 'No, I will die here' (1Ki.2.30#cl6).
The altar appears only as asylum — 'took hold of the horns of the altar' (1Ki.2.28#cl4, 1Ki.2.29#cl3); no offering or slaughter of a victim is made in the section.
The section names David, his descendants, house and throne (1Ki.2.33#cl1) but puts forward no new David; Solomon is simply 'the king'.
No clause here has a crowning or accession; 1Kgs 2:46 has only the kingdom being established in Solomon's hand, which is not a coronation

The oath by the LORD in 1Ki.2.42#cl3 and 1Ki.2.43#cl0 is the closest thing, but it is a royal sworn undertaking, not a covenant enactment or covenant formula; the stamp names the section's drift (David's throne secure) without any clause that enacts a covenant
The elders are summoned as a body who hear and reply, not as witnesses who attest to anything; no clause carries the idea.
The demand for silver, gold, wives and children and the siege of Samaria are the setting of the crisis, but no clause states sin, exile or death.
No clause here is a prophetic word: the clause at the cited verse is Ahab's taunt about armor, not a word from a prophet.
A crisis for Israel is present but no clause names covenant or the violation of it.
Ben-hadad's aggression is the general drift the stamp reads, but no clause describes an anti-kingdom power.
The taunt in 1Ki.20.11#cl3 is the only hint, and no clash or defeat is reported in this section, so the stamp cannot be pinned.

No procession or triumphal march appears; the only marching is the sortie to fight and Israel's pursuit after the rout. Closest would be 'So the Arameans fled, with the Israelites in pursuit' (1Ki.20.20#cl2), but nothing in v.20 depicts a victory procession.

The only prophet in the section is the unnamed prophet of the LORD whose word comes true (v.13 delivered into Ahab's hand; v.22 fulfilled in the next campaign). Nothing depicts false prophecy; the false counsel is Aramean military advice in 1Ki.20.23#cl1-3.

Aphek is a city people flee into (1Ki.20.30#cl0) and a wall falls on them (1Ki.20.30#cl1), but no clause speaks of an army besieging a city, blockading it or attacking its walls; a city wall that collapses is not by itself a siege.

No clause swears an oath: nothing is sworn by God, by a life, or with an oath formula. The nearest language is Ben-hadad's plea for his life (1Ki.20.32#cl5) and Ahab's "By this treaty I release you" (1Ki.20.34#cl5), a covenant-release formula rather than an oath; the text says they made a treaty, not that they swore.

No promise and no covenant faithfulness appears in this section: the only divine speech is a death sentence for disobedience (1Ki.20.36#cl1-5) and a sentence of life-for-life retribution (1Ki.20.42#cl1-4). The nearest thing to an obligation, 'Guard this man' (1Ki.20.39#cl9), is the prophet's invented parable, not a promise of God.

Chapter 21:1-7 contains no transgression: Ahab offers a lawful purchase (1Ki.21.2#cl5-cl7), Naboth refuses (1Ki.21.3#cl1), and only Jezebel's promise at 1Ki.21.7#cl5 prefigures the murder that comes later; nothing in these seven verses names an offence.
Naboth's 'inheritance of my fathers' (1Ki.21.3#cl1) is the family land allotment, not Abraham or the Abrahamic covenant, which no clause of 1Kgs 21:1-7 mentions.
No idol, image, or worship of another god appears anywhere in 1Kgs 21:1-7; the only religious note is Naboth's appeal to Yahweh at 1Ki.21.3#cl1.
The section has no prophet at all, true or false: speakers are Ahab, Naboth and Jezebel (1Ki.21.2#cl0, 1Ki.21.3#cl0, 1Ki.21.7#cl0), and none is called a prophet or speaks as one.
'Inheritance of my fathers' (1Ki.21.3#cl1, 1Ki.21.4#cl3) is ancestral landed property, not a covenant; no covenant, its parties, or its terms are named in the section.
No clause in 1Kgs 21:1-7 pronounces or depicts judgment; Ahab's sullenness and Jezebel's promise at 1Ki.21.7#cl5 only set up the judgment that falls later in the chapter.

There is no woe-form (הוֹי) anywhere in the section; the doom is delivered as 'thus says the LORD' sentences (19#cl2, 19#cl7, 21#cl0). The stamp fits the section's drift — an oracle announcing disaster — but no clause in particular states a woe.

Elements of a lawsuit are present (the LORD's charge, 'because of the provocation which you have provoked to anger' 22#cl1), but there is no rib pattern, no summons of witnesses, no indictment-and-verdict form; the speech is a prophetic announcement of judgment. General drift only.

No clause speaks of worship of other gods. The charges are murder and seizure of land (19#cl3, 19#cl4), doing evil (20#cl6), provoking the LORD to anger and causing Israel to sin (22#cl1, 22#cl2) — 'causing Israel to sin' is the Jeroboam formula and is not itself made idolatry here, and 'provoked to anger' likewise names no cult object.
Elijah is the true prophet in this section; Jezebel (23#cl2) is condemned as the doomed queen, not as a prophet or a false one. No clause speaks of a false prophet.

The section contains no promise and no display of covenant faithfulness; it is entirely an announcement of judgment. 'This is what the LORD says' (19#cl2, 19#cl7) is a messenger formula, not a promise. If the stamp is meant as the general theme of God keeping his word, it could be argued from the fulfilment of the doom, but no clause states it.

The section attributes the deferral of the calamity to Ahab's humbling, not to any divine promise or covenant faithfulness; no clause speaks of God keeping a promise. The oracle here is judgment, not promise.

The two men of worthlessness in 21:10#cl0 and 21:13#cl2 are false witnesses, not prophets: they testify (21:10#cl1 'let them testify against him') and are called 'men, sons of worthlessness', with no prophetic word, office or claim anywhere in the section. The stamp mislabels the role.

Nothing here is prophetic speech. The letters are Jezebel's forged royal instruction (21:8#cl0, 21:9#cl0), the testimony is the scoundrels' false charge (21:10#cl3, 21:13#cl4), and the only reported speech is Jezebel's to Ahab (21:15#cl4). No prophet speaks in this section.
The two kings seated publicly with the prophets before the gate makes the scene public, but no clause states anyone witnessing or testifying.

No clause in this section reports an act of judgment, a sentence, or its execution - the section gives an accession, a character verdict, and an idolatry report. The 'provoking to anger' in the Berean text is not a judgment event, and it is not carried by any clause id I was given.

No clause states sin leading to exile or death: the reign is two years, the evil is described, but no consequence (exile, death, judgment) is narrated here. At most a general backdrop of the sin-of-the-northern-kingdom theme.

Nothing in this section judges: there is no verdict, sentence, or punishment, only the report that Ahaziah did evil and worshiped Baal. The stamp is at best foreshadowed by the wider narrative, not spoken by any clause here.
No holy place, temple, or sanctuary appears anywhere in this section, and no idol is said to be placed in one; Baal-worship is charged to the king, not located in a holy place.

No priest appears: the burnt offerings and peace offerings of 3:15 are offered by Solomon, who is elsewhere expressly not a priest but a king (1 Kgs 3:3 notes his high-place sacrifice; the priestly role is Aaron's line, cf. 2 Chr 26:18).

The feast in 3:15 has no stated relation to a covenant and is not eaten of any sacrifice before the LORD; it is a royal feast for Solomon's servants, so nothing in this section makes it a covenant meal.
No clause presents anyone as a witness testifying to the facts; 1Kgs 3:22 has the two women disputing before the king, not witnesses.
The section shows the king's rule and Israel's awe (3:28), but no clause speaks of the kingdom as such; it is the general setting, not a stated idea.
The section is a list of officials (BSB 'chief officials'); no clause calls any of them a servant or bondservant. The cited verse 1Kgs 4:3 names secretaries, which is an office, not the servant idea.

No clause of 1Kgs 4:20-28 is supplied beyond v.20, and no clause here names Solomon or any king; the stamp was cited at 1Kgs 4:21, which is not among the clauses given. Cannot be pinned from this clause set.
Cited 1Kgs 4:25, and nothing in the clauses (people numerous, eating, drinking, rejoicing) states or implies a covenant with David.
Cited 1Kgs 4:21; no clause in the supplied set speaks of a kingdom or reign — 1Ki.4.20#cl0-#cl2 speak only of Judah and Israel as a numerous, rejoicing people.
Cited 1Kgs 4:25, which is not in the clause set; the supplied clauses state a present condition of multitude and rejoicing, not a promise or its fulfilment.
Cited 1Kgs 4:25 (dwelling securely under vine and fig tree), which is not in the clause set; nothing supplied concerns law or wisdom.
The section describes administrative districts and officials; 'Israel' appears in 1Ki.4.7#cl0 but only as the territory governed, not as an expression of the people of God theme

This section is an administrative list of Solomon's governors and their districts; it contains no statement of promise or divine faithfulness (the cited verse 1Kgs 4:19 names Sihon and Og but only as land boundaries)
Nothing in this section concerns law or wisdom; it is a roster of officials and districts, with no wisdom saying or legal matter

The Hebrew clause set supplied for this section does not contain the anointing: no clause mentions anointing, and the Berean words 'had been anointed' (1Kgs 5:1) have no clause in the list carrying them. The stamp cannot be pinned to any clause here.
None of the clauses of this section state a covenant or its terms; the section as broken into clauses speaks of rule, tribute, provisions and peace, not of the covenant with David.
No clause in the list mentions building a house or Solomon as builder; the clause set of this section contains no construction clause.
Nothing in these clauses speaks of destruction of the temple; the temple does not appear in the clause set at all.
No clause of this section names servants or servitude; the clause set has no servant clause.

Clauses mentioning peoples/kingdoms exist (1Ki.5.1#cl0-1: the land of the Philistines, border of Egypt; 1Ki.5.4#cl0), but they are named as territory and as ruled kingdoms, and no clause in this section speaks of nations acting as a character.
No clause here mentions the temple, the house, or the presence of the LORD in it.
No clause in this section states a promise made or kept; the clause set does not carry the idea.

No clause in this section identifies Israel as the people of God or speaks of them as such; the clause set names Judah and Israel only in 1Ki.5.5#cl0 dwelling in security, which is not a statement about them as the people of God.
No clause in this section speaks of destruction of the temple; 1Kgs 5:17-18 describe preparation for building it.
No clause here states law or wisdom; the section bespeaks royal organization, not wisdom.

The clause list supplied for this section is 1Ki.5.7#cl0 through 1Ki.5.12#cl1, and none of them contains the Berean wording "Blessed be the LORD this day" (1Kgs 5:7); the clauses at that position are about supplying Solomon's table (cl0) and nothing being missing (cl1). The clause set does not correspond to the Berean verses cited, so no clause carries this stamp.

The Berean 1Kgs 5:7 speaks only of the LORD giving David a wise son; no clause in the supplied list mentions David, a son, or a covenant (cf. 1Ki.5.9#cl0, which concerns Solomon's wisdom, not a covenant with David).

No clause in the supplied list speaks of peace or of a covenant; the Berean words 'There was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them made a treaty' (1Kgs 5:12) are absent from the clauses, which end at songs and proverbs (1Ki.5.12#cl1).
No clause in the list contains cutting, sacrifice, oath or treaty language; the nearest items (1Ki.5.12#cl0, 1Ki.5.12#cl1) are about proverbs and songs.
Nothing in the supplied clauses expresses a promise or its fulfilment; the Berean 'as He had promised him' (1Kgs 5:12) is not present in the clause list.
Nothing in this section speaks of destruction; the house is being built and described (6:1-4). The offering is the building of the temple, not its destruction.
'temple_destroyed' is not present; the passage concerns building the temple and God dwelling in it, with no destruction."
No clause states sonship; David is named as father, not Solomon as son.
The section says the ark was to be put in the inner sanctuary (1Kgs 6:19); nothing here speaks of the ark being preserved or surviving.
1Kgs 6:14 is the temple being built and finished; no destruction is spoken of anywhere in the section.
No priest or priestly act appears; 1Kgs 6:19 concerns placing the ark, not a priest.
The only covenant named is 'the ark of the covenant of the LORD' (1Kgs 6:19), not the Davidic covenant.
1Kgs 6:16 concerns the inner sanctuary's construction; no priest or priestly service is mentioned.
1Kgs 6:20 mentions the altar being overlaid with gold, but no sacrifice or offering is performed or named.
The section is about Solomon's temple doors and doorposts, not tabernacle furnishings; the stamp registers the general sanctuary-furnishing drift but no clause names a tabernacle item.
Solomon is the royal builder throughout (1Kgs 6:31), but no clause in this section names him as king or states kingship; it is the section's background, not a clause's content.
Carved cherubim and palm trees are temple decoration, not the image of God borne by humans; no clause in this section speaks of it.
