No clause in this section speaks of the kingdom, the throne or rule as such. Saul's kingship is the setting of 19:4-6 and 19:15, and that is the section's general drift rather than any clause's content.

The section's only promise is Saul's oath that David will not die (19:6#cl1-3), and he breaks it at 19:11 and 19:15. There is no promise from God and no divine faithfulness in these chapters; the stamp at most names the passage's general background.

David is innocent and persecuted (19:4#cl3, 19:5#cl0-1 and cl5), but nothing in this section presents him as a servant who suffers for others or bears their sin. That is the mark of the stamp, and no clause carries it; the section merely matches its general shape of an innocent sufferer.
v.10 speaks of God's future act for His king/anointed within the prayer, but no clause states a promise given or faithfulness kept; the stamp is the section's drift, not carried by a clause.
the whole prayer anticipates God's future reversal and the king (vv.4-10), but no clause names a prophet, a word from God, or the act of prophecy; the cited v.10 only announces what God will do.
Samuel is described only as ministering before the LORD, a boy in a linen ephod (1Sa.2.18#cl0-1); no clause in this section names or depicts him as a prophet.

The section presupposes a perpetual priestly grant to Eli's house (2:30 uses 'said', not 'covenant') but never speaks of Phinehas or of a covenant with him; the priestly covenant named in this passage elsewhere belongs to Levi (cf. Num 25:12-13), not Phinehas, and no clause here carries it.

1Sam 2:35 speaks of an enduring house for a faithful priest and walking before "My anointed one"; the anointed is presupposed but no clause says the covenant is with David or names him, so the stamp is an inference, not something this section states.

The section speaks of sin (1Sa.2.29#cl0, cl2) and of death (1Sa.2.33#cl3, 1Sa.2.34#cl2), but exile is nowhere in it and no single clause carries the tripartite idea; it describes the section's drift only.

The section never uses kingdom language or names a king; 'My anointed one' presupposes a king but the clause states the priest's standing before him, not a kingdom, so the stamp as worded is not carried by any clause here.
David is afraid and calls himself Jonathan's servant (1Sa.20.8#cl0), but nothing in these clauses makes him a suffering servant figure; the stamp's idea is not present as its own.
The clauses rest on a test and a sign ("know that it has been determined"), but no prophet speaks and no word of the LORD is given in this section.

The section has the hunted David (20:13 'harm on you'), but nothing marks him as the LORD's servant or as suffering on behalf of others; the nearest speech (12#cl1, 13) is an oath of a friend protecting David, not servant-of-the-LORD language.

This section is about Saul's hostility to David and Jonathan's parting from him; the clauses cited (Jonathan's grief) describe the grief of Jonathan, not the servant of the LORD, and no clause here presents the servant's vicarious suffering.
The section's drift concerns the breach between Saul and David, the LORD's anointed-to-be, but no single clause states or shows the people of God as a body.

Doeg is 'chief shepherd for Saul' in the Berean text, but the Hebrew here (אַבִּיר הָרֹעִים, 'mighty one of the shepherds') is a title; no clause in this section states a shepherd role as an idea, so it stands as part of the general cast rather than a clause-level pin.

The section's drift is David as hunted man among hostile Philistines, but no clause states enmity; Achish and his servants are hosts who receive him and then are alarmed by him, and Saul is only named as the one David flees from (1Sa.21.11#cl1).
The flight to a foreign king in 1Sa.21.11#cl1-cl2 is the exile pole; the section contains no exaltation clause, so the stamp is a reading of a wider arc rather than anything this section says.

The cited verse (v.9) does mention Goliath the Philistine 'whom you struck down' (1Sa.21.10#cl1-cl2), but the defeat is recalled, not enacted here, and nothing in this section has the weak overcoming the strong — David is fleeing, unarmed, and then feigns madness. The stamp projects the wider David story onto a section that shows the opposite of a victory.

The cited verse (v.11) is David's flight from Saul; no clause in the section shows an insider failing — Doeg the Edomite belongs to verse 8's clause list (1Sa.21.8#cl2-cl3) and is not in the reader's cited verse, and Ahimelech, Achish and the servants act as the text says. The stamp is not carried by v.11.

Four hundred men gather to David and he becomes their commander (1Sa.22.2#cl0, cl2, cl3), but the Hebrew calls them distressed, indebted and bitter of soul, not warriors, and the section has no fighting; the stamp is read in from David's later career, not from this text.
David flees to Adullam and Mizpah and lives in a stronghold, but he is never deported or taken out of his land as an exile event; the section's flight language is refuge, not exile.

The distressed, indebted and bitter gather to David and he becomes their commander (1Sa.22.2#cl0-cl3): the weak are gathered and given a leader, but no strong party is defeated anywhere in this section, so the reversal does not occur here.
David is on the run and hiding (1Sa.22.1#cl1, 1Sa.22.4#cl1, 1Sa.22.5#cl1) and is nowhere exalted in this section; only the exile half of the pattern is present.

David's "until I learn what God will do for me" (1Sa.22.3#cl3-cl5) presupposes God's commitment to him, but the section states no promise and shows no fulfilment; the stamp is only the drift behind his waiting, and no clause itself carries it.

Nothing in this section anoints, is anointed, or mentions anointing; the words cited are 'gave him provisions' ('provisions', not 'anointing'), and 'the son of Jesse' is a patronymic, not a reference to anointing.
The nearest clauses name 'the priests of the LORD' (1Sa.22.17#cl3), which is close but not the same term as 'people of God'; the stamp fits the section's drift rather than any clause.

No prophet, prophetic formula, or word of the LORD occurs in this section; speech in the scene is Saul's, Ahimelech's, Doeg's and David's, and 'inquired of the LORD' (1Sa.22.10#cl0) is priestly enquiry, not prophecy.

1Sam 23:5 has a rout and plunder (fought, drove away livestock, mighty blow, saved Keilah), but nothing in this section depicts a procession, triumph or celebratory march; the stamp's imagery is absent.
David is not called or shown acting as king in this section; he appears as the leader of a fighting band who inquires of the LORD. No kingship language or royal act in any clause.

The section gives no comparison of strength or reversal of it: David's men voice fear (1Sa.23.3#cl2), but the fight in 1Sam 23:5 is won with the LORD's pledged deliverance, not by a weaker party overcoming a stronger one in the text.

No oath is sworn or invoked anywhere in these clauses; the covenant of 1Sa.23.18#cl0 is made 'before the LORD' but no oath formula ('as the LORD lives', 'swear') occurs, and Jonathan's 'Even my father Saul knows this is true' is assurance, not oath.

The cited verse 24:6 has no covenant term; the section has oath-like formulas ('far be it to me from Yahweh') and an appeal to Yahweh's judgment but no covenant-making or covenant word. The stamp is at best the section's general frame, not carried by any clause.
Nothing about priests, priestly service or cult is said in this section; the only cult-adjacent term is 'anointed', which is kingship here, not priesthood.

The only covenant here is the oath David swears to Saul about Saul's descendants (1Sam 24:21-22); nothing in the section speaks of a covenant with David. The dynastic promise to David belongs to 2 Samuel 7.

No one is called to witness and no testimony is invoked; Yahweh is named only as the one Saul swears by and the one asked to reward David. The reader's citation of 1Sam 24:21 points at the oath, which is oath_swearing, not witness.

The section is conducted by oath, good dealing and its expected reward, but no clause states a promise or a divine faithfulness; the nearest clauses are the oath itself (1Sa.24.22#cl0) and the appeal for Yahweh to repay (1Sa.24.20#cl2), and I am neither sure the stamp belongs here nor which clauses carry it.
This section is an insider succeeding: David, one of Saul's own men and son-in-law, spares him and is blessed and sworn to. There is no failure by an insider in these clauses.

Abigail is no priest and makes no intercession for others before God; she petitions David for herself and her household and speaks of the LORD's restraint, but nothing in these clauses presents a priestly mediating office — the section has no priest, altar, sacrifice or intercession to God at all.
The section's drift is Abigail's abasement before David and David's blessing of her, and Nabal's fall; but no clause states a reversal of low to high.
Nothing reverses rank or precedence; Abigail's deference to David and Nabal's death are not the last becoming first.
No conflict is decided by the weaker party; David is restrained by Abigail's words and the LORD strikes Nabal, not a contest of weak versus strong.
Nabal's death in the last clause yields no life anywhere in the section; no life arises from it.
David acts with kingly authority over 400 men throughout, but no clause names or depicts a king; nearest are 1Sa.25.13#cl0 and #cl4, which give only 'David' and 'his men'.

Folly is present in this section's characters (1Sa.25.3#cl3 'harsh and evil of his dealings'; 1Sa.25.17#cl3 'he is such a scoundrel') but attached to the man, not a woman; as a stamp about a woman no clause says it.
'harsh and evil' (1Sa.25.3#cl3) and 'disaster / son of worthlessness' (1Sa.25.17#cl2, #cl3) are sin and death-adjacent, but no clause states exile or death.
No clause in the section shows mercy given or restoration; Abigail's intervention that resolves the crisis comes later (vv.18-35).
No clause speaks of a throne, realm or kingship; only David's personal command of men (1Sa.25.13#cl0, #cl4).
The section quotes only greeting, refusal and counsel; no clause presents a word from God (the later reference to Yahweh's restraining Abigail is outside this section).
The section ends with the strong arming against the weak; no clause narrates the reversal.
The one who believes David and acts on it (Abigail) responds in vv.18-35, outside this section; within it no clause shows an outsider believing.

Nabal is dead before the section opens (25.39 reports his death) and no clause names an adversary acting within these verses; the opposition is past and only recalled. This is the section's background, not something any clause here speaks to.

The section names individuals and households (Abigail, David, Ahinoam, Michal, Saul, Palti) but no clause speaks of a people, Israel, congregation, or covenant community. If the stamp means Israel as the people of God, no clause here carries it.

The stamp names belief/faith, but no clause in this section has a verb of believing, trusting or confessing, and no clause marks Abigail or anyone as an outsider to the people of God. Her words in 25.41 are service, not a confession. I do not see this stamp in this section.
Confidence in the LORD's vindication ('the LORD Himself will strike him down') is the section's drift, but no clause states a promise or divine faithfulness.
David is the pursued innocent, but nothing in these clauses speaks of a servant who suffers and bears it for others; the stamp is read into the section, not carried by it.
David's refusal rests on reverence for the LORD's anointed, a principled restraint akin to wisdom, but no clause of this section states law or wisdom.

No clause in the section shows mercy or restoration. 26:17 is only Saul recognising David's voice and the exchange of greetings ('Is that your voice, David my son?'), which is recognition, not mercy or restoration; the rest is accusation, a curse and a plea for his blood not to be shed.

No clause is a prophetic utterance or the report of one; 26:19 is David's own plea ('may my lord the king hear the words of his servant', 'If the LORD has stirred you up against me, then may He accept an offering') and the citation in it is the saying of David's pursuers, not a prophet's word. Nothing in the section introduces a prophet.

The cited verse 26:20 is David pleading that his life not be taken and belittling the pursuit ('to look for a flea... like one who hunts a partridge'); it asks for deliverance rather than reporting one, and no clause in the section shows God delivering anyone.

The cited verse is Yahweh repaying a man for his righteousness; no clause has anyone testifying or being called as a witness — the idea is the section's general drift of deeds seen and repaid, not a clause in particular.
No clause says anything about rule, throne or kingdom; only the title "king's spear" and the final parting are near the cited verse.
David is not exalted in this section: he flees, settles as a dependent of Achish, and ends as Achish's perpetual servant.
The raids kill unresisting populations; no stronger opponent is overcome by a weaker one, and Achish's gift of Ziklag is not a contest.
David's departure is prudent self-preservation, not a failure; he succeeds in escaping Saul's hand.
Israel appears only as territory Saul searches or as the people David is accused of stinking before; there is no covenant-people idea carried by any clause.
No divine promise is cited, invoked or fulfilled in the section; Ziklag's lasting ownership by Judah is a historical note, not a promise.
Although there is flight and killing, no clause presents this as sin leading to exile and death; the section presents escape and slaughter as David's strategy.
Samuel is named (1Sa.28.3#cl0) but no clause here calls him a prophet; prophecy appears only as the LORD's silence by prophets (1Sa.28.6#cl1), and Samuel's role as prophet is presupposed, not stated.
No clause states or depicts a judgment event: 28:5 has only Saul's fear at the Philistine camp (1Sa.28.5#cl1, cl2). Fear before a battle is not a judgment.
No clause contains an oath, vow, or swear formula; 28:6 has only Saul's inquiry and the LORD's refusal to answer.

This is a meal of hospitality and physical reviving for a distressed man, not a covenant/treaty meal (no covenant, oath, or covenant formula appears); the bread is even unleavened, i.e. a hurried ordinary meal.

Nothing in the section shows an insider failing: the commanders reject David (1Sa.29.4#cl1-#cl5) and David is sent home innocent, protesting his loyalty (1Sa.29.8#cl3-#cl4). The nearest candidate, David's defection (1Sa.29.3#cl5 'from the day he defected'), is past history predating the clause's point, which is Achish's verdict of no fault.

No humiliation and no vindication is narrated. David is publicly dismissed from the battle he wanted to fight (1Sa.29.8#cl3-#cl4; 1Sa.29.4#cl5), and the section ends with the Philistines going up to Jezreel (1Sa.29.11#cl3); the reader's 1Sam 29:5 is the taunt-song, a threat cited against David rather than a reversal accomplished.

No clause states a promise or covenant. The nearest things are human loyalties and verdicts — David's obedience to the king (1Sa.29.8#cl4) and Achish's 'found no fault' (1Sa.29.3#cl5, 1Sa.29.6#cl7) — which are not divine promise or faithfulness, so no clause in particular carries the stamp.

No prophetic speech in the section. 1Sam 29:5, the reader's citation, is the quoted victory song 'Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands' (1Sa.29.5#cl3-#cl4), sung by people in dances as a taunt against David, not a prophet's word; the only other quoted formulas are the commanders' orders and Achish's oath (1Sa.29.6#cl2).
No clause in the section names mercy or restoration; Eli's 'Let Him do what is good in His eyes' (1Sa.3.18#cl4) is acceptance of judgment, not mercy, so the stamp is general drift at best.
David is a king in the narrative, but no clause here names him king or shows him ruling; he appears only as leader of men.

David and his men are warriors of the narrative frame, but this section shows them arriving, weeping and being distressed, never fighting. The stamp is about who they are, not something a clause says.

This section has a city burned, captives taken and a people in grief, but no servant figure who suffers on behalf of others; David is distressed for himself and his own, and nothing here is vicarious or servant-shaped.

There is no reversal in this section: it records loss (raid, burning, captivity, threatened stoning) and ends with David still in distress. The exaltation the stamp implies comes later in the chapter, outside these six verses.
As above: the section gives humiliation (loss, tears, men speaking of stoning David) with no vindication within it. "David found strength" is endurance, not vindication.
No defeat of anyone occurs in this section; the strong (the Amalekites) have just defeated the weak, and David's men are too spent to weep. The reversal belongs to later verses.
The section opens with David and his men coming out and being met (30:21) and everywhere else speaks of plunder sent out as gifts; no clause describes a procession or triumphal return with the spoil.

30:29 does name Jerahmeelites and Kenites as groups and 30:26 Judah, but every clause about them is a place-of-residence or recipient formula ('those who were in the cities of the Jerahmeelites'); no clause treats a nation as an acting character.
'Israel' appears only as the addressee of a statute (30:25); there is no clause here about a kingdom, throne, reign or royal rule as such.
The cited verse (30:25) speaks only of a statute enduring 'from that day forward ... to this very day' — a custom's continuance, not a promise made or kept and not God's faithfulness.

David is not called king, does not command as king or act in any distinctively royal way; his authority is only as leader of the six hundred. It is the section's background drift rather than any clause.
The two hundred left at the Brook of Besor are the weak, and they never fight; the victory is won by the four hundred strong. The reversal idea is not in this section.
Nothing is exiled or exalted here: David's household is recovered from raiders and the plunder is brought back. No clause traces a fall followed by an elevation.
No clause in this section states or depicts a judicial act; the deaths are reported as battle outcome. At most the whole section is read as the outworking of judgment, which is drift, not a clause.

The section moves the other way: the king is wounded, fears being tortured by the uncircumcised, and kills himself. No clause shows humiliation turning to vindication; the reversal is from kingship to death.
Nothing in these clauses presents Saul or the men as a suffering servant; the clauses report hearing, retrieving bodies, burning, burying and fasting, not servanthood or vicarious suffering.
The section reports death, retrieval of corpses, burning, burial and fasting; no clause says the death produced life or any reversal from death to life.
The section shows the ark brought out to save Israel and then captured (1Sa.4.11#cl0); nothing here preserves the ark, so a stamp of ark preservation is not true of this section.
The only capture here is the ark's; no person is taken into captivity in this section (1Sa.4.10 has the slain and the fugitives, not captives).

No idol is brought into a holy place in this section; the ark (not an idol) is carried into the camp (1Sa.4.3#cl3, 1Sa.4.5#cl1), and the Philistines' word 'gods' is their reading of the ark (1Sa.4.7#cl2).
There is no temple in this section and nothing is desecrated in one; the ark's seizure (1Sa.4.11#cl0) is not a desecration of a temple.
The Philistines are the stronger side in this section and Israel the weaker; the defeat of the strong by the weak is the opposite of what these clauses say.
The ark is moved about and never harmed (5:1-5:12 passim), but no single clause states its preservation; this is the drift of the whole chapter.
The only combat is past and off-stage ("had captured the ark", 5:1); no clause in this section narrates a battle, though the capture is its background.
The Philistines are the enemy only in the presupposed capture (5:1); in these clauses they are the ones judged, not adversaries acting.
The chapter has no king, throne or kingdom; the "rulers of the Philistines" (5:8, 5:11) are city lords deciding what to do with the ark, not a kingdom. The stamp is misapplied here.
Nothing in the section swears an oath, invokes a deity as witness, or uses oath formulae; the Philistines' speech is consultation and instruction, not swearing.
No divine promise is made or recalled in this section; 1Sam 6:18's reference to the rock standing to this day is a note on the memorial, not covenant faithfulness.
The section's drift is the raising up of Samuel as judge, but no single clause carries the idea of a judge being raised; the clauses only record that he judged (1Sa.7.6#cl6, 1Sa.7.15#cl0).
Israel goes out of Mizpah and pursues a fleeing enemy (1Sa.7.11#cl0-cl2); that is a rout, not a victory procession, and no clause describes any procession or ritual return with spoils.

Samuel offers the burnt offering and intercedes (1Sa.7.9#cl1, #cl2) and builds an altar (1Sa.7.17#cl3), but the text gives him no priestly title, lineage or sanctuary role; I cannot determine that this section presents him as priest.
No clause names a priest, priestly line or priestly duty; the offering and altar are done by Samuel without priestly language, so I cannot pin the stamp.
No clause speaks of a king, throne or kingdom; 7:13 has the Philistines subdued under Samuel's judgeship, not a kingdom.

The section has the elements of covenant renewal — return, removal of foreign gods, service of the LORD alone (1Sa.7.3#cl2-#cl6), and the pledge not to sin (1Sa.7.6#cl5) — but no clause names a covenant, and I cannot tell whether the stamp is meant to cover it.
No clause states a law, statute, instruction or wisdom saying; the closest, the call to serve the LORD only, is a prophetic exhortation, not law or wisdom.

No clause in this section places an idol or false worship in a holy place; 'serving other gods' (1Sa.8.8#cl4) is apostasy by the people, with no temple, sanctuary or holy place mentioned anywhere in 1Sam 8:1-9.
Nothing in this section is stated as law, statute, or wisdom instruction; it is a prophetic declaration of what the king will do.

This section is about Israel demanding a king, Samuel relaying their words, and the LORD granting the request; the clause glosses contain no judging pronouncement or verdict (the only 'judge' is 1Sa.8.20#cl1, where the requested king is to judge Israel, not an act of judgment). The rejection in v.19 is the people refusing Samuel, not the LORD judging them.
the section's high place is a bamah for sacrifice (1Sa.9.12#cl7, 1Sa.9.13#cl7), not the temple; no clause speaks of God's dwelling or presence

No clause in this section carries 'prophet': the only role words are 'Paul and Silvanus and Timothy' (1Th.1.1#cl0), 'the church' (1Th.1.1#cl0), 'brothers' (1Th.1.4#cl1), 'imitators' (1Th.1.6#cl0), 'an example' (1Th.1.7#cl0), 'the believing ones' (1Th.1.7#cl0), 'to serve' (1Th.1.9#cl3). The Berean text has no 'prophet' here.
'sending' is not said here: 1Th.1.1#cl0 names the senders/authors, not a sending event, and the Berean text of this section has no 'sent/send'. Paul being 'sent' is not asserted in any clause.
The section has the Thessalonians' suffering ('great suffering', 1Th.1.6#cl1) but nothing of the servant of Isaiah or the Lord's own suffering; the Berean text has no servant figure suffering here.
No clause here uses 'kingdom' or kingship language; 1Th.1.1#cl0 names the Lord Jesus Christ but does not speak of a kingdom.

There is no divided or rival kingdom here; the only kingdom language is God's own kingdom into which He calls believers (1Th.2.12#cl2), and the opposition in vv.14-16 is persecution, not a kingdom set against a kingdom.
The one called the Lord Jesus here appears only as the one killed by the Jews (1Th.2.15#cl0); there is no clause in this section about his bearing suffering or being God's servant.
Nothing in this section names the Spirit; the nearest is 'we were bold in our God' (1Th.2.2#cl0), an implicit claim at best.
No clause in the section speaks of testifying, bearing witness or testimony; 1Thess 2:19 speaks of the Thessalonian believers themselves as Paul's hope and crown, not of witness.
Nothing in the section speaks of redemption, ransom, purchase or salvation; 'our Lord Jesus' is named, but no redemptive act or language is present.

2:17 speaks of Paul and his companions being 'torn away'/'bereft' (aporphanisthentes) from the Thessalonians, which is the missionaries' separation, not the Servant's vicarious suffering; no clause carries the idea.
No clause states a promise, covenant, oath or act of faithfulness; 2:18 narrates a thwarted intention and 2:19 asks a rhetorical question.
The 'torn away for a short time' of 2:17 and the longing to see them again express personal separation and desire, not mercy shown or restoration; no clause carries the stamp.
No clause mentions creation, renewal, newness of life or the transformation of the world; the eschatological note in 2:19 is the Lord's coming and the believers' presence with Him, not new creation.
The section nowhere mentions the Holy Spirit or spirit; 'in heart' in 2:17 is the human inward self, not the Spirit.
the section has senders and a messenger but no clause in which anyone bears testimony or testifies
the readers are addressed as 'you'/'yourselves' throughout but no clause names them as God's people
the section speaks of faith being tested and of labour proving vain, not of any promise or of God's faithfulness; the cited verse 3:5 has 'faith' (pistis), not a promise kept
no clause of 3:1-5 refers to the Spirit; 'faith', 'gospel' and 'God' appear but not 'spirit'

Nothing in 1Thess.3.6-13 speaks of redemption, ransom, or deliverance-from-sin; the section asks that God direct the way (3.11), make love abound (3.12) and strengthen hearts (3.13), with no redemptive act named.
No clause in the section speaks of creation, new birth or renewal of the cosmos; 'strengthen your hearts in holiness' (3.13) is sanctification, not new creation.
The Holy Spirit is not named or referred to anywhere in 1Thess.3.6-13; the cited verse (3.12) speaks only of the Lord causing love to increase.

4:7 speaks of God's call to holiness, not mercy or restoration; no clause in the section carries the idea of mercy or restoring the fallen (the forgiveness/mercy idea is absent even from 4:6, which states avenging).
Ascension is Christ going up; here the Lord descends from heaven and the living are caught up, the reverse direction.
No conflict, enemy or warfare anywhere in the section; the loud command, archangel's voice and trumpet are accompanied by no battle.
Nothing about creation, renewal of the world or new heavens; the hope stated is being with the Lord, not a re-created order.
Neither 'kingdom' nor rule, throne or reign appears; the coming of the Lord is not described as establishing a kingdom here.
No temple, sanctuary or dwelling imagery; the presence motif here is 'with the Lord' in the air, not a temple.
5:4 speaks of believers not being in darkness and of the day not overtaking them; there is no clause here about creation made new, no new heavens/earth, renewal or new birth language.

The clause forbids retaliation between people; it names no divine judgment, verdict or wrath. The nearest thing to a verdict idea is the summons to test all things (1Th.5.21#cl0), but that is discernment, not judgment, and the cited verse 15 does not carry the stamp.
Verses 16-22 are exhortations to joy, prayer, thanksgiving and discernment with no mention of reign, king or kingdom; the stamp is at best the general Christian life, so it attaches to no clause.

No clause mentions covenant, its making, or its parties; 5:28's 'grace of our Lord Jesus Christ' is eschatological greeting, not a covenant statement. If anything, the stamp fits the section's general Christian frame rather than any clause.
No clause states purchase, ransom, or redemption; 'the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ' (5:28) is the nearest wording but names grace, not redemption.

No clause speaks of creation, renewal of creation, or new heavens and earth; 'sanctify you completely' and 'blameless' are moral/eschatological, not creational. If the stamp means new creation in the individual believer via the coming of Christ, that is a stretch the clauses do not state.
No clause speaks of testifying or bearing witness; 'apostle' is a sending/commission, not a witness role, and the verse names no witness.
No clause calls anyone son: Timothy is 'my true child', and Christ Jesus is named 'the Lord', never 'Son'.
Nothing here speaks of ransoming, rescue or purchase; Christ Jesus appears only as the one through whom Paul is commanded and as 'our hope' and 'our Lord'.
No clause speaks of a people belonging to God; 'God our Savior' and 'God the Father' name God's relation to Paul and Timothy, not a corporate people.
Hymenaeus and Alexander are handed over for discipline for blasphemy; they are called blasphemers, not false prophets, and no prophecy or prophet language attaches to them.
No clause names a people, congregation or covenant community; the section's addressee is one man (Timothy) plus named opponents, so the stamp can only describe the section's drift.

False shepherd is a role of a leader who feeds or fails to feed a flock; this section speaks of men who want to be teachers of the law (1Ti.1.7#cl1) and of straying to empty talk (1Ti.1.6#cl1), but nothing here says they shepherd, teach wrongly a flock, or are charged with a flock. It would be read in from 1Tim 1:3's Ephesus only; nothing in the clauses speaks to it.

A witness is one who testifies. The nearest words are 'perjurers' (false witnesses, 1Ti.1.9#cl3) and 'entrusted' (1Ti.1.11#cl0), neither of which is a witness or an act of witnessing; that perjurers are named among the lawless no more makes a witness here than 'murderers' makes a murderer. Nothing in the clauses speaks to the stamp.

'the glorious gospel of the blessed God, with which I have been entrusted' (1Ti.1.11#cl0) names the gospel, but no clause states redemption, a redeemer, or Christ as the one who redeems; the stamp is the section's assumed background, not anything a clause says, so general true.
The sound teaching and the gospel entrusted to Paul (1Ti.1.10#cl1, 1Ti.1.11#cl0) are teaching and gospel, not prophecy, and no clause here says anything was foretold or spoken by a prophet.
No clause in this section speaks of God's people, a congregation, Israel or the church; Ephesus (1Ti.1.3#cl2) is a place, and the 'certain men' (1Ti.1.3#cl4) are false teachers, not a people of God.

Wrong for this section: 1Ti.2.7#cl1/#cl0 ('I was appointed as a preacher, an apostle, and a faithful and true teacher of the Gentiles') names herald, apostle and teacher, not prophet, and no clause speaks of prophetic utterance. The 'at just the right time' testimony (1Ti.2.6#cl1) is not prophetic speech.

Wrong for this section: no clause has servant, ministry or service language. The nearest idea, Christ giving Himself (1Ti.2.6#cl0, 'gave Himself as a ransom for all'), is stated as ransom/mediation (1Ti.2.5#cl1), not as service.

The section's concern is prayer for everyone and God's desire for all men to be saved; it has no clause naming a people belonging to God (no 'saints', 'Israel', 'church', or equivalent). 'On behalf of all men' (1Ti.2.1#cl1) is wider than any people-group. General drift only.

Wrong for this section: no clause speaks of a prophetic word or prophecy. 1Ti.2.7#cl1/#cl0 describes Paul's appointment as herald, apostle and teacher, and 1Ti.2.6#cl1 speaks of 'the testimony' of the ransom, neither of which is a prophetic utterance.

The section names 'kings and all those in authority' (1Ti.2.1#cl1, with 1Ti.2.2#cl0 'in authority being') only as the objects of prayer, so that believers may lead tranquil lives (1Ti.2.2#cl1). No clause speaks of God's rule, a kingdom, or an anointed king; the stamp is at most the section's general setting, not its idea.
The section gives conduct and teaching rules (apparel, learning, teaching, authority) but nowhere names law or wisdom; it reads as the section's general drift, not any clause's content.
No clause names an overseer as priest, sacrifice, or temple service. 'overseership' (episkope) is an administrative role, not priestly; treating it as priest misreads the Greek.
The list of qualifications is wisdom-shaped instruction, but no clause invokes law, wisdom, or a wisdom saying; the 'trustworthy saying' (1Ti.3.1#cl0) is a formula, not wisdom content.
The section is entirely qualification and warning (must be, must not, lest he fall); no clause speaks of mercy, forgiveness, or restoration.
The confession of 3:16 is the section's redemptive centre, but no clause states purchase, ransoming or salvation from sin in particular.
Nothing here is a prophet speaking or prophecy being given; the mystery is confessed, not proclaimed as prophecy.
No clause speaks of believers being in Christ or sharing his life; 3:16 is about Christ alone.

The section's role-word for the office is 'Deacons' (diakonos, servant), a distinct office from 'overseer/bishop' (3:1-7); no priestly, sacrificial or temple-cult term, temple duty, altar or mediation appears anywhere in 3:8-13. The cited verse 3:8 concerns deacons' moral qualifications (dignified, not double-tongued, not given to much wine, not greedy), not priesthood.

No clause speaks of bearing testimony, testifying, or being a witness; 3:9 speaks of holding to 'the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience', which is fidelity to the faith, not witness. If anything of the section's drift could be stretched toward a public testimony, it is only the general exemplary-conduct drift, not a clause that carries the idea.

No building, construction, or household-edification imagery occurs in 3:8-13. 'a good manager of his children and of his own household' (3:12) is household management (oikonomia/proistēmi), not building; treating 'household' as builder imagery is a metaphor the text does not make.

No clause names the congregation, the church, God's people, or Israel; the section speaks of deacons, women, wives, children and households. The corporate people-of-God idea is at best the general setting of the qualifications, not the content of any clause.

No clause cites or alludes to the law, and 'wisdom' is not a word of the section; the closest are the virtue words 'dignified', 'temperate', 'faithful' (3:8, 3:11), which express general moral wisdom rather than torah instruction.
Nothing in the section speaks of law or wisdom; the abstinence rules are the false teachers' commands, not law, and no wisdom saying appears. General drift only.
No clause speaks of mercy or restoration; the section's positive note (foods received with thanksgiving) is not mercy or restoration.
The prophecy in 1Ti.4.14#cl1 is a spoken word given to Timothy, not a person exercising the role of prophet; no clause here identifies anyone as a prophet.
The laying on of hands by the elderhood (1Ti.4.14#cl1) is an act of commissioning, not priestly service, sacrifice or mediation.

The Berean text of this section never uses anointing language (no 'anoint', no 'anointed'); the gift is given 'through prophecy' and 'at the laying on of the hands', which the text keeps distinct from anointing.
'You will save both yourself and those who hear you' (1Ti.4.16#cl2) is about salvation through persevering in life and teaching; the section has no healing, sickness, or cure.
No clause of this section mentions the Spirit, the Holy Spirit, or any work of the Spirit; 'the gift' (1Ti.4.14#cl0) and 'the prophecy' (1Ti.4.14#cl1) are named without the Spirit.

This section speaks of elders (presbyteroi) who rule and teach, and of honoring them with wages; no sacrificial, cultic or priestly role or language appears in any clause. The only sacrifice-adjacent words are the ox 'treading out the grain' and 'wages', which are about labor and pay, not priesthood.

There is no clause in 5:21-25 that states or cites law, commandment or wisdom instruction; the teaching here is church-order advice. If the stamp is meant as the section's general ethical-instruction drift, it applies only as general drift, not to any particular clause.

The section speaks of a remedy for Timothy's stomach (5:23) and of sins going to judgment (5:24), not of mercy shown or restoration of a person. Nothing in 5:21-25 restores anyone; the closest idea, healing of an ailment, is not mercy_restoration.

1Tim 5:4 speaks of children repaying parents ('recompense to give to parents', 1Ti.5.4#cl3) and of 'godliness' in the household; nothing in the section names a priest, priesthood, or cultic service. The cited verse contains only family devotion and repayment.

1Tim 5:8 does give a household rule with a stated ground ('he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever'), but no clause asserts law, commandment or wisdom as such; the section's mode is instruction and advice, so this reads as the section's general drift rather than a pinned clause.

The section's general drift is ethical instruction/household teaching, but no clause names law, wisdom or a specific maxim from the law; the one imperative in 1Ti.6.1#cl0 and 1Ti.6.2#cl6 is apostolic instruction, not citation of law or wisdom.

The section mentions belief ('having believing masters', 'they are believing [ones]') but nothing of redemption, Christ's work, ransom or salvation; redemption_in_christ is not stated or implied by any clause here.
Nothing in the section speaks of a man of lawlessness or an opponent of God; 6:14 speaks only of keeping the commandment until Christ's appearing.
No covenant is named or implied in 6:14; the verse concerns keeping the commandment until the appearing.
No sonship language in this section; 'man of God' does not itself say son.
No priestly or cultic language anywhere in the section.
No peace covenant or peace language in the section (6:11 has love, endurance, gentleness; not covenant peace).
Nothing in the section invokes David or a Davidic covenant; 6:14's covenant stamp was cited to 6:14 which has no covenant.
No creation or new-creation language in the section; 6:14 speaks of keeping the commandment, not renewal of creation.

1Tim 6:15 speaks of God's own timing ('which ... He will display') and of His sole sovereignty ('the King of those being kings and Lord of those being lords'); nothing in the section states judgment. The nearest clause, 1Ti.6.15#cl0, names God as 'the blessed and alone Sovereign' who displays (shows) it at His own season, and 1Ti.6.13#cl0 supplies 'to keep you the commandment ... until the appearing', which concerns keeping the command, not judging anyone. I could not determine any clause that carries a judgment idea.

1Ti.6.16#cl1 ('in light unapproachable dwelling', 'dwells in unapproachable light') and 1Ti.6.16#cl2/#cl3 ('whom has seen no one of men', 'nor can anyone see Him'; 'to see is able') speak of God's unapproachable, unseeable presence, but no clause in the section names a temple, a sanctuary, or a place of dwelling among His people; the idea is the section's general drift about God's own inaccessible glory rather than a clause in particular.

1Tim 6:12 speaks of 'the eternal life to which you were called' and 'the good confession before many witnesses' — calling and confessing, not mercy shown or restoration; 1Ti.6.12#cl1 ('Lay hold of the eternal life to which you were called and also did confess the good confession before many witnesses') rests on 'eternal life' and 'called', and 1Ti.6.12#cl3 ('you were called') on 'called', neither of which carries mercy or restoration. I could not determine any clause that carries the idea.
The stamp captures the section's overall shape (wise instruction about wealth) rather than being carried by any one clause; the paraenesis runs across the whole unit.
Nothing in the section is a prophetic utterance or refers to prophets/prophecy; the cited words are a charge to guard a deposit and avoid chatter, not prophecy.

The clauses describe a conceited teacher of another doctrine who disagrees with sound words (1Ti.6.3#cl1, cl2); nothing speaks of a man of lawlessness who sets himself up in the temple and exalts himself above God. The idea is foreign to this section.

The closest clauses name slander, evil suspicions and constant friction (1Ti.6.4#cl1, cl2), but these are vices coming out of a proud teacher, not an enemy or adversary figure. No clause speaks of opposition to God or his people as an enemy.

Nothing in 1Tim 6:5 or its clauses speaks of testimony, bearing witness or being a witness; the clauses name corrupt minds, being destitute of the truth, and godliness treated as a means of gain (1Ti.6.5#cl0, cl1, cl2). The stamp is unsupported here.
The section states the character and conduct of false teachers (1Ti.6.4#cl1, cl2; 1Ti.6.5#cl0, cl1, cl2) but no clause announces a judgment, verdict or sentence on them.
The section is wisdom-style teaching about godliness and contentment, but no clause names or invokes law or wisdom.
No clause in 1Tim 6:6-10 mentions Christ, redemption, or any saving act; the section warns about the love of money.
Solomon asks for wisdom for himself (2Ch.1.10#cl0), not on behalf of the people, and offers no intercessory prayer; the sacrifices (2Ch.1.6#cl2) are his own burnt offerings, not intercession.
The section speaks of God's loving devotion and the fulfilling of His promise to David, but no clause describes mercy or restoration as such.
The section states wealth and trade as fact; no clause gives, bestows or commissions blessing on Solomon or anyone.
No clause cites or evokes a divine promise, and nothing here presents the trade as fulfilment of one.
No battle occurs in this section: Hadoram is sent to the forced labor and is stoned by the people (2Chr 10:18), and Rehoboam flees; no armies, fighting or warfare are described.
The oracle in v.4 is a prohibition and command ('You are not to go up and fight... return home'), not a promise; nothing in the section promises anything.
No judgment is announced or executed; the word forbids the war and the men simply go home.

The section records Rehoboam's marriages, children and appointments; no clause mentions David, the covenant, or God's promise to David's line. The Davidic covenant is presupposed background, not stated here.
The section concerns the royal house of Judah but no clause speaks of God's people as such.
No clause mentions a promise or God's faithfulness; the only 'intention' is Rehoboam's own plan to make Abijah king.
Nothing in the section speaks of sin, exile or death; it reports marriages, offspring and provision.
The section shows fortification and arming, not a warrior figure acting; no clause names a warrior.
No fighting occurs in these verses; only defensive preparation (fortresses, officers, supplies, shields and spears).
Judah and Benjamin appear as tribes belonging to Rehoboam, but nothing in the section marks them as God's people.
Nothing in these verses refers to a divine promise or to God's faithfulness; the section is wholly about Rehoboam's building and garrisoning of cities.
The section names forsaking the Law of the LORD and unfaithfulness, but no idol, image or worship of another god is mentioned in any clause (2Ch.12.1#cl2; 2Ch.12.2#cl2)
No covenant is made, named or invoked in this section; 'the Law of the LORD' (2Ch.12.1#cl2) is the closest thing, but that is transgression language, not covenant language

The verse says nothing about the Davidic covenant (the promise to David of an enduring dynasty in 2 Sam 7). 'Chosen ... to put His Name' is the election of Jerusalem as the place of the LORD's name (cf. Deut 12:5, 1 Kgs 11:36), and 'the City of David' is a toponym, not a statement of covenant. The nearest notes — Abijah succeeding, dynasty continuing — are not voiced as covenant in this text.
The kingship and the two named sides (Abijah over Judah, Jeroboam) are the section's setting, but no clause names a kingdom as such.
Nothing in the section marks either army or either king as God's people; 2Chr 13:2 mentions only Abijah's mother Micaiah.
The section reports a battle being raised and armies mustered, with no verdict, sentence or divine judgment language.
Nothing in the section presents a procession or triumphal march; the victory is a rout and a pursuit (v.15-19), not a procession. Wrong for this section.

The golden calves are cited as Jeroboam's gods with his army (v.8) and in the charge about his own priesthood (v.9), but the section never places an idol in the holy place or temple; that is Dan/Bethel elsewhere. No clause here says it.
Asa's reign in his father's place is the Davidic succession, but no clause in this section names David or the covenant.

The speech states a conditional principle of divine favor and abandonment (2Ch.15.2#cl4, cl6-cl9) and reviews Israel's faithlessness (2Ch.15.3#cl0), but no clause brings a formal charge, summons witnesses, or pronounces covenant curse, which is what a lawsuit stamp requires.
2Ch.15.6#cl0-cl3 speak of nations and cities being crushed and of God disturbing them; no clause names a warrior, an army, or a human fighter as a role.
No priest or priestly act appears in this section; the only cultic act is Asa's sacrifice and altar restoration, both done by the king, not a priest.
Israel and Judah here are the covenant people gathered, not foreign nations acting as characters; no nation other than Israel/Judah is portrayed.
Ramah is fortified to block traffic (2Ch.16.1#cl1), not besieged; no city is besieged in the section; 2Chr 16:4 is conquest of cities by assault, not siege.
No procession or triumphal entry appears; 2Ch.16.4#cl3 is a list of conquered cities, not a procession, and no such scene follows.
No clause states a divine verdict or sentence; the section narrates only human diplomacy and warfare, so at most a general drift.
Judah and Israel are named only as kingdoms under kings (2Ch.16.1#cl0/cl1, 2Ch.16.4#cl3); no clause speaks of them as God's people.
No exile and no death appear in this section: Asa is imprisoned-adjacent in no way, the seer is put in prison and the people oppressed, and the penalty is war, not exile or death.
No prophet or prophecy appears: the officials sent to teach, the Levites and the priests hold no prophetic role (2Chr 17:7–9).
Nothing is judged or condemned: the dread of the LORD merely restrains war (2Chr 17:10), and no verdict, punishment or vindication appears.

The section speaks of war and kings going up to battle, but no clause describes a warrior or warrior role; k.3#cl3/cl5 'I am like you... we will join you in the war' is the nearest, yet it speaks of alliance, not a warrior.
No clause speaks of witnessing or a witness giving testimony. 2Ch.18.7 is about hating and disbelieving a prophet and a rebuke, not witness.
No oath, vow or swearing by God or man appears in the section; 2Ch.18.3 is a declaration of alliance ('I am like you...'), not an oath.
Israel and Judah are named (2Ch.18.3) but no clause speaks of them as God's people or of a people belonging to God; k.3#cl4 'my people' is Jehoshaphat's people in an alliance formula.
The man's shot is called aimless ('without taking special aim') and the section shows no judge, verdict, or sentence; the king's death is narrated as battle outcome, not as an act of judgment.
No clause in this section states or presupposes a judicial verdict; the wording is entirely battle narrative (struck, wounded, died).
No clause here contains a prophetic word, a prophet, or a fulfilment formula; the earlier prophecy (18:16) is outside the section and the text here never refers to it.

Wrong for this section: sin is present (2Ch.19.2#cl2–cl4, helping the wicked, loving those who hate Yahweh), but there is no exile and no death anywhere in 2Chr 19:1–3; and no clause in this section speaks of the sin-exile-death complex as such.
The section has disputes and 'incur guilt before the LORD' but no clause stages a covenant lawsuit (no indictment, witnesses, or verdict against the nation).
No clause in the section speaks of witnessing, testimony, or witnesses; the judges warn and settle disputes, but nothing is described as bearing witness.
The section describes royal administration across Judah, but no clause states the kingdom itself.
'the LORD, the God of their fathers' and 'incur guilt before the LORD' presuppose covenant, but no clause states covenant.

Nothing in this section speaks of destruction. Every clause about the house is future or present: 'I am about to build' (2Ch.2.4#cl1, 2Ch.2.8#cl3), 'will be great' (2Ch.2.4#cl0, 2Ch.2.8#cl2). The temple does not yet exist at this point in the narrative, so it cannot have been destroyed here.

The reading of the house's items is possible: incense, showbread (2Ch.2.3#cl4 'the row of continuity'), and the vessels implied by gold, silver, bronze, iron (2Ch.2.6#cl1). But this section is about building the house and its equipment, not about tabernacle furnishings; the row of bread and the altar smoke are the only furnishings named, and they belong to the temple being built, not to the tabernacle. I cannot pin this without a judgement I cannot make from the clauses alone.

No clause here names a priest, a son of Aaron, or a priestly office. The incense, the showbread row, and the burnt offerings are the duties priests perform, but the clauses name the acts and not the men. This stamp may be true of the section's background rather than of any clause in it.
No clause in this section speaks of a temple being destroyed; the only temple clause is about building one (2Ch.2.11#cl5, 'who will build a temple for the LORD').
The section builds toward the temple (2Ch.2.11#cl5) but no clause states the LORD's presence in it.
The section sets up the threat (2Ch.20.1#cl3, 2Ch.20.2#cl3) but no clause states rescue or deliverance; it is the general drift of the passage that a battle follows and deliverance is sought.
Nothing in the section states mercy or restoration; the fasting and seeking are the passage's general posture of dependence, but no clause carries the idea itself.
No clause speaks of judgment; the invasion is a threat, not a stated judgment. The stamp is the section's general frame at most, and I would not pin it to a clause.
There is a battle and a king named, but no clause describes anyone as a warrior or fighting; the point of the oracle is that Judah does not fight. The stamp fits only the section's drift.

The cited verse names Levites (Kohathites and Korahites) standing to praise, not priests; no clause in the section identifies anyone as a priest or describes priestly service such as sacrifice or mediation.
Divine rescue from the enemy is the section's drift, but no clause speaks of mercy, forgiveness or restoration from a fallen state.

The section speaks of Judah's deliverance, not of judgment on anyone; 'the battle does not belong to you, but to God' describes God fighting for Judah, not judging. Nothing in these clauses conveys divine judgment.
The Levites' standing to praise is Levitical, not priestly; no clause names priests, Aaronides, or priestly duties. As with 'priest', the cited verse does not carry the idea.
Worship 'before the LORD' with the Levites praising him is the section's drift, but no clause mentions the temple or a sanctuary; the presence is God's presence in the assembly.

No human warrior is presented as acting in this section: the doers are the singers (21) and Yahweh, who sets ambushes (22#cl0) and lets the nations destroy each other (23#cl0, cl3). The stamp reads a warrior role onto a passage that has none.

The section's outcome is the enemies destroyed and Judah enriched by plunder, which a reader may read as divine mercy to Judah, but no clause states mercy, restoration, or the theological point; the closest, 2Ch.20.21#cl7 ("His loving devotion endures forever"), is a liturgical formula sung before the battle rather than a statement about what happens here. General drift, not pinned to any clause.
2Chr 20:27-28 is a return from the battlefield to Jerusalem, not from exile; no clause says they were in exile or that they came back from a foreign land.

Nothing in these clauses speaks of repentance or religious renewal; #cl1 is blessing, not repentance, and the assembly at Beracah is for blessing, not confession (depending on the wider context of 2Chr 20:3-4, which is not in this section).
No clause states a judgment: 20:29#cl2 says Yahweh fought against Israel's enemies, and no clause announces a verdict, sentence or judicial act against anyone.
The verses name Jehoshaphat's father Asa, not David; no promise to David, no throne/lamp/forever language appears in any clause.

No clause in this section speaks of sin, exile or death: v.35 has the alliance and Ahaziah acting wickedly, v.37 the prophecy and the wrecking of the ships. The stamp is cited at v.35, but the clause there (2Ch.20.35#cl1) is wickedness of Ahaziah, not a sin-exile-death schema, and no clause names exile or death.

Jehoshaphat stands in the assembly in the temple court to pray (2Ch.20.5#cl0) but no clause gives him priestly acts or role (no sacrifice, no mediation, no priestly title); the standing is prayer, not priesthood.
No clause mentions David, a Davidic promise, or an eternal throne; the sanctuary and the Name (2Ch.20.8#cl1) are tied to the temple, not to the David covenant.
The temple is standing and prayed toward ('we will stand before this house', 2Ch.20.9#cl1; 'Your Name is in this house', 2Ch.20.9#cl2); nothing in the section says it is destroyed.
The section is prayer and standing before the LORD (2Ch.20.13#cl0), with no confession of sin or repentance language; the stamp fits the surrounding narrative rather than any clause here.
The section's drift is a plea for help on the basis of mercy, but no clause speaks of mercy or restoration in particular; the plea is for rescue ('save us', 2Ch.20.9#cl5).
2Chr 21:4 is a purge of Jehoram's own brothers and Israelite princes by the sword, not a battle between forces as the stamp's event_image implies; no clause describes combat.

No worship of other gods or idols appears; 2Chr 21:6 speaks of walking in the ways of the kings of Israel and doing evil, and the clause text given never names a foreign deity (the reader cited 21:6, not the later high places).
2Chr 21:6 records Jehoram's evil but no sentence, punishment or verdict is pronounced; the LORD's action in 2Chr 21:7 is the opposite, an unwillingness to destroy.
The section describes the fulfilment of Elijah's written word to Jehoram (2Chr 21:12-15), but no clause in these five verses itself states or reports a prophetic word.
Judah is the people of God under attack, but no clause in this section names or characterises them as such; 'Judah' appears only as the object of invasion.

The section presents rebellion and forsaking as the cause working itself out (Edom and Libnah freed from Judah's hand, 2Ch.21.10#cl0, #cl1), but no clause enacts a judgment: no verdict, no sentence, no agent judging. The stamp describes the drift rather than a clause.
Sin is present (2Ch.21.10#cl2) and loss of dominion (2Ch.21.10#cl0, #cl1), but no exile and no death appears in any clause; the stamp names a sequence this section does not carry.
As with judgment_ev: no clause states a judgment, only its outworking in the loss of Edom and Libnah.
The high places are on the hills of Judah (2Ch.21.11#cl0), not in the temple or another holy place; the section names no holy place and no idol object, only high places and prostitution.
Two human dominations break (Edom, Libnah), but no staff image or symbol of a broken staff appears in the clauses.

The section speaks of walking in the ways of the house of Ahab and doing evil, but no clause names a cult image, a foreign god or an act of worship; the idea is the general drift, not said by any clause.

The LORD's anointing of Jehu to destroy the house of Ahab (2Ch.22.7#cl4) is an act of commissioning, not a spoken prophetic word, and no clause in the section reports a prophet speaking or a word of the LORD delivered.
The section is about dynastic rule (royal house, the sons of the king, Athaliah reigning over the land) but no clause names the kingdom as such; 'over the land' in 2Ch.22.12#cl2 is rule, not kingdom.

Wrong for this section: the killing in 2Ch.22.10#cl3 and 2Ch.22.11#cl1 is Athaliah's own act ('she proceeded to annihilate', 'she stole him away from among ... who were being murdered'), not God's judicial act, and the section nowhere presents it as judgment. Nothing in it is declared or enacted as divine judgment.

No clause in the section speaks of testimony or witnessing. 'the Testimony' in 2Ch.23.11#cl1 is the object presented with the crown (the written testimony/covenant document), not a person giving witness; reading the stamp here would rest on an English word the Hebrew clause uses differently.

No clause states a law or a wisdom saying; the nearest is 2Ch.23.6#cl5 'the requirement of the LORD', which is a cultic duty (מִשְׁמֶרֶת) rather than law teaching. Fits only as general drift, if at all.

The only damage language in the section is Athaliah's sons breaking into the house of God and using its sacred objects for the Baals (2Ch.24.7#cl1, #cl2); the rest of the section describes repair and restoration (2Ch.24.12#cl3, #cl5; 2Ch.24.13#cl2), not destruction. Nothing in the clauses says the temple was destroyed.

The section does mention sin — 'the sons of that wicked woman Athaliah had broken into the house of God and had even used the sacred objects of the house of the LORD for the Baals' (2Ch.24.7), which is a trespass and apostasy. What no clause states is exile or death; Athaliah's death is not in this section. The composite stamp as named is therefore not carried here.

Jehoiada is the high priest, but no clause in this section names his priestly office or any priestly act; the verses speak only of his old age, death, burial and his good done for God and the temple. The stamp belongs to the section only by the identity of the person, not by any clause.
Nothing here is mercy or restoration: the section reports a death at 130, a burial with the kings, and good done for God and the temple. No clause speaks of mercy, deliverance or restoration.
Nothing here is testimony or witnessing; the nearest idea is the written record in 2Ch.24.27#cl1-cl2, which is a source citation for events, not a witness or the act of witnessing.
The section speaks of the LORD's giving Judah into an enemy hand because they forsook him, and of the ending of a dynasty's blessing; no promise and no divine faithfulness is expressed.

The section records Amaziah's execution of his father's murderers and his citing the Law of Moses; there is no accusation, indictment, or lawsuit speech by the LORD against Israel (no covenant lawsuit form here).
The section shows sin (idolatry) and announced death ("to destroy you"), but no exile or deportation is spoken of by any clause; the stamp fits only as the section's general drift.
The idols are set up as gods for Amaziah and sacrificed to (2Ch.25.14#cl4, cl6), but no clause enthrones an idol or presents one as ruling/seated on a throne.

The cited verse (2Chr 25:23) is a prisoner being brought to the enemy capital and a wall demolished, and 25:24 is looting and a return to Samaria. There is no procession of triumph over captives such as a victory parading: the king is captured and deported, not paraded.

A siege is the surrounding and investing of a city. In 2Chr 25:23 Jerusalem is not besieged: the wall is breached after the battle by a victorious king who already holds the captured king, and the text has no encampment, blockade or assault.

The cited verse (2Chr 25:24) says the gold, silver and articles of the house of God were taken away by Jehoash; the building is plundered and its treasures carried to Samaria, not destroyed. No clause reports its demolition.

Nothing in 2Chr 25:25-28 speaks of a divine promise or of faithfulness kept; the section reports apostasy, conspiracy, killing and burial, and the nearest thing to continuance is the burial 'with his fathers' (28#cl1), which is a burial formula, not covenant faithfulness. The reader cited 2Chr 25:28, but that verse carries no promise language (no 'swore', 'covenant', 'forever').
The section records a battle victory at the Valley of Salt, but no procession, parade, or triumphant entry is described; the 10,000 of Seir are struck down and the captives are executed, not paraded
The raid on the cities of Judah (25:13#cl3) is a plundering raid, not a siege; no encirclement, siege works, or city under siege is described
No procession or victory march appears; 2Chr 26:8 has tribute brought and fame spreading, which is not a procession.
The temple is neither destroyed nor damaged; Uzziah merely enters it to burn incense (2Chr 26:16).
Uzziah's leprosy is not healed; he remains a leper until his death (2Chr 26:21).
Uzziah suffers judgment for his own unfaithfulness (2Chr 26:16), not as an innocent servant bearing others' sin.

The section reports war and defeat of the Ammonites and tribute paid, but no procession, entry or triumph ritual is described in any clause (no clause of 2Ch.27.5 speaks of a procession).
