2Co.13.12#cl0 is a command to greet one another with a holy kiss; the greeting is an act of affection toward insiders, not bearing witness or testimony to anyone.
The clause names 'the Lord Jesus Christ' only as the source of the grace in the closing wish; nothing in the section speaks of redemption, ransom or purchase.
'All of you' (2:5) and 'the majority' (2:6) name the congregation as a body, but no clause states the idea of a people belonging to God; it is the section's background drift.
'Satan' and 'schemes' in 2Co.2.11#cl0/#cl1 speak of being outwitted by the adversary, not of sin, exile or death.
No ransom/buying-back language in these clauses; 2:14 speaks of triumph and fragrance, and 'captives' if anything suggests the opposite.
Nothing in this section speaks of a servant's suffering; 2:15 concerns aroma.

Clause 2Co.3.6#cl0 names the role 'ministers' (Greek diakonoi) of a new covenant, not priests (hiereis); the section never uses priestly language or imagery, and no clause here carries the idea of a priest.

The clauses of 3:2 say the Corinthians are a letter 'known and read by all men' (2Co.3.2#cl0/#cl2), which is public attestation/recommendation, not witness in the sense of testifying or bearing witness; the letter is the evidence about the apostles, not a witness speaking.

The section addresses the Corinthian congregation as 'you' throughout (2Co.3.2#cl0, 2Co.3.3#cl1), but no clause states they are God's people or uses people-of-God language; it is only the section's general drift.

3:3 speaks of a letter 'from Christ' written by the Spirit (2Co.3.3#cl1/#cl3), and 3:4 of confidence 'through Christ' (2Co.3.4#cl0), but nothing in the section speaks of redemption, ransom, or being bought/purchased; the idea is not present.

The clauses 'a letter of Christ' (2Co.3.3#cl1) and 'confidence... through Christ' (2Co.3.4#cl0) express origin and mediation, not the believer's being in Christ or Christ in the believer; no clause carries union with Christ.
The section's whole argument contrasts the old covenant with the ministry of the Spirit; no single clause names the new covenant.
The transfiguration is the shining of Jesus' face on the mountain; this section only recalls the glory on Moses' face being veiled and fading, and never mentions Jesus' face or the mountain.

The section's drift is transformation by the Lord who is the Spirit, but no clause says the believer is in Christ or Christ in the believer; 'in Christ' (2Co.3.14#cl3) is about the veil being removed.
The section treats the law as the ministry of death and condemnation engraved on stone, never as wisdom or instruction.
The contrast between what fades away and what endures (2Co.3.11) carries the general contrast, but no clause speaks of a promise or of God's faithfulness.

The section does show God's power 'not from us' (2Co.4.7), resurrection hope (2Co.4.14) and renewal (2Co.4.16), which a reader may take as God keeping his commitment; but no clause speaks of a promise, of God's word, or of his faithfulness. General drift only.

Renewal of the inner self (2Co.4.16), the contrast of seen/temporary with unseen/eternal (2Co.4.18) and the eternal weight of glory (2Co.4.17) can be heard as new-creation language, but there is no creation word, no 'new', and no regeneration clause; the stamp describes the drift and no clause states it. Reported as general rather than wrong.

No clause in 4:7-18 speaks of purchase, ransom, blood, or being redeemed, though it cites 4:18. 'us through Jesus will raise up' (2Co.4.14#cl1) and the glory produced for us (2Co.4.17#cl0) are the only remotely redemptive clauses, and both say resurrection and glory, not redemption; the stamp sits at the section's overall drift, so empty with general.

The clause closest to the stamp (2Co.5.4#cl5, 'may be swallowed up the mortal by - life') speaks of the mortal being swallowed up by life at being clothed with the heavenly dwelling; nothing in this section says a resurrection (raising of the dead) occurs, and no clause mentions resurrection.

2Co.5.1#cl0/#cl1/#cl2 speak of an eternal house in the heavens belonging to the individual believer, not of new heavens and a new earth as a renewed cosmos; the reader cited 2Cor 5:1 but no clause there carries the stamp.
2Co.5.5#cl0/#cl2 speak of God preparing us and giving the Spirit as a pledge (down payment); nothing in this section speaks of a covenant, and no clause names or implies a covenant of peace.

2Co.5.10#cl0/#cl1 use 'revealed'/'appear before the judgment seat' in the sense of being laid bare for judgment, not of bearing witness or testifying; no clause in the section names a witness or act of witnessing.

The 'building from God ... not built by human hands' (2Co.5.1#cl0/#cl1) is the believer's eternal dwelling, not a temple nor God's presence dwelling in a temple; the Spirit is called a pledge (2Co.5.5#cl2), not temple presence.

No clause speaks of a new creation or renewal of the created order; 2Co.5.1 speaks of a building from God and 2Co.5.4#cl5 of the mortal swallowed up by life, which is about the individual's clothing with the heavenly dwelling.

The cited verse concerns the groaning for and clothing with the heavenly dwelling (2Co.5.2#cl0-#cl2, 2Co.5.4#cl0/#cl3/#cl4); no clause in this section speaks of the believer's union with Christ, and 'at home with the Lord' (2Co.5.8#cl3) is presence, not union.
2Co.5.8#cl1/#cl2/#cl3 express confidence and preference for being absent from the body and at home with the Lord; nothing in this section speaks of redemption, ransom or being bought back.

The cited verse (2Co.5.4) states the groaning and the wish to be clothed so the mortal is swallowed up by life (2Co.5.4#cl0/#cl3/#cl4/#cl5); no clause in the section speaks of mercy, forgiveness or the restoration of what was lost.

Paul never names or evokes Adam here; the section's corporate language is 'in Christ' (new creation), not a second-Adam typology. The one who brings corporate newness is Christ himself, not a counterpart to Adam.

No one is sent in this section. The ministry, word and message of reconciliation are said to be 'given' (2Co.5.18#cl2), 'put into us' (2Co.5.19#cl2) and carried out through present appeal (2Co.5.20#cl1), not through a commission in the pattern of an apostle or the Spirit being sent.

The section presents Christ as the sin-bearer made sin by God, not as the Servant who suffers and is despised; there is no language of affliction, rejection, wounds or vicarious bearing of the Servant songs (cf. Isa 53).
God's action here is described as reconciling and not counting trespasses; no oath, promise or covenant-faithfulness language occurs anywhere in the section.

The section is about the missionaries' conduct and openness, not about bearing witness/testimony to an event. The nearest words, "no one can discredit our ministry" and "truthful speech" (2Cor 6:3, 6:7), concern reputation and speech-quality, not witness; no clause here carries the stamp.

No clause in 2Cor 6:1-13 speaks of a people/corporate body belonging to God; 6:11 names the Corinthians as addressees and 6:13 calls them "my children", but neither makes a people-of-God claim. Unsure whether the stamp is meant so broadly; no clause specifically carries it.

"Grace" (2Co.6.1#cl2, "the grace of God") and "day of salvation" (2Co.6.2#cl4) are the nearest ideas, but no clause states redemption, ransom, or being bought/redeemed, and Christ is not named in this section. The stamp as stated is not carried by any clause here.
Christ is not mentioned anywhere in 2Cor 6:1-13; the paired clauses in 6:8-10 contrast states of the servants without any "in Christ" or union language. Stamp not carried here.
No clause in this section speaks of rank, order, or reversal of first/last positions; the reversals here are conditions (sorrow/joy, poor/enriching), not status ordering. Stamp not carried here.
The pairs in 6:9-10 are lived paradoxes (dying/yet living; poor/yet making many rich), not weakness overcoming a stronger opponent; no clause sets weakness against strength. Stamp not carried here.

Nothing in 6:14-18 speaks of God's covenant with creation (Noah/Gen 9); the only covenant language is the temple-of-God promise formula in 6:16, which is covenant with Israel/the new covenant, not creation.
The temple in 6:16 is the community as God's dwelling ('we are the temple of the living God'); there is no destruction of a temple anywhere in the section.
The section speaks of 'unbelievers' and 'Belial' as those to be separated from, not of the nations as a character in the narrative.
The section speaks of separation from unbelievers and of God's fatherhood/temple-dwelling, not of a covenant of peace.
No oath sworn to the patriarchs is in view; 6:18's 'I will be a Father to you' is the fatherhood promise, not the oath to the fathers.
The 'unequally yoked' image in 6:14 is about partnership with unbelievers, not a marriage covenant; no marriage is spoken of in the section.

2Cor 6:18's 'I will be a Father to you, and you will be My sons and daughters' is the Nathan oracle form (2 Sam 7:14), not the Abrahamic covenant's promises (land, seed, blessing to nations, Gen 12/15/17); no clause here speaks of Abraham or of his promises.

The Noahic covenant's clause content (ark, flood, never again, the bow in the cloud) appears nowhere in these clauses; 2Cor 6:16's temple/dwelling language is Sinai-Zion covenant language, not Noahic.
No clause mentions circumcision, flesh, or the sign of the covenant (Gen 17); 'the temple of God' and 'I will dwell in them' at 2Cor 6:16 do not carry it.

Nothing in these clauses matches the Shechem covenant of Josh 24 (choose this day whom you will serve, the stone of witness); 2Cor 6:17's 'come out from among them and be separate' is Isaiah's call, not Joshua's Shechem assembly.
The Phinehas covenant (Num 25:12-13, a covenant of peace and everlasting priesthood) has no counterpart in these clauses: no clause mentions priesthood, zeal, or a covenant of peace.
Salt, and the covenant of salt (Num 18:19; 2 Chr 13:5), is not in the text of any clause here.

The David-Jonathan covenant (1 Sam 18:3; 20:16-17) is not what 2Cor 6:14's 'Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers' speaks of; the clause forbids a mismatched bond, it does not narrate or cite that covenant.

No clause names sin, exile, or death. The nearest thing is the separation called for in 2Co.6.17#cl0-cl2 ('come out from among them and be separate. Touch no unclean thing') and the 'wickedness'/'darkness' of 2Co.6.14#cl0-cl2, but these speak of defilement and idolatry to be left, not of sin, exile or death as such. The stamp describes the section's background drift only.

No clause in this section names God as Father or speaks of fatherhood; 2Cor 7:1 addresses 'beloved' and speaks of 'the fear of God', which is not a father image. The cited verse 7:1 supplies no father language in the Berean text.
This section does not describe the Servant of the LORD; it describes Paul and his companions' afflictions. No clause carries the idea of the suffering servant figure.

2Cor 7:10 speaks of 'repentance that leads to salvation', not of redemption in Christ; no clause in this section mentions Christ, his blood, or redemption. The stamp is imported from elsewhere, not present in this section.

No clause here speaks of being in Christ or joined to him; 7:4 says 'Great is my boldness toward you, great my boasting on behalf of you' and 'I overabound with joy', which concern Paul and the Corinthians, not union with Christ.

No clause in this section speaks of a covenant, its making, or its terms; 7:3's 'to die together and to live together' is a statement of mutual devotion, not covenant language, and the cited verse contains no covenant idea.
Clause 2Co.8.6#cl0/cl1 speak only of completing 'the grace this' (the collection); no covenant, covenant-making, or covenant formula appears anywhere in the section
2Cor 8:9 has 'He became poor' but no cross, death, blood or crucifixion; the section never mentions his death
No raising, resurrection or resurrection appearance is spoken of in this section
2Co.8.7#cl1 lists faith, speech, knowledge, earnestness and love as things the Corinthians 'abound' in, but the Spirit is not mentioned and none is called a gift of the Spirit
'love', 'knowledge' and 'earnestness' appear in 2Co.8.7#cl1, but the Spirit is not named here; this is a list of the Corinthians' own excellencies, not the fruit of the Spirit
2Co.8.2#cl0 speaks of 'much proof of tribulation' and deep poverty, not of mercy or restoration; the theme of relief for the poor is not the same idea
The section speaks of Christ's poverty and our enrichment through it, but never of believers being in Christ, with Christ, or sharing his life
2Co.8.14#cl2/#cl0 speak of material 'equality' between surplus and need (echoing the manna of 2Co.8.15), not of new creation
No meal, table, bread, cup or eating anywhere in 2Cor 8:16–24; the "gracious gift/offering" (v19–20) is a collection of money, not a meal.
Nothing in the section speaks of mercy, forgiveness, or restoration: the section is about arranging and commending the collection and its couriers.

No redemption, ransom, blood, or cross language here. The nearest candidate is v19's "the gracious gift we administer", but that is the collection for the saints (charis = the gift/offering), not Christ's redemption.
The Spirit (pneuma) is never mentioned; "earnestness/devotion" in Titus's "heart" (v16) is zeal, not the Holy Spirit, and "heart" is kardia, not pneuma.
The cited verse 9:7 speaks of giving by one's own decision, 'not out of regret or compulsion'; no clause describes a sacrifice or sacrificial offering.
The cited verse 9:2 mentions only 'the Macedonians' and 'Achaia', particular regions/peoples, not nations as a character or the nations generally.
Verse 9:13 and the section speak of 'the gospel of Christ' and generosity; nothing names or describes a covenant, new or old.
The cited verse 9:13 speaks of glorifying God for confession of the gospel and generosity; no clause in the section speaks of a kingdom, king, or reign.
The cited verse 9:10 speaks of sowing, reaping and an increased harvest of righteousness; nothing in the section describes new creation or renewal of the created order.

No clause in the section speaks of a covenant: no covenant-making, covenant parties, or covenant formula ("I will be your God", etc.). The nearest material is the greeting's chosen/elect lady, truth abiding in us and the grace-and-peace wish, none of which says covenant.

No clause speaks of redemption: nothing about buying, ransoming, saving, sin or the cross. "Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father" (2Jn.1.3#cl0) names Christ but states no redemptive act, and the greeting's grace, mercy and peace are a benediction, not a redemption.

Nothing in 2Jn.1.12 speaks of mercy or restoration. The only clause of the cited verse with content (2Jn.1.12#cl3 and its parts) is about the writer hoping to come, speak face to face, and have 'our joy ... complete' — joy/completion, not mercy and not restoration. Paper and ink, writing, coming and speaking carry no mercy or restoration idea either.

The section speaks only of 'commandment' (singular, εντολή) received from the Father and from the beginning, and of walking in truth and love; it never names or alludes to the ten commandments of Sinai, nor to any set of ten.
There is no accusation, indictment, summons, witness or judgment speech here; the section is exhortation to love and walk in obedience, with no lawsuit imagery in any clause.
The joy at finding children walking in truth is the section's general drift of good news about the community's faithfulness, but no clause states mercy or restoration as such.

No clause in the section describes anyone bearing witness or testifying; the closest is confessing (2Jn.1.7#cl1), which is confession, not witness, so the stamp applies only as general drift of the letter.
The refuse-to-greet clause concerns greeting and sharing in evil deeds, not bearing witness; nothing in 1:11 testifies.
No clause speaks of redemption or purchase; the section speaks of confessing Christ and remaining in his teaching, which is the letter's general frame rather than a clause about redemption.
The section has deceivers, an antichrist and a refusal of hospitality, but no beast, no kingdom and no empire; it is about false teachers, not an anti-kingdom.

The section has Ahaziah inquiring of Baal-zebub and a king who sends captains against the prophet, but no clause names or describes a man of lawlessness; the stamp's figure is not present in this text.
The idol Baal-zebub belongs to Ekron, a Philistine city, not to Israel or the temple; no clause places an idol in a holy place, so the stamp does not hold for this section.

Nothing in these clauses presents an act of judgement. Ahaziah's death is stated in cl0 as fulfilment of Yahweh's word ('according to.the.word of.Yahweh'), not as a sentence being executed; cl2/cl3 and 1:18 cl0-cl2 (succession, no son, the chronicles) carry no judgement. If the reader meant the earlier sentence on Ahaziah (2Kgs 1:16), that verse is outside this section.
2Kgs 10:15 has Jehu's question whether Jehonadab's heart is as true as his and the giving of the hand, but no oath, vow or swearing by God or man is spoken anywhere in the section.

The temple in 2Kgs 10:26-27 is the temple of Baal, a pagan shrine, not a holy place of the LORD; the sacred pillar is native to it, not an idol introduced into a holy place. The section's one 'holy place' reference (2Ki.10.23#cl4, 'no servants of the LORD here') asserts the opposite: the LORD's servants are absent.
No altar is mentioned anywhere in these clauses; the objects destroyed are the sacred pillar (2Ki.10.26#cl0-1, 2Ki.10.27#cl0) and the temple building (2Ki.10.27#cl1-2).

The clause the reader cites (2Ki.10.23#cl4, 'there are no servants of the LORD here') denies the presence of the LORD's people; the people gathered and named throughout are the servants of Baal (2Ki.10.18#cl0, 2Ki.10.21#cl1).

The cited verse (2Kgs 10:19) contains no word of a prophet; the speech there is Jehu's own command ('summon to me all the prophets of Baal'), and the prophets named are prophets of Baal, not speakers of the LORD's word.

Bethel and Dan are not the holy place and the calves are not said to stand in a holy place; the text states only that the calves were worshiped 'at Bethel and Dan' (2Ki.10.29#cl3-5), so the stamp as worded does not hold here.

Nothing in these three verses speaks of a promise kept or of God's faithfulness to his word; the section is the closing regnal formula for Jehu. If the stamp is meant only as a distant thematic echo of the dynasty continuing, no clause carries it.

Israel is named only as the object of Jehu's reign ('over Israel', 10.36#cl0/cl1) and as the title of the royal annals ('kings of Israel', 10.34#cl2); no clause speaks of Israel as God's people or of God's relation to them.
In 11:2 the only kinship named is Jehosheba as daughter of Joram and sister of Ahaziah; the clause does not itself carry the mother idea
No clause in 11:3 names a king or the kingdom; the verse only names the LORD's house and Athaliah's rule
No clause states a promise or divine faithfulness; the preservation of Joash is narrated as human action
The ardor and reform of the narrative as a whole, but no clause states repentance or revival; cl0 rejoicing over the king and cl1 quiet are the result of Athaliah's death, not of turning from sin.

The Jerusalem temple is the scene throughout ("the house of the LORD"), but no clause of this section speaks of God's presence dwelling there; the temple is referred to only as a place entered, guarded or left.
The section's only image-idolatry is Baal's temple, altars and idols, which are torn down and smashed (2Ki.11.18#cl1, #cl2); no idol is said to stand in the LORD's holy place.
Clause 2Ki.11.12#cl1's 'the Testimony' is the עֵדוּת, the document/tablet of the covenant placed on the king, not a person bearing witness; no clause mentions witnesses.
The house of the LORD is the setting and store (2Ki.11.4#cl2, 2Ki.11.10#cl2, 2Ki.11.11#cl3) but no clause speaks of Yahweh's presence in it.
The people appear only as bystanders in 2Ki.11.12#cl4-cl5 (clapping, 'Long live the king'); no clause names them as God's people.
No clause speaks of a promise kept; the oath at 2Ki.11.4#cl4 is exacted from the guards by Jehoiada, not God's faithfulness to David.
No clause states rescue; the saving of Joash is enacted across the narrative, and this section only shows protective arrangements and his investiture.
No clause concerns the law or wisdom; 'the Testimony' in 2Ki.11.12#cl1 is the object presented, not the law taught or obeyed.
The temple is damaged and in need of repair (2Ki.12.6#cl1 'the damage of the house' and passim), not destroyed; nothing in the section says the house was destroyed.

The verse cited (2Kgs 12:6) is the priests' failure to repair the temple; there is no sin offering, exile or death in this section except the money of guilt and sin offerings in 2Ki.12.16#cl0, which is income for the priests, not a theme of sin, exile or death.
The killing of Joash is a conspiracy of his own servants, not a divine judgment pronounced or executed in this section; nothing here names God as judge or states judgment.
The Davidic promise to keep a lamp for David (1 Kgs 11:36; 15:4) is the general backdrop only; no promise or divine faithfulness is spoken in these clauses.

The only likely footing is the cited 13:8, which mentions 'all his accomplishments and his might' (2Ki.13.8#cl0), but that is historical record, not divine promise or covenant faithfulness — and no clause in this section states a promise, a covenant, or God's faithfulness. The LORD's listening and giving a deliverer (13:4-5) are his mercy to an entreating king, from the story, not from a promise named in the text. I judge this stamp unsupported for this section rather than merely general; if it must go somewhere, it is at best general drift.

The section contains sin (2Ki.13.11) and death/burial (2Ki.13.13), but the theme's third element, exile, is not spoken of in any clause: the narrative stays in Samaria and ends in the tomb of the kings of Israel. No clause carries the whole theme.
The section's drift is military victory (2Ki.13.17#cl7-8, 2Ki.13.25#cl4-5), but no clause depicts a procession: nothing here shows anyone marching, entering, or being paraded.

The one restoration here (2Ki.13.21#cl7 'he.lived', cl8 'he.arose on feet his') is of a dead man to life, a revival/resurrection, not the healing of a sick or injured person. Elisha's own illness (2Ki.13.14#cl0-1) issues in death (2Ki.13.20#cl0), not recovery.

The only clause that names the fathers' covenant is 2Ki.13.23#cl2 ('on.account.of covenant his with Abraham Isaac and Jacob'): it says 'covenant' (בְּרִית), not 'oath' (שְׁבוּעָה). No clause in this section mentions an oath sworn to the fathers; an oath is a different element of the tradition from the covenant named here.

The section reports the defeat of Edom and the capture of Sela but no procession, triumph, or celebratory return; nothing in the clauses describes a victory procession. The nearest clause (2Ki.14.7#cl1, taking Sela) is a capture, not a procession.

No clause in this section speaks of a promise, covenant or divine faithfulness. 16#cl2 (Jeroboam succeeds) may echo the dynastic promise to Jehu, but nothing in the words says it; the surrounding text is the war with Amaziah and Jehoash's death notice.

The section speaks of kings, their wars and their burial; no clause speaks of a people belonging to God. 'the kings of Israel' (15#cl3, 16#cl1) and 'the kings of Israel' in Samaria name a dynasty/kingdom and its royal graves, not the people of God, and 'rested with his fathers' (16#cl0) is about ancestors, not the covenant people.

Nothing in this section speaks of a promise or of faithfulness: it is a reign summary, a conspiracy, a killing and a burial. The nearest formula, 'with his fathers' (2Ki.14.20#cl1), concerns burial, not covenant promise.
nothing in these two verses speaks of a divine promise or of faithfulness being kept; restored is Elath restored to Judah, not a promise fulfilled

The clause ('he did not turn aside from all the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat') says 'sins' but names no cult object, image, altar or foreign god; the Hebrew here is chatta'ot, not 'idols'. The stamp may be true of Jeroboam historically, but no clause in this section carries idolatry in particular.

The section reports a boundary restored and cities recovered, but there is no procession, entry, march or cultic celebration; no clause depicts a victory procession. A conquest result is not a procession.

The section records evil done and no turning away, but records no sentence, verdict, punishment or disaster. 'He did evil in the sight of the LORD' is an evaluation of conduct, not an event of judgment.

The only movement after the victory is the victor's return to his own capital (2Ki.14.14#cl2 'he returned to Samaria') and the entry into the defeated city to strip it (2Ki.14.13#cl1 'he came Jerusalem'); there is no ceremonial procession of triumph, and the cited verse 13 shows plunder and wall-breaking, not a procession.
This section has defeat, flight and plunder (2Ki.14.12–14) but no sin, no exile and no death; the cited verse 12 speaks only of Judah being routed and the men fleeing.

2Ki.15.5 speaks of the LORD striking the king with a skin disease, not of healing; the English 'leprosy' in the Berean text renders the Hebrew skin-disease term and no curing or restoration is narrated here.
the section's general subject is the throne of Judah under Azariah and its transfer to Jotham, rather than any one clause carrying the idea of 'kingdom'
the Davidic throne continuing through Azariah to Jotham is the section's general drift, but no clause states a promise or divine faithfulness in words; there is no explicit promise language here.
the king struck with skin disease in 2Ki.15.5 is Azariah, a Judean king, and the text gives no servant-of-the-LORD figure, vicarious suffering or restoration.
the text says Pul invaded the land (2Ki.15.19#cl0) and withdrew (2Ki.15.20#cl2-3); no fighting, army or combat is described
no city is besieged or surrounded; the encounter ends in tribute and withdrawal, the opposite of a siege
no temple or sanctuary appears in the whole section
no one is taken captive or deported; Menahem buys the invader off and the Assyrian goes home
Pul's incursion is described in political terms (tribute, support) and the section states no verdict from God or punishment on the section's own terms
no curse is pronounced or referred to in this section
there is no deportation: the king of Assyria 'withdrew and did not remain in the land' (2Ki.15.20#cl2-3)
only the general drift of the section (a bad reign followed by submission to Assyria); no clause states a judgment
2Ki.15.21#cl2 is the annalistic source citation, not a prophetic word; no prophet appears in the section

The clause names 'the sins of Jeroboam' and not turning aside from them, but does not itself say the sin was idolatry; the stamp is the section's general drift (evil in the LORD's sight), not a word here

Pekah's act is a conspiracy and a killing at the citadel (2Ki.15.25#cl0, cl1, cl3), not a battle: no armies engage, no fighting is described; the fifty Gileadites are accomplices, not a fighting force
No battle is narrated: the Assyrian king simply 'came and captured' cities and deported the people; no fighting, army or defeat is stated in any clause (15:29).
No siege is described: 15:29 says only that he came and captured the cities and took the people captive; nothing of surrounding, walls or starving a city appears.
Hoshea is a conspirator and usurper (15:30), not a judge or deliverer raised up by God; the stamp does not fit this section.
No prophet speaks and no prophetic word is given in this section; 15:30 reports a conspiracy, not a prophecy.
v.37 says only that the LORD began to send Rezin and Pekah against Judah; no battle, fighting or defeat is narrated in this section (2Ki.15.37#cl0-1 end with the sending, not with any combat).
v.38 records only Jotham's death, burial and Ahaz's succession; nothing in this section states or assumes a divine promise or God's faithfulness (contrast the Davidic-promise formulas elsewhere).

the only candidate is 2Ki.15.37#cl0-1 (the LORD began to send Rezin and Pekah against Judah), which reports the start of hostile action, not a judgment pronounced or executed; nothing here says why or that it is judgment.

No clause names an idol, image, Baal, Asherah, high place or any object or act of worship. The clause says only 'the sins of Jeroboam' generically; the Hebrew of 2Kgs 15:9 (חטאות ירבעם) carries no word for an idol. The reader cited only 2Kgs 15:9, which does not state idolatry.

2Ki.15.10#cl1/cl2 are a coup and assassination ('conspired', 'struck him down', 'killed him in front of the people'), not a battle between forces; there is no army, no fighting, no opponent in the section.
the section gives no image or idol placed in a holy place; 16:4 cult is at high places, hills and trees, and the temple appears only in 16:8 as the source of silver and gold
16:8 strips the house of the LORD of its silver and gold for a foreign king — a real assault on the temple, but it is spoliation, not the defilement/desecration the stamp names, so I pin no clause

Ahaz copies a foreign (Damascus) altar and its pattern, but no clause here names an idol, an image of a god, or worship given to one; the altar is an altar to the LORD on which offerings are made (2Ki.16.13#cl0-cl2, 2Ki.16.15#cl2-cl3). Foreign cultic imitation is not the stamp 'idolatry' as an event involving images.

The temple is not destroyed: parts are dismantled and altered (2Ki.16.17, 2Ki.16.18) and its vessels remain in use for offerings at 2Ki.16.15#cl2-cl3. Vandalism/dismantling is not destruction as an event.

No idol or image of a deity is said to stand in the temple here. The Damascus altar Ahaz copies (2Ki.16.10#cl2-cl4, 2Ki.16.11#cl0) is an altar for the LORD's offerings (2Ki.16.15#cl2-cl3), and the word for the pattern sent (2Ki.16.10#cl4) is a plan/likeness, not a god-image set in the holy place.
No clause enthrones, installs or seats an idol or deity: the 'great altar' is made and used for offerings (2Ki.16.15#cl2-cl3), and the only thing 'put' is the displaced bronze altar (2Ki.16.14#cl3).

No clause here speaks of sin leading to exile or death; Ahaz's death is an ordinary royal burial (2Ki.16.20#cl0-cl1), and no exile or deportation is described, only a temple change made 'on account of the king of Assyria' (2Ki.16.18#cl0).
No clause pronounces or depicts judgment: the section is narrative of Ahaz's cultic acts and his burial, with no verdict or penalty stated.

No clause mentions the temple or the LORD's presence dwelling in a place; 2Ki.17.29#cl2 refers to shrines of the high places, not the temple, and the stamp's referent (God's presence in His sanctuary) is nowhere in this section.

The prophets in this section are the LORD's true prophets and seers whom He sent to warn Israel (2Ki.17.13#cl0, 2Ki.17.13#cl5, 2Ki.17.23#cl2-cl3); no false prophet appears or is described.

The section names no sin, no exile and no death of the people; the distress is from the Assyrian threat, not from guilt or deportation.

The section names foreign gods only to deny their power to rescue; no idol is set up in the temple or holy place.
No claim is made against God's presence or temple; the gods named are other nations' gods, and this section does not attack YHWH's presence.

The salt here is only a physical element Elisha casts into the spring (2Ki.2.21#cl1, “cast the salt into it”); nothing in the section speaks of a covenant, and the phrase “covenant of salt” (Num 18:19; 2 Chr 13:5) does not occur. The section concerns the healing of existing waters, the land and its unfruitfulness (2Ki.2.19#cl4–cl5; 2Ki.2.21#cl4–cl5); no clause speaks of creating, making, or originating anything.
Hezekiah's prayer (2Ki.20.2#cl1, 2Ki.20.3#cl2) is the king's own petition, not a priest interceding for others; nothing in the section involves a priest or priestly mediation
No procession or triumph is narrated; the only movement toward the house of the LORD is Hezekiah's predicted going up on the third day (2Ki.20.5#cl7), which is not a victory procession

The section has Hezekiah's mortal illness and prayer, but no servant of the LORD who suffers on others' behalf; the 'servant' mentioned is David (2Ki.20.6#cl2), and Hezekiah is called ruler, not servant

No clause in this section states a divine promise or an act of faithfulness: the only spoken word of the LORD is the judgment of 2Ki.20.16#cl1 through 2Ki.20.18#cl3, and 2Ki.20.19#cl1 ('The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good') only calls that judgment good. If the stamp is meant as 'the LORD's word stands', it is carried by no particular clause here.
Nothing in 2Kgs 20:20-21 cites, recalls or fulfils a divine promise; a dynastic succession is not itself a statement of God's faithfulness, and the stamp's cited verse has no such words.
Judah/Hezekiah/Manasseh are the people of God, but no clause singles the idea out - the section's clauses are about building works, a chronicle source and a royal succession.

The house of the LORD is polluted with altars and an Asherah pole (21:4-5, 7) but nothing in this section says the temple was destroyed; destruction of the temple is only the threatened/implied background, not stated.
No curse is pronounced or described here; 21:8 states the conditional promise of land ("if only they are careful to do all I have commanded them") rather than a curse.
No exile occurs or is announced in this section; the land/feet language in 21:8 is the positive promise of not wandering, not an exile event.
Moses is called "My servant" (21:8) and no prophet or prophetic role appears in this section.
The mediums and spiritists (21:6) and the Asherah pole are not prophets: no false prophet figure or prophecy is in this section.
The opposite: 21:3 says he rebuilt what Hezekiah had destroyed, and 21:9 that the people did not listen; there is no return or repentance.

No clause in the section performs a curse (no 'cursed be', no oath-formula); the judgment of vv.12-14 is declared by Yahweh as his own act against Jerusalem. The stamp can only be attached to the section's general drift of doom, not to any clause.
The section has sin (2Ki.21.20#cl0) and a death (2Ki.21.23#cl1), but no exile and no link between the sin and the death; the stamp names a whole pattern the section does not speak of.
No divine promise and no divine act of faithfulness is spoken in this section; Amon's reign, death and Josiah's succession are reported without any reference to a promise.

The stamp is cited to 2Kgs 22:2, but neither the section nor verse 2 mentions the law, a book, wisdom, instruction or teaching; the only data there are Josiah's right doing and his walking in David's ways, which is covenant fidelity, not law or wisdom. There is no divine oath or covenant-faithfulness formula ('I will never forget my covenant', oath, everlasting promise) anywhere in these clauses; the promise here is a specific sparing of the king (2Ki.22.20), which is a different stamp.

No clause names a servant; Shaphan is 'the scribe' (2Ki.22.3#cl1) and the doorkeepers and workmen are their own roles. The stamp at best describes the scene's drift — men sent on the king's errand — but no clause carries 'servant'.

No clause of this section speaks of law or wisdom: the money put into the hands is not to be accounted for 'since they work with integrity' (2Ki.22.7#cl2, 'in faithfulness they are working') — trust in the workmen's honesty, not law or wisdom, and the reader cited 2Kgs 22:7 for it.

No prophet appears or is named in this section; the delegation in 22:12-13 goes to priest, scribes and servants to 'inquire of the LORD', and no prophetic figure or prophetic speech act is stated. The reader cited 22:13, but that verse names no prophet.

Nothing in this section speaks of mercy or restoration: the movement is finding the book, the king's distress, and the announcement of wrath kindled against the people. The nearest note, that Yahweh may be inquired of, is not mercy or restoration stated; the stamp is not supported here.
2Ki.23.27#cl3 speaks of rejecting the city and the house, not of the temple being destroyed; no clause in the section says the temple was destroyed.
The law is already written and found (2Ki.23.24#cl2-cl4); no clause in this section gives law, so law-giving is not present.
The Book of the Covenant is cited in 2Ki.23.21#cl2/cl3, but no covenant is cut or made in this section; covenant-cutting is absent.

The section's Passover obedience and Josiah's wholehearted turning are the section's positive note, but no clause states mercy or restoration, and the LORD does not turn from His anger in 2Ki.23.26#cl0.

No clause in this section speaks of sin or of exile; the only death is Josiah's violent death at Megiddo, which is not presented here as the judgment of sin, and Jehoahaz's removal to Egypt and the exile lie outside these verses. The section says only that Jehoahaz 'did evil in the sight of the LORD' (2Ki.23.32#cl0); no idol, image, altar, or worship of other gods is mentioned anywhere in 23:31-35.
No prophet, prophecy, or divine word appears in 23:31-35; the cited verse 23:34 has only Pharaoh Neco's acts (making Eliakim king, renaming him), which is royal decree, not prophetic word.
The 23:20 clauses are about killing and defiling, not about a people belonging to God; nothing in the section names the people of God as such.
The section has an invasion, vassalage, raiders and a rebellion, but no clause says the city was besieged or invested.
Removal from the land is implied by 'destroy Judah' (2Ki.24.2#cl1) and 'to remove them from His presence' (2Ki.24.3#cl0, cl1), but no clause in this section states a deportation of people.

The description given is 'event_images', but there is no clause here pronouncing or depicting a curse: no 'cursed be', no blessing/curse formula, no curse as an event. If the stamp means 'covenant curse threatened in Deuteronomy executed', I could not determine it from this section.

No human is called or depicted a warrior. The Chaldeans, Arameans, Moabites and Ammonites are 'raiders' (2Ki.24.2#cl0) and Nebuchadnezzar is 'king' (2Ki.24.1#cl0); if 'raiders' counts as a warrior role, then 2Ki.24.2#cl0 is the pin. I am unsure which side of that line the stamp sits.

The only idea close to it is that the word the LORD spoke came true (2Ki.24.2#cl1, 2Ki.24.3#cl0), but the word kept is a word of destruction, not a promise, and no clause speaks of the LORD's faithfulness to a promise.
The text records spoliation of the temple's treasures and gold articles (2Ki.24.13#cl0, #cl1), not the destruction of the temple building; no clause speaks of it being destroyed.
The section narrates exile and slaughter-free deportation as the outcome of Judah's fall, but no clause states sin; the theme is the section's drift, not carried by any clause.

No clause in this section says anyone was carried away or deported; 2Ki.24.7#cl2 (words on the Berean text "had taken all his territory, from the Brook of Egypt to the Euphrates River") describes the king of Babylon taking territory, not an exile of people. The clause cited with verse 9 (2Ki.24.9#cl0) says only "he did evil in the sight of the LORD"; no clause in this section mentions idols, images, other gods or worship of them.

The section's general drift (a king doing evil, then exile and death of the kingdom) matches the theme, but no single clause states the theme; "he did evil" (2Ki.24.9#cl0) is sin only, and the rest is report of accession, reign and death.

No clause in this section reports a word of Yahweh, a prophet, or a fulfilment formula; the section is narrative report (death, accession, Egypt's reduced territory, Jehoiachin's age and reign, his evil). The reader's citation of v. 7 supplies no prophetic speech.

Exile (2Ki.25.7#cl3) and death (2Ki.25.7#cl0) are present as events, but no clause in the section names sin or states that sin caused them; the theme is carried by the section's drift, not by a particular clause.

The section ends in exile and mutilation (2Ki.25.7#cl1-cl3) and contains no reversal: no return, restoration or exaltation is stated in any clause. The stamp is a shape of a later narrative, not an idea of this section.

The section presupposes a city recently taken and its remaining inhabitants seized, but no clause states a siege (no besieging, surrounding, or investment of the city); 'from the city' in 2Ki.25.19#cl0 identifies a location, not a siege.

Nothing in these clauses mentions the temple or its destruction; 2Ki.25.18 names the chief priest, a second-rank priest and three doorkeepers, who are persons taken, and the 'keepers of the threshold' are temple staff, not the building. The cited verse does not carry the stamp.
Gedaliah's oath in 2Ki.25.24#cl0 is a sworn assurance to the commanders, not God's promise or covenant faithfulness; no clause speaks of a divine promise kept.

The text describes an assassination of Gedaliah by Ishmael and ten men, not a battle: no armies engage, no combat is narrated; the only military body named (the commanders of the armies, 2Ki.25.26#cl0) appears solely as those who flee.
The section has Jehoiachin released from prison in Babylon and given a seat and a daily portion; nothing says he returned from exile to Judah or to his land, which is what return_from_exile names.

The section shows kindness to Jehoiachin and a lasting provision, which a reader takes as the general drift of God's promise to David's line being kept; no clause here states a promise or its fulfilment.
No clause states the LORD's presence; the house of the LORD is spoken of only as being burned.
Victory here is pursuit and devastation (2Kgs 3:24-25), with the Moabite king's son offered on the wall (3:27); nothing in the section pictures a procession or triumphal entry.
2Kgs 4:2 shows the widow's poverty and Elisha's question, not a wise woman; no clause in the section carries this idea.
The woman telling the man of God what happened is report, not witness in the sense of testimony; the stamp describes the drift of the section, not a clause.
Nothing in the section depicts conflict or a reversal of strength; the widow's deliverance is by provision, not by defeating a stronger party.
The section's drift is the prophet's word/authority at work, but no clause here states a prophetic utterance; 2Ki.4.36#6 is a direct command rather than a prophetic word.

No suffering servant here: the suffering is the child (2Ki.4.19#1-2, 2Ki.4.20#3) and the mother (2Ki.4.27#6), and the one who acts is the prophet; 2Ki.4.34 is the prophet's own body over the boy, not a servant's affliction for others.
Nothing in this section speaks of kingship, throne or realm; the actors are a prophet, a woman, her household and servants.

No servant suffers here. The one who serves is Elisha himself, acting without cost to himself; the company is poisoned food, not a suffering servant. The stamp belongs to Isaiah's servant figure, not this scene.

No one is sick or cured in this section: the woman is childless and her husband old (2Ki.4.14#cl4, cl5); the outcome is conception and birth (2Ki.4.17#cl0-1), not healing. The stamp would be right only for the later Shunammite narrative (2Kgs 4:18-37).
No clause of this section shows anyone testifying to an event or bearing witness; Elisha and the girl are agents in the narrative (sending messages, speaking), not witnesses.

No clause in this section has an outsider confessing or believing; the girl's words are a wish ('If only my master would go'), Naaman resists, and the section ends with the healing and no statement of faith.
No healing occurs in 5:15-27; the only skin-disease clause (27#cl0, cl2) is the infliction of leprosy on Gehazi, the reverse of healing. The healing of Naaman is in 5:14, outside this section.
No priest, Aaronic or otherwise, appears here; Elisha is called 'the man of God' (15#cl0), a prophetic, not priestly, title, and no priestly act is performed in 15-27.

The section's drift is a prophet acting and speaking, but no clause here is a prophetic utterance (no 'thus says the LORD' or word of the LORD); Elisha only gives directions ('Go', 'I will come', 'Where did it fall?', 'Lift it out').
The section presents famine (2Ki.6.25#cl0) but no clause reports provision or relief; the stamp describes the section's drift as a reversal and nothing in these clauses speaks the provision pole.
Aramean soldiers' blindness is removed so they can be captured and led away; the opening of eyes is a punitive wonder and a reversal, not the healing of a sick person

The siege is the situation presupposed by the price oracle (the gate of Samaria, famine prices), but no clause in this section states the siege; the clauses only speak of flour and barley prices at the gate.
No clause in this section speaks of a siege; the section concerns the fulfilment of Elisha's word, the cheap grain, and the officer's death.

No fighting occurs anywhere in 2Kgs 7:3-15; 2Ki.7.6#cl3 has Israel's king hiring Hittite and Egyptian kings 'to attack us', but the Arameans flee at the sound without a battle, and no combat clause exists in the section.
Nobody processes in triumph; 2Ki.7.15#cl2 shows the road littered with discarded clothes and equipment, and the only movement is scouts tracking a fleeing army to the Jordan.
The gatekeepers of 2Ki.7.10#cl1 and 2Ki.7.11#cl0 shout news from the gate; they are not posted lookouts reporting what they see, and no watchman clause appears.
No individual fighting man is described; the Aramean army flees without a soldier being portrayed, and 2Ki.7.6#cl0-3 speaks only of the army's sound and the kings hired against it.

The section contains no prophetic speech or fulfilment formula; the king's speech in 2Ki.7.12#cl2-11 is his own guess about Aramean tactics, not a prophet's word, and no clause cites a prophetic utterance.

No clause announces or executes judgment. The famine and deaths threatened are siege conditions and the men's own reasoning (2Ki.7.4), and the Lord's action in 2Ki.7.6 is heard as terror by the Arameans, not framed as judgment in this text.
No promise is quoted and no fulfilment of a divine word is marked in these clauses; 2Ki.7.6#cl0 simply narrates that the Lord caused the sound to be heard.

The chapter presupposes that the promise implicit in the prophet's word to the woman holds and that the king restores her property; no clause in this section states a promise or an act of faithfulness, so it is a section-level characterisation I judge true only in that general sense.

Nothing in the clauses exalts anyone: the woman returns from a seven-year sojourn and the king restores her property. If the stamp means 'loss to restoration' one could cite 2Ki.8.3 and 2Ki.8.6, but 'exile to exaltation' is not what this section says.

The famine is emphatically named (2Ki.8.1#cl6, with 'seven years' in cl7), but no clause mentions food, harvest, rain or any provision; the presumed deliverance is not in the text, so I treat this as the general reverse of the section's situation rather than a pinned idea.

The clauses say only that Jehoram walked in the ways of the kings of Israel / the house of Ahab (2Ki.8.18#cl0, #cl1) and did evil in the eyes of Yahweh (#cl3); no idol, image, or worship of another god appears in this section, so the specific idea 'idolatry' is not carried by any clause.
The section shows sin (2Ki.8.18) and the threat of destruction (2Ki.8.19), which is the general drift of the theme, but no clause here speaks of exile or death.

The section's drift — rebellion against the house of David, Libnah falling away, and Jehoram's death — fits the theme, but no clause names a sin, an exile or a death as such; the death is only 'rested with his fathers'. Nothing in particular can be pointed at.

Nothing in this section pronounces or depicts judgement: Edom and Libnah's rebellion is political, Jehoram's night attack is not presented as divine retribution, and the report of his death and burial is standard regnal formula. The section says Ahaziah walked in the ways of the house of Ahab and did evil, referred to the house of Ahab as a dynasty and marriage tie (2Ki.8.27#cl0, cl1, cl2), but names no idol, cult object or worship of another god; 'the ways of the house of Ahab' is the nearest thing and it is not stated as idolatry here.
General drift only: the evil of 27 belongs to the pattern that leads to death, and the wounding of Joram (28#cl1) to a fatal wound, but no clause states exile, death or its cause here.
General: Israel and Judah are named as the covenant nations (2Ki.8.25#cl0), but no clause speaks of them as the LORD's people.
The section has Elisha announce that Hazael will be king over Aram (2Ki.8.13#cl5-6), but nothing is poured or anointed: no anointing act appears in any clause of 2Kgs 8:7-15.

The only words near the citation are Elisha's 'You will surely recover' (2Ki.8.10#cl3) and the same report in 2Ki.8.14#cl6; these state Ben-hadad's illness, not a divine promise or act of faithfulness, and no clause speaks of God keeping a promise.
the section is an anointing and an oracle of destruction; no clause speaks of a promise being kept or of God's faithfulness

The section asks for grace and peace to be multiplied, which is the general drift of a blessing-wish, but no clause speaks of mercy or of restoring anyone.
Christ is named as the one through whose righteousness faith is received and as Lord, so the section's drift is toward the shared faith of those in him; no clause states union with Christ itself.

The verses cited (2Pet 1:4) speak of 'precious and magnificent promises' and becoming 'partakers of the divine nature' (2Pe.1.4#cl0, #cl1), but no covenant, covenant-making, or covenant formula appears anywhere in the section; a covenant is not merely a promise, and nothing here names or enacts a covenant.

2Pet 1:11's clause 2Pe.1.11#cl0 has 'the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ' — a kingdom is spoken of, but no clause names or depicts Christ as king; 'Lord and Savior' are the titles used, not 'king'.
The cited verse 2Pet 1:11 names 'our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ' (2Pe.1.11#cl0) but nowhere in the section is anyone called 'Son' or addressed as son; the sonship idea is absent.
