The stamp names a person (witness), but no witness appears; the LORD speaks his own word, and the cited verse has no human witness to corroborate anything.
No clause speaks of a promise or of God's faithfulness; this belongs to the section only as the larger David narrative's drift.
The section is a murder and a beheading reported to David; no clause shows mercy or restoration.
The covenant made here is between David and the elders of Israel before the LORD, not the divine covenant with David of 2 Sam 7; the stamp is a different covenant from this one.

The davidic covenant is the dynastic promise of 2 Sam 7 ('your throne shall be established forever'), which is not in this section; here the LORD's word is a commissioning of David as shepherd/ruler over Israel, and the covenant made is with the elders.

David is the younger brother who becomes king over all Israel (his brothers are not mentioned here), so the idea is the section's general drift; no clause in this section states the elder/younger relation.

The section says only that the LORD had established David as king and exalted his kingdom; it contains no covenant, no promise of an eternal dynasty, and no offspring promise. Nathan's oracle (2Sam 7) is absent here.

The clauses report that God had established and exalted David; there is no promise made or recalled and no word of faithfulness, covenant loyalty or keeping an oath anywhere in 2Sam.5.12-16. God's past act is stated, not a promise kept.

Nothing in the section describes a procession: 2Sa.5.25#cl2 is a pursuit-and-strike route ('from Gibeon to Gezer'), not a parade or entry, and no clause mentions movement in triumph or a city entered.

The section never presents David as the weaker party; the Philistines are defeated because the LORD delivers them into his hand (2Sa.5.19#cl6), so victory is attributed to divine help, not to weakness.
The idols appear only in 2Sa.5.21#cl0, abandoned by the Philistines at Baal-perazim; no clause places an idol in the temple or any holy place, nor mentions the temple.
David enters by stealth and capture (2Sa.5.7#cl0); the only movement text is an approach to Jerusalem to fight, 2Sa.5.6#cl0 — no procession or triumph is described.
2Sa.5.10#cl1 states the LORD was with him, not a covenant grant; no covenant-making speech or parties occur in this section.
No temple, sanctuary or divine presence is spoken of here; 2Sa.5.9#cl0/#cl2 concern David's stronghold and Millo, and 2Sa.5.11#cl1 a palace for David.
The only corporate body named is Israel under David ("his men", 2Sa.5.6#cl0); no clause speaks of the people of God as such, so this is the section's drift rather than a pinned idea.
David is not in exile here; he moves from campaign to capture to residence and greatness (2Sa.5.6#cl0, 2Sa.5.9#cl0, 2Sa.5.10#cl0), with no exile or return.
Hiram's envoys bring cedar and craftsmen in a diplomatic/commercial gesture (2Sa.5.11#cl0); nothing in the clause expresses belief, and he is not reported as believing.
The gathering of chosen men and the thirty thousand read as a muster, but no clause speaks of fighting, an enemy or a battle; nothing here says a battle is waged.
The movement in 6:2-6:4 is a transport of the ark, not a triumph after a victory; no clause names a victory or a defeated foe.
No clause reports an appearing or manifestation of God; the ark is called by the Name of the LORD of Hosts, which is a title, not a theophany.
Nothing in this section speaks of a covenant with David; the cited verse 2Sam 6:12 is the ark's removal from Obed-edom, and the Davidic covenant is 2Sam 7 (not this section).
The ark's move toward the City of David and the presence 'before the LORD' are the drift, but no clause here speaks of a temple; the temple is not built until Solomon.
No promise, oath or divine faithfulness is spoken of in these four verses; the blessing of Obed-edom (cl2) is a past act, not a promise kept.
No clause speaks of mercy or restoration; blessing of a household (cl2) is not restoration, and the narrative's reversal from the ark's danger (2Sam 6:7) is outside this section.

2Sam 6:21 speaks only of the LORD choosing David over Saul's house and appointing him ruler over Israel; no covenant, covenant formula, or oath is stated in this section (the Davidic covenant is 2Sam 7). The cited verse does not carry this stamp.
The place named is a tent David had pitched, and the presence marked is the ark of the LORD (2Sa.6.17#cl1, 2Sa.6.16#cl1); there is no temple and no temple-presence language in this section.

The sacrificing and blessing in 6:17-18 are the general priestly drift of the passage, but no clause names a priest, Aaron, Levi, Zadok, or any priestly office; the actors are David and (possibly) the bearers of the ark.
Wrong for this section: there is no enemy, no fighting and no warfare here, only celebration, the ark's transport, Uzzah's death and the ark's stay at Obed-edom.
Nothing in 2Sam 7:1-17 speaks of a temple being destroyed; 7:13 speaks of Solomon building a house, and 7:6 says the LORD has not dwelt in a house — the opposite of destruction.
2Sam 7:8 says the LORD took David from the pasture to be ruler, with no anointing or pouring of oil; the stamp is not present in this section.
2Sam 7:9 speaks of cutting off enemies but there is no procession or triumphal march in the text.
2Sam 7:10 promises Israel will dwell in their own place and be disturbed no more; the section reports no deportation or exile.
2Sam 7:2 mentions the ark and the tent but names no furnishings (lampstand, table, altar, etc.); the stamp is not carried by any particular clause.
Nothing in this section presents David's descendant as a new Moses; the exodus in 7:6 is recalled as past history, not as a role the offspring takes up.
God's dwelling in tent/ark is the old order being replaced, not a renewed Israel-character; 7:10 speaks of Israel as the people, not a new Israel figure.
No clause speaks of a surviving remnant; 7:10 promises security to Israel as a whole.
The nations appear only as David's enemies (7:1, 7:9), never as an acting character in this section.
God acts against enemies, but no human warrior role is predicated here; 7:14's rod and blows are discipline, not warfare.
Nathan speaks at 7:3, but nothing in the section frames him or anyone as a witness.

Wrong for this section. David prays for himself and his own house ('Your servant and his house', 7:25-29); there is no priest, no intercession for others, and no sacrificial or cultic act. In 7:18 he simply 'went in, sat before the LORD' and spoke — a royal prayer, not priestly intercession.

No clause in this section speaks of a temple or of God's dwelling presence. The 'house' of 7:25-27 and 7:29 is the dynastic house of David (the word-play with 'I will build a house for you' in 7:27), not a building; 7:18 has David sitting 'before the LORD' but no temple. The stamp is therefore at best the general drift of the wider chapter and gets no specific clauses here.

The section is a sequence of triumphs, but no clause depicts a procession or parade (no entry, escort, display of captives or spoil); the closest, bringing the gold shields to Jerusalem (2Sa.8.7#cl2), is a single act of transport, not a procession.

Nothing here is covenant language: no covenant, oath, promise, or 'forever'/'house' formula. 2Sam 8 reports David's victories; the unconditional covenant with David is narrated in 2Sam 7 (not this section) and Yhwh's favour in 2Sa.8.6#cl2 / 2Sa.8.14#cl3 is victory, not covenant-making.
The section is about David and the foreign nations; Israel is never named (the 'subdued'/'subject' clauses name Moab, Aram, Edom and the rest), so no clause carries the idea.

The gold shields brought to Jerusalem (2Sa.8.7#cl2) and the silver, gold and bronze dedicated to the LORD (2Sa.8.11#cl0) are acts of storage and dedication, not temple, dwelling or presence language; no house, temple, ark or presence is mentioned in the section.

Nothing in the section is framed as the weaker overcoming the stronger; David is the powerful aggressor who defeats and subjugates nations (2Sa.8.1, 2Sa.8.2, 2Sa.8.5), so there is no reversal clause to point at.

No exile or return-from-exile appears; David 'returned' from striking down Edomites (2Sa.8.13#cl1) is a return from battle, not from exile, and making a name (2Sa.8.13#cl0) is exaltation without the exile counterpart.

The only boundary drawn among people is between those put to death and those spared in the cording of Moab (2Sa.8.2#cl3, 2Sa.8.2#cl5), an act of slaughter, not a reversal of rank; no clause makes the last first or the low exalted.

Joab's post is named (2Sa.8.16#cl0: "Joab son of Zeruiah was over the army"), but no clause in the section shows fighting, a warrior, or a warrior's act; an administrative appointment is not a warrior.
No clause here speaks of a covenant, promise, or its making (nothing in 2Sa.8.15#cl0-cl1 or the officials list); the section's theme is David's administration, not a covenant with him.

Nothing in the section speaks of a covenant with David; the only loyal-love shown is David's to the house of Saul for Jonathan's sake (2Sa.9.1#cl3; 2Sa.9.7#cl2), which is the Jonathan-David bond, not the Davidic covenant. The reader cited 2Sam 9:7, but 2Sa.9.7#cl3-cl4 concern land and table, not a covenant with David.

The only bodily condition named is lameness, which is never healed here: 2Sa.9.3#cl4 says he is 'stricken of both feet' and 2Sa.9.13#cl2 repeats 'he was lame in both feet' at the end. No clause describes a cure or healing.

No clause mentions a firstborn or birth order. Mephibosheth is called Jonathan's son (2Sa.9.3#cl4; 2Sa.9.6#cl0) and Mica is called a young son (2Sa.9.12#cl0), but neither is said to be firstborn. The reader cited 2Sam 9:11, where the point is eating at the king's table 'like one of the king's own sons' — status as an adopted son, not firstborn rank.

Mephibosheth is no stranger or sojourner: he is an Israelite of Saul's own house living in Jerusalem (2Sa.9.13#cl0), brought into the king's household and fed at the king's table. No clause speaks of a foreigner or resident alien.

The section nowhere speaks of testimony, testimony-bearing or being a witness (martyrs); 1:4 speaks of endurance under persecution, not of witness. Closest words are 'perseverance and faith', which is endurance, not witnessing.
The section's suffering belongs to the persecuted Thessalonians (1:4), not to a servant figure bearing it for others; nothing here evokes the suffering servant.
1:2 speaks of grace and peace, not mercy or restoration; no clause in the section states mercy or restoration.
The clause 2Th.1.5#cl1 gives 'the kingdom of God' but nothing in the section divides a kingdom into parts (as in the divided-kingdom image); only 'being accounted worthy of the kingdom' is in view.
The section has vengeance and affliction (2Th.1.8#cl0, 2Th.1.6#cl1) but no battle, armies, weapons or combat; nothing here depicts a final battle.
2Th.1.9#cl0 speaks of 'the penalty of eternal destruction, separated from the presence of the Lord' — there is no book, no opening of books, no recording of deeds.
2Th.1.10 speaks of Christ's coming and being marveled at by 'all who have believed' — no raising of the dead, no resurrection of anyone is stated in any clause.
2Th.1.11 is prayer that God will count them worthy and fulfill every good desire; no one is commissioned, called to a task, or sent.
The suffering here is that of the Thessalonian believers ('for which you are suffering', 2Th.1.5#cl2), not the Servant of Isaiah; nothing in the section describes the Servant.
The section prays and describes the coming revelation of the Lord; no clause speaks of prophecy, a prophet, or a prophetic writing.

No clause speaks of a covenant or of peace; 2:16 only says God 'by grace has loved us and given us eternal comfort and good hope' — comfort is not covenant. The stamp belongs to passages where a covenant of peace is named (e.g. Ezek 37:26), not here.

Nothing in the section names or describes a covenant, new or old; 2:13's 'chosen you from the beginning to be saved' is election/salvation, not covenant-making. The reader cited 2:13, which has no covenant language.
The only candidates are 2:14 'called you through our gospel', which is calling/preaching, not sending; no clause has God or Christ sending anyone. Sending is not the idea carried here.
2:15 speaks of 'the traditions we taught you, whether by speech or by letter' — teaching/handling down tradition, not bearing witness/testimony. No clause says anyone testified to anything.
The section names brothers, the Lord, God the Father; no clause presents anyone as a servant or in servant role. 2:13's 'we ought to give thanks' is the writers' action, not servanthood.

2:13's 'chosen you from the beginning' is God's election of the whole addressed community, not a remnant surviving out of a larger group; no clause has the remnant idea (a faithful few left from many).
No clause in 2Thess 2:13-17 mentions suffering, opposition or persecution; the reader cited 2:15, which speaks only of standing firm and holding to traditions. Nothing here carries the idea.

The section is thanksgiving, exhortation and prayer; it never mentions the coming of the Lord or the day of the Lord (contrast the immediately preceding 2:1-12, not quoted here). The cited 2:13 has 'has chosen you from the beginning unto salvation', not the day.

No clause in this section mentions the Spirit. The Greek of 2 Thess 3:5 is εἰς τὴν ἀγάπην τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ εἰς τὴν ὑπομονὴν τοῦ Χριστοῦ ('the love of God and the steadfastness of Christ' — genitives of God and Christ, not 'of the Spirit'). The Berean text confirms: 'into God's love and Christ's perseverance'. The stamp was cited at 2Thess 3:5, perhaps under the influence of the variant reading πνεύματος, but that reading is not reflected in the clause text or the Berean text here, so the stamp does not hold for this section.

The clause says 'the Lord of peace' and asks him to give peace; it names no covenant, no covenant formula ('my covenant of peace', as in Num 25:12; Ezek 37:26), and 'peace' here is the closing wish of a letter.
Only a general motif at most: the Lord being 'with all of you' is presence language, but no clause names the temple, sanctuary or dwelling place.
Christ is named as 'our Lord Jesus Christ' in a grace-wish, but no clause in this section speaks of redemption, ransom or purchase.
The section's drift is a wish of peace and grace, but no clause names mercy or restoration.
Nowhere in 2Thess 3:6-15 is anyone called a slave or bondservant; 3:8 speaks of 'labor and toil' and refusing to be a burden (2Th.3.8#cl0, #cl1), not of slavery, and no clause carries the idea.
3:9 is about 'an example for you to imitate' (2Th.3.9#cl1, #cl2) and 3:7 about imitating Paul — exemplary conduct, not bearing witness/testimony; no clause here speaks of witnessing.
3:12 speaks of working quietly to 'earn their own living' (2Th.3.12#cl1, #cl2) — everyday labour, not redemption or any saving act in Christ; no clause carries the idea.
Paul is called 'an apostle', not a prophet; nothing in either clause names or describes a prophet.
'apostle' (2Ti.1.1#cl0) is an envoy/commissioned role, not a servant; the Greek diakonos/doulos does not appear in the text as given.
The section speaks of 'the promise of life in Christ Jesus' and 'grace, mercy, and peace', but no clause says anything about redemption, ransom or being bought back.

No clause in this section has anyone bearing testimony to a fact or person; 2Ti.1.16#cl0 speaks of Onesiphorus' mercy, refreshment and lack of shame about Paul's chains, not of witness or testimony. The stamp is misassigned to this section.
No sacrificial, cultic or priestly language or figure appears; 'he served' in 2Ti.1.18#cl3 is ordinary service to Paul, not priestly ministry.
Contrary to the cited verse, 2Ti.1.15 speaks of desertion by 'everyone in the Province of Asia' and names Phygelus and Hermogenes; no clause presents a body of God's people.
2Ti.1.18 asks for mercy 'on that day' and recalls Onesiphorus' service in Ephesus; no clause states a promise or divine faithfulness, so the stamp does not belong here.
Clause 2Ti.1.11#cl0 lists 'preacher (herald), apostle, teacher' only; no prophet or prophetic office appears in this section.
No priestly terminology; the closest word, 'I serve' (2Ti.1.3#cl1), is service to God rendered by prayer, not cultic priesthood, and the stamp is cited to v.11 where no priest stands.

2Ti.1.10#cl1 speaks of Christ 'having abolished death' and cl2 of 'life and immortality' brought to light; these are the effects of Christ's victory, not an event of rising from the dead anywhere in the section.
The section speaks of grace given 'in Christ Jesus before time eternal' and of a holy calling, which carry covenant grace generally; no clause names a covenant, its making or its parties.
The only candidate clause, 2Ti.2.4#cl0, is about a soldier pleasing 'the one who enlisted him' (a commander, not a servant); there is no servant/master relation or servant role in this section.
2Ti.2.8 states Jesus is 'descended from David' (Davidic descent), which is not the same as an image of a new/second David; no clause presents Jesus as a new David figure.
The section's only kingship language is 'we will also reign with Him' (2Ti.2.12), which describes believers reigning, not a king figure or king role; Christ is named as Lord and Christ, not as king.
2Ti.2.9 presents Paul as the one suffering and chained, not Christ; nothing in the section portrays Christ as the suffering servant of Isaiah.
The section has no kingdom of God language; 'we will also reign with Him' (2Ti.2.12) is believers' co-reigning with Christ, not the kingdom itself.
Nothing in 2Ti.2.10 or elsewhere in the section speaks of new creation (no new creation, new heaven/earth, or renewal language); the verse speaks of obtaining salvation with eternal glory.

Hymenaeus and Philetus are condemned as men who have deviated from the truth and overturn the faith of some (2Ti.2.17#cl1, 2Ti.2.18#cl0, 2Ti.2.18#cl1), but no clause in this section casts them as shepherds who feed or lead a flock.

The cited verse (2 Tim 2:19) speaks of God's firm foundation, the seal, and turning away from iniquity (2Ti.2.19#cl0, 2Ti.2.19#cl4) — the opposite of a man of lawlessness; no clause in the section presents a lawless individual.

There is no word for covenant in this section; the seal and the Lord's knowledge of those who are His (2Ti.2.19#cl1, 2Ti.2.19#cl2) are the closest Old-Testament-flavoured covenant language, but nothing names a covenant, new or otherwise. Unsure whether the stamp is meant to belong here.
The only peace in the section is the object of pursuit in 2Ti.2.22#cl1 ("pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace"), not a covenant; no clause names a covenant of peace.
No clause in the section mentions any piece of armour, belt, shield, sword or helmet; it speaks of fleeing, pursuing and gentleness, not of arming for battle.
2 Tim 2:25 speaks of repentance and knowledge of the truth, not of healing; no clause in the section uses healing, sickness or cure language.
"Having been sanctified" (2Ti.2.21#cl2) means set apart, but the section never uses anointing language, oil, or pouring; sanctification here is a result of cleansing, not an anointing.
The vessels of 2Ti.2.20#cl0 and the vessel for honor of 2Ti.2.21#cl0 are household vessels from a great house, and the role named in the section is bond-servant (2Ti.2.24#cl1), never priest.
No clause in the section mentions a vine, vineyard, planting, pruning or any cultivation image.
There are no guests, visitors or table-fellowship in the section; the great house of 2Ti.2.20#cl0 is populated only by vessels.
No clause in the section addresses the nations or peoples as a collective actor; 2 Tim 2:26 speaks of the devil's snare and individual captives.

No clause in this section carries the watchman idea (a figure who warns of coming danger and is answerable for blood not warned). The role language present is 'bond-servant of the Lord' (2Ti.2.24#cl0) and 'workman' (2Ti.2.15#cl1); neither is a watchman, and 2Tim 2:24 says nothing about watching, warning or bloodguilt.

No clause presents anyone as a prophet or as speaking prophetic revelation. 2Ti.2.15#clcl2 ('accurately handling the word of truth') concerns handling the word rightly, not prophesying; the false teachers of 2Ti.2.18#cl1 assert that the resurrection has already occurred, which is false teaching rather than prophecy.

No clause in the section speaks of a king, kingship or rule. 'Master' in 2Ti.2.21#cl0 (Gk. despotēs) is a household master, and 2Ti.2.24#cl1 has 'bond-servant of the Lord' — neither is royal language.

No clause carries judging or a judge. The nearest thing is God's knowing those who are His (2Ti.2.19#cl2), which is knowledge, not judgment; 'discipline' in 2Ti.2.24#cl0/2Ti.2.25#cl0 is instructing opponents, not judging.
No clause names a son or uses sonship language. 2Tim 2:19 speaks of those 'being His' (2Ti.2.19#cl3) and of those 'naming the name of the Lord' (2Ti.2.19#cl5); neither says 'son'.

No clause names God as Father or uses father language. 2Tim 2:19 has 'the Lord' (2Ti.2.19#cl2, cl5) and 'God' appears elsewhere only as the one charged before (2Ti.2.14#cl0) and the one who gives repentance (2Ti.2.25#cl2); neither says father.
No clause carries firstborn status or language anywhere in the section.
No clause speaks of a stranger, sojourner, resident alien or outsider. The vessel imagery of 2Ti.2.20#cl0-2Ti.2.21#cl0 is household vessels, not sojourners.

No clause carries military or warrior imagery. 2Tim 2:22 ('Flee from youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace', 2Ti.2.22#cl0-cl1) is athletic/ethical pursuit language, not warfare; nothing in the section mentions weapons, soldiering or battle.

The section has verdict-like notes (the firm foundation with its seal, 'the Lord knows those who are His', vessels unto dishonor, ruin/subversion) but no clause states a judgment event, sentence or day of judgment, so no single clause carries the stamp.

Nothing in the section speaks of being in Christ or of union with him. 2Tim 2:21's vessel 'for honor' (2Ti.2.21#cl0) describes usefulness to the Master, and 2Tim 2:19's 'those who are His' (2Ti.2.19#cl3) is possession by the Lord, not the union-with-Christ idea.

No clause speaks of redemption, ransom, purchase or deliverance in Christ. 2Tim 2:19 has God's firm foundation and seal (2Ti.2.19#cl0-cl1) and 2Tim 2:26 escape from the devil's snare (2Ti.2.26#cl0), but escape from a snare is not stated as redemption, and Christ is not named as redeemer here.

The Holy Spirit is not named or referred to in any clause of the section. 'Pure heart' (2Ti.2.22#cl2) is a moral condition, not the Spirit, and God's granting of repentance (2Ti.2.25#cl2) does not mention the Spirit.

The idea is present in the section's drift — God's firm foundation stands and bears the seal 'The Lord knows those who are His' (2Tim 2:19) — but no particular clause states a promise or an act of divine faithfulness; the standing foundation and seal are the guarantees, and pinning them would be reading the stamp in rather than out.
No clause speaks of a kingdom, kingly rule or reign. The image is a 'large house' with vessels (2Ti.2.20#cl0) and a 'Master' (2Ti.2.21#cl0) — household imagery, not kingdom.
The section's men are described by vices (self-lovers, money-lovers, boastful, v.2) but nothing marks the single figure of lawlessness; 'oppose the truth' (v.8) is the only opposition language.
No ruler or reign appears; the vice list (v.4) describes private character, and the only named figures, Jannes and Jambres, are magicians opposing Moses.
No suffering, violence or persecution of the godly appears; the women are 'led astray by various passions' (v.6), and the opponents are the ones exposed (v.9).
'the last days' with 'terrible times' (v.1) is a general period of moral decline, not the day of the Lord's coming in judgment.
Same as the character-role stamp: the section names a class of men opposing the truth, not the man of lawlessness.
Paul's own conduct and teaching set before Timothy is the general drift, but no clause names testimony or testimony-bearing.
The section addresses 'you' and 'the man of God' rather than a people; no clause names the people of God as such.
In this section Paul is the persecuted one and Timothy the learner; Christ is named only as the one in whom one lives piously and believes (2Ti.3.12, 2Ti.3.15), never as the one who suffers.
The one thing the section calls trustworthy is what Timothy has learned and firmly believed (2Ti.3.14#cl1); it contains no promise and no statement of God's faithfulness.
The Lord's rescue (2Ti.3.11#cl2) is deliverance from persecutions, not mercy or restoration; the section has no restoration to a former state.
Evil men advance and deceive (2Ti.3.13#cl0) but no sentence of judgment is pronounced on them here.
The making complete and equipping of 2Ti.3.17#cl0-1 is fitness for every good work, with no language of new creation.
No clause in this section names a priest, priesthood or cultic mediation; the reading is at most the section's general atmosphere.
Nothing in this section speaks of renewal or new creation.
The section is a charge and a farewell; no clause speaks of mercy, forgiveness, or restoration.
The section speaks of Paul's defense before a court and of the message being proclaimed through him, but no clause names a sending or a sender; the idea is at best the section's general drift.

No clause in this section speaks of a king or of kingship; "the Lord" (2Ti.4.17#cl0, 2Ti.4.18#cl0/cl1/cl2) is addressed as Lord, deliverer and bringer-into-the-kingdom, but kingship is not predicated of him in any clause, and the kingdom named in 2Ti.4.18#cl2 is the heavenly kingdom, not a king.
The section names "His heavenly kingdom" (2Ti.4.18#cl2), which is a kingdom, not new heavens and a new earth; no clause speaks of the heavens and earth being made new.

The section has Paul's confidence that "the Lord will rescue me" and "will bring me safely into His heavenly kingdom" (2Ti.4.18#cl1, #cl2), which rests on the Lord's faithfulness, but no clause states a promise or an act of faithfulness as such; the stamp is the section's general drift rather than anything a clause says.

The proclamation named in 2Ti.4.17#cl2 is "the message" (to kerygma) that Paul proclaims, not a prophetic word or prophecy; the section never speaks of prophecy or of a prophet being fulfilled. [My general knowledge of Greek, not this section alone, tells me kerygma means proclamation; if that is wrong, the pin is wrong.]

The clause cited (2Ti.4.16#cl1: "all me deserted") and its neighbour (#cl0: "no one me has stood with") describe everyone abandoning Paul, and 2Ti.4.17#cl3 names "all the Gentiles" as those who hear. No clause names a people of God, Israel, the church or any collective belonging to God; "the Gentiles" hearing is the closest and it is not the same idea.

The section's deliverance language ("delivered out of the mouth of the lion", "will deliver me ... from every deed evil") and its "in His heavenly kingdom" are the general shape of redemption, but no clause names Christ in this section (the actor is "the Lord") and no clause speaks of being bought, ransomed or saved from sin.

No clause speaks of a new creation, new birth or the old passing away; "His heavenly kingdom" (2Ti.4.18#cl2) is entrance into a kingdom, and "every deed evil" (2Ti.4.18#cl1) is rescue from evil deeds, neither of which is new creation.
No clause speaks of testifying or bearing witness; 4:21 names people who send greetings, which is not witness.
Erastus and Trophimus are simply named as remaining or left behind; nothing in the clauses calls them servants or describes service.
Trophimus is left ailing; the clause states illness, not a healing.
No clause mentions opposition, arrest or suffering for the faith.
Trophimus is left sick and Erastus remains behind; the clauses report circumstance, not mercy or restoration.
No clause mentions Christ, his death, or redemption; 'The Lord' and 'Grace' do not by themselves state redemption.

Nothing in 2Tim 4:9-15 speaks of witnessing or testimony: Alexander is said to have opposed the message (2Ti.4.15#cl1) and harmed Paul (2Ti.4.14#cl0), the reverse of bearing witness; no clause describes anyone testifying.
The section names Luke, Mark, Timothy, Tychicus and others, the people around Paul, but no clause states the idea itself.
No clause speaks of a prophet, prophecy or a word from God; the only word mentioned is 'our message' (2Ti.4.15#cl1) - the gospel Paul preaches and Alexander opposes - not a prophetic utterance.
The section speaks of the elder's love, joy and the brothers' testimony; nothing in the text mentions mercy, forgiveness or restoration.
The truth language in 1:3 is about walking/witnessing in truth, not about a promise or covenant faithfulness; no clause states or implies a promise.
Christ is not named or implied in these four verses; walking in the truth is not stated as union with Christ.

Nothing in 3John 1:13-14 speaks of mercy or restoration; the section is about the writer's wish to write less, his hope to visit and speak face to face, and greetings. Neither forgiveness, reconciliation, nor restoration language appears in the Berean text or the clause glosses.

No clause in 3John 1:5-8 speaks of a servant or service role; 1:7 speaks of those who 'went out on behalf of the Name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles' and 1:8 of 'fellow workers', neither of which is a servant.
The section reports apostolic writing, counsel and testimony, not a prophetic word; no clause carries prophecy as such.

The clauses promise a baptism with the Holy Spirit "not after many these days" (Act.1.5#cl1), but no clause names the feast of Pentecost, the day of the Spirit's outpouring, or any event of that day: the reader cited Acts 1:5, which speaks of the promise, not of the feast. If the stamp means the eschatological event image indexed to Acts 2 rather than a named day in this section, I could not determine it from the text given.

The Gentiles' reception of the Spirit is the section's drift of God's favour reaching outsiders, but no clause in it carries the idea of mercy or restoration in words.

The vision, read in Acts, is about who belongs among God's people, but no clause in the section names a people or a community.

No clause mentions the Spirit; Act.10.11#cl1 is "heaven opening", not the Spirit descending.
The opening of heaven in Act.10.11 is not the temple or its presence; no clause mentions a temple, house of God or divine dwelling.
Peter is on a housetop, not in a sanctuary, and no clause mentions a priest, altar or service.
No clause contains covenant language (no covenant, treaty, oath or making of one).
No clause speaks of rule, king or kingdom; the vision is about clean and unclean foods.
Nothing in the clauses states a promise or its fulfilment.
No clause speaks of judgement; God's act is to cleanse (Act.10.15#cl2), not to condemn.
No clause describes a rescue or deliverance from anything.

Christ is nowhere mentioned in the section, and no clause speaks of being in him.
The animals of Act.10.12#cl0 are created kinds but no clause speaks of the image of God or of humans as such.
The section sets up the mission to the Gentiles, but no clause in it contains a commission or a blessing.

The section presupposes the believing community (church, disciples, brothers) throughout but no single clause states the theme itself.
The chapter speaks of the Lord, faith and salvation but never of a kingdom or reign; 'turned to the Lord' and 'hand of the Lord' are not kingdom language.
No clause in this section speaks of a promise, covenant or divine faithfulness; the famine is foretold and relief sent, which is not the same.

Acts 12:20 is Herod's angry dispute with Tyre and Sidon over food and the securing of Blastus's support; nothing here is done against the church or believers, which is what persecution names.

No prophecy or prophetic utterance occurs anywhere in Acts 12:5-19; the angel's commands (Act.12.7#cl5, Act.12.8) are instructions, not prophecy, and 12:11 is Peter's own realization.

The word/idea of the kingdom does not appear; the only reign in view is Herod's (Act.12.19#cl0), which is the stamp "king", not kingdom.
The movement is prison-to-freedom, but no exile or exaltation is in view: Peter is not exalted or restored to honour in the section, he leaves for another place (Act.12.17#cl6).
No death or life comes from a death in this section; Peter is delivered from the threat of death, not brought through it to life.
No clause in this section states a blessing; the section's drift is commissioning for mission, not blessing, so no clause in particular carries the stamp.
Acts 13:38-39 speaks of forgiveness of sins and justification through Jesus; no covenant, new or otherwise, is named or described in the section.
Acts 13:17 says 'with an uplifted arm He led them out of that land' — the exodus from Egypt; it is not a crossing of the sea, and no sea is mentioned in the section.
No priest, priesthood, or priestly act appears in the section; Acts 13:15 refers to the reading from the Law and the Prophets and to synagogue leaders, not priests.

The rejected-stone/cornerstone image is absent here; the rulers' failure (Act.13.27#cl2, #cl5) is stated without any building or stone metaphor.

Acts 13:11 is the opposite of a healing: Paul pronounces blindness on Elymas and it falls on him; no one is healed in this section.

Nothing in Acts 13:4-12 shows mercy or restoration: the judgment on Elymas is temporary only in extent ('for a time'), and the one who receives grace, the proconsul, is said to believe, not to be restored.

No clause in the section describes a servant who suffers for others, or quotes Isaiah's servant; 13:50 reports persecution of Paul and Barnabas as an event, not a servant's vicarious suffering.

The section reports rejection and opposition on both sides, not the fulfilment of a promise; 13:47 quotes a command, and 13:48 says 'appointed', not promised. No clause in the section states a sending (Paul and Barnabas are already at work in Iconium in 14:1); the 'fled to ... Lystra and Derbe and to the surrounding region' of 14:6 is movement away from persecution, not a commissioning or sending.
The section speaks of persecution of the missionaries (14:5), but no clause speaks of the Suffering Servant: no servant of the LORD, no bearing of sin or vicarious suffering is referred to here.
The cited 14:3 has grace affirmed and signs granted (mercy in a broad sense), but no clause speaks of restoration or of being restored; the stamp as worded is not carried by this section.
The gospel is preached (14:7) and 'the message of His grace' is named (14:3), but no clause says anything of redemption, ransom, cross or Christ's work of redemption.
The hardships here are the missionaries' own ("us", Act.14.22#cl3/cl4); no clause speaks of a servant who suffers for others, and the suffering-servant idea (Isaiah 53) is nowhere in this section.
No clause in this section mentions the Spirit; the Spirit is not named in Acts 14:21-28, and the reader's cited verse (14:27) speaks of God and faith, not the Spirit.
Acts 14:20 reports only that Paul left for Derbe with Barnabas; no clause says anyone was sent, commissioned or dispatched.
Acts 14:15 has Paul and Barnabas preaching the gospel, not delivering a prophetic oracle; no clause says a prophet or the Spirit speaks (contrast Acts 14:14) beyond the speech act itself.
The idolatry here is at the city gates of Lystra, not in the temple or a holy place; no clause has anything set in a sanctuary.
The crippled man is healed but overcomes no opponent; Acts 14:19 has the crowd and the Jews prevailing against Paul, the reverse.
The section records dispute and debate, not persecution; no clause speaks of hostility, violence, or suffering inflicted on anyone.
The only reference is 'the custom of Moses'; no clause speaks of a covenant, its making, or its terms.
The section only debates being saved by circumcision; no clause names Christ or his redemptive work.
Clause Act.15.4#cl2/cl3 says 'all that God had done', not the Spirit; the Spirit is not mentioned in this section.

The section's drift is encouragement and strengthening (Act.15.31, Act.15.32, Act.15.35), which a reader may read as restoration, but no clause says mercy, forgiveness or being restored.

The Holy Spirit is not named or implied in any clause of Acts 15:30-35 here; the only candidate (Act.15.32#cl0/cl1, prophets exhorting) rests on inference from Acts 15:28, which is outside this section.

No opposition, hostility or suffering appears anywhere in this section; the sharp disagreement is between Paul and Barnabas, not persecution. The stamp's cited verse (15:39) contains only their parting.

The Jerusalem council's deliberation is Acts 15:1-35, not this section; here there is no council, no gathered discernment, only a personal dispute and departure. Closest candidates (15:38 thought fit, 15:39 disagreement) are one man's judgment and a quarrel, not conciliar discernment.
Nothing in these verses presents a servant who suffers; Mark's withdrawal in 15:38 is his desertion, not suffering, and the suffering-servant theme belongs to Christ, nowhere in view here.

No clause in this section states a promise or divine faithfulness; Act.16.4 reports deliberated decrees being delivered, which is not the same as God's promise kept. If the stamp is meant as the section's general drift (growth of the churches), no particular clause carries it.

Nothing in these clauses speaks of mercy or restoration: the section reports a journey, a circumcision, delivery of decrees and church growth. Church growth (Act.16.5) is increase, not restoration of the broken.

The section's conversion does presuppose the Spirit's work, but no clause names the Spirit: the actor in Act.16.14#cl3 is 'the Lord', and baptism in Act.16.15#cl0-#cl1 involves only water and the household. No clause in particular speaks to this stamp.

Christian conversion is the section's general drift, but no clause states redemption, purchase, ransom or being 'in Christ': the closest are 'the Lord opened her heart' (Act.16.14#cl3) and 'faithful to the Lord' (Act.16.15#cl5), neither of which says redemption or names Christ. The conflict here is a mob attack, arrest and beating (16:22), i.e. persecution, not warfare/battle imagery; no clause in the section speaks of battle.

Paul and Silas are beaten and imprisoned (16:22-23), but the section nowhere presents them as the Servant who suffers for others (no servant/Servant-of-God language or allusion); the stamp as used of this section is not supported by any clause.
The servants of the Most High God (16:17) are God's people, but no clause states a people-of-God idea in particular.
No clause speaks of sin, exile or death; 16:23 is an imprisonment (thrown into prison, guarded securely), not exile or death.

Nothing in the section states the arrest, beating or imprisonment as an event; the only clauses of v25 present are prayer and praise, and the prisoners' listening (Act.16.28#cl3 'we are all here') shows no hostility, so no clause here carries persecution.

Paul's protest in 16:37 is about his legal rights as a Roman citizen, not testimony to the gospel; the section only reports the message about release being relayed, with no clause in which anyone bears witness to what God has done.

Nothing here is judged by God or by a court: the magistrates' alarm (cl1-cl3) is fear of the law, not a verdict, and no clause pronounces or executes a judgment. The closest clauses at best presuppose the illegal beating of v.37.

No clause in this section speaks of anyone being sent: Paul and Silas arrive and are dragged before officials, but nothing in the text is a sending.
The section has the Christ suffering and rising and being proclaimed, but no clause speaks of redemption, ransoming or being bought back.
The city officials hear the crowd and collect bond, but no clause in this section speaks of judgment, condemnation or a verdict on anyone.
Death appears only as the dead from whom the Christ rose (Act.17.3#cl3), which is not sin, exile or death as the section's subject; no clause speaks of sin or exile at all.

The discussion at the Areopagus concerns a 'new teaching', 'strange notions' and knowing what they mean; the kingdom is never mentioned in the section.

Paul's reasoned proclamation in the synagogue and marketplace and his hearing at the Areopagus are the setting in which the message is offered, but no clause speaks of mercy or restoration.
Acts 17:31 speaks of judgment and resurrection, not of a covenant; no covenant-making language occurs anywhere in the section.
The section mentions an altar TO AN UNKNOWN GOD as an object Paul found while surveying Athenian worship; there is no holy place defiled by an idol.

The section records arrivals (Silas and Timothy coming down from Macedonia, Paul coming to Corinth) but no clause speaks of anyone being sent; mission sending is the section's general drift, not something a clause says.
The speaker in the vision is the Lord, not a prophet: Act.18.9#cl0 ("the Lord spoke to Paul in a vision"). No clause names or describes a prophet.

Not wrong as a category, but no clause in this section carries it: Paul's service is described as testifying, teaching and working a trade (Act.18.5#cl2, Act.18.11#cl1, Act.18.3#cl2), none of which uses a servant image. I am unsure the stamp belongs here at all.

"Do not be afraid" (Act.18.9#cl1) and the promise of safety (Act.18.10#cl1, cl2) are encouragement and protection, not mercy or restoration in the text's sense; no clause speaks of mercy or restoration. I am unsure which clauses could carry it, or whether it belongs here.

No clause in this section carries the idea of a prophet or prophesying. Acts 18:25 speaks of Apollos' fervour in spirit and his accurate teaching about Jesus; the only candidate word is 'spirit', which is presence/sphere, not the prophetic gift. Apollos 'powerfully refuted the Jews in public debate' (Acts 18:28) and was opposed in argument, but the section records no persecution of anyone; nothing in the cited verse or elsewhere here speaks of harm suffered for faith.

The word is not used in the section, so this cannot be judged on its merits; taking it in its plain sense there is no council meeting, deliberation or corporate decision. Nothing in the section states a promise or God's faithfulness to it; 'those who by grace had believed' (Acts 18:27#cl7) and 'Jesus is the Christ' (Acts 18:28#cl2) touch the theme only as the section's general drift, with no clause asserting it.
Act.18.27#cl7 ('those who by grace had believed') and cl5 ('helped greatly') touch grace and help, but no clause states mercy or restoration; the theme is only the section's general drift.
The section's drift is the incorporation of the twelve Ephesian disciples into the church, but no clause says it; cl4 only calls them 'certain disciples'.

Baptism 'into the name of the Lord Jesus' is naming and identification, not the section's redemption idea; no clause speaks of being redeemed, ransomed or saved (contrast the repentance/faith clauses in v.4).
The prophesying in v.6 is an act of Spirit-inspired speech by the twelve, not a prophetic word (Scripture/utterance from God) as such; no clause presents a prophetic message.
Nothing in the section speaks of mercy or restoration; v.4's call to believe in Jesus is repentance and faith, not a stated act of mercy or restoration.
No covenant is mentioned or implied in these clauses; 'in the name of the Lord Jesus' is not a covenant formula here.

The section ends with the crowd dismissed and no harm recorded (he dismissed the assembly, 19:41, now Act.19.40#cl5) and Paul's companions unharmed; no clause states any act of mercy or restoration.
The section speaks of 'the word of the Lord' being heard, but no clause here presents a prophet or prophecy.
The 'spirits' of Acts 19:12 are evil spirits that depart; nothing in this section speaks of the Holy Spirit.
Nothing in this section speaks of mercy or restoration; the gathering of nations is stated as fact and no clause rests on mercy or restoring.

Not spoken of here. Nothing in this section speaks of a covenant, new or old; Act.2.39#cl0-cl1 speak of 'the promise' to hearers and their children, which the text does not call a covenant, and no clause uses covenant language.

No clause here speaks of redemption, ransom or purchase; the forgiveness clause (Act.2.38#cl2) names forgiveness 'in the name of Jesus Christ' but not redemption, so the stamp's specific idea is not carried by any clause in this section.

No clause here speaks of the kingdom, a king, or reign. Act.2.47#cl2's 'the Lord added to their number daily those who were being saved' is about salvation and growth of the community, not the kingdom, and 'Lord' there is the risen Jesus acting, not a kingdom reign described in the text.
No clause names Paul or anyone as servant, or describes service; only a general characterisation of Paul's ministry roles, so it attaches to the section as a whole rather than to any clause.
Nothing in the section speaks of mercy or restoration; encouragement (Act.20.1#cl3, Act.20.2#cl2) is the nearest idea and no clause carries mercy or restoration itself.

Nothing in the section speaks of redemption, the cross, or Christ's saving work; Acts 20:6 (the cited verse) is only a travel note about the Feast of Unleavened Bread and sailing from Philippi.

Acts 20:13 narrator/travel detail only (ship, Assos, Paul going on foot); the word 'pilgrim' appears nowhere in the Berean text. 'Pilgrim' is a role for the section's travellers as a whole, not carried by any clause here.
Acts 20:14 is pure itinerary (Assos, Mitylene); no clause in it names or characterises the travellers as pilgrims.
Acts 20:15 is pure itinerary (Chios, Samos, Miletus); no clause in it names or characterises the travellers as pilgrims.

No clause in Acts 20:13-16 contains a prophetic utterance, citation or fulfilment; the reader cited Acts 20:16, whose clauses concern sailing past Ephesus and Paul's haste to reach Jerusalem for Pentecost.
No clause speaks of priesthood or priestly service; the church is said to be purchased with His own blood, and the overseers' task is shepherding, not priestly mediation.
Paul testify to you this day is a solemn witness, not an oath or vow; no clause contains swearing, an oath formula, or a self-curse.
The cited verse records kneeling and praying, not a shared meal or the breaking of bread; no clause mentions bread.
The section's general drift is about the word of His grace, the purchased church, and an inheritance among the sanctified, but no clause names a covenant.

Acts 20:28 speaks of the whole church/flock purchased with blood; no clause in this section marks out a remnant (no 'the rest', no part-of-Israel subset). The Berean text has only 'the whole flock' and 'the church of God'.
No bridal image anywhere in the section: the church is called 'the church of God' which He 'purchased with His own blood' (20:28); no bride/bridegroom language, no wedding image.
Same as bride: Acts 20:28 has no bridegroom language, only God purchasing the church with His own blood.
No firstborn language or idea in the section; Acts 20:28 speaks of purchased blood and shepherding, not a firstborn.
Acts 20:28 has the Holy Spirit 'has made you overseers' and God's own blood, but no anointing language or act anywhere in the section.

No covenant-cutting rite (sacrifice, blood of a covenant, divided animals) in the section. 20:28's 'blood' is the blood of God's own Son in purchase, not the cutting of a covenant between parties.
No meal in the section at all; the prayer in 20:36 is not a table scene and nothing is eaten.

No clause in this section names, mentions or alludes to the Spirit; the reader's citation of Acts 20:10 rests on "the life of him in him is", which is Paul's word about the young man's life, not the Holy Spirit.
Eutychus's death is reversed, not the means of life: no clause says the death produced anything, only that he was picked up dead and taken home alive.
Nothing in these clauses speaks of union with Christ; Paul's embracing the young man (Act.20.10#cl0/cl3) is a physical act, and no clause expresses a believer's union with Christ.
No clause here reports testimony, proclamation or bearing witness; Acts 21:4 has the disciples 'telling Paul not to go up to Jerusalem', which is a warning, not witness to Christ or to events.

No meal, loaf or table fellowship is mentioned; the believing community appears only in prayer and farewell.
No washing or baptism is mentioned in the section; verse 5's 'knelt down on the beach to pray' is prayer, not baptism.
No oath, vow or swearing is in the section; there is a prayer and a farewell, not a vow.
Verse 5 contains only prayer and an escort out of the city; nothing there is testimony or proclamation.
No priest appears in this section. The men in the temple are Paul and four vow-takers, not priests; the sacrifice is brought by them, not offered by a priest named in the text.
The section mentions only a rumor about Paul's teaching and the threat of a crowd hearing he has come (Act.21.22#cl1); no persecution, arrest, or violence is narrated or predicted.

No clause contains prophecy, scripture or a prophet speaking; Act.21.28#cl0 is a crowd's accusation ('This is the man who... teaching'), not prophetic speech, and the Agabus prophecy lies in Acts 21:10-11, outside this section.

Nothing in Acts 21:37-40 or its clauses speaks of a prophet or prophecy: Paul claims only to be a Jew from Tarsus, a citizen (Act.21.39#cl0-cl2).

Paul is being taken into the barracks under arrest, but no clause carries the servant-of-God or vicarious-suffering idea of Isaiah; the section gives the arrest only as narrative setting (Act.21.37#cl1-cl2).

The Spirit is nowhere named in the section; the trance at the temple (Act.22.17#cl3) and the voice from heaven are not called the Spirit here

Paul's speech in this section is defensive ('Is it lawful...?'), not testimony about Christ/God; no clause here carries the witness idea, so it is only the section's general drift or, more strictly, absent.

Acts 23:34 has Felix the governor (hegemon), not a king; no clause of this section names or describes a king.

Acts 23:33 has the horsemen delivering the letter and presenting Paul, not the fulfilment of a promise; no clause of this section speaks of a promise or of faithfulness to one.

The section contains no echo of the servant of Isaiah and no statement of innocent suffering borne for others: Paul does not speak here; the only clauses about him are accusations (Act.24.5#cl0, Act.24.6#cl0, Act.24.6#cl2). Acts 24:21 mentions only the resurrection of the dead as the point of the trial; no clause in this section speaks of Christ, his death, or redemption. The stamp is not present here.
Acts 24:20 has Paul ask his accusers to name any crime found in him before the Sanhedrin; there is no reference to the Servant, his suffering, or vicarious suffering in this section.
Paul is confined but the section shows no servant who suffers; he is guarded, unharmed, allowed ease and friends' ministry, and hopes raised of a bribe. No clause speaks of suffering.

The section's drift is delay and the passing of two years with Paul still held; but no clause states a divine promise or its faithfulness. 'Two years having been completed' only measures the delay. Marked general; the clause is given as the closest, not a claim that the stamp is stated there.
Deliberation exists (chief priests and leaders, Festus's reply and proposal), but cl4/5 are Festus's unilateral answer and venue choice, not a council's discernment; the stamp fits only the drift.
Nothing restores or shows mercy; cl4 is Festus declining a request, and no release or healing appears. Only the general drift of an unsettled case fits.

No oath, vow, or swearing formula appears anywhere in these clauses (nothing corresponding to an oath in the Berean text of 25:10-12). The appeal 'To Caesar I appeal' is a legal appeal (provocatio), not an oath.

Nothing in these clauses is a prophetic utterance or a divine word; the speech is Paul's legal defense and the appeal to Caesar, and Festus's administrative reply. A prophecy that Paul must go to Rome does exist in the book (Acts 23:11), but not in these clauses.
No clause speaks of God's people as such; the Jews appear only as accusers (25:15)
Nothing in the section is a prophetic utterance or fulfilment of prophecy
No Servant-of-YHWH language; Paul is a defendant, not the Servant figure, and the stamp is not in view
No clause names a promise or God's faithfulness; the section is narrative of Festus' handling
No clause in this section mentions Christ, his blood, purchase, or release from sin; the only 'send' is Festus sending Paul to the Emperor (Act.25.25#cl4). Wrong for this section.
26:6 speaks of the promise made to 'our fathers' generally, with no mention of David or of anything distinctly Davidic; the stamp is not supported by this section.

The section never calls anyone 'son' (not even 'Son of God'); 'Jesus of Nazareth', 'the Christ' and 'Lord' are used, so the stamp is not carried by any clause here.
No firstborn language or imagery occurs; 26:23 says 'the first to rise from the dead', which is protos ek nekron, not 'firstborn'.
Nothing in this section mentions washing, water, immersion or baptism; 26:20 is repentance and turning to God, not baptism.
Moses is mentioned only as a prophet whose predictions are being fulfilled (26:22); there is no giving of the law and no Sinai scene here.
Acts 26:7 speaks of the twelve tribes' hope of the promise (resurrection/fulfillment), not of an exile event; no clause here describes deportation or life in exile.
No clause speaks of a return from exile; 26:7's 'earnestly serve God day and night' refers to ongoing hope, not restoration from exile.
Acts 26:20 calls Gentiles to 'repent and turn to God', but no clause names idols or idol-worship.
Acts 26:20 has 'repent and turn to God', not the sending away of a scapegoat; no clause carries the ritual at all.
Acts 26:23 has 'the Christ would suffer' but no clause names a sacrifice or the offering of a victim.

Acts 26:23 has 'the Christ would suffer' and rise, but no clause enthrones or crowns him.
No clause mentions armor, weapons of the Spirit, or standing armed; 26:16's 'stand on your feet' is literal.
Acts 26:20's 'performing deeds worthy of their repentance' is a call to repentance, not fruit of the Spirit.
Acts 26:16 promises appearing and witness, but no gift of the Spirit is named.
Acts 26:16 speaks of Christ appearing and commissioning; the Holy Spirit is nowhere named in these clauses.

The only charge here is Festus's 'You are insane, Paul!' (Act.26.24#cl2) and the false accusation is not persecution; Paul's chains are mentioned as a present fact ('except for these chains', Act.26.29#cl2) but no clause of this section narrates anyone persecuting him.
No clause here says anyone serves or is a servant; Paul asks that his hearers 'become what I am' (Act.26.29#cl2) but no servant language appears.
No oath, vow or swearing occurs in the section; 'I wish to God' (Act.26.29#cl1) is a wish, not an oath, and Caesar is named only as the court of appeal (Act.26.32#cl3).

No clause in Acts 27:1-12 speaks of a shipwreck: the voyage is still under way and the only forward-looking words are Paul's warning of "disaster and great loss" (Act.27.10#cl2/cl3), which is not a shipwreck stated as happening (no wreck, no loss of the ship as an event); the section ends with the decision to sail on from Fair Havens (Act.27.12#cl1).

Acts 27:1 has Paul as a prisoner being handed over (Act.27.1#cl0, "Paul and some other prisoners were handed over to a centurion"), which is custody/transport, not persecution as an event spoken of in this section; no clause states hostility, opposition for faith, or violence against believers.

The section's general drift is travel through foreign ports under Roman custody, but no clause in particular carries the idea of being a stranger or sojourner; Act.27.1#cl0 (Paul and other prisoners handed over to a centurion named Julius of the cohort of Augustus) and Act.27.2#cl4 ("Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, was with us") are the nearest clauses, but they state custody and origin, not sojourning, so I leave the list empty.

No clause calls Paul a prophet or presents him as speaking a word from the LORD; Act.27.9#cl3 / Act.27.10#cl1-2 give his own judgment ("I can see/understand that"), and the centurion rejects it (Act.27.11#cl0), which is forecast, not a prophetic role stated in this section.

Paul's speech (Act.27.9#cl3, Act.27.10#cl1-2) is introduced as his own advice/insight ("I can see that our voyage will be filled with disaster"), and the centurion rejects it (Act.27.11#cl0); no clause marks it as a word from God or a prophecy, and the coming true of a prediction is not stated in this section (the section ends at the decision to sail).

The only suffering words refer to the ship's cargo and the lives of all on board (Act.27.10#cl2-3, "great loss, not only to ship and cargo, but to our own lives as well"), not to a servant of the LORD bearing suffering for others; no clause here echoes the servant figure.

No clause narrates a rescue or being handed over out of danger; Act.27.3#cl1 ("Julius treated Paul with consideration, allowing him to visit his friends and receive their care") is a concession, not a deliverance, and the section contains no escape or salvation event.

The section names no people of God as a body; the only possible point is Paul's visit to "his friends" (Act.27.3#cl3-4), which is unspecified and not the people of God as such. I judge this not carried by any clause rather than wrong: the reader's citation (Acts 27:3) shows the company around Paul, but the clause does not itself say who they are. Empty list.

Nothing in the section mentions a promise of God or its fulfilment; Act.27.1#cl0 is a transfer of prisoners to a centurion and the rest is voyage narrative (winds, ports, decisions), so the stamp is not present here.

Act.27.10#cl2-3 speaks of coming "disaster and great loss... to ship and cargo... and to our own lives" — a forecast of damage, not divine judgment on anyone; no clause pronounces or depicts judgment.

Act.27.1#cl0 shows Paul being handed over as a prisoner to a centurion named Julius of the cohort of Augustus — the humiliation/ custody side only; no clause in the section shows a reversal or exaltation, so the pattern is not complete here.
Act.27.3#cl1-2 (Julius's considerate treatment of Paul) is only the favourable half; no clause shows prior humiliation or Paul being vindicated, so the reversal is not spoken of in this section.
No clause reports anyone, Gentile or otherwise, coming to faith; Julius's consideration (Act.27.3#cl1) and the crew's decisions (Act.27.11#cl0, Act.27.12#cl1) are kindness and seamanship, not belief.
No clause of this section speaks of fighting, weapons or soldiery; the storm-struggle is seamanship, not warfare.
Paul says 'I believe God', which is trust, not an oath; no oath, swearing or self-imprecation appears in this section.

Acts 27:21 says only that the men had gone a long time without food; the Greek (cl0, 'Much time without food there being') reports the fact as a circumstance, not a deliberate religious fast, and no clause describes fasting as an act.
The section's deprivation and hopelessness are at sea in a storm (cl0, cl2), with no desert, no wandering and no Israel-in-the-wilderness language; the stamp is not carried by any clause.
A violent wind (14#cl0) is weather, not combat: no opponents, no fighting, no weapons in any clause.
Struggle with wind and sea is not battle imagery; the clauses describe a ship overpowered by weather (15#cl0-cl2), not armed conflict.
Throwing cargo and tackle overboard (18#cl1; 19#cl0) is a storm emergency, not battle.
The storm's battering (20#cl1) and lost hope (20#cl2) are peril at sea, not battle; 'batter' is weather, not combat.
Standing before Caesar (24#cl2) is a trial appearance, not a triumphal procession, and the granting of lives (24#cl4) is a rescue, not a victory parade; no clause depicts a procession.
The preservation promised in 24#cl4 is rescue from drowning, not healing of sickness; no clause speaks of disease or cure.
Promised survival (22#cl2; 24#cl4) is escape from death at sea, not a resurrection of the dead; no clause mentions rising.

Paul appears as the one whose ignored advice is vindicated and who is beaten by the storm with the rest, but no clause in this section carries the Servant's vicarious suffering; the sense is the section's drift rather than any clause.
The loss of hope and threat of death at sea (20#cl2) is not presented as sin, exile or the death that follows sin; no clause names sin or exile.
No combat: the soldiers' plan to kill the prisoners (27:42) is an execution to prevent escape, not a battle; nothing in the section describes fighting.
Paul speaks as an authoritative adviser to centurion and soldiers (27:31, 27:33-34) and the centurion acts to spare him (27:43); no clause presents anyone as a servant or in service to another.
Paul is a prisoner in danger (27:42-43), but no clause describes him as a servant or as suffering on others' behalf; the cited verse 27:34 is his exhortation to eat for their preservation.

No clause here speaks of God's reign or kingdom; the healings of Act.28.9 are not described in kingdom terms by anything in this section.
The islanders' changed verdict (Act.28.6#cl7-#cl9) is their own inference from Paul surviving, not a clause about God's promise or faithfulness.
This section has no death, and no life coming out of one: Paul does not die but suffers no ill effects (Act.28.5#cl0). This is deliverance from expected death, not death producing life.
No clause names or describes the Spirit; the healing is attributed to Paul's praying and laying on of hands (Act.28.8#cl4, #cl5). If the stamp means the Spirit's action, it is not stated here.

Nothing in these clauses states or restates a promise of God or an act of divine faithfulness; the arrival at Rome is fulfilment of Acts 23:11 etc., but that is not said in this section, so no clause in particular speaks to the stamp.

Paul's service is the drift of the whole section (preaching, teaching, receiving all who came) but no clause names a servant or servanthood; the nearest wording, 'Paul stayed there two full years ... welcoming all who came to visit him' (Act.28.30#cl0/#cl1), is hospitality, not servant language.
No clause in Acts 3:1-10 names the Spirit, the Spirit's filling, or any Spirit-work; the healing is credited to the name of Jesus (Act.3.6#cl4), not the Spirit.
The reversal stamp 'weak defeats strong' does not fit: no contest or adversary appears; a man lame from birth (Act.3.2#cl2) is simply healed and no strong party is defeated.

No death and no raising from the dead occurs in this section: the man is lame from birth (Act.3.2#cl2) and is healed, so 'death produces life' is not spoken of here.
No clause in Acts 3:1-10 speaks of the kingdom, a king, or rule; the only name invoked is Jesus Christ of Nazareth (Act.3.6#cl4), which names the person, not the kingdom.
No clause in this section calls Peter (or anyone) a prophet or describes prophetic speech; Peter's speech is framed as testimony (witness) and Spirit-filling, not prophecy.
No clause here presents Jesus (or Peter) as servant; the words used are name, Jesus Christ of Nazareth, crucified, raised, stone, cornerstone, salvation.
The section speaks of "the people" as Peter's audience, of "the people of Israel," and of "men" to be saved; it nowhere presents them as God's people/covenant community.
No clause pronounces or describes judgment; the hostile action is limited to seizure, custody and questioning (persecution, council_discernment).

No clause gives mercy or restoration as an act or attitude; the healing is cited as an accomplished fact in the speech (Act.4.9#cl1, Act.4.10#cl0) rather than described as an act of mercy or restoration.

Nothing in this section is a prophetic utterance, scripture citation or fulfilment; the only speech is the Sanhedrin's deliberation and Peter and John's reply, and no word here is presented as prophecy.
The persecuted ones here are Peter and John, the apostles, not the Servant; and there is no quotation or allusion to Isaiah's Servant in these clauses.
No clause speaks of God's rule or kingdom; the dispute is only about the name of Jesus and the healed man.
The Spirit is nowhere mentioned in Acts 4:13-22; the boldness of Peter and John (4:13) is stated without reference to the Spirit in this section.
No promise, oath or covenant is cited or alluded to in these clauses; obedience to God in 4:19-20 rests on what they had seen and heard, not on a promise.
The name of Jesus is invoked in 4:17-18, but nothing in the section speaks of redemption, atonement or salvation through him.

The section is about bold speech of the word and the apostolic report, but no clause is a witness/testimony event; 'reported how much to them the chief priests and the elders had said' (Act.4.23#cl2) is a report of events to the community, not a witness stamp. The stamp belongs to the section's drift rather than a clause.

Pentecost is the event of Acts 2 (the day of the Spirit's outpouring); here the meeting place is shaken and they are filled with the Spirit again (Act.4.31#cl2, cl4), which is a distinct filling, not Pentecost. The section does not speak of Pentecost.

The section opens with the apostles' release ('Having been let go', Act.4.23#cl1) and asks for boldness under threat, but no clause states a rescue/deliverance event; the stamp is the section's drift, not a clause's content.

Act.4.28 says the conspirators 'carried out what Your hand and will had decided beforehand would happen' — God's predetermined plan, not a judgment/sentence on anyone. No clause in the section pronounces or depicts judgment.
No clause in the section says mercy or restoration; the nearest material is the practical relief of the needy, which is benevolence rather than the mercy-restoration theme itself.
The Spirit is not named or alluded to in this section: 4:33 speaks of great power and abundant grace, not the Spirit. Nothing in these clauses carries the stamp.
The section mentions the resurrection of the Lord Jesus but no redemption, cross, blood or saving work; the stamp is not present in these clauses.
No kingdom, reign or king language occurs in the section; the cited verse 4:34 is about property and need, not the kingdom.

Nothing in the section describes hostility against the church from outside: the deaths come from God through Peter's word, and the fear falls on the church itself (Acts 5:11). The church is not being persecuted here.

Nothing in 5:12-16 describes opposition, arrest or hostility: 5:13 says the people regarded them highly and no one dared join them, and 5:14-16 report growth, healings and crowds from the towns. The reader cited 5:13, which is about awe/reputation, not persecution.

The section nowhere speaks of the kingdom, reign or rule of God; the cited verse 5:12 has no kingdom language. If any clause were stretched to it, it would be the healing/believing growth, but that is the church's growth, not a kingdom statement.

The section has no servant, no vicarious suffering, no quotation of Isaiah's servant. Read cited 5:15, which is about Peter's shadow healing the sick; the 'sick/afflicted' are those healed, not a suffering servant.

The growth of believers is the fulfilment of the promised increase, but no clause states a promise or God's faithfulness; the stamp is only the section's drift, so the list is a single clause at low confidence.
The angel's command in v.20 is a commission to speak a message, not a prophet's oracle from God; no clause has prophetic speech.
Nothing in the section speaks of God's reign or kingdom; v.20 says 'this new life', not kingdom.
Acts 5:17 reports the high priest's jealousy and arrest; no clause states a judgment, verdict or condemnation.

No clause in Acts 6:1-7 speaks of witness, testimony or bearing witness. No ruler or beast-like figure appears; the Sanhedrin is a council and no one is described as ruling.
No king in the section; the only ruler-like words are 'Sanhedrin' and 'the people, elders, and scribes'.
Duplicate stamp. No priest appears in the section, and the custom-Moses accusation in Act.6.13#cl3/Act.6.14#cl4 does not mention one.
Nothing in the section speaks of a Davidic king, throne, or covenant; the cited verse is about the temple and the customs of Moses.

No 'son' language: no father-son relation, no 'Son of God' or 'Son of Man' title anywhere in the section.
No service or servant wording; Acts 6:15 speaks of Stephen's face like an angel's, which is about vindication, not service.

No royal vocabulary, throne or reign in the section.

Same as the Acts 6:14 pin: nothing Davidic in the section, and Acts 6:15 (Stephen before the Council) has no royal content.
The cited verse only has the high priest's question about charges; no clause in this section states a hostile act against anyone.
