Egypt and the Egyptians appear (Act.7.21#cl1 'Pharaoh's daughter', Act.7.22#cl0 'the wisdom of the Egyptians') but only as a setting and a source of instruction, and the woman acts as an individual. No clause personifies Egypt/the nations as an acting character in the sense the stamp names; what the stamp names is the drift of the passage's setting, not a claim of any one clause.

No clause in 7.20-22 reports a rescue: Moses is born, nursed (cl2), exposed (Act.7.21#cl0), taken and raised (cl1-cl2), and educated (Act.7.22#cl0). The taking up of the child is an adoption, not a deliverance of Israel, and the exodus deliverance is not narrated here. The stamp does not fit this section's clauses.

The section contains no statement of belief, faith or conversion, and the people in it - Moses, his parents, Pharaoh's daughter - are not presented as outsiders coming to faith. Pharaoh's daughter acts within her own house; nothing in Act.7.20-22 speaks of an outsider believing.
Nothing in this section presents Moses as a new Moses or a second deliverer figure; the parallel belongs to the book's wider argument, not to a clause here.
The section narrates Moses' deed and rejection but contains no prophetic utterance or word of God; this belongs to Stephen's speech as a whole, not to a clause here.
Within this section Moses moves from presumed leadership to flight and rejection; the vindication is later (Exodus, and Moses' return) and is not stated in these clauses.
The section ends in exile ('I will send you into exile beyond Babylon', Act.7.43#cl3); no clause here speaks of return or exaltation, so the reversal is not present in these verses.
No clause describes the temple being destroyed; Acts 7:47 mentions only that Solomon built the house.
Acts 7:58 is a stoning by a mob; the clauses speak of stones (Act.7.58#cl0 'began to stone him') and of garments laid down (Act.7.58#cl2), not of crucifixion, which the section never mentions.

Acts 7:59 speaks while Stephen is being stoned, of his spirit being received by Jesus (Act.7.59#cl3 'Lord Jesus receive the spirit of me') — Stephen's death, not a resurrection; no clause of the section states a resurrection.

The section narrates Stephen's death (Act.7.58#cl0, Act.7.59#cl0, Act.7.60#cl3 'he fell asleep') but no clause speaks of life coming from that death; the idea is the section's general drift, not carried by any particular clause.

The cited verse 7:13 speaks of Joseph, his brothers, his family and Pharaoh; Egypt appears earlier only as a place ('in Egypt'), never as an acting character here, and no nation is given agency in this section.

Nothing in these clauses states a promise made or kept; the section narrates events (sale, rescue, famine, sending for Jacob). Closest is 'God was with him' (7:9#cl2), which is divine presence, not a promise-fulfilment statement. If the reader means God's ongoing care of the patriarchs generally, that is a reading of the section as a whole rather than something a clause says.
Nothing in these clauses speaks of sin, exile or death as such; Stephen's killing is referred to only as Saul's consent (Act.8.1#cl0) and the scattering is of the church, not an exile for sin.

The suffering servant idea belongs to Stephen's speech and death (Acts 7); in these verses the only clauses about Stephen are his burial and lamentation (Act.8.2#cl0, Act.8.2#cl1), which do not carry the servant theme.
No persecution is narrated or quoted here: the deprivation of justice in Isaiah 8:33 is judicial humiliation of the servant, not persecution of anyone in the section.
No healing occurs in this section; Acts 8:39 is the Spirit carrying Philip away, not a cure.
No clause states a deliverance or rescue; the section's drift (one who was far off brought to Christ) is all this can rest on.
The scattering (Acts 8:1, 3) lies outside this section; within these verses no clause states the persecution itself, only the resulting scattering.
No clause speaks of anyone being sent: cl0/cl1 state the believers were scattered (passive) and cl0/cl2 that they went about preaching; Acts 8:4 is a consequence of persecution, not of a sending.
Philip is presented as an evangelist/proclaimer (a city named and the Christ proclaimed), not as a prophet; no clause uses prophet language or speech attributed to God.

Pentecost is the specific Jerusalem event of Acts 2; nothing in this section marks that day — the Spirit here is received in Samaria through the apostles' laying on of hands (Act.8.17#cl1), which is a distinct occasion.

No clause in this section has anyone persecuting anyone: the conflict is Simon's attempted purchase (Act.8.18#cl0) and Peter's rebuke (Act.8.20#cl0); the clause at 8:23 ('captive to iniquity') describes Simon's own moral bondage, not persecution of the church.
The only duration in this section is "three days" (Acts 9:9); there is no forty-day period here, so the stamp does not belong to this section.

No servant of the LORD who suffers is spoken of here: the section has Saul persecuting, and "whom you are persecuting" (Acts 9:5) refers to Jesus as the one persecuted, not as a suffering servant figure described in the text.
The Holy Spirit is not mentioned or referred to in any clause of this section.
Nothing in this section reverses an order of first and last; Saul's conversion is an unexpected choice, not a reversal of rank.

Nothing in this section has anyone acting or speaking as a prophet: Saul proclaims (cl0/cl1), the hearers are amazed (9.21#cl0), and Saul proves (9.22#cl3] — the words are "proclaim", "astounded", "confounded", "proving", not prophet or prophesying; the content proclaimed is "He is the Son of God", a title of identity, not a prophetic utterance.
No kingship language anywhere: the titles given are "the Son of God" (9.20#cl1) and "the Christ" (9.22#cl4); "the chief priests" (9.21#cl7) is priestly, not royal.
The section's drift is that Saul now proclaims Jesus as Son of God and Christ (9.20#cl1, 9.22#cl4), but no clause states redemption, salvation or purchase.
The words are proclaiming (9.20#cl0), proving and confounding (9.22#cl1, cl3); no clause presents a prophetic word or Scripture being fulfilled.
No reference to the Spirit or to being filled/empowered by the Spirit; "was empowered" (9.22#cl0) has no stated agent in these clauses.
No clause in this section is a prophetic utterance or a word of prophecy; 9.27 describes what Saul saw and spoke, which is testimony, not prophecy.
The Spirit is not mentioned anywhere in Acts 9:26-30; the bold speaking is attributed to the name of the Lord, not to the Spirit.

Nothing here speaks of the Servant of Isaiah or of suffering borne as the Servant; the hostile Jews' attempt to kill Saul (9.29) is persecution, not the suffering-servant idea, and the stamp cites 9.29.
No clause states or rests on a promise; the verse cited (9:42) reports belief, not God's faithfulness to a word.
The servant figure here is Dorcas, whose suffering is only narrated (sick, died, washed), and she is not the servant of Isaiah; nothing in 9:39 carries the idea.
The Spirit is never mentioned or implied in 9:40 or anywhere in the section; Peter prays, but no clause names the Spirit.
Faith in "the Lord" is reported (9:42), but no clause speaks of redemption or of Christ's redemptive work.
The raising resembles new life at the level of the section's drift, but no clause names or rests on new creation.
Nothing in 9:40 or the section describes being in Christ; the named actor is Peter.
This is a healing, not a contest; no clause shows weakness overcoming strength.
9:41 records a presentation of the restored woman to the saints and widows; no clause speaks of rank reversal.
Death and raising is not exile and return; no clause carries exile.

Amos 1 is oracles of judgment against the nations; no clause here speaks of a promise or of faithfulness kept — the only covenant word, "broke a covenant of brotherhood" (Amo.1.9), records a broken covenant, not faithfulness, and the cited verse Amos 1:3 contains only transgression and judgment.

No clause here speaks of a kingdom as such (rule, throne, dominion); the cited verse Amos 1:15 names a king who will go into exile, which is a person, not a kingdom, and the surrounding clauses only cut off rulers and destroy citadels.
The section speaks of Israel being brought up out of Egypt (2:10) and of destruction at home (2:13-16), with no deportation or exile described.
The fire against Moab in 2:2 is announced by the LORD as judgment He Himself sends, not as a spoken curse or curse-formula.
Amos 3:9-15 has no "Woe to..." formula; 3:9-12 goes to the citadels and 3:13-15 is a hear/testify summons. The closest thing is the "therefore" oracle at 3:11.
Amos 3 never uses the phrase or its motifs; "the day" at 3:14 is "the day I punish Israel", a punishment day, not the day of the LORD (contrast Amos 5:18).
No clause here carries the day-of-the-LORD symbol; the trumpet and lion at 3:6/3:8 are general warnings, and Amos's only day-of-the-LORD text is 5:18-20.
No clause desecrates or destroys the temple; 3:14 demolishes the altars and horns of Bethel, a northern royal sanctuary, not the temple, and Bethel is not Zion.
No darkness, night or light imagery appears anywhere in Amos 3.
No fire in Amos 3; the destruction of 3:14-15 is by cutting off, falling and tearing down, not burning.
No nation is shaken by God here; 3:9-11 has foreign citadels summoned as observers and an unnamed foe surrounding Israel, which is the reverse sense.
No staff or rod appears in Amos 3. The nearest image is the cut-off altar horns at 3:14#cl3, which is a different object and symbol.

Amos 3:12 speaks only of a remnant rescue — 'having just the corner of a bed or the cushion of a couch' — a deliverance of scraps, with no note of exaltation or restoration to honour; the direction of the stamp is not present in this section.
Amos 4:1 has no woe (hoy); the verbless 'Hear this word' is a summons, not a hoy-oracle, and the clause list contains no woe formula.
No clause in Amos 5:1-3 names the day of the LORD or its cosmic signs; the section's drift is lament and decimation, not the day-of-the-LORD motif.

The section has the form's materials (I/you address, accusations over worship and idols in 5:21-26, sentence in 5:27) but no clause states a charge-and-indictment proceeding; the closest, 5:25 cl0, is rhetorical question only. General drift, no particular clause.

The section as a whole is addressed to Israel as the LORD's covenant people in breach (rejected worship 5:21-23, idols 5:26, exile 5:27), but no single clause states the covenant relationship itself; the closest, 'O house of Israel' (Amo.5.25#cl1), is address only.

Nothing in these verses holds out mercy or restoration: they announce wailing, darkness, rejected offerings and exile. The one apparent positive, 5:24 ('let justice roll on...'), is an indictment-demand, not a promise of restoration.
Amos 5:7 has no woe/hoy: the Hebrew is a plain participial accusation ("There are those who turn..."), and the Berean text has no "woe" anywhere in this section.

I could not find any clause in 5:4-15 that names or depicts the day of the LORD; 5:8 (the cited verse) speaks of the constellations and of the LORD's cosmic power, not of the day. It is present in the book's other verses (5:18-20), not here.

No clause names a king. The nearest is 'the distinguished ones of the foremost nation' (Amo.6.1#cl1), which is a description of the dignitaries of Israel, not a king; no royal title, person or act appears in the section.

No clause in 6:8-14 contains a hoy/woe form; the nearest hoy is 6:1 (outside this section). The section is accusation and announced judgment without the woe particle, so the stamp names the drift but no clause carries it.
No clause in 6:8-14 names a king or royal figure; the cited 6:13 has 'Lo-debar' and 'Karnaim' and 'the joyful people', not a king.
Yahweh is speaker and avenger here but no clause gives warrior imagery (no sword, bow, battle cry); the raised nation has no warrior description either.
Judgment by fire that consumes the deep and the land is the general tenor of day-of-the-Lord texts, but no clause here names 'the day of the LORD' or its signs.

Same as day_of_the_lord: the fire and locust judgments carry the general mood of day-of-the-Lord symbolism, but no clause in this section states the day of the LORD or its signs (darkness, trumpet, etc.).

No clause says anyone is a false prophet. Amaziah's charge is political conspiracy (Amo.7.10#cl2), and Amos denies being a prophet at all (Amo.7.14#cl2/cl3); the section answers a true prophet with an accusing priest, not a false prophet.

The section's drift is the LORD's word to Israel being refused (Amo.7.16#cl0-cl3) and the resulting national ruin (Amo.7.17), which is what the stamp names; no single clause names a covenant or frames the crisis as a covenant breach, so the pin is the section as a whole rather than a clause.

Nothing in this section scatters sheep or uses shepherd/sheep imagery. The only flock reference, "the LORD took me from following the flock" (Amo.7.15#cl0), is about Amos's own calling; the outcomes named in Amos 7:17 are a prostitute wife, children slain, land divided, death on pagan soil and exile — the people are never called sheep.

Amos 8:10 and the section speak of mourning rites (sackcloth, shaved heads, lamentation) and a famine of hearing the word, but nowhere of abstaining from food as a practice; fasting as an event is not said here.
Amos 8:11 announces a famine of hearing the words of the LORD; it is announced by God as judgment, not spoken as a curse formula or imprecation, and no clause utters a curse.

Amos 8:11 announces a famine, but of hearing the words of the LORD, and there is no provision or restoration of food anywhere in the section; the reversal is judgement on word-hearing only, so the stamp's provision side is absent.
The section is unrelieved judgement: no clause offers mercy, return, or restoration, and the last words are "they will fall, never to rise again" (Amos 8:14).
Amos 9:10 states the doom of the sinners ('will die by the sword'); it contains no 'woe' (hoy) cry or 'woe to you' address, so the woe-oracle form is not present in this section.
The scattering language of Amos 9:9 is grain sifted in a sieve, and the other dispersion clauses speak of captivity and hiding; no sheep, flock or shepherd imagery occurs in this section.
Amos 9:15 promises permanent possession of the land; it has no covenant-making language, no party formula, no 'new covenant' term. The stamp names a covenant the text here does not state.
Security in the land is asserted, but nothing in the section says a covenant, let alone a covenant of peace; the clause speaks of planting and not being uprooted.
Amos 9:15 has gift-of-land and permanence language but no covenant term or covenant ceremony; the idea is the section's drift, not carried by a particular clause.
Paul's apostleship is stated as a status ('an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God'), with God's will as its source; no clause of this section speaks of anyone being sent or of a sending.
Neither clause has any word for testifying, bearing witness, or attesting; 'faithful brothers' is faithfulness, not witness.
The only kinship terms are 'brother' (Timothy) and 'Father' (of us); no clause speaks of a son.

Nothing in these two verses speaks of redemption, rescue, forgiveness or purchase; 'in Christ' here describes the brothers' position, not redemption, and the verse cited (Col 1:2) contains no such word.

'the blood of the cross of Him' (Col.1.20#cl0/#cl1) is atoning blood, not a covenant word: no clause in this section contains covenant vocabulary (diatheke/covenant, 'new covenant', covenant-making language) or the covenant formula. Col.1.23 mentions 'the gospel', not a covenant.

No clause uses priestly vocabulary or imagery: no sanctuary, altar, offering, intercession or priestly mediator role. Col.1.20#cl1's 'blood' is the reconciling blood of the cross, not a priest's offering, and Col.1.23#cl6 'minister' (diakonos) is not a priest.
The section presents Paul as a servant/minister proclaiming the word, not as a prophet; no clause names a prophetic role or mediation of a prophetic oracle.
Paul's suffering and ministry are described as filling up Christ's afflictions and serving the church, with no priestly or sacrificial language; nothing in the clauses makes him a priest.
The section's drift of God revealing the mystery and presenting everyone perfect touches restoration, but no clause in particular carries the idea of mercy or restoration.
The hidden-for-ages mystery now revealed carries an undertone of God's long purpose being kept, but no clause states a promise or God's faithfulness.
Col 1:9 has Paul praying and asking God to fill the Colossians with knowledge; no priest, priesthood, temple, altar or mediating office appears in any clause of the section.
Col 1:14 gives 'redemption, the forgiveness of sins' in Christ; the section has no covenant, covenant formula, covenant meal, or 'new' anything.

Col 2:2 names 'the mystery of God, namely Christ', but the stamped idea is the act of giving a name. No clause performs a naming; the naming is carried by the English gloss 'namely' and the clause 'of God [which is] Christ' in Col.2.2#cl0, which asserts identity rather than a naming event.

Nothing in the section mentions a covenant, its inauguration, its parties or its terms. 'mystery of God, namely Christ' (Col 2:2) and 'in whom are hidden all the treasures' (Col 2:3) do not state a covenant.

Christ is named but no clause predicates kingship of him. 'all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden' (Col 2:3) and 'the mystery of God, namely Christ' (Col 2:2) are about revelation and knowledge, not rule.

No clause in the section has anyone speaking or acting as a prophet, or Christ presented as one. The 'mystery' (Col 2:2) is made known to the saints, but the section does not describe prophecy or a prophet.
There is no sacrificial, mediatorial or temple-priestly language anywhere in the section. 'a struggle I am having for you' (Col 2:1) is Paul's pastoral toil, not priestly service.

Col 2:4 speaks of preventing deception by persuasive speech; it does not describe testifying or bearing witness to anything. The contrast is between Paul's plain 'I say this' and the deceiver's speech, not a witness.
the body joined to the head in Col 2:19 is the church as a body with joints and ligaments growing, not a bride; the section has no bridal language or imagery
the cross is present (Col 2:14) but no sacrificial killing, altar, blood or offering is spoken of; the stamp is the section's drift only
no clause of this section names the Spirit; Col 2:11 has 'not by human hands' and Col 2:18 'unspiritual mind', neither of which is the Holy Spirit
the section addresses believers as one body (Col 2:19) but no clause states the corporate identity of God's people
Col 2:15 is Christ's triumph over the powers, not a judgment scene, and Col 2:16's judging is human judging of believers about food and festivals, not God's judgment
The 'no Greek or Jew' clause is about the new humanity's unity, not a covenant made or its members named.
No clause in this section mentions the Spirit or his work.
No clause in this section names a mother; Col 3:20 speaks only of 'parents' (and 'children'), so the mother role has no clause here.
The section speaks of 'children' (Col 3:20, Col 3:21) and 'Fathers'/'parents', but no clause names a son.
This section is the household code for wives/husbands, children/parents and fathers; no clause mentions slaves or bondservants (that material is Col 3:22 onward, outside this section).
The section is hortatory instruction on household conduct, but no clause states a law, commandment formula, or wisdom saying.
The section is paraenesis (household duty) with a retribution principle, but no clause itself carries a law or wisdom idea.
The section speaks of the Lord, inheritance and reward, but no clause names a kingdom, kingship or reign.
The section addresses slaves' service, reward and retribution; no clause states the reader's being in Christ.

No intercession for others: the praying is for God to open a door for the word and for Paul (Col.4.2#cl0, Col.4.3#cl0), not a priestly prayer of atonement or mediation on a people's behalf; the drift is apostolic prayer, but no clause carries the idea.
No servant/role-of-serving language in this section; the closest term is 'slaves' (Col.4.1#cl0), which is the slave_bondservant role, and 'Master' in heaven (cl1/cl2) is God, not a servant.
The community is addressed throughout (masters and slaves, 'us' in Col.4.3#cl0-2, 'outsiders' in Col.4.5#cl0), but no clause speaks of the people of God as such.
'redeeming the time' (Col.4.5#cl1) is 'buying up the opportunity' — ethics of time, not redemption in Christ; nothing in the section speaks of redemption in Christ.
The Holy Spirit is not mentioned in Col.4.1-4.6; prayer and thanksgiving (Col.4.2#cl0-1) do not name or specifically speak of the Spirit.
No kingship/reign language; 'a Master in heaven' (Col.4.1#cl1-2) names the masters' heavenly Master, not the kingdom.

The only candidate words are the closing wish “Grace be with you” (Col.4.18#cl2), which is a farewell benediction; nothing in Col 4:15–18 speaks of redemption or of Christ's work, and the stamp was pinned to v.18, not to grace.

“Remember my chains” (Col.4.18#cl1) states Paul's imprisonment, i.e. his suffering as an apostle, but the stamp names the Servant — the figure of Isaiah 52–53, who suffers on behalf of others — and no clause here has that figure as its subject; Paul's chains are not said to be vicarious or redemptive.
no clause in this section speaks of a promise or of God's faithfulness: God appears only as the one who delivers Jehoiakim into Nebuchadnezzar's hand (Dan.1.2#cl0)
no prophetic speech, vision or word of the Lord occurs in these clauses
Nothing in the section has anyone testifying, attesting or bearing witness; the king examines and finds the four better than the magicians, which is assessment, not witness.
The outsider here (the chief official) fears the king, and the steward simply consents; no one in verses 8-16 comes to belief.

The section speaks of 'the latter days'/'the end of the days' (Dan.10.14#cl2) as the time of the vision's fulfilment, but no clause describes the day of the LORD - judgment, cosmic signs, or the LORD's coming.
Michael appears here (Dan.10.13, Dan.10.21) but there is no dragon, serpent or Satan in this section; the conflict named is with the princes of Persia and Greece.
Dan.10.14#cl2 says only that the vision is 'for the days'/'the latter days'; no clause says God judges, pronounces verdict, or executes judgment.
No clause in this section names the temple, sanctuary or a place of worship; the shining figure of Dan.10.5-6 is not said to be in the temple.
Dan.10.21 speaks of the 'Book of Truth' and 'Michael your prince', not of a covenant or its making/keeping.
The weak party here (Daniel) is strengthened but does no fighting and defeats no one; the fighting named in Dan.10.13 and Dan.10.20 is between angelic princes, with no reversal of weak over strong.
No beast or monstrous kingdom appears in this section; the opposing powers named are 'the prince of the kingdom of Persia' and 'the prince of Greece' (Dan.10.13, Dan.10.20).
No clause in Dan 10 speaks of nations shaking. The nearest is Dan.10.13#cl0/#cl2 — a prince opposing and a heavenly helper — which is angelic conflict, not the shaking of nations.

Nothing in the section has angels holding or restraining winds. Dan.10.13#cl0, Dan.10.20#cl3 and Dan.10.21#cl4 concern the prince of Persia, the prince of Greece and Michael, i.e. princely/angelic opposition, not winds.

Cited verse 11.35 (and the section's ending) speaks of refining, purifying and 'the time of the end' / 'the appointed time' — Daniel 11 has no day-of-the-Lord imagery of the day of YHWH's coming in judgment; the clause set is the wise falling and being refined, not the day itself. The stamp does not belong in this section.

Cited verse 11.33 (those with insight falling by sword, flame, captivity, plunder) is the suffering of the wise/righteous many, not the singular Servant figure of Isa 52-53; Daniel 11 contains no servant-of-the-Lord figure. The stamp is wrong for this section.

The section shows a self-exalting king who defies God and does as he pleases, but no clause says he sets aside law or covenant; the idea is a NT characterisation of the section's drift, not something any clause here states
Dan 11:44 has only 'news from the east and the north will alarm him' and he goes out in fury — reports and warfare, with no collapse of sun, moon, stars or heavens anywhere in the section
Nothing in Dan 11:36-45 (including 11:45, the cited verse) says the sanctuary or a holy place is defiled; 11:45 only has him pitching tents near 'the beautiful holy mountain'
No clause in Dan 11:36-45 mentions sacrifice, offering, altar or its cessation (that language is in Dan 8, 9 and 12, not here)
Michael 'will rise up' (Dan.12.1#cl0) and 'a time of distress' (Dan.12.1#cl2) are all the section says; nothing here names a warrior, arms or fighting.
Dan.12.11 speaks only of the daily offering being abolished (a cultic event, sacrifice_ev), not of anyone serving as priest; the section names no priest.
The periods in this section are a time, times and half a time (Dan.12.7#cl5), 1,290 days (Dan.12.11#cl0) and 1,335 days (Dan.12.12#cl2); no period of forty (days/years) appears.
The section speaks of nations as a whole ('from the beginning of nations', Dan.12.1#cl3) and of 'your people'; no divided kingdom is described.

Dan.12.11 names the abolishing of the daily offering and the setting up of the abomination (Dan.12.11#cl1, #cl2) and Dan.12.7 names the shattering of the holy people, but no clause says the temple/house is destroyed.
No clause mentions a covenant, a covenant formula or covenant-making in this section.
No clause mentions a covenant of peace or any covenant; deliverance at Dan.12.1#cl4 is not joined to a covenant in the text.
Dan.12.7 contains an oath (Dan.12.7#cl4), but it is sworn by Him who lives forever about the times; no clause mentions the fathers or an oath to them.
The section speaks of Michael, distress, deliverance and resurrection; no clause mentions David or a covenant with him.
No clause mentions Abraham, his seed, or a covenant with him; 'your people' (Dan.12.1#cl0, #cl4) is not that covenant in this text.
No clause mentions Sinai, the exodus, or the making of a covenant at Sinai.
No clause mentions Noah, the flood, or a covenant with him; the 'waters of the river' (Dan.12.6#cl2, Dan.12.7#cl2) are not that covenant.

Dan 12:1 speaks of Michael, the prince over Israel, a time of distress, and deliverance of the named in the book; nothing in the section concerns a covenant with Noah or creation, and no clause mentions creation or a covenant.
Dan 12:1 treats angelic warfare and the distress and deliverance of Israel, not the salt covenant of Numbers 18:19; no clause mentions salt or priestly food dues.
No clause in Dan 12:1 names Shechem or a covenant renewal there; the verse speaks of Michael, distress, and the book of the delivered.
Nothing in Dan 12:1 concerns Phinehas or a covenant of perpetual priesthood; no clause names a priest.
No clause in Dan 12:1 mentions circumcision; the reference to the sons of your people is a designation of Israel, not a circumcision covenant statement.
No clause in the section speaks of marriage or a husband-wife covenant; Dan 12:1 concerns angelic conflict and Israel's deliverance.
Nothing in Dan 12:1 corresponds to the covenant between Jonathan and David; no clause mentions either figure.

The section's drift is the fate of 'your people' (Israel) in the last distress, but no single clause states 'new Israel'; the phrase 'your people' (cl0, cl1, cl4) names the existing people, not a renewed one.
No clause in the section presents a Davidic figure; the only royal title is 'the great prince' Michael (cl0), an angel, not a new David.
No clause mentions Moses or a new lawgiver; Dan 12:1 names Michael, not a Mosaic deliverer figure.
Dan 12:3 portrays the wise shining like the heavens and stars, an eschatological glory that resonates with new-creation imagery, but no clause states a new creation.

Dan 12:1 has Michael the great prince 'rise up' (cl0) as protector of Daniel's people in a time of distress, but there is no heavenly battle, no combat, and no opposing angelic force anywhere in this section; the only 'war'-like act is the shattering of the holy people (Dan.12.7#cl8), which is not a war in heaven.
Dan.12.7#cl8 speaks of the holy people's power being smashed/shattered, not of them being scattered; no clause in this section speaks of dispersion or scattering of the people.

The reader cited Dan 12:3, but Dan.12.3#cl0 and Dan.12.3#cl1 speak of the wise shining and of leading many to righteousness — no kingdom, king, throne or reign is mentioned anywhere in Dan 12:1-13; 'delivered', 'inherit' (Dan.12.13#cl2) and 'prince' (Dan.12.1#cl0) are not kingdom language.

No clause in Dan.2.1-13 carries a prophetic word; the dreams here are the king's troubling dreams and their interpretation, not a divine prophetic utterance. The stamp describes the book's general drift, not this section.
No clause speaks of a kingdom or of kingdoms as such; the section concerns a king's rule and decree, which is activity, not the theme of kingdom.
The threatened deaths in Dan.2.12-13 are the king's decree against his own wise men, not sin, exile or death as the section's theme; no clause names sin or exile.

Daniel receives revelation and speaks for God here, but no clause names or portrays him as a prophet; it is the section's general drift, not a clause-level idea.
Daniel's public praise before others could be read as witness, but no clause states testifying or bearing witness.
