the heifer's neck is broken in place; nothing is sent away or driven off, which is what the stamp names (the live goat sent to Azazel, Lev 16:21-22)
this is the unsolved-murder rite; atonement is made through the broken-necked heifer and the elders' declaration, not by the Day of Atonement ritual (Lev 16)
the section's drift is answering for innocent blood and purging guilt, but no clause in it runs a lawsuit; the nearest, Deu.21.5#cl4, only names the priests' ordinary ruling
The whole section is casuistic law ('if... then'), but no single clause states law or wisdom as an idea.

'the LORD your God' (10#cl1) marks Israel as God's people only by address, and the section never speaks of God's people as an idea; the subject is the treatment of a foreign captive woman. No clause carries the stamp itself.
The section is an Israelite inheritance ruling but no clause names Israel, the assembly, or the people; the stamp is only the section's general setting.
No clause speaks of a promise, oath, covenant or God's faithfulness; the section concerns a man's duty in inheritance and the birthright.

No clause here speaks of a servant or of vicarious suffering; the hanged man is a sinner executed under God's curse, and the section nowhere says he suffers for others. The connection is only made later, in the New Testament's reading of this verse.
Nothing in the section speaks of redemption or of Christ; it is a burial-and-cleansing statute. The link to Christ is a New Testament use of the verse, not an idea carried by any clause here.

Clause 22.5#cl2 calls cross-dressing 'detestable to the LORD your God', an abomination verdict, not the covenant-lawsuit form (summons, indictment, witnesses, curse) that stamp names; no suit is brought and no party is charged in a lawsuit.
The cited verse and the whole section address 'your brother' / 'your countryman' (22.1#cl0-1, 22.3#cl2); the outsider category the stamp names does not appear.
The straying animal's owner is 'your brother' / 'your countryman' (22.1#cl1, 22.1#cl3), never a slave or bondservant; the stamp is absent.

Deut 22:10 forbids plowing with an ox and donkey yoked together (22.10#cl0), an agricultural yoking, not warfare; nothing here concerns a warrior or battle. (The plowing is the only candidate and I judge the stamp wrong, not general.)

No priest, sanctuary or cultic act appears; the tassels of 22.12 ('tassels you will make for yourself on the four corners of your covering', 22.12#cl0) are a lay command, not priestly. Treating the tassel command as priestly is possible by typology, which is why I do not mark it wrong, but no clause carries priesthood.

The cited verse (26) does show mitigation — the young woman is spared and guilt is assigned only to the man (Deu.22.26#cl0, cl1) — but no clause in the section speaks of mercy or restoration; the chapter's outcome is death, fine or forced marriage.

The only candidate is 'because the LORD your God loves you' (Deu.23.6#cl3) and the earlier oath to the fathers, which the section does not state; the reader's cited verse Deut 23:8 speaks of the third generation being admitted, not of a promise kept. The stamp reads more as the section's general drift (Yahweh's durable commitment to Israel) than as any clause in particular.

Nothing in this section is a lawsuit/rib speech: no summons, no accusation of covenant breach, no witnesses, no indictment. It is casuistic/apodictic instruction and motive clauses ('so that the LORD your God may bless you', 'you will be guilty of sin'). Guilt language ('you will be guilty of sin', Deu.23.22#cl4, Deu.23.23#cl2) is not a covenant lawsuit.

The section names no priest, Levite, sacrifice, altar or cultic officiant; the cleansing in Deu.23.11#cl2/Deu.23.12#cl1 is self-administered ('he must leave', 'he must wash with water'), and the camp's holiness in Deu.23.14#cl5 is grounded in Yahweh's own walking, not in a priesthood. 'Priesthood' is not a feature of this section.

No clause stages a lawsuit or indictment; the nearest is the cry of the unpaid hired hand to the LORD, which is a complaint to God, not a covenant lawsuit. General drift of the section's legal material, not pinned to a clause.

The cited verse (Deu 24:16) concerns putting to death for one's own sin, not judging; no clause in this section names judges, judging, or a court. The only judging language is 'do not deny justice' (Deu.24.17#cl0), which is about the parties' conduct, not a judge role.
The Hebrew word used (Deu.24.16#cl0 'parents') is the usual 'fathers'; no clause in this section names a mother. The stamp is not carried by any clause here.
No clause speaks of a witness, testimony, or evidence. Deu 24:16, the cited verse, is about liability for one's own sin, not witnesses.
There is a legal dispute and adjudication, but nothing marks it as YHWH's covenant lawsuit; the section's drift is ordinary civil litigation. No clause carries 'covenant_lawsuit' specifically.
The whole unit is case law with a wisdom-tinged rationale ('lest your brother be degraded'), but no single clause states a wisdom theme.

Nothing in the section names Sinai, the covenant, or its making; the land and its gift are referred to, but that is not the Sinai covenant event. The reader's cited verse (25:19) speaks of rest and inheritance, not of Sinai.
The whole section is case law with rulings ('you are to cut off her hand', 'she must not marry outside the family'), and no single clause states the theme of law or wisdom as an idea in itself.

The chapter names commandments given to Moses and sworn oaths to the fathers, but no clause speaks of Sinai, the mountain, or the covenant made there; the reader's citation of 26:13 points only to 'the commandments You have given me'.
The basket of firstfruits is taken by the priest and placed before the altar (26:4), but nothing is slaughtered, burned, or offered as a sacrifice; placing firstfruits is not a sacrifice event.
The historical summary runs from the wandering Aramean to Egypt, oppression, and the exodus straight to 'this place' (26:5-9); no clause speaks of Israel's wandering or journey in the wilderness.
The sojourn in Egypt (Deu.26.5#cl3-4) is a stay in a foreign land before the exodus, not an exile event; no clause speaks of deportation or captivity away from the land.
Deu.26.8 says only 'brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, with great terror, signs, and wonders'; no clause mentions the sea, its parting, or a crossing.
Deu.26.9 speaks of being brought to this land from Egypt (the exodus and entry), not of a return from exile; no clause speaks of exile or return from it.
The chapter speaks of commandments being kept ('I have not transgressed or forgotten Your commandments'), but no clause connects the law with wisdom, understanding, or the fear of the LORD.
Deu.26.4 places the basket of firstfruits before the altar but nothing is slaughtered or offered on the altar in this section; no clause names a sacrifice or offering.
Deu.26.14 is a declaration of innocence about the sacred portion—no eating in mourning, no removal while unclean, none offered for the dead—and contains no clause of judgment, verdict or punishment.
The Aramean ancestor of Deu.26.5 is Israel's ancestor who went down to Egypt, and the affliction in 26:6-7 is Israel's; no clause speaks of a servant who suffers for others.
Deu.26.11 names the foreigner as a fellow rejoicer over the good the LORD has given, which is inclusion in Israel's joy, not an outsider coming to faith.

No clause in this section speaks of famine, hunger or want being reversed; the nearest clause, Deu.26.9#cl0-cl1, speaks only of being brought to and given the land, and the only eating/filling clauses (Deu.26.12#cl3-cl4) concern the Levite, foreigner, fatherless and widow eating and being satisfied from the tithe, not a reversal of famine. The stamp is a plausible deduction from Israel's Egyptian sojourn in Deu.26.5#cl3-cl5 and hard labor in Deu.26.6, but no clause carries the idea.

The section's statutes/ordinances are the Deuteronomic covenant terms, but no clause names Sinai, Horeb, the mountain, or the events at Sinai; it is the section's setting, not something a clause says.
No oath, swear, or vow appears in any clause: Deu.26.17#cl0 says only '(et) Yahweh you.have.declared this day' — a declaration/affirmation, not the swearing of an oath.

The promises to the fathers are referred to only as 'just as he.spoke' / 'just as he.spoke' (Deu.26.18#cl2, Deu.26.19#cl4); no clause names Abraham, Isaac or Jacob, so the Abrahamic covenant in particular is not in the text.
No clause uses king, throne, reign or kingdom; the mutual taking of Yahweh as God and Israel as His people is the general framework kingship language builds on, not a statement of it here.
Mount Ebal, where the stones and altar are set up, is named (Deu.27.4#cl2); Shechem is never mentioned in this section, so the clause list cannot show this stamp here.
The section presents the law as to be written, kept and obeyed, but no clause states or implies wisdom, understanding or discernment; only the general drift of law-keeping touches it.

The section speaks of an altar and of rejoicing 'in the presence of the LORD your God' (Deu.27.7#cl2), but there is no temple, sanctuary, house, ark or dwelling-place in any clause; only an altar of stones on Mount Ebal is commanded.

The section is set in Moab on the day Moses commands the people before crossing the Jordan (Deut 27:11-12); nothing in it names Sinai, Horeb, or the mountain where the law was given. The 'words of this law' in v.26 are the Moab covenant words, not the Sinai giving.
The section states a curse for not putting the words of the law into practice (Deu.27.26#cl0-cl1); it nowhere frames the law as wisdom, understanding, or a wise way of life.
The covenant form (command, curse, all Israel, 'this law') runs through the whole section without being one clause's idea.
Deut.27.15#cl2 says the idol is set up 'in secret', not in the sanctuary or holy place; no clause places it in a holy place.

The only 'abomination' here is the carved or molten image itself, 'the work of the hands of a craftsman', set up in secret (Deut.27.15#cl1-cl2); there is no desolation, no holy place, and no apocalyptic desolating abomination in the section.
The section is wholly blessing for obedience; mercy after failure and return from exile are absent, so the stamp describes only the general drift of the chapter, not any clause of this section.

The section is a conditional curse-list ('If ... you do not obey ... all these curses will come upon you'), not a 'Woe to ...' oracle: no clause contains a woe/interjection; the Hebrew of Deut 28:15 is a conditional protasis with weqatal curses, not הוֹי.
Deut 28 has no 'day of the LORD' language: no clause names a day of Yahweh or its darkness/coming; the closest (28:67) is dread because of terrifying sights, not a day-of-Yahweh scene.
No clause in the section speaks of fire as event or symbol (28:24 is rain turned to dust and powder); the only burning imagery is locusts/worms consuming crops, which is not fire.
The movement here is exaltation to exile (prosperity and increase reversed into destruction and being uprooted, Deut 28:62-63), not exile to exaltation; the stamp is inverted for this section.
Deut 28:43 has the foreigner rising and Israel sinking - humiliation with no vindication; nothing in the section reverses Israel's humiliation.

The reversal of rank in Deut 28:43-44 (sojourner above, Israel below; he the head, you the tail) is a rank reversal, but it reverses the covenant order rather than being the kingdom's last-first principle.
Deut 28:63 speaks only of destruction and annihilation ('it will please Him to annihilate you and destroy you'); no life comes out of the death here.
Deut 28:48 moves the opposite direction, into hunger, thirst, nakedness and lack ('you will serve your enemies ... in famine, thirst, nakedness, and destitution'); no provision follows.
Israel's defeat of Sihon and Og is a battle victory with no procession, no carrying of spoils and no entry rite; nothing in the section depicts a victory procession.

There is no procession or celebratory march anywhere in these verses; the verbs are 'came out to meet us in battle' (Deu.3.1#cl2), 'delivered into our hands' (Deu.3.3#cl0) and 'we struck them down' (Deu.3.3#cl1). A victory is narrated, but no procession or entry rite is described.
Nothing in the section shows a procession (cultic or triumphal); the crossing of Deu.3.18#cl4 is an armed advance, and the ark-led procession idea has no words here.
The land here is described as given by Yahweh and already taken (Deu.3.18#cl2), with no mention of Abraham, his offspring, or an oath to the fathers; the reader's cited verse does not carry it.
No oath, and no fathers sworn to, appear anywhere in this section; the gift of land in Deu.3.18#cl2 and Deu.3.20#cl3 has no oath formula attached.

Nothing in the section presents Moses as a priest or any priestly act; Deut 3:23 is Moses' plea to the LORD (Deu.3.23#cl0 'I.sought.favor to Yahweh'), not a priestly role. 'servant' (Deu.3.24#cl2) is a servant of Yahweh, not priest.

No clause in this section indicts Israel or summons witnesses/judges; Deut 30:1 mentions the blessings and curses already set before them, but the section speaks of restoration and obedience, not a lawsuit charge.
No clause in this section mentions the Spirit or God's Spirit; the heart-circumcision of Deut 30:6 is not a spirit clause, and reading the Spirit into it would go beyond the words.
The material does speak of blessing/life and of entering the land, but no clause carries a commissioning of a bearer of blessing to others; the notion is only general here.
The section offers life as a live option, but contains no rescue, forgiveness or restoration of the failed; the stamp is not carried by any clause here.
No clause reports a rescue or deliverance, only the life that follows obedience; nothing in the section speaks of being delivered.

No temple, sanctuary, dwelling or glory is mentioned; the section's presence language (Deu.31.6#cl5/#cl6, Deu.31.8#cl1/#cl2/#cl3) is about Yahweh going with and being with his people, which is the general drift of the stamp rather than a temple clause. If the stamp means God's presence among his people unconditionally, I would move those four clauses here.
The section presents the written law as Moses' complete, authoritative deposit, but no clause in it carries the wisdom idea itself.

Nothing in this section has the shape of a lawsuit/rib: no summons, no indictment, no witnesses, no accusation. vv.9-13 are Moses writing and depositing the law and commanding a septennial public reading; the only covenant word is the ark of the covenant (Deu.31.9#cl2), which is furniture, not litigation.

The section is set on the plains of Moab, at the end of Moses' life, with the crossing of the Jordan still ahead (Deu.31.13#cl4, cl5); it never mentions Sinai, Horeb, the mountain, or the events there. The ark of the covenant (Deu.31.9#cl2) is not Sinai.

The section's horizon is Israel in the land (Deu.31.13#cl4), not creation or the created order. Yahweh is named as 'the LORD your God' to Israel (Deu.31.11#cl2, Deu.31.12#cl4, Deu.31.13#cl3); no cosmic or creation-wide covenant is in view.

The land as something the hearers will possess (Deu.31.13#cl4, cl5, cl6) rests on Yahweh's promise and his pledge to be their God (Deu.31.11#cl2, Deu.31.12#cl4, Deu.31.13#cl3) is the same bond the reading renews; but no clause states either promise or covenant fidelity itself. It is the section's general drift, carried no doubt of nothing said.
The only rock-and-provision clause here is honey/oil from the rock; water from the rock is not in this section.

The cited verse 26 (and verse 43) speaks of cutting Israel to pieces and blotting out their memory, and of the sword making them childless; the section nowhere uses shepherd/sheep/scattering language, and the nations are not scattered here.

The cited verse 30 says the opposite of the stamp: it asks how one man could pursue a thousand and is explicit that this happened only because 'their Rock had sold them, unless the LORD had given them up' (Deu.32.30#cl0–cl3). The weak do not defeat the strong here; the strong overrun them by God's act.

The cited verse 4 gives the 'Rock' title for God ('He is the Rock, His work is perfect', Deu.32.4#cl0), which is why the reader likely cited it, but the section nowhere speaks of a rejected stone that becomes the head/cornerstone. The stamp's idea does not occur.
Sinai appears only as the place the LORD came from in the theophany; no clause states a covenant made or given there.
No clause mentions Abraham, his seed, or the promises made to him; the verse cited is a blessing on Israel's salvation and the nations cowering.
No clause speaks of an oath sworn to the fathers; the land-and-descendants oath is nowhere expressed in this section.
Deut 33:2 has no word for the Spirit (Hebrew ruach); it speaks of the LORD coming with myriads of holy ones and flaming fire, which the stamp's cited verse does not state.
The cited verse 33:17 names Ephraim and Manasseh (Joseph's sons) but states no reversal of elder and younger; the birthright-over-birth-order motif (Gen 48) is not expressed in this clause pair.
The mourning period is thirty days, not forty (Deut 34:8).
Land, tribal territory and Pharaoh's officials are the nearest thing here, but no rule, throne or kingdom is named; general drift only.
Moses is called servant, but the stamp is the suffering servant of Isaiah 53; nothing here has vicarious suffering or bearing sin.
4:13 has Yahweh declaring and writing a covenant, but nothing in this section cuts, slaughters, passes between pieces, or otherwise enacts a covenant-cutting rite; the stamp's event is absent here.

No clause mentions a sea or its crossing; Exod.4:20 names the exodus from Egypt/'iron furnace' (Deu.4.20#cl1) and the Jordan to be crossed is a river (Deu.4.21, 4.22, 4.26) with no water-crossing event recorded.
No clause describes Israel walking through or being tested in the wilderness; Deut 4:21 speaks of Moses not crossing the Jordan into the land, not of the years of wandering.

Every idol in the section is one the people make 'for yourselves' (Deu.4.16#cl1, 4.23#cl3, 4.25#cl3); no clause places an image in the sanctuary or the holy place, and no clause mentions the temple or its desecration.

No clause in this section states a law, statute or command to be kept, nor any wisdom, understanding or teaching; the only commands are the negative warnings 'be careful' / 'do not make an idol' (Deu.4.15#cl0, 4.16#cl1), which are the forbidden act itself, not law or wisdom.
The section moves toward obedience to statutes given 'today' (4:40), but no clause narrates the giving of the law at Horeb; the fire/voice clauses are about hearing, not receiving laws.
Nothing here is a lawsuit/indictment against Israel with witnesses and charges; 4:32-40 is a summons to remember and obey, not an accusation in covenant form.
No figure presented as a new Moses; the speaker addresses Israel without typological framing.
No prophet or prophetic office is referred to; only God's own voice is heard.
Egypt is mentioned, but no sea, crossing, or water is spoken of in any clause.
No procession or triumphal entry; 'brought you out' is exodus, not a victory march ritual.
No deportation or exile of Israel is described; Egypt is the place they left, not a place of exile in view.
No return from exile; the only 'bringing in' is the entry into the land under Joshua.
Abraham is not named; 'your fathers' and 'descendants' evoke the fathers broadly, and the verse's oath motif is absent here.
David and his dynasty are nowhere in the section.
'Prosper' and 'live long in the land' are covenant blessings, not a peace covenant.
Creation appears only as a time-marker for the question of 4:32, not as a covenant with creation.
Heaven and earth are not invoked as witnesses, and no witnessing role is assigned; 'ask from one end of the heavens to the other' is inquiry, not testimony.
No servant or servant role is named or implied.
No king, throne, or royal rule is spoken of; the LORD is God, not depicted as king here.
No judging, judgment, or judge figure appears.
No priest, altar, or cultic mediation is in the section.

Deut 4:37 speaks of 'your fathers' and 'their descendants' (Deu.4.37#cl0, cl1), not of a firstborn; the Hebrew behind cl1 ('offspring his after him') is זַרְעוֹ, seed/descendants, no firstborn term anywhere in this section.

The nearest wording is 'children your after you' (Deu.4.40#cl3) and 'their descendants' (Deu.4.37#cl1); neither is a son (בֵּן) nor a father-son relation as an idea of the section. No clause carries 'son'.
No clause in the section mentions a sojourner, resident alien or stranger; Israel is described as being brought out and brought in (Deu.4.38#cl1-3), never as sojourning.
Nothing in the section speaks of a surviving remainder; the nations are dispossessed whole (Deu.4.38#cl1) and Israel is brought in whole (Deu.4.38#cl2-3).
The section's movement is a national exodus and conquest ('he brought you out ... from Egypt' Deu.4.37#cl2; 'to drive out before you nations' Deu.4.38#cl1), not a pilgrimage or journey to a shrine.
No clause has anyone receiving or hosting guests; Israel's role is dispossessor and inheritor (Deu.4.38#cl1-3), not host.
The land is given as an inheritance (Deu.4.38#cl3), not as hospitality to a guest; no guest or host language appears.
No clause in this section mentions building, a house or a city.
No clause mentions a vineyard, vine or wine.
No clause mentions fishing, fish or water; the only water-adjacent event is the exodus from Egypt (Deu.4.37#cl2), which is not fishing.

The section's substance is the covenant relation — 'the LORD is God; there is no other' (Deu.4.35#cl1/cl3/cl4; Deu.4.39#cl1/cl3/cl4) and 'Keep His statutes and commandments' (Deu.4.40#cl0) — but no clause names a covenant, oath or covenant-making, so no particular clause carries the stamp.

Deut 4:32's 'ask now ... has anything as great as this ever happened' (Deu.4.32#cl0, cl3, cl4) is rhetorical appeal to history, and the only speech-from-God clauses are about his voice at Horeb heard by Israel (Deu.4.33#cl1, Deu.4.36#cl0-3), not a prophet speaking or a word of prophecy given through a prophet.
These are the law Moses proclaimed in the plains of Moab after the exodus, not the covenant made at Sinai (Horeb); the section says nothing of Horeb, the mountain, or the making of a covenant.
The section speaks of coming out of Egypt and of land already taken from Sihon and Og; no clause mentions wandering, or the wilderness period between the exodus and this point.
Deu.4.47 describes the conquest as taking possession of land, not as a procession; no clause shows a procession, or movement in triumph with spoil or captives.
The section introduces the law with no predicate or term of wisdom; no clause calls the law wise, or connects it with wisdom in any way.
The verbs are Moses' setting the law before Israel and Israel's taking the land (ירש); nothing in the section states a promise or God's fulfilling of one, and God is not named.
Sihon and Og are called kings and their territories are named, but no clause speaks of kingship, rule, throne or realm as such.

Though the gloss renders it "judgments", that word is מִשְׁפָּטִים, the laws Moses set before Israel, and the section contains no act of judging or verdict; the defeat of Sihon and Og is narrated as conquest, not as judgment.

The section presents the statutes and judgments as what Moses declares and Israel must hear, learn and observe (Deu.5.1#cl3, cl5, cl6) — obligation and command, not wisdom, insight or understanding; nothing here praises the law as wisdom.

The section cites Deut 5:3, but that verse draws a contrast of covenant recipients ('not with ancestors our ... but with us'), which is about the present generation, not about God keeping a promise; no promise and no act of faithfulness is spoken of in these clauses.
Deut 5:4 speaks of Yahweh speaking from the fire on the mountain (Deu.5.4#cl0) — a theophany at Horeb, not a temple or sanctuary; no house, dwelling place or cultic site is mentioned in the section.

No priest appears in this section. The people ask Moses, not a priest, to go near and hear on their behalf (Deu.5.27#cl0, Deu.5.27#cl1), and Moses is called mediator, not priest; no sacrificial or priestly act is mentioned.
Nothing here is a lawsuit: no accusation of covenant breach, no witnesses, no indictment. The section is commandment-giving and the people's obedient response, not a charge against them.
No temple or dwelling place of God appears. God's presence here is the Sinai theophany of fire, cloud and darkness (Deu.5.22#cl0, Deu.5.23#cl2), which the people call glory, not a temple.

Nothing is lost or ruined here to be restored. The only mercy-sounding clause, 'If only they had such a heart' (Deu.5.29#cl0, Deu.5.29#cl1), expresses God's wish for present obedience, not restoration after judgment.
No judgment is enacted or threatened in this section. The fire (Deu.5.25#cl1) is feared destruction, not a sentence pronounced on anyone, and no act of God judging sin is described.

The section is the giving of the Decalogue as command and its grounding in deliverance; nothing in these clauses speaks of wisdom, understanding or instruction as wisdom (no wisdom term in the clause glosses).
This section's only image language is the prohibition of making an idol/image (Deu.5.8#cl0), which is the opposite of the image-of-God idea; no clause speaks of humanity as made in God's image.

The section never names Sinai, Horeb, or a covenant made there; Deut 6:1 refers only to 'the commandments and statutes and ordinances' commanded through Moses, and the only oath mentioned is the one sworn to the fathers (6:10), not a covenant at Sinai.

The section speaks of commandments, statutes and ordinances generally (6:1, 6:2, 6:17) but never of ten, never of the Decalogue as a set, and never of the Sinai tablets; the stamp is background drift, not something a clause here states.
The clauses speak of driving out enemies (6:19), which is expulsion in battle, not a procession or triumph celebration; nothing in the section depicts an ordered march or victory parade.
No clause in the section mentions a king, a throne, or royal rule.
No clause in the section mentions a priest, altar, or sacrificial service; the only 'serve' is serving the LORD generally (6:13).
No clause in the section names a prophet or prophetic speech.
No clause mentions bearing witness, testimony in court, or being a witness; the 'testimonies' of 6:17 are commandments, not a person's testimony.
No clause shows a judge, judging, or a legal verdict; the 'judgments' of 6:1 are ordinances given, not an act of judging.
No clause speaks of a surviving remainder; 6:3's multiply and 6:19's expulsion of enemies are the opposite theme.
No clause shows a host, army, or one receiving guests; the only acts are entering the land and driving out enemies.

The 'guest' role is read out of Deut 6:10-11's 'cities that you did not build' and 'houses ... you did not fill them' (Deu.6.10#cl4 'not you.built'; Deu.6.11#cl2 'not you.filled'), but no clause names a guest, a host, or anyone received into a house. The section is addressed to Israel as the incoming possessor; nothing in it casts anyone as guest.

The only building clause is negative of Israel — Deu.6.10#cl4 'not you.built' (cities) and Deu.6.11#cl0 'houses ... which not you.filled' — so no clause in this section presents anyone as a builder; the point is that Israel did not build.

Vineyards and olive trees appear only as what Israel did not plant: Deu.6.11#cl0 'vineyards and olive.trees which not you.planted' / Deu.6.11#cl1 'not you.planted'. No clause has anyone tending or dressing a vine.

Deut 6:7 is cited, but its clauses are about teaching and speaking — Deu.6.7#cl0 'you will.repeat.them to children your', Deu.6.7#cl1 'you.will.speak in them ...' — with no flock, no tending, no shepherd. The role is not present in this section.

Deut 6:5 is cited, but Deu.6.5#cl0 is 'you.will.love (et) Yahweh God your with all heart your ...' — covenant love directed to God, with no marriage, spouse or bridegroom terms anywhere in the section.

Same clause as above, Deu.6.5#cl0 'you.will.love (et) Yahweh God your with all heart your and with all being your and with all strength your'; nothing in the section speaks of a bride, wedding or marriage.

Deut 6:7 concerns instructing children — Deu.6.7#cl0 'you will.repeat.them to children your' — but the actor is 'you' (Israel), and no clause names a mother, nursing or childbearing; the role is not carried by any clause.

Deut 6:2 is cited, but its clauses are Deu.6.2#cl0/#cl1 (fearing, keeping statutes), Deu.6.2#cl3 'you and child your and the.child your.child your' and Deu.6.2#cl4 'they may.grow.long days your' — generations and long life, with no firstborn, birthright or primogeniture.

The speaker's teaching role is real here (Deu.6.1#cl0/#cl1: 'he.has.commanded Yahweh God your to teach you'), but he is Moses, not a 'new Moses'; no clause marks a typological or eschatological successor. General drift only.

Deu.6.4#cl1 'O.Israel' and Deu.6.4#cl2 'Yahweh God our Yahweh [is].one' address Israel as Israel; nothing in the clauses presents a renewed or restored Israel beyond the addressee. General drift only.

Deut 6:13 is cited, but its clauses are Deu.6.13#cl0 'Yahweh God your you.will.fear', #cl1 'him you.will.serve', #cl2 'in name his you.will.swear.oaths' — fear, service and oath, with no king, David, throne or anointed figure in the section.

Deu.6.16 is a prohibition on testing God backed by the Massah incident; no clause in the section states or presupposes a wisdom element (no wisdom saying, no 'fear of the LORD is wisdom', no wise/understanding person), and the clause carries law alone. The stamp as cited at 6:16 does not belong to this section.
Deut 7:9 speaks of the covenant of loving devotion kept for a thousand generations, not of a covenant made at Sinai/Horeb; nothing in the section locates a covenant at Sinai.
The section commands keeping the commandments this day but nowhere links the law to wisdom or understanding; the drift is law-keeping, not wisdom.
The oath sworn to the fathers (7:12-13) is the Abrahamic/paternal oath, not the Sinai covenant; the section names no Sinai event.
The section speaks of conquest and annihilation, but no marching, procession or triumph ceremony is described.
"a great and awesome God" (7:21) names Yahweh's greatness, not a visible manifestation (fire, cloud, earthquake, appearance); no theophany scene in this section.
The section forbids images and bringing a detestable thing into one's house (7:25-26); it says nothing about an idol set in a holy place, and speaks of destroying the images, not consecrating one.
The vocabulary of detestation and destruction (7:25-26) is here applied to the nations' images and plunder, not to an eschatological abomination standing in the sanctuary.
Deut 8:18 speaks of the covenant sworn to the fathers (the patriarchs), not a covenant with creation or with Noah; no clause here concerns creation.
Deut 8:3 states that man lives on every word from the mouth of the LORD; nothing here concerns a servant who suffers, nor the Servant of Isaiah.
The land is described as good and fruitful (Deut 8:7-9) but no clause gives a commission to be a blessing to the nations; as a description of the section's drift it stays general.
Deut 8:19 speaks of going after other gods generally, not of an idol set in a holy place.
The section's drift is the contrast between Israel's unworthiness (stiff-necked, no righteousness of their own) and the nations' wickedness; no clause names Israel's sin, an exile, or a death.
General drift only: the taking of the land and driving out nations implies Israel becoming a settled people, but no clause speaks of a king, throne, reign or kingdom.
The section is Moses' retrospective accusation and plea, not a lawsuit speech with summons, witnesses and indictment; no clause formally frames a rib against Israel here.

No priest, priesthood, or cultic office appears in the section; Moses acts as mediator and intercessor but is nowhere called or described as a priest here. Aaron is mentioned only as an object of wrath.
The molten calf was made at the foot of the mountain while Moses was on it (Deu 9:12, 9:16), not set up in the holy place or sanctuary; nothing in the section places an idol in a holy place.
The section speaks of futility, toil and weariness (Ecc.1.2, 1.3, 1.8), but no clause refers to sin, to exile, or to death; the stamp's ideas are not present, only a generally bleak mood.
The cited verse (Ecc.1.11) is about remembrance and forgetting, not about divine judgment; no clause in the section speaks of judging, verdict, or retribution.
The section speaks of God's giving men a burdensome business and of futility under the sun, but there is no judging, verdict, sentence or court scene in any clause — nothing here is a judgment event.

Wisdom is spoken of in Ecc.1.16#cl5/cl7 and Ecc.1.17#cl1, but it is the Teacher's own wisdom ("I have grown and increased in wisdom", "my mind has observed a wealth of wisdom"), not a woman or a personified woman Wisdom.
"Madness and folly" in Ecc.1.17#cl2 is a thing the Teacher set his mind to know, an abstract quality, not a woman or personified figure.
The Hebrew of this section has no torah/law term; the clauses rest on חׇכְמָה (wisdom), דַּעַת (knowledge) and סׇכְלָה (folly) only, and the English "wisdom" does not carry law with it.

The grief and pain of Ecc.1.18#cl0/#cl1 and the burden of Ecc.1.13#cl4 are the Teacher's own and humanity's, not a servant of the Lord who suffers for others; the section names no servant, no vicarious suffering and no Servant figure.

Folly is spoken of here as a quality or as the fool (Ecc.10.1#cl2, 10.3#cl3, 10.6#cl0, 10.13#cl0), never as a woman; the earlier-reader's citation of Eccl 10:1 is a reading of the English 'folly' as the personified woman Folly of Proverbs, which this Hebrew does not say. No clause in the section names a female figure.

The ruler of 10:4 and the king of 10:16f are characterised by temper, youth and feasting, not by beast-like imagery; the only animal in the section is the snake that bites (Ecc.10.8#cl3, 10.11#cl0), which is not the ruler.
The blessing of the well-ordered land at 10:17 is the nearest thing to a positive counterpart to the woe, but no clause in the section speaks of mercy or of restoration after loss.

No clause in 11:1-6 contains a divine promise, a word of God, or an act of God keeping faith; 11:1's 'after many days you will find it again' is a consequence of the human act of casting, and the cited verse 11:1 has no Hebrew term for a promise (the noun is not present). The stamp as written does not belong to this section.
The section's drift is wisdom instruction (carpe diem tempered by accountability, 11:9-10), but no clause names law, commandment, or Torah; the nearest is the judgment clause.

Eccl 12:7 has the spirit returning to God who gave it, but nothing in any clause describes God judging, evaluating or rendering a verdict; the reader's cited verse is the only candidate and it does not carry the idea.
No clause speaks of the dead being raised or of life after death restored; 12:7 says dust returns to the ground and the spirit returns to God, which is dissolution/return, not resurrection.
Nothing in the section speaks of renewal, restoration or a new created order; the movement is toward decay and death (12:1-7), ending in 'Everything is futile!' (12:8).

The stamp names the scene of books being opened (as in Dan 7 / Rev 20). This section has books only as things that are endlessly made ('There is no end to the making of many books', Ecc.12.12#cl2); no book is opened, and no book is brought to judgment. The judgment clause Ecc.12.14#cl0 mentions deeds and hidden things, not books.
Ecc.12.12#cl0 is 'my child my' (Hebrew beni), an address of a teacher to a pupil; the section nowhere names a father. The cited verse supplies the 'son' address, not a father role.

The section speaks only of judgment for deeds ('whether good or evil', Ecc.12.14#cl1-2); it has no clause on sin, exile or death, and Eccl.12.9-14's only mention of death is not present in these clauses.

The section's drift — everything under the sun ends in futility, nothing gained — matches this theme, but no clause names sin, exile or death; Ecc.2.11#cl5 ('futility and striving of wind') and #cl6 ('no advantage under the sun') speak only of futility, not of any of the three named ideas.

The cited verse and its neighbours describe building, planting and irrigation by Qoheleth (houses, vineyards, gardens, parks, fruit trees, reservoirs) — human projects, not creation. The Berean text has no act of divine creation and no creation vocabulary (no 'made the heavens and the earth', no 'created') in Eccl.2.1-11. If the stamp is meant more loosely as 'the natural world / fruitfulness of the earth', that is not what this section is about, so I judge it wrong here.

The section has no blessing and no commission: no divine speech, no command to anyone, no promise. Ecc.2.10 (the cited verse) is Qoheleth's own self-reward — 'this was the reward for all my labor' — which is the opposite of a blessing given by God, and Ecc.2.11 immediately calls the whole labour futile; the creation blessing/commission language of Gen.1 is absent.

The stamp names a woman/role ('woman_wisdom'), but no clause here presents wisdom as a woman or personified female figure; the cited verse Ecc.2.13 only says wisdom has an advantage over folly. Nothing in the section supports a female wisdom role.
As with woman_wisdom: folly appears in Ecc.2.13#cl1 merely as the lesser of two compared things ('wisdom exceeds folly'), never as a female person. No clause supports a woman/folly role.

No clause pronounces or describes a judgment; the single 'fate' (Ecc.2.14#cl3/cl4) is a shared mortality, not a judicial verdict, and nothing addresses God as judge. The word does not carry the stamp.
The whole movement of vv.14–16 is the opposite: one fate overtakes both, and the wise die like the fool with no remembrance. No clause offers mercy, rescue or restoration.
Ecc.2.16#cl1–cl2 speak only of being forgotten in the days to come, and the section ends in hatred of life and work under the sun (Ecc.2.17#cl0–cl3). Nothing here implies new creation.
The cited verse's grief, sorrowful task and unresting mind (Ecc.2.23#cl0-cl2) are the section's drift of toil and sorrow, but no clause in it speaks of sin, exile or death.
"sons of men" (Ecc.3.10#cl1/cl2) is the idiom for humankind, not God as father; the section nowhere presents God in a father role.
The section's 'two are better than one' companionship has no covenant-people reference; it is the general drift of the stamp, not any clause.
Nothing in the section portrays the king as beast-like or as a beast; the king is called 'old but foolish' and unable to take a warning, which is a failure of discernment, not beastliness.

Eccl 4:16 speaks of the endless crowd and the successor being uncelebrated, and closes with futility ('pursuit of the wind'). There is no sin, no exile and no death in the clause, and 'futile' is not one of the three ideas the stamp names.

The Hebrew of 5:1 (MT 4:17) has 'give ear to listen' and no word for sacrifice; the clause list for this section contains no clause about offering a sacrifice. The English 'sacrifice of fools' is the translator's supplied reading (cf. 1 Sam 15:22), and the digest says an English word the Hebrew does not have is not evidence. No clause carries the idea.

No clause names sin, exile or death. Only #cl1/#cl3 speak of missing the mark ('inadvertence', שְׁגָגָה) and #cl5 of ruin of one's work. Sin, exile and death are three separate ideas; the section carries at most a word for inadvertent wrong and no exile or death, so the stamp does not fit.
No clause names mercy, forgiveness, restoration or return; the section's only movement is warning (God's anger, ruin of work, fear God), with no note of pardon or restoration in the clauses given.
No clause mentions a covenant, its parties, stipulations or signs; the vow clauses (Ecc.5.3#cl0/#cl1, Ecc.5.4#cl0-#cl3) are voluntary vows, not covenant language (בְּרִית does not occur).
The cited verse's labourer is a hired day-worker (Hebrew "laborer/worker"), not a slave or bondservant; no clause in the section speaks of slavery or bondage.
The gift in the cited verse is wealth, riches and the power to enjoy them given to every man, not the Spirit or a spiritual gift; no clause in the section speaks of the Spirit or of spiritual gifts.

This is the section's general wisdom drift (the carpe diem/"this is his lot" wisdom of Ecclesiastes), but no single clause states law or wisdom as such; the nearest clauses (Ecc.5.17#cl4/#cl5/#cl11) only describe eating, drinking, enjoying one's toil and one's portion.
The cited verse's giving is a gift to enjoy, not mercy shown to the guilty nor a restoration; no clause in the section speaks of forgiveness, rescue or restoration.

The cited verse's creation theme is only the earth and its produce as background to the section; no clause states God's creating, and Ecc.5.8#cl0 ("profit of a land") and Ecc.5.8#cl2 ("a king to a field he has been served") are land/field, not creation. General drift only.
The cited verse has God giving wealth, riches and the power to enjoy them, with no commission, mandate or charge to the man; no clause in the section speaks of being sent or commanded to a task.

Nothing in the section speaks of mercy or restoration: God withholds enjoyment (Ecc.6.2#cl4), the dead child has only rest/darkness (Ecc.6.4#cl0-cl2, Ecc.6.5#cl2), and all go to the same place with no reversal (Ecc.6.6#cl2). The stamp is the opposite of the section's drift.

Nothing in Eccl.7.1-14 speaks of mercy, forgiveness, or restoration; 7:3 (sorrow is better than laughter; a sad countenance is good for the heart) is a wisdom maxim about sorrow's benefit, not mercy or restoration, and no clause carries those ideas.

The verse cited (7:19) is about wisdom making a man stronger than ten rulers in a city; no clause in this section speaks of law/Torah. The one clause that might suggest it, Ecc.7.18#cl3, says only one fearing God will follow both warnings.
Eccl 8:8 speaks of death and wickedness not releasing its owners; no clause in this section describes an act of judging or a verdict.
The section's drift — the king's supreme word, the right time and procedure, wickedness not releasing its owners — touches accountability, but no clause in it names a judgment.
No clause in Eccl 8:10-13 states a curse; 8:13 says only that it will not go well with the wicked and their days will not lengthen, which is a consequence stated as fact, not a curse pronounced.
The section's only positive note is commendation of eating, drinking and joy under the sun (Ecc.8.15#cl0, cl3); nothing speaks of mercy, forgiveness or restoration.
No judge, judging, or courtroom figure appears anywhere in Eccl 9:1-6; the cited verse 9:1 speaks of God's hand holding the righteous, wise and their deeds, not of God as judge passing verdicts.
No king or royal figure is named or implied in these clauses ('God' in Ecc.9.1#cl3 is not a king stamp); the section is about the common fate of all humans.
The cited 9:2 contrasts righteous/wicked, clean/unclean, sacrificer/non-sacrificer — all individuals, not nations; 'all' ((the) all) is humanity in general, not nations acting as a character.
Nothing in 9:3 (or the section) speaks of a curse, cursing, or cursedness; 'This is an evil' (Ecc.9.3#cl0) is a moral judgment on the common fate, not a curse.
The section speaks only of death and the dead joining the dead (Ecc.9.3#cl5, Ecc.9.5#cl2-3, Ecc.9.6#cl0); no raising, reviving or coming back to life is stated or implied.
The 'dog' and 'lion' of 9:4 (Ecc.9.4#cl3, Ecc.9.4#cl4) are compared for being alive versus dead; no shepherd, flock or herding image appears.
The animals in Ecc.9.4#cl3-cl4 ('a live dog is better than a dead lion') are a proverb about hope for the living, not a ruler depicted as a beast.
'They have no further reward' (Ecc.9.5#cl4) and 'their memory is forgotten' (Ecc.9.5#cl5) describe the dead's loss of share under the sun, not a judgment event or verdict.
No books, records or opening of books appear; the only 'remembering' language is the negative 'the memory of them is forgotten' (Ecc.9.5#cl5).
The wise deliverer is explicitly 'a poor wise man' (Ecc.9.15#cl0, 'a man poor wise'); no woman and no woman's wisdom appears in the section.
The section's cited verse contrasts wisdom with 'strength' and no warrior or fighting man is named; the king of 9:14 is not called a warrior.
Wisdom here is practical deliverance of a city and the worth of calm words (Ecc.9.15#cl1, Ecc.9.16#cl1, Ecc.9.17#cl0); nothing about law, Torah, or legal wisdom is said.

No clause names law, Torah, commandment or wisdom instruction; the section's imperatives to eat, drink, be white and enjoy life are not law-teaching. The reader's citation of 9:7 does not hold: 9:7 is blessing/joy, not law or wisdom. At most a distant wisdom-theme drift (Ecc.9.10#cl0 'do with strength your do' echoes a wisdom maxim), but no clause in particular carries law_wisdom.

Ecc.9.12 says no man knows his time and that evil time suddenly falls on men like a net or snare — that is calamity/fate, not divine judgment: no clause has God as judge, no verdict, no court, no sentence. Ecc.9.7#cl3 says God has already approved your works, which is approval, not judgment. The stamp fits the section's general drift of sudden ruin but no clause in particular carries judgment, so empty with general: true.

None of the three clauses carries the idea of witnessing/bearing testimony; cl0 gives Paul's office ('apostle ... by the will of God') and the addressees' identity, cl1 their location, cl2 a greeting. An apostle is a sent one, not a witness, and nothing here says Paul testifies to anything.
Eph 1:2 names 'God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ' but never calls Jesus the Son. The Greek behind Eph.1.2#cl0 has no 'son' word; the stamp is not carried by any clause of this section.
No clause here speaks of redemption, purchase, blood or deliverance; 'in Christ Jesus' in Eph.1.1#cl0 is an identifying phrase for the saints, not a statement of redemption.

The 'faithful' in Eph.1.1#cl0 is an adjective describing the addressees ('the faithful'), not God's faithfulness or a promise kept; Eph.1.2#cl0 has 'grace and peace' with no promise or covenant term. No clause states faithfulness or promise as such.

The only possible hook is 'Grace and peace' (Eph.1.2#cl0), which is a greeting/blessing, not mercy or restoration; no clause mentions mercy, forgiveness, healing or restoring. At most this is the letter's general drift, not something any clause says.

The section says God put everything under His feet (Eph.1.22#cl0) and subjected all things to Him as head (Eph.1.22#cl1), but there is no procession, no captured enemies led in triumph, and no train of captives or spoils in the text; the image of a triumph is read in from elsewhere.
The church is called His body and the fullness of Him who fills all in all (Eph.1.23#cl0, Eph.1.23#cl1); no bridal language, no husband/wife, no marriage appears in these verses.
The stamp requires temple or dwelling-place imagery; Eph.1.23#cl1 says He fills all in all, which is fullness and filling, not a temple, sanctuary or house where God dwells with His people.

The section speaks of redemption through His blood and forgiveness, but no clause names or describes a covenant; the stamp is a general theological reading of the passage rather than one carried by particular clauses.
No clause in the section uses firstborn language; the nearest is "we, who were the first to hope in Christ" (Eph.1.12#cl1), which is about prior hope, not firstborn status.
Nothing in the section speaks of judgment; the closest is "the redemption of those who are God's possession" (Eph.1.14#cl0), which is redemption, not judgment.
Eph 2:8 ("by grace you have been saved through faith") speaks of salvation by grace, not of a covenant; nothing in the section mentions a covenant, its parties, or its making.
No clause in this section names Christ as priest or describes priestly mediation; the section speaks of access to the Father, not of a priestly office.
No clause in this section calls Christ the Son; He is named as Christ Jesus only.

No clause in this section speaks of a covenant or its making: the section speaks of citizenship, household, foundation, building, temple and Spirit, not of a covenant (contrast 'covenant' language, absent here).
The temple here is being built up and growing (Eph.2.21#cl0), not destroyed; no clause mentions destruction.
The dwelling place spoken of is a building/temple being built of people, not new heavens and earth; no clause mentions a renewed cosmos.
The section's drift (reconciliation and building in Christ) touches redemption, but no clause names redemption, ransom, blood, forgiveness or cross.
Christ is called the cornerstone, but no clause says a stone was rejected; that element is absent from this section.

Eph.3.6 speaks of Gentiles as fellow heirs, fellow members of the body and fellow partakers of the promise in Christ, but no covenant, its newness, nor covenant language ("covenant", "new") appears anywhere in this section; "the promise" is a promise, not stated as a covenant.
No clause in this section uses covenant language; Eph.3.6's "the promise in Christ Jesus" is the nearest thing, and it is a promise, not stated as a covenant.

The only candidate is the posture 'I bow my knees' (Eph.3.14#cl0), but the clause carries no priestly role, cult, temple or mediation language; there is no named intercessor-priest here, and the section is a prayer-report/doxology, so the stamp is not pinned by any clause.

The petition 'that He might give you according to the riches of His glory' (Eph.3.16#cl0) is a request for divine giving; no single clause states a blessing as an event, so the stamp describes the section's drift rather than any clause in particular.
Eph.3.17#cl0 speaks only of Christ dwelling in the hearts through faith; no covenant formula ('I will be your God', 'new covenant') is stated or alluded to in the clause.

cl0/cl1 ask God for the Ephesians ('I ask that He might give you ...'), but a petition for another's benefit is not intercession performed in a priestly role; nothing in the clauses mentions a priest, altar, or mediation.
Eph.3.17#cl0 has 'Christ may dwell in your hearts' — no David, no throne, no offspring/kingdom promise is mentioned in the clause.
The clause has Christ indwelling believers, not the Word becoming flesh / God sending His Son in the flesh (the direction is the reverse of incarnation).
Eph.3.17#cl0 contains no rising, tomb, or raising language; the indwelling of Christ is not the resurrection event.
No ascent, heaven-taking, or enthronement language in the cited clause or section.
The Spirit is named ('through His Spirit', Eph.3.16#cl1), but nothing states the coming of the Spirit at Pentecost (no tongues of fire, no sound, no 'when the day of Pentecost came').
No clause speaks of God or anyone sending (ἀποστέλλω/πέμπω); 'He might give you' (Eph.3.16#cl0) is giving, not sending of a messenger.
'together with all the saints' (Eph.3.18#cl1) is the company the Ephesians comprehend with, not a role of witnessing or testifying; the clause has no witness content.
Eph.3.20 is a doxology ('to Him be the glory'); the clause 'being able to do exceedingly above all things' (Eph.3.20#cl1) has power but no kingship, throne, reign or royal title.
No servant language, service role, or servant figure in the cited clause or the section.
Eph.3.14#cl0 names only 'the Father'; no 'Son' is named or addressed in the clause (Christ appears only later, in Eph.3.17#cl0, as dweller, not as Son to the Father).
'the church' (Eph.3.21) is the body in which glory is given, but nothing in the clause makes the church a bride (no husband/wife, wedding, or bridal imagery).
Nothing in Eph.3.21 (or the section) presents Christ as bridegroom; 'in Christ Jesus' is a sphere, not a marriage role.
'all the saints' (Eph.3.18#cl1) is the community of believers; the clause states no Israel identity, twelve tribes, or new-Israel idea.
'all the saints' (Eph.3.18#cl1) is explicitly all, not a remainder; no remnant language in the clause.
'every family in heaven and on earth' (Eph.3.15#cl0) is not 'the nations' as a character; the clause is about naming, not about the nations as an acting party.
No peace, covenant, or reconciliation language in Eph.3.17 or its clauses.
'every family in heaven and on earth' (Eph.3.15#cl0) mentions creation, but the clause speaks of deriving a name, not of a covenant made with creation.
No oath, promise to the patriarchs, or 'fathers' (=ancestors) language; 'the Father' (Eph.3.14#cl0) is God, not the patriarchs.
Eph 3:17 speaks of Christ dwelling in believers' hearts through faith and of being rooted and grounded in love; nothing about marriage or a marriage covenant appears anywhere in the section.
No mention of David, kingship, or an everlasting dynastic covenant; Eph 3:17's 'dwell in your hearts' is indwelling, not a Davidic covenant.
Eph 3:15's 'every family in heaven and on earth derives its name' is naming/derivation from the Father, not the Abrahamic covenant of blessing and descendants.
No flood, no sign, no Noahic covenant language; Eph 3:15's 'every family' is not the Noahic covenant.
Nothing of Sinai, law-giving, or the Mosaic covenant in the section; Eph 3:17 concerns Christ dwelling in the heart by faith.
No salt, no enduring-priestly/royal covenant motif; the cited verse Eph 3:17 does not speak to it.
No priesthood, zeal, or perpetual priesthood language anywhere in Eph 3:14-21.
No Shechem, no covenant-renewal scene; the section is a prayer for strengthening and comprehension.
The only candidate is 'the bond of peace' (4:3), which is Paul's exhortation, not a named covenant; no covenant is made or named in this section.
Eph 4:7 speaks of 'grace ... given according to the measure of the gift of Christ', not of purchase, blood, ransom or release; nothing in the section carries redemption.
Eph 4:13-16 speaks of maturity, growth and building up, in the image of a body, not of creation renewed; no creation language (kainos, ktisis, new birth, re-creation) appears.
Eph 4:10 has 'ascended above all the heavens' and 'fill all things' — dominion language, but no kingdom, king, reign or rule is named in this section.
Eph 4:6 has God 'over all and through all and in all' — omnipresence, not a temple; no house, dwelling, sanctuary or temple is named in this section.
The section's oneness statements and the citation of Ps 68:18 presuppose God's faithfulness, but no clause makes a promise or an act of faithfulness; general drift only.
Eph 4:2 has 'bearing with one another in love' and 4:15-16 growth in love — mutual forbearance and growth, not mercy shown or restoration to a former state.

Eph 4:8 is a citation of Scripture ('This is why it says'), but the section nowhere speaks of prophecy as utterance or of prophetic speech; 'prophets' in 4:11 is a church role, not the prophetic word.
Eph 4:1 names Paul as 'a prisoner in the Lord' and 4:9 Christ's descent — neither is the servant of Isaiah's songs bearing sin; nothing in this section carries that idea.
Eph 4:4 has 'one body ... one Spirit ... one hope' and 4:5 'one Lord, one faith, one baptism' — a confession of oneness, not a covenant made or named; no covenant language in the section.
Eph 4:13 has 'as we mature to the full measure of the stature of Christ' — conformity to Christ's measure, not the image of God (no eikon, no Gen 1 wording).
This is a section about the church as the body of Christ; nothing in it speaks of the created order (heaven and earth, creatures, Gen 1 wording).
Nothing here speaks of a covenant or its making; 4:24's 'new self' is the new man, not a covenant.
Cited verse is only 'do not give the devil a foothold'; the armor (Eph 6:10-18) is absent from this section.
Paul contrasts the kingdom of Christ and of God with the disobedient (5:5-7), not a kingdom split against itself over a ruler; no clause here speaks of a divided kingdom.
5:6 says the wrath of God 'is coming' on the sons of disobedience; the text names no day, no coming of the Lord, and no day-of-the-Lord language.
The 'sons of disobedience' in 5:6 are a moral category, not a nation or people-group standing as a character in the narrative.
Nothing in 5:1-7 speaks of being in Christ or joined to him; 'partakers with them' (5:7) concerns the disobedient, not union with Christ.
The section's horizon is Christ's self-offering 'for us' and escape from wrath, but no clause states mercy, forgiveness or restoration.

Eph.5.31#cl0-cl2 quote Gen 2:24 ('leave...be united...one flesh'), a marriage ordinance/one-flesh union, not a covenant-making; nothing in the section says 'covenant', and the husband-wife relation is made a figure of Christ and the church (Eph.5.32#cl1), so a marriage covenant is not asserted here.
The Greek mysterion in 5:32 is the Christ-church secret just revealed, not diatheke; no covenant-making, blood, or covenant formula appears in any clause here.
No clause names a covenant, covenant-making, oath, or covenant formula; the one-flesh quotation in Eph.5.31#cl0-cl2 is marriage language used as a figure (Eph.5.32#cl1), not a covenant.
Eph.5.24 mentions only the church's subjection to Christ, with no king, kingdom (basileia), rule, throne or reign language anywhere in the section.

'redemption', 'ransom', 'blood', 'cross' do not occur in this section, and the clause the reader cites (Eph.6.19#cl0-1, boldness to make known the mystery of the gospel) is about proclamation, not redemption. A key NT redemption phrase does occur in the parallel passage Col.4.3 ('mystery of Christ'), but that is not this text. Nothing in this section states the idea.

'kingdom' does not occur in the section, and the powers named in Eph.6.12#cl0 ('rulers', 'authorities', 'cosmic powers', 'spiritual forces of evil') are the hostile powers, not the kingdom of God; the clause is evidence of conflict, not of the kingdom as a theme of this section.

The reader cites Eph.6.19#cl0, but that clause asks for 'utterance'/'word' to proclaim the gospel; the word revealed is 'the mystery of the gospel', not prophecy. 'prophecy'/'prophet' does not occur in the section; the only 'word of God' clause (Eph.6.17#cl1) is the sword of the Spirit, not a prophetic word.
The only clause that could carry it, Eph.6.24#cl0, is a closing grace-wish addressed to 'all those loving the Lord of us Jesus Christ'; nothing in the section says covenant, new, or its mediation.
No clause here speaks of purchase, ransom or release; Eph.6.24#cl0 asks grace for those who love the Lord, not redemption.
The section's drift is encouragement and peace (Eph 6:22-23), but no clause names mercy or restoration.
Eph.6.9#cl3 says 'the master is in the heavens' (ho kyrios), not a king or kingship; 'your Master and yours' is lordship, and no clause here speaks of a king.

No clause here speaks of a people or nation belonging to God; the section addresses 'slaves' and 'masters' (Eph.6.5#cl1; Eph.6.9#cl0) as categories of household, and 'slave or free' (Eph.6.8#cl4-5) is not a people.
Eph.6.9#cl3 says 'the master is in the heavens' — a place of rule, not a kingdom; no clause names a kingdom or its citizens.

Esth 1:6 lists palace furnishings (hangings, silver rings, marble pillars, gold and silver couches) in the king's garden court, not an idol or an abomination standing in a holy place; there is no idol and no holy place in the clause, so the stamp is wrong for this section.
Persia and Media are named only as the king's realm and its provinces here; no nation is presented as a speaking or acting character.
Disobeying the king's command is not sin in this text, nobody is exiled, and no death is spoken of; the stamp's three elements are all absent.
The “peoples” here are the empire's subject populations addressed by decree; Israel is not named or referred to, so the stamp does not apply to this section.

Nothing in Esth.1.9-12 speaks of sin, exile or death: Vashti's refusal, the king's anger, and a banquet are all that this section contains. The theme's second and third elements have no clause at all here.

No clause adjudicates or sentences anyone: the king's anger (Est.1.12#cl3, Est.1.12#cl4) is wrath, and Vashti's refusal (Est.1.12#cl0) is the deed, not a verdict. If the stamp means divine judgment it is wrong here; if it means the king's displeasure as a precursor to Vashti's deposition, that verdict falls outside this section.

No covenant, oath, or covenant party appears in Esth.1.9-12; the king's marriage to Vashti is nowhere framed as covenant, and the section is a Persian court banquet and refusal, so the stamp does not apply.

No clause presents Mordecai (or anyone) as a servant. He is 'second only to King Xerxes' (Est.10.3#cl0) and one 'whom he had made great' (Est.10.2#cl1) — a subordinate royal official, but the text never uses servant language; 'second to' is rank, not service.

No clause in this section states a divine promise, or God's faithfulness in keeping one; nothing in the text is attributed to God. If the stamp means the narrator's faithfulness in recording events, the text does not say that either. What is present — the king's favour to Mordecai and Mordecai's good to his people (10:3) — is not covenant promise.

Nothing in these four verses speaks of exile or of exaltation; Israel's exile is not referenced. The reader cited Esth 2:4, but the clause there, Est.2.4#cl0, is the choice of a young woman to become queen, not a reversal of fortune of an exile and no such clause is here. At most the section is the general antecedent of that reversal (Esther's later elevation), which the text does not state in this section.

No clause here speaks of belief, faith, or an outsider coming to faith; the section is about gathering beautiful young women and the king's favour, and Esther is not named (only 'the young woman who pleases the king'), and nobody believes anything. The reader cited Esth 2:3, but no clause there carries this idea.

The Hebrew of 2:17-20 never calls Esther a bride or describes a marriage; cl0 speaks of the king's love and cl1 of her finding favor, and the crown/queenship of cl2-cl3 is a royal appointment, not a wedding. Calling her 'bride' reads marriage into the text.

No clause in the section has anyone observing, testifying or attesting anything; the nearest is Mordecai sitting at the gate (cl2 of 2:19), which is presence, not witness. The stamp can only be said to fit the section's general drift, if at all.

Mordecai 'was sitting at the king's gate' (Est.2.19#cl2) — the Hebrew verb is sitting, not guarding or keeping; he is a bystander at the gate, and no gatekeeping role or act is stated. The Berean text says 'sitting', not 'guarding'.
This section shows no exile or exaltation; no clause carries the movement. Only the cited verse number matches.
No clause speaks of belief or of an outsider coming to faith; the eunuchs conspire, Mordecai reports, the officials are hanged. The stamp does not belong to this section.
The section records a plot, a report and executions; no death here produces life or deliverance in the clauses given.

Esther is not presented as a bride: Est.2.13#cl3 and Est.2.16#cl0 say only that she was taken to the king, and Est.2.14#cl1–cl2 place her not with a husband but among the concubines in the second harem, to be sent for again only if the king delighted in her (Est.2.14#cl3–cl5). No clause names a marriage.

The same ground as bride: Xerxes is never called a bridegroom, and the only clauses about the king in this connection (Est.2.14#cl3–cl5, Est.2.16#cl0) describe his palace and concubine harem, not a wedding.

No clause of Esth.2.5–16 states faith or belief, and the outsider status that is present (Est.2.5#cl0, Est.2.6#cl0) is not tied to believing anything; what Est.2.9 says is Hegai’s favour toward Esther (she bore favor before him), not her trust in God.
No clause in this section states a promise or covenant, nor God’s faithfulness to it; the cited verse (Est.2.6) speaks only of the exile to Babylon (Est.2.6#cl0–cl3).
The section has plotted death and an exilic scattering, but no clause in Esth 3 names sin or exile as such; the stamp describes the book's larger drift rather than anything this text says.
Nothing in this section moves from humiliation to vindication; Mordecai's refusal and Haman's exaltation only set up later reversal.
No outsider comes to faith anywhere in this section; Mordecai is the one standing firm (3:4), and no non-Jew is said to believe anything about God.
The one clause that could fit, Mordecai's refusal (3:2), is his faithful dissent, not a failure of an insider; the section contains no insider failing.
No clause here speaks of a surviving remnant: 4:14 says the Jews as a whole will be delivered, and 'you and your father's house will perish' is the reverse idea.
4:16 speaks of fasting and of Esther risking death ('if I perish, I perish'), not of humiliation reversed into vindication.
The section has no servant of the Lord who suffers for others and is vindicated; Esther's self-offering in 4:16 is not the Servant motif.
No divine promise or covenant oath is quoted or invoked anywhere in these clauses.
No clause here speaks of restoration; 4:14 speaks of relief and deliverance in the crisis, not of restoration after judgment.
No clause speaks of exile or of return from exile; the section's drift is Esther's rise in the court, not exile.
No clause names Israel, the Jews or a people; the stamp is the book's larger frame, absent from this section's clauses.
The stamp fits the section's banquet setting, but the clauses present Esther only as the one who prepared the feast and invited, not as acting the host in any clause here.
The clauses speak of Haman's promotion only; nothing here states a prior exile or low condition from which he rose, so the reversal is not present in this section.
Mordecai's refusal to rise is the one dishonored party's stance in the clauses, but no clause shows Mordecai humiliated and then vindicated; his vindication lies outside this section.
The section moves toward a death (the gallows), which is the 'death' side of the pattern, but no clause speaks of sin or exile.
No clause here enacts or announces a judgment: Est.7.5#cl2–cl3 ask who devised the scheme and only identify a culprit; the king's condemnation of Haman is not in this section.

The section speaks of Esther's plea for her life and her people's lives being sold to destruction (Est.7.3#cl5–cl6, Est.7.4#cl0), not of a movement from exile to exaltation; no clause carries that reversal.
As a theme the section shows accusation and terror, not judgment executed or declared; the king only asks who the schemer is (Est.7.5#cl2–cl3) and no sentence is passed.

The clause at Est.7.4#cl0 ('we have been sold... to annihilate, to kill and to destroy') is a whole people sold to death plus the speaker, not a servant who suffers on others' behalf; the stamp's servant figure is not present.

No clause in this section speaks of exile or of exaltation: Haman is hanged and the king's fury subsides, and Mordecai's elevation comes later (Esth 8). The verse cited (7:10) contains the hanging, not a return from exile or a rise to honour.
No priest appears in this section; Esther is a queen, not a priest, and nothing here concerns cultic mediation between God and people.
Nothing in these clauses presents Esther as a wisdom figure; she weeps, begs, and petitions, none of which is a wisdom motif in the text.
The king here awards an estate, extends the scepter and receives a petition; no clause depicts him as beastly or tyrannical, unlike the cited verse's context in Daniel.
No clause pronounces judgment; the section reports the king's gift and Esther's petition, and judgment against Haman is only implied by the estate's transfer.
No clause in this section speaks of a promise or of faithfulness to one; the deliverance comes by royal decree, not by appeal to a promise.
No clause describes a procession, parade, triumph, or celebratory march; the only movement is armed assault (Est.9.1#cl4, Est.9.2#cl0) and no clause names a return or a public display of captives.

Exile_to_exaltation needs exile and return from it; no clause in the section mentions exile, captivity, deportation, or a return, and Est.9.4 (Mordecai's greatness) is the cited verse's content without the exile half.

The section has no procession, triumph, parade or public display of captives/spoils. The Jews assemble (Est.9.15#cl0, Est.9.16#cl0), kill, and rest; the only public display is of Haman's sons' bodies on the gallows (Est.9.14#cl3), which is an execution, not a victory procession.

The section is full of killing by armed groups (Est.9.15#cl2, Est.9.16#cl4), but no clause in it presents the Jews, the king, or anyone as a warrior: there is no armor, weapon, fighting, or named combatant. The deeds of the 'warrior' are here while the warrior, as a role, is not.

No nation (goy) is named or personified in this section. The agents are named individuals/groups: the king, Esther, the Jews, Haman, and 'those who hated them'. A collective enemy does not make nations a character here.

The cited verse Esth 9:13 is Esther's petition about who may act tomorrow, not a rise from exile to honour.
Haman's plot is described as a plan to destroy the Jews (cl0) and a lot cast to disturb and destroy (cl2); nothing in this section narrates fighting, armies, or combat.
The section has rest from enemies (Est.9.22#cl1) and feasting, but no procession, march, or public triumph.
Est.9.27 has the Jews imposing the custom on themselves and their descendants, not swearing an oath or invoking a curse on themselves.
Est.9.25 records the king's counter-decree returning Haman's scheme on his own head; there is no indictment, plaintiff, or covenant charge.
Est.9.28 speaks of every generation, family, province and city remembering the days; there is no surviving residue-after-judgment idea.
Mordecai and Esther are named by title and lineage, not as servants or slaves; no service relationship is predicated of anyone in the section.
Est.9.29 has Esther and Mordecai writing with full authority, which is authority within the Persian court rather than return from exile; nothing here speaks of exile or restoration to the land.
The only ingathering language is 'all who join them' (Est.9.27#cl0), which is about joining the Jews' observance, not about an outsider coming to faith.
Joseph's death and the generation passing is not suffering servanthood; no clause in this section speaks of a servant who suffers, and the stamp's own citation (1:6) is about dying, not affliction.
The section's affliction is of the Israelites as a people under forced labor, not of a servant figure who suffers for others; nothing points to an individual suffering servant.
No covenant, covenant formula, or covenant-making appears anywhere in this section; the midwives' fear of God (Exo.1.17#cl0; Exo.1.21#cl1) is not a covenant statement.

The section concerns the tenth plague and Israel's distinction, but no clause speaks of the passover rite or the passing over of Israelite houses; the stamp is the drift of the surrounding narrative, not any clause here.

No clause in this section states a covenant, covenant formula, or covenant-making act; Exod 12:13 speaks of a sign and of passing over, not of a covenant, and the section's nearest neighbours (12:14-20) are where the ordinance is made perpetual.
No clause indicts, accuses or brings a case against anyone; the section is instruction and narrative, not lawsuit.
The tenth plague on the firstborn is not stated; 12:23 says the LORD strikes the Egyptians and the destroyer strikes the houses, with no mention of firstborn.
No priest appears in the section; the cited 12:28 names only Moses and Aaron, and Aaron is not called priest here.
No prophet or prophetic speech occurs; Moses is not called or presented as a prophet in this section.
No servant figure or service of a servant to a master is spoken of.
No priestly office or cultic personnel appear; the hyssop and blood action at the door is done by each household, and the cited 12:21 concerns the elders slaughtering the Passover.

The slaying of the firstborn is the event the Passover is named for and follows the Passover instructions, but no clause in these two verses names or describes the Passover itself; its clauses are about the LORD, the firstborn, Pharaoh's rising, the wailing and the dead.
Israel is never mentioned in these two verses; the strike on Egypt is the turning point by which Israel is delivered, but no clause here speaks of Israel's release or going out.
