No clause in this section speaks of Sinai, the mountain, or the covenant made there; Exo.12.49#cl0 speaks of the same law for native and sojourner (a legal parity rule), not of the Sinai covenant. Possible mis-citation or a very loose thematic link.
The section ends with the exodus from Egypt 'by their divisions' (Exo.12.51#cl1); nothing here mentions the sea, the crossing, or the Egyptians drowning.
The law as sign, memorial and teaching on the lips (Exod 13:9) is a general legal-pedagogical drift; no clause in this section presents the law as wisdom per se.

The section speaks only of redeeming firstborn donkeys and sons (Exo.13.13#cl0, #cl3; Exo.13.15#cl5); nothing in the text refers to Christ, so the stamp is a later Christian reading, not an idea these clauses carry.

The section is the aftermath of the Exodus ("When Pharaoh let the people go"; "the Israelites left the land of Egypt"), but no clause performs or narrates the deliverance itself — the departure is presupposed throughout. General drift: true.
The pillars of cloud and fire are a theophany guiding Israel in the wilderness, not a temple or sanctuary presence; no tabernacle or temple is in view in these clauses.
Joseph's words in 13:19 are a deathbed oath and its fulfilment-instruction, not prophecy; nothing in this section is a prophetic utterance about the future.
The section is the approach to the sea and the encampment by it (Exo.14.2#cl2, Exo.14.9#cl1), but no clause narrates a crossing; the cited verse (14:13) speaks only of seeing the LORD's deliverance.

The section ends with Israel seeing the Egyptians dead on the shore and fearing/believing the LORD (14:30-31); there is no procession, no triumphal march, and no entry into a city or sanctuary anywhere in these verses.
Moses acts exactly as the LORD commands him (14:16, 21, 26-27), fulfilling his existing role; nothing in the section presents him as a new or second Moses.
Pharaoh's rule is only the object of the honor the LORD gains (14:18); the section names no kingdom, king, throne or reign as an idea of its own.
The section tells of rescue by the destruction of the Egyptian army, not of mercy or of restoration after ruin; no clause speaks of mercy or restoring.
The section has no covenant, oath, or covenant formula; Israel's response is fear and belief in the LORD and in Moses (14:31), which is not a covenant-making.
No clause in the section names a servant; the people are called redeemed/bought (Exo.15.13#cl0, Exo.15.16#cl4), not servants.
No clause speaks of a firstborn; nothing in the Hebrew glosses of this section carries the idea.
No clause speaks of a remnant; the whole people pass by (Exo.15.16#cl2, #cl4).
Exo.15.13#cl0 has only 'your covenant loyalty' (hesed), not a covenant with Abraham named.
No clause mentions an oath or the fathers (cf. Exo.15.2#cl3, which names 'my father's God' but not an oath).

The section speaks of Yahweh redeeming Israel out of Egypt in the past/exodus ('you have redeemed', 'the people You have bought'), which is the exodus redemption, not redemption in Christ; no clause in this section names or implies Christ or a messianic redemption. The stamp is a NT theme being read onto a historical exodus song.

The song is future-oriented (will lead, will bring them in, nations will hear, the LORD will reign), but no clause in the section is a prophetic utterance by a prophet or an explicit 'thus says the LORD' word. It is a victory song with future confidence, not a prophetic word in the narrow sense; the drift is general.
No rock and no water from a rock here: the bitter water of Marah is sweetened by a log cast into it (Exo.15.25#cl1, Exo.15.25#cl3).
There is no accusation, no summons and no indictment: the LORD gives statute and ordinance and tests Israel (Exo.15.25#cl4, Exo.15.25#cl5), then blesses obedience.
The section speaks of statutes, commands and doing right (Exo.15.26), but no clause presents law as wisdom.
No servant of the LORD bears suffering here; the sick are the Egyptians (Exo.15.26#cl5) and Israel is promised healing.
Moses receives and relays the LORD's word, but no clause in this section names or portrays the role of prophet; nothing in 16:6 (cited) does.
Aaron and Moses appear, but no clause here presents priestly action or role; 16:6 ('you will know that it was the LORD who brought you out of the land of Egypt') is about deliverance, not priesthood.
Egypt is mentioned only in the clauses of Israel's going out ('from the land of Egypt'); no clause in Exod 16:1 portrays a nation acting as a character in the narrative.

Sinai covenant is established in Exod 19-24; in Exod 16:22-30 the only covenant-linked language is 'My commandments and instructions' (Exo.16.28#cl1), which is Sinai law anticipated, not the covenant-making at Sinai itself. The English chapter context names Mount Sinai only later (Exod 19).
Nothing in the section frames obedience as wisdom; the Sabbath command is stated as divine command and reported as obeyed (Exo.16.24#cl0, Exo.16.30#cl0) rather than as wisdom teaching.

The jar of manna is placed before the LORD / before the Testimony (Exo.16.33#cl3, 16.34#cl2), not in the tabernacle's furniture; no item of tabernacle equipment (ark, lampstand, altar, table) is named here.

the section has no sin, exile or death: the people's failure is contention and testing (Exo.17.2#cl0, Exo.17.2#cl5, Exo.17.2#cl6; Exo.17.7#cl1, Exo.17.7#cl4), and they are still in the wilderness, not exiled, though death by thirst is wished for in Exo.17.3#cl5

Nothing in this section depicts a procession or triumphal march; Joshua's victory is a battlefield rout with the sword (Exod 17:13), and the only movement is Moses and the elders going up the hill and the stone being placed for Moses to sit on.
No judge is raised, appointed or commissioned here; Joshua is chosen as a military commander (Exod 17:9) and Moses judges nothing, and the section names no deliverer who judges Israel.

The section contains no oath: Moses builds an altar and names it (Exod 17:15), and the LORD's declaration in Exod 17:16 is a divine assertion, not a sworn oath formula with the usual 'as I live' or imprecation.
Jethro is called a priest (Exo.18.1#cl0), but the section shows no priestly office, line or function beyond the title; the stamp is the section's general background rather than carried by any clause.

The section recounts the LORD's completed acts for Israel (Exo.18.1#cl1, Exo.18.8#cl1) but nowhere mentions a promise, oath or covenant being kept; only the general drift of God's goodness to His people is in view.

The Sinai covenant itself is not narrated here; Israel is only named (25:25#cl0 'from all Israel') and God's statutes/laws are mentioned, but no covenant-making, mountain, or covenant formula occurs in these verses. I flag this as a stamp that may belong elsewhere.
The section is command and covenant address, not wisdom instruction; no clause speaks of wisdom.
God's carrying of Israel is past deliverance, not mercy on the guilty; no restoration or mercy to the failing appears in this section.
No clause in this section states or narrates the giving of the law; the section is the theophany, the boundary warnings and Moses' descent. The law's words begin at 20:1, outside this section.
The section contains no clause about wisdom or the wisdom of the law; at most the boundary command ('Put a boundary around the mountain and set it apart as holy') is law, not wisdom.

The clause at 19:24 is a prohibition with a threat ('must not break through … or He will break out against them'), not an act of mercy or restoration; nothing in the section restores or spares anyone.
No clause in this section speaks of kingship, a kingdom or rule; the divine descent in fire and smoke does not state it.
"firstborn" is not in the text of Exod 2:1-10; the section says only she conceived and bore a son ("a son", not a firstborn), and whether this child is firstborn is never stated.
This section is the birth and naming of Moses himself; there is no second figure presented as a new Moses here, so the typology has no clause in this section.
No clause in this section states or appeals to a promise of God; the theme is only an inference from the wider Exodus narrative.

No clause here has an outsider believing anything; Pharaoh's daughter shows compassion (Exo.2.6#cl4) and speaks of the child, but belief/faith is nowhere in the text, and the stamp describes the section's general drift at most.
No clause in this section speaks of death; the child is preserved alive throughout (hidden, drawn out, nursed), so the reversal is not present.
The section has no victory or defeat; the child is hidden, and no conflict between the weak and the strong is stated.
The section shows exile only (Moses flees and sojourns in Midian); no clause reverses it into exaltation — he stays a foreigner (Exo.2.22#cl3).
Moses helps the daughters and is given Zipporah and a home in Midian, but no clause presents him as humiliated and then publicly vindicated.
No clause records anyone believing or coming to faith; the 'Egyptian' theme at Exo.2.19#cl1 is a misidentification by the daughters, not belief.

The section speaks only of God remembering His covenant with the fathers; no clause mentions an oath, swearing, or the fathers as recipients of a sworn promise. The Hebrew here (berith) is covenant, not oath (shevu'ah).
The Hebrew of 20:7 is 'take the name... for emptiness' (נשא שם לשוא), a prohibition of misusing the LORD's name, not of swearing oaths; the clause text here has no oath-taking word.
The section gives the law of the divine king, but no clause names a kingdom, king or throne.
The section speaks to the fear of God and refraining from sin, which is wisdom's summary; no clause states wisdom or teaching, so the stamp is only the section's general drift.
No clause in this section speaks of mercy, forgiveness or restoration: the words here are fear, testing, distance, thick darkness and not sinning.
The section is apodictic prohibition and cultic instruction; no clause states or reasons from wisdom, and no motive clause here is a wisdom saying.
The section forbids making gods at all (20:23) and regulates the altar (20:24-26); no clause places an idol in a sanctuary, and there is no sanctuary in view.

Two notes: (a) Exo.21.9#cl0 is the only clause that actually makes the son a party ('for son his he will designate her'), so the stamp's cited verse is genuine; (b) but the 'son' here is a person to whom the servant-woman is designated, not a role that acts, and the closing slave release in v.11 has no son in it. The stamp is thin/general for this section; I include v.11 only as the outcome of v.9's arrangement, not as itself about a son.

The stamp is the section's general frame (case law given to Israel), not carried by any particular clause.
No clause speaks of a stranger/sojourner; v.35 is about a neighbour's ox.

No clause in the section names a sojourner, resident alien, or foreigner; the parties are 'a man', 'his neighbor', 'the owner', 'the judges'. No clause names Sinai, Moses, or the making of the covenant; the section is simply part of the legislation given there. The stamp is the general setting, not something a clause asserts.
The section is legal material, but no clause expresses wisdom reflection or motive in the wisdom style; it states enforceable statutes. I find no clause in this section carrying the theme.

The section's drift is legal instruction (you shall not / do not throughout), but no clause in particular states or carries the wisdom idea; the reader cited v.1, whose clauses are prohibitions about a false report and a malicious witness.
The section is part of the Sinai covenant speech, but no clause names Sinai, the covenant, or its making; the cited verse Exod 23:10 only gives the sabbatical-year law.
The section is legal instruction (sabbatical year, sabbath, no other gods), fitting the law/wisdom theme as a whole, but no clause states wisdom, teaching, or the fear of the LORD.

The section stands within the covenant legislation and opens 'everything I have said to you', but no clause speaks of covenant, its parties, or its making; the cited verse Exod 23:13 concerns other gods.
The section is case law (apodictic festival and offering rules) with no wisdom idiom, motive clause or appeal to understanding anywhere in these clauses.

No clause in the section speaks of a new Moses or of Moses as a figure to be recapitulated; the idea is not present.

Egypt's royal authority is the backdrop (Pharaoh, his officials, his palace, his magicians) but no clause states a kingdom or reign; the section's point is Pharaoh's refusal, not rule.
Nothing in 7:8-13 frees anyone; the sign only hardens Pharaoh, and the exodus deliverance has not yet happened.
The section touches the theme only as background (Pharaoh's hardening), with no clause about sin, exile or death.

The clause list supplied contains Exod 8:16-19 of a different passage (gnats narrative is Exod 8:16-19 in English; the clauses given are Exod 8:16-19 Hebrew numbering = Exod 8:20-23 English), so no clause here shows magicians' contest; I cannot pin it from these clauses
The clauses supplied contain no warrior imagery: Yahweh acts by sending a swarm and by making a ransom/separation (Exo.8.17#cl1, Exo.8.19#cl0), not as a fighting man

The throne, the glory and the voice are throne-chariot imagery; nothing in the clauses names a temple, sanctuary or house, so no clause in particular carries 'temple presence' as against 'theophany' in general.

Nothing in the section speaks of mercy, pardon or restoration; the closest clauses are the prophet's falling facedown and hearing a voice (Ezk.1.28#cl4, cl5), which is awe and commissioning, not restoration.

No clause in 1:4-14 contains speech, a word of the LORD, or a commissioning to speak; only the seer's vision is narrated. General to the book, not this section.
Fire and lightning are present but no clause states a judgment, verdict, or object of judgment; the reader's citation of 1:13 is the fire imagery, not judgment as such.

Wrong for this section: nothing here is collapsing, being dissolved or destroyed. The storm, fire and lightning are the ordered appearance of the living creatures and the glory; the heavens do not give way.

The glory is departing the city and standing on the mountain east of it (Ezk.11.23#cl1), not dwelling in the temple; no clause here speaks of the temple.

Ezk.12.25 is a first-person declaration, "I will speak ... and bring it to pass", not a woe; no clause here pronounces "woe to ...".

"None of My words ... delayed ... will be fulfilled" (Ezk.12.28#cl2, #cl5) is the section's drift - the announced end of delay upon a rebellious house - but no clause in this section narrates a judgment event.

No clause in this section mentions sin, exile or death; its subject is the proverb's delay and the fulfilment of the word.

Ezek 13:9 denies the false prophets a place in 'the council of My people', the register of the house of Israel and the land of Israel; that is exclusion from the people, not a remnant preserved or a remnant described in any clause here.

The section works out the breach between God and Israel (false prophecy, failed wall, exclusion from land and people) but never states covenant, oath or its stipulations; no particular clause names the covenant.

The idols are set up in the heart and the stumbling block 'before his face' (Ezk.14.3#cl1-2; Ezk.14.4#cl4-5), not in the temple or any holy place; no clause here places an idol in the sanctuary, which is the apocalyptic-crisis idea
The chapter lists sword, famine, wild beasts and plague as divine judgments; no clause mentions a besieging army, siege works or a city under siege, so the stamp is wrong for this section.

The clauses speak of wild beasts making the land childless and desolate so that no man passes through, and of cutting off man and beast; no sheep, flock, shepherd or scattering appears in this section.
No clause names the day of the LORD, darkness, or a coming day of visitation; the section is a sequence of four judgments with a remnant, not a day-of-the-LORD text.
The section is the comparison of Jerusalem to the wood of the vine in Ezek 15:2-5, but no clause in it reports Ezekiel performing an acted sign.
The section has no woe ('oy/hoy') and no curse-form address; it is a question-and-answer comparison ending in 'declares the Lord GOD' (Ezek 15:2-8).
No cutting, dividing, or oath-ratifying rite appears; the Hebrew verb here is כרת ('cut') only in the idiom 'cut a covenant', and nothing in the section enacts a cutting ceremony.

The section contains accusation and an indictment of adultery, but no lawsuit form here: no summons, no charges formally brought, no witnesses, no sentence — the rib genre's markers are absent; only the bare metaphor remains.

Idols are made and worshipped (Ezk.16.17-19), but no clause places an idol in a holy place — no temple, sanctuary or holy site is named in this section; the shrine-language is the 'lofty shrines' and 'mounds' of 16:24-25 that belong to the shrines themselves.

The section has 16:27's 'I stretched out My hand against you and reduced your portion', but there is no staff, no bread-staff, no breaking of a staff or image of a support removed; the stamp's image does not appear.
No sheep, flock, shepherding or scattering image occurs anywhere in Ezek 16:1-34; the giving over to the Philistines (16:27) is not a scattering of sheep.

The section speaks of Sodom, Samaria and Jerusalem being restored from captivity, but no clause narrates the exile itself as an event; the closest, Ezk.16.53#cl0, is about the reversal of captivity, not the exile.

The clause mentions detestable idols as the partners of Jerusalem's promiscuity, but nothing says an idol is enthroned, seated, or set up in God's place; the stamp's distinctive element is absent from the section.

The clauses here speak of an everlasting covenant and of establishing His covenant (Ezk.16.60#cl1; Ezk.16.62#cl0) but the word peace never appears; nothing in this section identifies the covenant as one of peace.

The only sacrificial language is the verb "I make atonement" (Ezk.16.63#cl3), which names no sacrifice, victim, altar or offering, so no clause here speaks of a sacrifice.
No clause in the section names a king or royal figure; the eagle, vine, cedar and seed are images with no explicit royal referent in this text.
The section presents trees, vine and seed as a political allegory whose referent is a kingdom/dynasty, but no clause names a kingdom or king explicitly.
This section (vv.1-10) is entirely threat: the vine is planted only in order to be uprooted and withered (vv.8-10); restoration after judgment comes in Ezek 17:22-24, beyond this section.

Nothing in the section describes the ruler as a beast, by animal imagery or otherwise: the king of Babylon and the vassal king are spoken of only as kings, and the only animal language (birds in the branches, 17:23#cl4) is not applied to a ruler

David is nowhere named and no clause identifies the shoot with a Davidic figure; the image is a cedar sprig, which in this chapter stands for the kingdom (cf. 17:4), so the Davidic reading is an inference, not something a clause says
Babylon, Egypt and 'all the trees of the field' (17:24) are named or imaged but none is given speech, agency as a character, or personified role in any clause of this section
The section has no staff, rod or broken-staff image in any clause; the oath and covenant are 'despised' and 'broken', and the supporting figure is a cedar, so the image is not verbally present here
No clause names vindication or a status of being humiliated then cleared; Ezk.17.24 restores status but no clause speaks of vindication.
The section's planting produces life but no clause states that a death is what produces it; that idea is not stated here.
The figurative role here is a lioness mother and her cubs, not a shepherd; no flock, feeding or failing-to-feed imagery occurs in the section, and the cited verse Ezek 19:2 names only a lioness.

The section is a lament (qina) over princes already fallen, with no 'woe to you' address, accusation or threatened judgment on a named addressee; the Hebrew lament form here is not a woe oracle, so none of the cited or surrounding clauses carries the stamp.

Nothing in the section restores: the mother's loss of hope and taking of another cub (Ezk 19:5) is the pivot to a second doomed lion, and the ending is lacking a branch fit for a scepter. The cited verse contains no mercy or restoration clause.

The section's drift is a mission of judgment to a rebellious house, but no clause in Ezek 2:1-10 pronounces judgment; the lamentation, mourning and woe scroll (Ezk.2.10#cl2) is content to be delivered, not an act of judgment, and the cited verse 2:10 only describes the scroll.

The suffering-servant figure (Isa 52-53) is absent: 2:6 only commands Ezekiel not to fear briers, thorns and scorpions, which is a threat of hostile hearers, not a servant suffering for others, and no clause here speaks of one being pierced, bearing sin, or being afflicted.

The chapter is divine speech throughout, but no clause in this section is a prophetic word spoken to the people; the nearest speech-acts (Ezk.20.18#cl0 'I said to their children') are commands, not prophecy.

No clause places an idol in the sanctuary or any holy place; this section's idolatry is 'hearts ... went after their idols' (Ezk.20.16#cl4) and 'idols of their fathers' (Ezk.20.24#cl3), and the uncleanness of Ezk.20.26 is by 'gifts—the sacrifice of every firstborn in the fire', not an idol set in a holy place.

No 'woe' (הוֹי) or equivalent cry of doom appears in any clause here; 20:32 is an oath that their plan will not happen ('what you have in mind will never come to pass'), which is a denial, not a woe-oracle. The stamp does not belong to this section.

No clause in this section mentions an altar (מִזְבֵּחַ) or its profanation. The cultic acts in 20:28 and the defilement in 20:31 are located at high hills, leafy trees and 'Bamah', not at the altar. The stamp is not true of this section.
No priest, Levite or priestly role appears in the section; offerings are made by the whole house of Israel (Ezk.20.40#cl2), not by priests.

No beast imagery attaches to the ruler here (no horns, beasts or animals at all in this section); the king of Babylon is presented as a diviner and besieger, not a beast.

The section has no flock, shepherd or scattering imagery at all; Ezek 21:12 speaks of the sword being 'wielded against My people' and princes 'tossed to the sword', not of sheep being scattered, so the stamp is wrong for this section.

Ezek 21:7 describes individual bodily terror ('every heart will melt... every knee will turn to water'), not nations or the earth shaking; no clause in the section speaks of the nations being shaken.

The Servant songs of Isaiah are not in view: Ezekiel is not a servant bearing sin for others; he is a sign who suffers the loss of his wife as an enacted oracle.
Nothing here marks a 'day': the text says 'when I lay My vengeance upon them', not 'in that day'. The oracle is a judgment saying; the day-of-the-Lord frame is not in these clauses.
The section never pronounces 'woe' (Hebrew hoy) over Moab; Ezek 25:8-11 is a 'because ... therefore' judgment oracle with no woe cry in the Berean text or the clause list.
Every speech act in the section is against Moab, Seir and the Ammonites; nothing is promised to Israel or any addressee within these clauses, so 'promise' mislabels the genre.
Nebuchadnezzar is presented as a human king with horses, chariots and troops (Ezk.26.7#cl1); nothing in the section figures him as a beast or beast-like ruler.
The section is unrelieved destruction of Tyre; there is no mercy or restoration anywhere in these clauses (the only 'again' is 'You will never be rebuilt', Ezk.26.14#cl2).
Jerusalem appears only as the object of Tyre's taunt (Ezk.26.2#cl1/#cl2); no clause addresses Israel as God's people or speaks of their standing with him.
Ezk.26.20 speaks of being brought down to the Pit, not of exile followed by exaltation; the section has no exaltation for Tyre.
Ezk.26.2 has Tyre gloating over Jerusalem's ruin and expecting to be filled; there is no reversal of first and last in the section.
The strong (Nebuchadnezzar, many nations) defeats Tyre; the section has no weak party overcoming a strong one.

The stamp needs an insider whose own position or privilege fails him. In Ezek 26:2 Tyre is an outsider gloating over Jerusalem's fall (Ezk.26.2#cl2, cl5, cl6: 'it.has.been.turned.over to me', 'I.will.be.filled'), and Tyre's own judgement in vv.3-21 is the subject, not an insider's failure. Being a reversal stamp about a privileged party losing standing, it does not fit a foreign city's schadenfreude; the only 'insider' element (Jerusalem's gate broken) is the object of the taunt, not a reversal of the taunter.

Ezek 26:20 is descent to the Pit and the land of the living with no raising up: Ezk.26.20#cl0 'I will send you down with those who have gone down of the pit', Ezk.26.20#cl1 'I will cause you to dwell in the earth of the lowest parts like waste places from long ago', Ezk.26.20#cl2 'not you.may.remain'. The section ends in non-existence (Ezk.26.21#cl1 'you.[will] not.[be]', cl3 'not you.will.be.found again forever'), so no clause yields life out of death; the cited verse is judgement-language only.

Ezek 26:6 is the slaughter of Tyre's mainland villages by the sword (Ezk.26.6#cl0 'daughters its which [are].on the land with the sword they.will.be.killed'), and the surrounding verses scatter or destroy Tyre and its people (Ezk.26.3#cl4, Ezk.26.4#cl0, Ezk.26.11#cl1) with no gathering of the scattered anywhere in the section. The nearest thing to gathering is plunder taken by the nations (Ezk.26.5#cl3 'it.will.become (into) spoil for the nations', Ezk.26.12#cl0), which is the opposite of a return.

The section is a lament over Tyre, not an address opening with 'Woe to you'; the nearest rhetorical utterance is the lament refrain at 27:32, but no clause pronounces woe. General drift rather than a specific clause.
Tyre is addressed as a city/merchant ship, not as a king; 27:33 mentions 'the kings of the earth' only as those Tyre enriched, which does not make kingship a theme of the section's clauses.
The section ends with 'you have come to a horrible end and will be no more'; it contains no word of mercy, restoration or return, and the cited verse 27:36 says the opposite.

The section never depicts the ruler of Tyre as a beast or with beast imagery; the words are heart/pride, wisdom, wealth, trading, swords and death. The stamp describes the tradition's later reading of such a figure, not anything a clause here says.
Nothing in the section presents Tyre or anyone as a witness; v.9 speaks only of the doomed ruler's boast in the presence of those who slay him, which is not bearing witness to anything.
The section speaks of a human ruler of Tyre, not of a beast or an anti-kingdom; v.2 says explicitly 'you are a man and not a god', and no beast imagery occurs anywhere in vv.1-10.

No clause presents the king of Tyre as a beast or beast-like ruler; he is a lamented human king, an anointed cherub, and a profaned tradesman. The passages' animal imagery belongs to other chapters, not here.

Wrong for this section: there is no beast, no anti-kingdom bloc, and no kingdom opposed to God. Tyre's king is a single anointed cherub-king who falls; 'kings' in 28:17 are spectators, not a competing empire.
Wrong for this section: nothing here opposes or rivals God's presence. The figure is a creature stationed within the holy sphere who profanes and is expelled; no false presence is set up against God.
Wrong for this section: the sequence is unmixed humiliation (28:17-19). This figure is never vindicated or restored; the section ends 'you will be no more'.
Wrong for this section: the death here produces nothing. The fire consumes him, he is reduced to ashes, and he 'will be no more'; no new life follows.

The section has revival (coming to life, Ezk.37.5#cl3, Ezk.37.10#cl2-3) but no clause in it speaks of repentance, confession, turning or mourning over sin; Ezek 37:14 has only Spirit-given life and return to the land.

Ezk.39.17#cl6#'a sacrifice great on the mountains of Israel' is a sacrificial feast, not a royal court. So the stamp is general to the section's drift and no clause carries it specifically.

The section has restoration, return and the outpouring of the Spirit, but no covenant is made or named: no clause contains 'covenant' (בְּרִית), no 'I will make/cut a covenant', and none of the covenant formula 'I will be their God and they shall be My people' (cf. which appears nowhere here). 'Hiding/not hiding My face' is idiom for favour or its withdrawal, not temple presence. The stamp is close to the section's drift but no clause states it, and as applied here it is a mismatch, so the list is empty.

No clause of Ezek.4.1-8 speaks of watching, warning or a watchman's office; v.7 has Ezekiel 'prophesy against' Jerusalem with his arm bared, which is siege-sign language, not the watchman role (that belongs to Ezek.3.17; 33.1-9). The stamp was cited from v.7 but no clause there carries it.

The section has Ezekiel bearing Israel's and Judah's iniquity (Ezk.4.4#cl2, Ezk.4.5#cl1, Ezk.4.6#cl2) and being tied up (Ezk.4.8#cl1), but nothing marks him as a servant, and no clause carries the servant figure of Isaiah 52-53 that this stamp names. It is vicarious sign-bearing, not the suffering servant.
No clause in the section mentions covenant, oath, or covenant formula; 'a day for each year' (Ezk.4.6#cl3) is a reckoning, not covenant language. The stamp does not belong to this section.

The section assumes the siege (rations by weight and measure, hunger, 'cut off the supply of food in Jerusalem'), but no clause in Ezek 4:9-17 names the siege or besieging. The siege proper is narrated in the preceding verses (Ezek 4:1-8).

The period in this section is 'three hundreds and ninety day[s]' (Ezk.4.9#cl3); no forty-day period is stated, and the reader cites the same verse (4:9) for it. The forty days of the sign belong to Ezek 4:6, not to this section.

The servant of Isaiah 52:13-53:12 is not in view; Ezek 4:14 is the prophet's protest about his own ritual purity ('I have never defiled myself'), not a servant bearing others' sin. The stamp's cluster is the servant songs.

The section moves in the opposite direction: from an ample mixed-grain loaf (Ezk.4.9#cl0-cl2) to starvation rations and lack of bread and water (4:10-11, 4:16-17). No clause reverses famine into provision.
The section states only that Ezekiel was carried in vision to the land of Israel; no clause speaks of a return of the exiles from Babylon, and 'our exile' (cl0) is the exile's continuation.
This section calls Ezekiel to see and to report what he is shown; no clause warns of coming judgment or makes him a watchman over Israel (cf. Ezek 3:17; 33:7).

The vision's aim is the temple (cf. Ezk.40.3#cl5 'standing in the gateway'), but no clause of this section states the LORD's presence in the temple; v.1's 'the hand of the LORD was upon me' is the prophet's commissioning, not temple presence.
The section has a very high mountain and a city-like structure, but those clauses describe what Ezekiel is shown, not creation language or a new creation.

The section's whole drift is restoration - God's hand on the exiled prophet, the vision of the land and the city-temple - but the clauses name only exile (cl0) and being brought to the land (v.2), with no clause about mercy or restoration.

The section is wholly about measuring the outer-court north gateway (walls, chambers, pillars, steps, gateways); no clause states or enacts a divine presence, glory, or presence theme. The stamp describes the passage's overall temple setting rather than any clause in particular.
No clause mentions priests, Levites, sacrificial service, or cultic personnel; the gate chambers (Ezk.40.21#cl0-cl2) are architectural rooms with no indicated priestly function in these clauses.

The passage presupposes the restored temple of the vision but no clause speaks of a king, throne, reign, or dominion; the gates and courts (Ezk.40.20#cl0, Ezk.40.23#cl0) are architecture, not kingdom language.

The section describes gates, gateways, gate chambers and their measurements, but no person who keeps or guards a gate is mentioned or implied; the stamp fits only the general subject-matter of the vision.
The text presents the gateways, pillars, porticoes and steps as already existing and measured; no one is described building them.
Nothing in these clauses speaks of destruction; the gates, pillars and palm trees are intact and being measured by the man.
No clause here reports building or rebuilding; the architectural features are simply surveyed (measured, counted, inspected), which is not the same event.
Though this vision is priestly in provenance, no priestly person or act appears in these clauses.

The section is a survey of a finished structure, 'he measured' repeated; there is no clause of building, making or constructing (no verb of building), so the builder role is not carried by any clause here.
Nothing in the section speaks of destruction; the temple is intact and being inspected and measured. This is the rebuilt temple vision, so destruction does not speak here.
The section is part of the vision of the eschatological temple with all its courts, gates, steps and measurements, but no clause states rebuilding; the building is already standing in the vision.

The section calls them 'the priests the Levites, the sons of Zadok' (Ezk.44.15#cl0); the priestly covenant in view is the one with Zadok's line (cf. the sons of Zadok alone are admitted), and no clause mentions Phinehas or a covenant with him. The stamp is not true of this section.
The closest clause is Ezk.44.23#cl0-cl1, but 'instruct/make known' is teaching, not the watchman's warning against coming danger; no clause in this section has the watchman idea.

Ezk.44.22#cl1 (marriage to 'a virgin of the descendants of the house of Israel') and cl2 are about who a priest may marry, not about a stranger or sojourner living among Israel; the section contains no such figure.

The clauses cited by the reader under Ezek 44:30 are cl0 (the best of all the firstfruits and every contribution) and cl1-cl2 (the first of your dough, that a blessing may rest on your house); 'firstfruits' and 'first of your dough' are not the firstborn, and no clause in this section mentions the firstborn.

Ezk.44.27 does have a sin offering on the day the priest enters the sanctuary, and 28:25 has a seven-day cleansing, but a single priest's entry-day sin offering is not the Day of Atonement, and no clause here names that day.

The passage says nothing about a surviving remainder of Israel; the Levites are not described as a remnant but as men punished and demoted to temple service. The clause cited (44:10) is about their going astray and bearing iniquity.

The section does not name the altar or any altar rite. 44:7 concerns defiling the temple by offering the fat and the blood, and 44:13 mentions the most holy things only to bar the Levites from them; the altar is absent, so the stamp is unsupported here.
The section is divine instruction for apportioning the land (lot, measured cubit dimensions), a general drift; no clause states law or wisdom as such.

The stamps given for this section name only 'law_wisdom (themes; cited Ezek 45:10)', with no definition; on its face the section is a legal regulation of weights and measures (the Berean text of Ezek 45:10-12 states commands and equivalences: 'You must use honest scales, a just ephah, and a just bath', 'the homer will be the standard measure for both', 'The shekel will consist of twenty gerahs'), so a stamp about law/regulation is the section's general drift rather than an idea carried by one clause in particular. If instead 'law_wisdom' is meant as the wisdom theme, I could not determine it: no clause here carries a wisdom saying (no 'fear of the LORD', no proverbial 'better than', no wise/foolish contrast), and 'wisdom' appears nowhere in the Berean text shown, so the pin would be wrong; with the stamp undefined I cannot distinguish these two readings and give an empty list.

The section names no Day of Atonement; Ezek 45:18-20 and 45:25 describe the first-day-of-the-month and seventh-month purifications/feasts, with no mention of the tenth day of the seventh month, the fast, or the scapegoat, and 'make atonement' atonement here is for the sanctuary/temple, not the named day.

The section speaks only of Israel: the prince, 'My people', 'the house of Israel according to their tribes'. No foreign nation appears as a character; the stamp is cited to Ezek 45:8 but the verse names no nation other than Israel.
No clause states or alludes to a covenant with David; the inheritance clauses (Ezk.46.16) speak of the prince's sons and descendants, not of the Davidic covenant.
Nothing in this section concerns a firstborn: the cited verse (Ezek 46:16) is about a gift of inheritance to the prince's sons, and no clause mentions birth order or a firstborn.
No clause in this section speaks of a stranger or sojourner; the cited verse (Ezek 46:9) concerns the people of the land entering and leaving by the gates at the appointed feasts.

This section legislates the service of a standing, functioning temple (gates, prince, priests, daily offerings); no clause concerns a destroyed temple, and the cited verse (Ezek 46:1) describes the inner court's gate.
The cited verse (Ezek 46:13) prescribes a daily morning burnt offering, not the Day of Atonement; no clause in this section mentions the Day of Atonement or its rites.
The cited verse (Ezek 46:11) speaks only of 'the festivals and appointed feasts' with grain-offering quantities; no clause names Passover or its distinctive features.
No clause in this section contains an oath, a swearing, or an oath formula; the cited verse (Ezek 46:16) concerns a gift of inheritance.
No clause in this section describes a divine appearance; the cited verse (Ezek 46:1) gives regulations about the gate of the inner court.
No clause in this section mentions anointing; the cited verse (Ezek 46:5) concerns the grain offering of an ephah with a hin of oil, where the oil is food for the offering, not an anointing.
No clause in this section describes a coronation or the installation of a king; the cited verse (Ezek 46:2) concerns the prince entering to worship and the priests sacrificing.
No clause in this section speaks of a witness, testimony or witnessing; the cited verse (Ezek 46:3) concerns the people bowing in worship before the LORD.

Nothing in this section watches, warns or announces danger; the gate-keeper idea is a closed or opened gate (Ezk.46.1#cl3), not a watchman. The cited verse Ezek 46:1 speaks only of shutting and opening a gate.
No fighting, weapon or enemy anywhere in Ezek 46:1-18; the prince offers sacrifice and bows (Ezk.46.2#cl2, Ezk.46.2#cl3), he does not fight.

The section describes use of an already-built gate and courtyard, not building. No clause names construction; the nearest words are architectural nouns ('gate', 'portico', 'gatepost') not the act of building.
No nation is addressed or acts in this section; the actors are the prince, the priests and 'the people of the land' (Ezk.46.3#cl0), Israel not the nations.
No woman, and no personified wisdom, appears in Ezek 46:1-18.
No woman, and no personified folly, appears in Ezek 46:1-18.
The prince here is bound by statute, provides for his sons and does not seize the people's land (Ezk.46.18#cl0); nothing animal-like or bestial is predicated of him.
This section's prince is the negative opposite of a false shepherd: he must not evict the people from their property (Ezk.46.18#cl0, Ezk.46.18#cl3).

The section presupposes the restored temple and land, but no clause states mercy or restoration; the nearest is the prohibition in Ezk.46.18#cl0 against displacing the people, which is a safeguard, not a statement of restoration.
Nothing in these verses speaks of destruction; they describe the temple's chambers, courts and kitchens in working order.
The section moves through the temple courts and chambers, but no clause states God's presence dwelling there; it is the setting, not a clause's idea.
The temple, altar and man with the measuring line are present, but no clause names a priest, states anyone's role, or shows priestly service; the stamp is only the section's drift.
No clause mentions new heavens or a new earth; the life-giving river is the vision's drift only.
The water here issues from under the temple threshold, not from a rock struck in the wilderness; no clause speaks of a rock.
The temple is standing and functioning as the source of the river; nothing in the section speaks of its destruction.
The restored land and sanctuary are the setting of the vision, but no clause states a return of exiles.
This section has no covenant formula ('I will be their God'), no law written on the heart, and no covenant-making speech; it speaks of water, fish and trees.
Nothing in these verses makes or names a covenant of peace; the vocabulary is water, healing and fruit.
The only non-Israelites here are individual foreigners resident among the tribes, not nations acting as a character.

The section's drift is the allotment of the land to the tribes as promised; no clause in this section itself asserts a promise or God's faithfulness — the clauses only name tribes and portions, so the stamp is general.

The section is part of the vision of the restored land, which a reader may take as the new creation's drift; but no clause in this section speaks of creation, renewal or newness — only tribal boundaries — so it is general at most.

Nothing in these clauses speaks of renewal, restoration or a new creation; the section is a land-survey (measurements, produce, city workers). The stamp can only be said of the chapter's general drift as a vision of the restored land.
The prince is set over against the holy contribution and the sanctuary (cl0, cl5): the priestly portion is what he does not own, and no clause names a priest or priestly act.

No clause here states or presupposes a divine promise being kept; v.29 is a concluding formula of allotment ('this is the land you are to allot...declares the Lord GOD'), which reports a command/institution, not the fulfillment of a promise. The section is land allotment to tribes, with no covenant or promise language.
The section names gates and the tribes inscribed on them (Ezk.48.31#cl2-4, etc.) but no person or role who keeps or guards a gate; 'gatekeeper' as a character role has no clause here.
No king, ruler, throne or reign appears: the city's name is 'THE LORD IS THERE' (Ezk.48.35#cl1/cl2) and the gates bear tribal names; nothing speaks of a human king.
The new city with its measured sides and the LORD's name is the section's general drift; no single clause states new creation.
No clause speaks of a surviving remainder; the Zadokites are distinguished by faithfulness ('kept My charge and did not go astray'), not by being a remnant of Israel.
No clause mentions Phinehas or a covenant of perpetual priesthood; the Zadokites' claim rests on keeping charge, not on Phinehas (Num 25).
The only cultic object named is the sanctuary itself ('the sanctuary of the LORD'), which is the sanctuary, not tabernacle furnishings (ark, lampstand, table, etc.).

The scattering here is of hair, a third of the hair, and of the remnant to the wind (Ezk.5.2#cl4, Ezk.5.10#cl3); no sheep or shepherd language appears in the section. The stamp's shepherd/sheep image is absent, though the scattering idea is present.
The section is an oracle of judgment announced throughout; it uses no 'woe' form or address, so it is a description of the section's drift rather than anything a single clause says.
No clause has a witness, testimony or third-party observer; the nations appear only as spectators of Israel's ruin ('in the sight of all who pass by', Ezk.5.14#cl0), which is not witnessing.
Nothing in this section speaks of fire; the judgment agents named are plague, famine, sword, wild beasts and bloodshed, with no flame or burning anywhere.
The image here is the arrows of famine (Ezk.5.16), not bowls poured out; no bowl, cup or libation appears in any clause of this section.
No 'woe' (הוֹי) cry here; the speech is an announcement of coming destruction ('I am about to bring a sword'), not a woe-oracle.
Nothing in the section speaks of a siege: no besieging army, siege works or blockade. 6:6 has city ruin but by direct divine destruction, and 'sword' (6:3) is not a siege.
The idols here are in the open high places/altars of the land (6:4-6), not set in a holy place; nothing in the section puts an idol inside the temple or sanctuary.
No performed sign-act appears anywhere in Ezek 7:1-13: there is no gesture, object or enacted demonstration (contrast the sign-acts of Ezek 4-5); the passage is speech only.

No clause in Ezek 7:1-13 states deportation, removal from the land, or being carried to another land; the ruin is total destruction, not exile (the verse the reader cited, 7:11, speaks of violence, a rod and none remaining, not of exile).
Nothing in the section names siege works, an encircling army, starving city or siege-ramp; the cited 7:10 ('the rod has budded, arrogance has bloomed') is the blossoming of doom, not a siege engine.
No clash of armies, weapons or combatants is narrated; the violence of 7:11 is a growth image ('grown into a rod'), and the cited 7:12 is about buyer and seller and divine wrath, not fighting.
The section nowhere pronounces 'woe'; 7:25 ('Anguish is coming!') is a plain announcement of coming distress, not the hoy-oracle form with an addressee and threatened doom.

The cited verse is mourning and shame imagery (sackcloth, shaved heads), not darkness; the only near-candidate is 'terror will overwhelm them', which is dread, not the darkness symbol. I judge this stamp wrong for this section.
Fire is never named or described in Ezek 7:14-27; the cited verse 7:15 has sword, plague and famine, no fire.
Ezek 7:26 names instruction from priests perishing and counsel from elders, not the end of sacrifice or the cessation of the cult; no clause in the section speaks of sacrifice stopping.
The profanation is of sanctuaries and of the treasured place generally, not of the altar specifically; no clause names the altar.
Ezek 8:18 is a first-person declaration of wrath ('I will respond with wrath... I will not listen'), not a woe-oracle; the word 'woe' never appears in the section.
The seventy elders (8:11) are elders who burn incense (8:11#cl3-4), and 8:16 has twenty-five men bowing to the sun; the Hebrew text has no 'priest' or priestly role in this section.
The watchman image (Ezek 3:17; 33:7) is absent here: no wall-watch, trumpet or warning role is named; 8:7-8 is a hole dug through a wall, not a watchman's post.
The section has 'abominations' (8:6, 9, 13, 17) but no 'abomination of desolation'—no setting up of a desolating object in the temple; 8:18 declares wrath but no desolation.
The section names 'abominations' but never names an idol, image or other god; the abominations are not specified as idolatry here (9:9 calls them bloodshed and perversity).
No watchman, warning, trumpet or blood-on-hands language anywhere in Ezek 9:1-11; the reader cited 9:4, which is about marking the sighing, not warning anyone.
Nothing in Ezek 9:1-11 is offered to God on an altar; the killing is judicial slaughter, and the only altar reference (9:2) is where the men merely stand.
No clause in the section shows anyone testifying or bearing witness; Jeremiah is cited as the mouth of the LORD's word, not as a witness, and nothing else speaks to it.
Nothing in the section speaks of David or of a covenant with him; v.5 names Judah, Benjamin, priests and Levites, not the Davidic promise.
The section has no word of an oath sworn to the fathers; only the fulfilling of Jeremiah's word is stated.
The section speaks only of the vessels being brought out and counted; no clause mentions building or rebuilding the house.
Mithredath is called treasurer and Sheshbazzar prince of Judah; neither is called a servant or given a servant role.
The section narrates the restoration of the temple vessels as part of the return, but no clause states mercy or restoration as an idea.
The return and the recovery of the vessels fit the theme of God's promise kept, but no clause in this section names a promise or God's faithfulness.
The Law is cited as an existing norm to obey ("Let it be done according to the Law"), which is law-keeping/application, not the giving of law; no clause presents the Law being given.
No clause uses remnant language or singles out a surviving remnant; "there is hope for Israel" speaks of hope, not of a remnant.

Nothing in Ezra 10:18-44 speaks of a return from exile: the section is a list of men who had married foreign women and their pledge to send them away. The return is narrated earlier in Ezra (chs. 1-2), not here; the stamp is wrongly attached to 10:44.
The section as a whole pictures the community's post-exilic restoration (dealing with the foreign-wife problem), but no clause names mercy or restoration; only the general drift.
The setting presupposes the return (the 'exiles' are in Judah and Jerusalem), but no clause here narrates a return; 10:7-17 concerns the foreign-wife crisis.
This is the section's general drift (return from exile as fulfillment); no clause states a promise or God's faithfulness.

Ezra 2:69 records a freewill donation of gold, silver and garments to the treasury, not an offering by slaughter or altar rite; the Hebrew verb here (hiphil of נדב/'offer freewill offerings') denotes a voluntary gift, and no sacrificial victim or altar appears in any clause.

No clause uses remnant language (no 'remaining', 'survivors', 'left'). The section's drift — the returned community resettling in its towns — can be read as the remnant restored, but no clause in particular carries the word or idea.
'As it is written in the Law of Moses' (Ezr.3.2#cl3) presupposes the Law as already given; nothing in this section narrates the giving of the law.
The feast kept here is Booths/Tabernacles (Ezr.3.4#cl0), not Passover; no Passover is mentioned in the section.
The Law of Moses is cited as a written authority (Ezr.3.2#cl3), but no Sinai covenant-making is spoken of here.

No clause in this section names a servant or servant role; the overseers and workers are named as Levites, priests and family heads, not servants (cf. Ezr.3.9#cl0, Ezr.3.8#cl2). The reader's citation of Ezra 3:8 does not support it.
No clause says the temple was destroyed; the section only speaks of rebuilding the temple and the exiles' return.
Verse 5 speaks of hiring counselors against them to frustrate their plans, not of a council discerning anything.
The building commanded by Cyrus may imply it, but no clause states a promise or God's faithfulness.
No servant figure appears; the suffering here is opposition to the Judahites' building, not a servant bearing it.
No judgment is pronounced or described; verse 5 is human opposition, not divine judgment.

Ezra 4:19-21 is a royal administratative decree and search, not divine or judicial judgment; v.19 found the city's rebellion (Ezr.4.19#cl2-4), and v.21 orders the work stopped (Ezr.4.21#cl0-3) — no clause pronounces judgment on anyone.
The section's drift — the temple work halting under a foreign king's decree — fits the exile-return setting, but no clause here speaks of sin, exile or death.
The section speaks of a written accusation, an investigation of records, and rebuilding; no besieging or military encirclement of a city is mentioned.
The only destruction mentioned is of the city ('this city was destroyed'), not the temple.
Nothing in the section is a prophetic utterance; it is an administrative letter and accusation, and no prophet speaks.

The section asserts that the decree of Cyrus exists and that the house was being built; no clause appeals to a promise or to God's faithfulness, and the reader cited Cyrus's decree in 5:13, which is a royal decree, not a divine promise.

No clause of this section contains a prophetic word: it is a report of an official inquiry, testimony of elders, royal decrees and a request to search the archives; the reader cited 5:17, which is a request for a royal decision, not prophecy.

The section speaks of vessels taken from the temple and carried to Babylon, and of the house being rebuilt; no clause states that the temple was destroyed. Plundering is not destruction, and Ezr.6.5 (the cited verse) only says Nebuchadnezzar brought the articles out and carried them to Babylon.
No clause in this section records an oath or a swearing; 6:11 is a royal decree with a penalty, not an oath, and contains no oath formula.

The clauses of 6:12 are a petition that God overthrow offenders and a command that the decree be carried out; no clause uses a curse form or invokes a curse on anyone. (The impalement of 6:11 is a legal penalty, not a curse.)
Nothing in the section appeals to or recalls a divine promise being kept; 6:5 is a decree that the vessels be restored, with no promise language and no mention of God's faithfulness.
The section presupposes a restored community in Yehud, but no clause speaks of the return itself; 'the Jewish elders' and the temple being built assume it rather than state it.
This section reports the temple's completion, not its destruction; nothing in Ezra 6:13-15 speaks of destruction.

The completion of the temple in the sixth year of Darius is the fulfillment of prophetic promise (cf. Hag 2:9; Zech 4:9), but no clause here states a promise or God's faithfulness; the section only narrates the outcome.
The completion/dedication of the house of God is presupposed, but no clause of this section states building; the dedication is named, not the rebuilding.
The section's drift is restoration (exiles, dedication, offerings, ordered service), but no clause states mercy or restoration; the joy and the sacrificial acceptance are not in the text as such.
the section's drift (a journey up to Jerusalem) but no clause names a pilgrim or a pilgrimage; the travellers are named by tribe (Israelites, priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants)
nothing in the section states or recalls a promise; the hand of God upon Ezra (Ezr.7.6#cl3, Ezr.7.9#cl1) is favour, not a promise kept, and the verse cited (7:1) is only a chronological note
Nothing in the section says the temple is destroyed or lies in ruins; the house of God is spoken of as standing and being served, with the temple in use at Jerusalem.
The section is a royal rescript of permission, provision and penalty; the sanction of Ezr.7.26 is the king's court enforcing the law, not a lawsuit in which God indicts His covenant people.
The letter/decree is written testimony of the king's grant, but no clause in the section presents a witness, testimony or witnessing act.
The permission to return and the king's freewill offerings presuppose a gracious turning, but the section states permission, provision and duty, not mercy or restoration in so many words.
No clause rests on a divine promise or on God's faithfulness; the section is the king's grant and command, so the stamp fits only the section's general drift, if at all.
No clause names or marks a servant; the king is called 'the king' and Ezra speaks in the first person.
The chapter records survivors of the exile returning; nothing in these verses states a promise, covenant, or God's faithfulness. No clause names it.
The section as a whole is a return to the land, which a reader may read as restoration, but no clause in these verses speaks of mercy or of God acting; the closest is 'returned from Babylon'.

The intercession here is Ezra's own proclamation of a fast and petition (8:21 'I proclaimed a fast'; 8:23 'we sought from God our on this'), not a priestly act on behalf of others; nothing in the clauses marks priestly mediation, and the earlier reader cited only 8:23 which is a communal petition and answer.

The section speaks of 'we/our little ones/our property' seeking a safe journey but never uses remnant language or a remnant idea; this is the returning community, not characterised as a remnant in these clauses. Clauses offered as medium if a reader takes 'our.little one[s] and all property our' (cl0/cl2) as the surviving community, but no clause carries the idea itself.

Cl.31 cl0/cl1 ('we set out from the Ahava Canal to go to Jerusalem') describe a journey of departure, not a return from exile; the section's general drift is the return to Jerusalem, but no clause here says 'return' or 'exile'.
The section as a whole shows the safe return and the completion of the temple service, but no clause names or appeals to a promise or to God's faithfulness.
cl3 states the peoples' abominations as the pattern from which Israel failed to separate; it does not itself assert idolatry (no worship of other gods, no idols) anywhere in 9:1-4.
the section shows only Ezra's grief and appalled sitting; no confession, prayer or turning (that begins at 9:5).
the section shows the sin (mixed marriages) but no clause states exile or death as its consequence.
the unfaithfulness is reported and mourned; no sentence, verdict or divine judgment appears in 9:1-4.
nothing in the section speaks of mercy or restoration; the reader cited 9:4, where only grief and the evening offering stand.

Nothing in this section refers to Sinai; the commandments are attributed to "Your servants the prophets" (Ezr.9.11#cl0, Berean "that You gave through Your servants the prophets"), not to the mountain.

No covenant word or covenant-making statement appears in these clauses; 'gave Himself for our sins' and 'deliver us from the present evil age' are not stated as a covenant, and the section's 'will of our God and Father' is not called a covenant.

Nothing in these clauses speaks of a promise made or kept: 'through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised Him from the dead' names the source of Paul's apostleship, not a promise, and 'according to the will of our God and Father' states God's will, not a promise. If anything is at stake it is the section's general drift of God's saving initiative, not any particular clause.
The general drift of the section is Paul defending his gospel and its divine origin; no clause names a prophet.
Paul's testimony is the section's drift, and Gal.1.20 is an assurance of truthfulness, but no clause uses witness language.
Gal.1.12 speaks of receiving the gospel by revelation from Jesus Christ, not of redemption; no clause in the section mentions redemption, ransom or being bought.
The revelation in view is the gospel Paul received and preaches, not a prophetic word or prophecy; no clause names a prophet or prophecy.
Conveys the drift that God's purpose for Paul, set apart from the womb, came to pass; no clause speaks of promise, oath or faithfulness.
No clause in the section mentions the Spirit, the Holy Spirit or anything done by the Spirit; God's calling is "by His grace" (Gal.1.15#3), not by the Spirit.
The section's change in Gal.1.23 is from persecuting to preaching, not rescue or deliverance from captivity; no clause speaks of being saved or set free.
No clause speaks of judgment, condemnation or God's verdict; Gal.1.10's "servant" and Gal.1.20's "no lie" are not judgment.
Persecuting and destroying (Gal.1.13#1, Gal.1.13#2) is opposition to the church, not sin, exile or death as a theme; no clause speaks of exile or death.
No clause mentions a covenant, its making or its parties; "the traditions of my fathers" (Gal.1.14#1) is ancestral custom, not covenant.
No clause in the section mentions a kingdom, a king or reign.
Gal.1.17 is Paul's travels to Arabia and Damascus, not an exile followed by exaltation; no clause expresses that reversal.
No clause speaks of Paul's humiliation or subsequent vindication; Gal.1.23 is a change from persecuting to preaching, not from being humbled to being vindicated.
The section contains no statement about first and last, ranking or reversal of order; the persecutor turning preacher is not that saying.
No clause speaks of scattering, dispersion or gathering; being zealous for ancestral traditions (Gal.1.14) is not it.

No clause in this section speaks of redemption, purchase, or being bought back. Gal.1.6#cl2 has 'having called you in [the] grace of Christ' — calling by grace, not redemption — and the section's argument is about desertion and a contrary gospel. The stamp does not belong to this section on the clauses given.

Nothing here is a prophetic utterance, oracle, or fulfilment of prophecy. Gal.1.8#cl1 mentions 'an angel out of heaven' only as a hypothetical alternative preacher, and Gal.1.9#cl0/#cl1 ('we have said before', 'now again I say') refer to Paul's own earlier teaching, not to prophecy. If the stamp meant merely 'authoritative apostolic declaration' it would be a different kind, not this one.

The word 'circumcised' occurs only as a group-label in Gal.2.3#cl0 ('not even Titus ... was compelled to be circumcised'), Gal.2.7#cl3, Gal.2.7#cl4, Gal.2.8#cl0, Gal.2.8#cl1, Gal.2.9#cl5, all describing circumcision as the mark distinguishing peoples, not the covenant God made with Abraham (Gen 17); no clause here speaks of the covenant of circumcision as such, so the stamp is the section's background rather than any clause, hence general.

Gal 2:9 speaks of James, Cephas and John 'recognizing the grace that I had been given' and giving the right hand of fellowship — a recognition of Paul's commission, not anyone bearing witness/testimony to a fact or event; none of the clauses is an act of witnessing.

No clause in this section mentions a servant, slave or serving: Gal.2.10#cl1 speaks of remembering 'the poor', and the nearest language of slavery, Gal.2.4#cl4 ('us they will enslave') and Gal.2.5#cl0 ('did we yield in subjection'), concerns being enslaved by the false brothers, not a servant role; the stamp is at most the section's general drift.

The verse cited (Gal 2:5) says 'so that the truth of the gospel would remain with you' (Gal.2.5#cl1); no clause in this section speaks of redemption, ransom or purchase, and 'in Christ Jesus' appears only in Gal.2.4#cl3 describing the freedom we have.
No clause here speaks of a promise or of faithfulness: 'I went in response to a revelation' (Gal.2.2#cl0) is guidance, not a promise, and Gal.2.2#cl3/#cl5 speak of running in vain.
The cited verse (Gal 2:10) says 'They only asked us to remember the poor' — almsgiving to the poor, which is generosity rather than mercy restoring someone; no clause here speaks of restoration.

The Spirit is not mentioned in this section: Gal 2:2 says 'I went in response to a revelation' (Gal.2.2#cl0), and the only 'in Christ Jesus' is Gal.2.4#cl3; a revelation is not the Spirit as such, so the stamp is at most the section's general drift.
No council is convened and no joint deliberation is narrated; the section is a public rebuke and an argument about justification, not a council reaching a judgement.
Nothing in these clauses names a covenant, its institution, or covenant members; 2:16 contrasts works of the law with faith in Christ, which is justification language, not covenant language.
The section contrasts Spirit with 'the flesh' only at Gal 3:3 (finishing in the flesh); it never mentions works of the flesh, and the 'works' named in 3:2 and 3:5 are works of the law.
No clause in the section names sin, exile or death; 'the flesh' at Gal 3:3 is the sphere of being perfected, and the suffering at Gal 3:4 is undefined and not identified with judgment.

The crucified Christ of Gal 3:1 is named as the object of portrayal, and no clause gives him the servant's suffering or its vicarious purpose; the 'you suffered' at Gal 3:4 is the Galatians' own experience.
The section speaks of the law's curse, Abraham's blessing and the promise of the Spirit; no covenant is made or named here, and "new covenant" is nowhere in the text.
"Redeemed" (ἐξηγόρασεν) is slave-market language, but no clause here speaks of a slave or bondservant, and the one who acts is Christ, not a slave.
The Spirit himself is promised, but no gifts of the Spirit are mentioned in any clause.
The law is spoken of here as a curse and as not based on faith, never as wisdom.
The section's covenant (Gal 3:15, 3:17) is the earlier covenant with Abraham, contrasted with the law that came 430 years later; nothing here speaks of a new covenant, and 'new' never appears.
Paul speaks of a promise/covenant to Abraham, not of an oath sworn to the fathers; 'oath' does not occur in this section.
No creation covenant is in view; the covenant here is the one made with Abraham (3:16-17).
The law is treated as added because of transgressions and as a guardian/custody, not as wisdom or instruction for wise living.
No clause in this section speaks of a new covenant; the promise named in 3:29 is Abraham's.

Nothing in Gal 4:1-7 speaks of a covenant made or renewed. The passage's contrast is slavery under the stoicheia/law versus sonship and adoption through God's sending of the Son and the Spirit (4:3-4:7); 'new covenant' is not the idea the clauses state, even though sonship and the Spirit are covenant-adjacent elsewhere.

No clause names a promise, an oath, or God's keeping of one. The nearest material — 'until the date set by his father' (4:2) and 'when the time had fully come' (4:4#cl1) — speaks of an appointed time being reached, not of a promise being fulfilled, so no clause carries the stamp.

Paul speaks of his travail as a mother, not of a prophet or prophetic office.
