No shaking of the heavens or the created order; the section's 'shaking' is political reversal (Hab.2.7) and the earth being filled with knowledge (Hab.2.14), not cosmic collapse.
No sun, light, or darkening anywhere in Hab 2:16; the cup and disgrace clauses have no solar imagery.
No moon or blood-of-the-moon language in Hab 2:16 or the section; 'bloodshed' (Hab.2.8, Hab.2.17) is human bloodguilt, not a darkened moon.
No angels and no winds in the section; the only agents of restraint or release are human creditors (Hab.2.7) and the LORD's cup (Hab.2.16).

The section presents Yahweh as sovereign over earth and nations (Hab.3.3, 3.6, 3.12), but no clause states a kingdom, throne or reign; the theme is the chapter's general drift, not any clause's content.
Nothing in the section mentions the temple, sanctuary, Zion or the presence of God in a house; Hab.3.3 speaks of God coming from Teman and Mount Paran, which is theophany, not temple.
No clause speaks of covenant, covenant-making or covenant obligations; 'Your people' and 'Your anointed' in Hab.3.13 presuppose a relationship but no clause carries the covenant idea itself.

The section's afflicted figure is the enemy's victim ('gloating as though ready to secretly devour the weak', Hab.3.14), and the anointed of Hab.3.13 is the object of salvation, not a servant who suffers; nothing here carries the suffering-servant idea.

Hab 3:17 says the fig tree does not bud, no fruit on the vines, the olive crop fails, fields produce no food, flock and cattle gone; 3:18-19 speak of exulting and of strength, not of anything being restored. No clause carries mercy or restoration.
Hab 3:19 has 'GOD the Lord', 'my strength', feet like a deer's and walking on the heights — no king, throne, reign, dominion or people ruled. 'the Lord' in the vocative is not a kingdom clause.
Nothing in 3:17-19 speaks of creating, making new, or a renewed world; 3:19's 'he makes my feet like those of a deer' is the poet's own enabling, not creation.

The famine half is explicit (no bud, no produce, olive crop fails, fields produce no food), but no clause states food, harvest or provision arriving; Hab 3:18-19 give exulting and strength, not provision. The stamp's 'to' half has no clause here.
Hag 1:11 is a drought on fields, crops, man and beast, with no day-of-the-LORD imagery (no coming day, darkness, fire, cosmic upheaval); the stamp is not supportable from this section.

Nothing in this section says the people returned from exile; it is set in Jerusalem with the temple work already being resumed. The only clause that might look like it, Hag.1.14#cl1 ("they came"), is the leaders coming to do the work, not a return from Babylon.
Zerubbabel appears only as 'governor of Judah' (Hag.2.2#cl0), never as king; nothing in the section names or describes a king. The stamp is wrong for this section.
The section has no 'day of the LORD', no day formula; v.6 says only 'Once more, in a little while' (Hag.2.6#cl1) and the shaking is an announced divine act, not a day. The stamp is wrong here.

Verse 3 (Hag.2.3#cl0) asks who 'is left' who saw the former house — a question about survivors, not a statement of return; the only exodus mentioned is Egypt (Hag.2.5#cl2), not Babylon. Nothing in the section states a return.
Verse 6 speaks of shaking, not of a kingdom, reign or throne; no clause in the section mentions kingship or dominion. (Zerubbabel is 'governor', Hag.2.2#cl0, not king.) The stamp is wrong here.
The section speaks of the temple's foundation being laid, not its destruction; no clause mentions destruction.
No clause speaks of exile or return; the section concerns the temple foundation and blessing.
Nothing in the section depicts a procession or triumph; the only movement is chariots and horses going down (Hag.2.22#cl2-cl3), which is defeat, not a victory march.

The section's only cultic act is 'having provided purification for sins' (Heb.1.3#cl4) and the Son is never called a priest here; the priestly argument belongs to Hebrews 5-10. The Berean text of Heb 1 does not contain the word 'priest'.

Heb 1 mentions no covenant, no covenant formula and no covenant mediator formula; the 'Father/Son' and 'I will be His Father' language of Heb.1.5#cl3-#cl5 is dynastic (2 Sam 7:14), and nothing in the section says a new covenant is made or inaugurated.

Heb 1 predicates things of the Son (radiance, creator, purifier, enthroned) but never states the believer's union, indwelling or being 'in Christ'; the only 'in whom/through whom' phrases (Heb.1.2#cl0, Heb.1.2#cl1) are about agency in speech and creation, not union.

Heb 10:12 speaks of the priest 'having offered' and then sitting down at God's right hand: the offering and the session, not a raising of Christ; no clause in the section mentions Christ being raised or rising.

The section quotes Ps 40 on sacrifice not desired and the prepared body and applies it to Christ's offering, but no clause speaks of the servant's suffering: no wounding, affliction, or rejection, and the psalm quoted in vv.5-7 is not itself a servant-song.

No clause in the section mentions new creation, a new heart, or renewal of the world: 10:16 gives laws written on hearts and minds, and 10:17 forgiveness, but neither the word nor the idea of creation is in any clause.

Heb.10.29 names the Son of God trampled on, the blood of the covenant treated as common and the Spirit of grace insulted — but that is the punishment of apostates, not the servant who suffers for others; no clause in this section speaks of the suffering servant. The clause cited (Heb.10.29#cl2 'the Son - of God having trampled upon') has the Son as the one trampled by the sinner, the reverse of the theme.

Heb.10.32-33 describes the readers' own endurance of persecution ('a great conflict of sufferings', 'revilings and tribulations'), not the servant of the LORD who bears others' suffering; the section nowhere speaks of the servant. The persecution material is pinned under the persecution stamp instead.

Heb 11:2 speaks only of the ancients being commended for their faith ("In this were commended the ancients"); the section names no promise and no act of God's faithfulness, and the reader's citation of 11:2 does not supply one.
Heb 11:22 speaks of Joseph's word about the exodus and his bones; no oath, and no oath sworn to a patriarch is mentioned in any clause of 11:20-22.
Heb 11:21 names Jacob blessing each of Joseph's sons and nothing about birth order or a younger being set over an elder.
The clauses of Heb 11:22 speak of a future exodus and of Joseph's bones; no exile endured and no exaltation is stated.
This is a role read off the whole passage (Moses and his parents, the exodus, the Red Sea); no clause in this section states the typology 'new Moses'. It is the drift of Heb 11:23-29, not a clause.

Wrong for this section. Heb 11:23 speaks of Moses' parents hiding him and not fearing the king's edict (cl0, cl2, cl4); there is no clause about being a stranger, sojourning, or living as an alien — 'hidden three months' is concealment of an infant, not sojourn. The stamp's cited verse does not carry it here.

Wrong for this section as a reversal. The movement here is the reverse of the stamp: Moses gives up the palace (refusing to be called Pharaoh's daughter's son, Heb 11.24#cl2; choosing affliction and reproach over Egypt's treasures, 11.25, 11.26#cl0). No clause in Heb 11:23-29 shows him brought up from exile to exaltation; the exaltation is only 'the reward' he looked ahead to (Heb.11.26#cl1), which is hope, not the reversal stated.

Wrong for this section. Heb 11:29 has the Egyptians trying to follow and being drowned (cl1, cl2) — attempted pursuit, not belief; and the believing subject throughout 11:23-29 is Moses and Israel. No clause in the section has an outsider believing.
Heb 11:40 speaks of God's better plan and being made perfect, but no clause names a covenant, let alone the new covenant.
The section's sufferers are the faithful many (Heb 11:36-37), not the servant of Isaiah; no clause carries that figure.
Heb 11:40 promises perfection with us, not a new creation; no clause describes creation made new.
The section never names Christ or his redemption; it speaks of faith, promises and perfection.

Heb 11:5 speaks of Enoch being taken up so as not to see death, which is the opposite of resurrection: the text explicitly denies death, and nothing in these clauses describes a raising from the dead.

The Noah clause in this section (Heb.11.7#cl0) mentions only the divine warning, the ark, the salvation of his household, the condemning of the world and his becoming heir of righteousness; no covenant, and no covenant-making word or sign, appears.
The flood is the assumed setting of Heb 11:7, but no clause names the waters or the deluge: cl0 has only the warning, the ark and the saving of the household.
These verses are about the faithful (Abel, Enoch, Noah) rather than about a people as such: no clause names a people, and the nearest is the household saved in the ark (Heb.11.7#cl0).

Nothing in Heb 11:4 speaks of a servant of the Lord bearing suffering or sin; Abel's offering and his being commended as righteous are the whole of the clause, and Abel is not presented as a servant figure here.
Heb 11:5 has Enoch translated so as not to see death and not found; that is a removal from the present order, not the making of a new creation, and no clause speaks of new creation.
No clause in Heb 11:4 names the Spirit or any activity of the Spirit: Abel's offering, the testimony about his gifts, and his still speaking after death are all that is said.
No clause in this section speaks of an oath or of God swearing to the fathers; the nearest thing is 'the promises' (Heb.11.13#cl1, Heb.11.17#cl3), which does not name an oath.

This section lives off the Abrahamic covenant (promise, inheritance, descendants) but no clause states a covenant, a covenant-maker or covenant language; it is background to the whole passage. (Heb.11.8#cl4 'to receive for an inheritance' is the closest, and even it does not say covenant.)
Nothing in this section speaks of new creation, new heavens and earth, or renewal of creation; the heavenly country and prepared city are said of God's own making but not of creation made new.
No clause here speaks of the servant of the LORD, of vicarious suffering, or of one bearing sin; Isaac is offered but not described as suffering for others, and there is no servant language at all.
The section's exhortation to run the race looking to Jesus assumes believers are bound up with him, but no clause states being in Christ, with Christ, or sharing his death and life — the drift only.

No clause shows mercy given or restoration: the section names the witnesses (cl1), the sin laid aside (cl3), endurance (cl0/cl1), and warns against growing weary (Heb.12.3#cl2). Christ's endurance and his seat at God's right hand are not presented here as mercy or restoration.

Nothing in Heb 12:14-17 speaks of sin as exile or of death; the cited verse Heb 12:16 speaks only of sexual immorality and Esau selling his birthright for one meal - a profane act and a lost inheritance, not exile or death.

If anything the section is the opposite of mercy and restoration: Esau is rejected, finds no place of repentance though he seeks the blessing with tears (12:17); no clause speaks of mercy received or restoration.
No clause speaks of God's promise being made or kept; the only promise-like element, the blessing, is one Esau sought and did not obtain (12:17).
Heb 12:28 speaks of one unshakable kingdom being received, not a kingdom split into parts; nothing in the section divides a kingdom.
The section speaks of sons, fathers and the Father of spirits (a household/family image), not of a covenant people or community; no clause refers to the people of God as such.

The section is about the readers' discipline and endurance as sons (Heb 12:4-11), not about a servant of the Lord who suffers on behalf of others; the only 'servant' language is the quotation's 'My son' (Prov 3:11), a son, not a servant.
No clause in Heb 12:4-13 speaks of new creation; the fruit of righteousness and peace (Heb.12.11#cl5) and healing (Heb.12.13#cl2) are the closest, but the section does not carry this idea.
Christ is not named in the section; the Father-son relation in view is discipline by 'the Father of our spirits' (Heb.12.9#cl2), not union with Christ, so no clause carries the stamp.

The section calls for remembering prisoners and the mistreated (Heb.13.3#cl0, Heb.13.3#cl2), but no clause speaks of mercy shown or of restoration; the idea is the section's general drift rather than anything said in particular.

Nothing in these clauses is stated as law or as wisdom instruction: the imperative clauses (Heb.13.1#cl0; Heb.13.2#cl0; Heb.13.3#cl0; Heb.13.4#cl0; Heb.13.4#cl1) are exhortations to brotherly love, hospitality and marital purity, with no law citation and no wisdom saying, and the reader cited Heb 13:4 only for its morality wording.

Heb 13:18-19 is a request for the congregation's prayer, not an act of intercession by a priest on the people's behalf; nothing in the section has a priest interceding. The verses the reader cited mention prayer by the community, so the stamp does not fit this section as named.
No priestly term, office or cultic act appears in any clause of this section; the idea is at best the general drift of Hebrews, not said here.
cl2/cited verse has 'word of exhortation' and 'I have written to you', which is exhortation/testimony, not the role of witness; no witness clause.
cl1 says Timothy 'has been released', implying prior detention, but the clause names release, not persecution; no clause states persecution.
'Those from Italy' are a local group of believers greeting the readers, not nations as a character; the section has no nations.
No clause in 13:5-14 speaks of renewal or new creation; the nearest is the future city (Heb.13.14#cl2), which is the city that is to come, not new creation language.

The section speaks of 'such a great salvation' being 'declared by the Lord' and confirmed, but no clause names Christ, his death, blood, or the purchase of redemption: the atonement is not stated here, only announced. I could not pin a clause that carries redemption as such.

Nothing in the section says Jesus was raised or exalted from the dead; Heb 2:9 speaks of his being crowned with glory and honor after/through suffering death, not of resurrection, and no clause states he was raised.

No clause describes a sacrifice as an event; Heb 2:17 speaks of making atonement/propitiation for sins, and Heb 2:9 of tasting death, but no sacrificial offering (altar, victim, offering rite) is stated.
The word 'firstborn' and the idea of a firstborn never appear in this section.
No clause mentions a covenant, new or otherwise; Heb 2:17's high-priestly atonement is not a covenant statement.
The section nowhere calls Jesus or anyone a servant; the servant language of Isaiah is not quoted here.
No clause names a sacrifice or sacrificial offering; Heb 2:17 states atonement for sins but does not itself carry the sacrifice idea.

The section contrasts Jesus with Moses (greater glory, Son over house vs servant in house) but never states that Jesus is a new Moses; the comparison is the section's general drift rather than a clause carrying the stamp.
Nothing here is a test or contest: Heb.3.16 asks who heard and rebelled; 'heard and rebelled' is disobedience, not trial, and the cited verse supplies no contest image.
The cited verse says they were 'unable to enter' the rest; exclusion from entry is not deportation or exile, and the section names no exile.
The cited Heb.3.13 calls for mutual exhortation to prevent hardening; it is a warning against sin, not an act of mercy or restoration, and nothing in the section shows God restoring anyone.
Nothing in the section promises or shows God's faithfulness; 'My rest' appears only in the oath barring entry (Heb.3.11#cl0), and the fathers' failure is the point.
No clause offers mercy or restoration: the section ends on anger and exclusion from rest (Heb.3.11#cl0-cl1), with no restorative note.
No clause of Heb 4:1-11 speaks of a covenant, its making, or its promised newness; 'Today' and 'a Sabbath rest for the people of God' do not name a covenant.
The section speaks of rest remaining and of entering God's rest, not of a new creation or renewal of creation; no clause names it.
The section names Jesus the Son of God and a great high priest (Heb.4.14) but never states redemption, buying, blood or release; it is the section's drift, not said in any clause.
Heb 5:5-6 have God speaking ('You are My Son', 'You are a priest forever'), a declaration and a citation of Psalm 110, but no oath formula and no swearing anywhere in the section.
The section speaks of priesthood in the order of Melchizedek and eternal salvation, not of a new covenant; no clause mentions a covenant at all.
Heb 5:7 has loud cries, tears and being saved from death, but no cross, no death and no crucifixion is narrated in this section.
Heb 5:7 says He 'was heard' by the One able to save Him from death, which presupposes deliverance but never states a resurrection.
Heb 5:4 speaks of the honor of the high priesthood and Aaron's calling; no covenant, covenant-making or covenant formula appears in the section.
Nothing in these verses speaks of sin, exile or death; the failure described is dullness and immaturity, not sin-exile-death.
The section rebukes immaturity and calls for growth; no mercy, forgiveness or restoration is spoken of.
Nothing in Heb 6:1-12 mentions an oath or swearing; the cited 6:12 speaks of faith and patience inheriting promises.
No priest, altar or sacrificial-cult term occurs in Heb 6:1-12; the cited verse 6:2 speaks of baptisms and laying on of hands. Only the epistle's later argument makes it apt.

Nothing in the section speaks of a new covenant: the covenant/promise in view is God's oath to Abraham (6:13-15), and 6:20 speaks of priesthood, not a new covenant. The word 'covenant' does not occur in these verses.
Heb 7:2 mentions only Abraham giving a tenth (Heb.7.2#cl0); no covenant, and no covenant-making with Abraham, is spoken of in this section.
Heb 7:5 is about Levitical priests collecting a tenth (Heb.7.5#cl0/cl1/cl2); no sacrifice or sacrificial rite appears anywhere in the section.
Heb 7:6 speaks of Abraham as 'the [one] having the promises' (Heb.7.6#cl3), not of an oath sworn to the fathers.
The section's general drift (Melchizedek as a type of the Son of God, Heb.7.3#cl1) but no clause speaks of redemption.
No clause speaks of being in Christ; the only 'in' is Levi in Abraham's loins (Heb.7.10#cl0).
No covenant is mentioned in the section; Heb 7:6 rests on Abraham 'having the promises' (Heb.7.6#cl3).

The section never presents the priest as suffering: the only reference to His self-offering is “He offered up Himself” (Heb.7.27#cl4), which is stated as cultic sacrifice, not as suffering or servant humiliation, and there is no suffering, rejection or bearing of grief anywhere in these clauses.

The people appear only as those who received the law (Heb.7.11#cl2) and for whom sin-offering is made (Heb.7.27#cl2); no clause states that they are God's people, so the stamp is the section's background rather than a clause-level idea.
Heb.7.28#cl3's “made perfect forever” is perfection of the Son's priestly status (cf. Heb.7.11#cl1, perfection by priesthood), not the renewal or new creation of anything.

Heb.7.26#cl0 describes the high priest's own moral attributes (“holy, innocent, undefiled, set apart from sinners”), and cl1/cl2 his separation from sinners and exaltation above the heavens — the opposite of the believer's union with him, which no clause here expresses.
The section speaks of the tabernacle itself (Heb.8.1#cl2, Heb.8.2#cl0, Heb.8.5#cl2-3) and its pattern, but names no furnishing (ark, lampstand, altar, table) of it.

The only covenant besides the new one named here is the one made with the fathers when they were led out of Egypt (Heb.8.9#cl2, Heb.8.9#cl3); nothing in the section speaks of a covenant with creation or with Noah.
The section names no son: Jesus appears only as the mediator of a better covenant (Heb.8.6#cl0), and no sonship relation or address is spoken of anywhere here.

The section speaks of a new covenant, not of new creation: Heb.8.13#cl0-4 concern a covenant being made obsolete and vanishing, and no clause mentions creation, a new heaven and earth, or a making-new of the world.
Heb.9.10 says only that the external regulations were imposed 'until the time of reform'; no clause names or describes a new covenant. The reference is an implicit forward look.
The section describes the insufficiency of the old arrangement (9:9 'unable to cleanse') up to 'the time of reform' (9:10), pointing forward, but no clause names Christ or redemption.
the section has Christ entering heaven and appearing again, but no clause speaks of Him being raised from the dead

"the day of Jezreel" in 1:11 is the nearest thing to a day-of-the-LORD formula, but no clause states a day of Yahweh's visitation in the established sense; the stamp is at best the section's drift toward a decisive day.
Sin is present (1:2) and judgment is announced, but no clause here speaks of exile or death; the stamp names a whole pattern the section only partly touches.

Unsure: the section does accuse (10:13-15) and has an 'oath/covenant' clause (10:4), but no clause frames a legal charge/rhetorical lawsuit against a covenant partner; the reader cited 10:4, which is the covenant-making clause and could equally support covenant themes rather than a lawsuit form.

Nothing in this section is instruction in the law or wisdom teaching: the closest is Hos.10.12's agricultural imperatives ('sow ... reap ... break up your unplowed ground'), which is prophetic exhortation to repent in covenant terms, not torah/ḥokmah instruction, and the clause glosses contain no 'law' or 'wisdom' word.

There is no staff, scepter or rod in the section; Hos.10.7's 'like a twig (gloss: a.twig) on the surface of the water' is a twig carried off in water, and 10.11's 'yoke on her fair neck' is the closest rod-like image, neither being a breaking of a staff. I could not find a clause the stamp describes.

No sheep, flock or shepherd appears in the section; the cited Hos.10.7 is about Samaria's king carried off 'like a twig on the surface of the water', which is not a scattered flock, and the people are named as Israel/Ephraim/Judah in metaphor (10.11) but never as sheep.
The terror-language of the hills and mountains (10:8) is a cry to creation, not a description of creation collapsing; no clause here says the cosmos itself gives way.
The section is about ruined altars, high places and fortresses; it never speaks of a house or temple left desolate.
Hos.10.12 offers repentance and promised rain, but no clause in this section moves anyone from humiliation to vindication; 10:15 ends in the king being cut off.
No clause in this section has the lawsuit form (no summons, charge, indictment, verdict); the drift is the husband/father's plea against Israel's apostasy, so the stamp is only general at most.
The section is prophetic speech throughout, but no clause itself speaks about a prophetic word; nothing names the speaking or the word.
No clause states a covenant or its terms; 11:1's love, sonship and Egypt recall it but do not assert it.
General drift: the whole unit is divine speech, but no single clause in this section is itself a promise formula; the cited verse Hos 11:8 is lament/rhetorical question, not promise.
Paternal stance is the drift of Hos 11:8 (grief over a child, compassion stirred), but the Hebrew clauses here name no father or father-language; no clause carries the role explicitly.
No clause in Hos 11:8-12 speaks of a king, kingship, throne or royal rule; Hos 11:9 speaks of God, the Holy One, not a king.
The section presupposes exile (Egypt, Assyria as lands of residence) but narrates no deportation or exile event; Hos 11:11 is the return, not the exile.
Lies and deceit (Hos 11:12) are not idolatry, and no clause in the section names false gods, images or their worship.
Hos 12:9 speaks of dwelling in tents as in the days of the appointed feast — a past/restoration image of the wilderness, not a return from exile; no clause here mentions exile or return to the land.
Hos 12:4 concerns Jacob struggling with the angel and finding God at Bethel; no clause speaks of an oath sworn to the patriarchs.
Hos 12:5 states that the LORD is His name of renown; it is a doxological assertion, not a narrative of naming.
Hos 12:1 names Ephraim and Judah but the clauses speak of deceit, violence, and covenants with Assyria and Egypt — not the division of the kingdom.
No clause in this section narrates an exile; Hos 12:1's covenant with Assyria and oil to Egypt are diplomacy, not deportation.
The altars of Gilgal are destroyed, not an idol set up in the holy place; the clause names no idol and no holy place.

No clause in Hos.13.1-8 names or depicts a prophet; the cited verse Hos 13:1 has Ephraim, Israel, Baal and death only. The section as a whole presupposes a prophetic speaker, but no clause pins the role.

The reader cited Hos 13:3, whose clauses are all simile imagery of dissolution; no clause in the section says 'the word of the LORD' or reports a divine speech as such. The whole section is prophetic speech, but no clause pins the stamp.
This section is accusation and announced destruction (13:7-8 tear open, devour, tear apart); nothing in it restores or shows mercy. Hosea 14 does that, not these eight verses.
The section has idols (Hos.13.2#cl2-cl4, cl6) but identifies no holy place — no sanctuary, temple or high place is named in any clause. The apocalyptic-crisis stamp is not carried here.

The clause list supplied contains only Hos.13.15#cl0–cl5; no clause ids for Hos.13.16 were given, so the clause ids I would need ('Hos.13.16#cl2' etc.) are not in the allowed set and I cannot cite anything I was given. More substantively: no Hebrew word in these clauses expresses a curse (אָלָה/קְלָלָה); the text states the disaster itself as coming judgment, and reading 'curse' into it would be importing an idea the wording does not carry. I flag this as unsure whether the stamp is simply mis-cited to v.16 rather than wrong for the section.

No clause id in the supplied list names a battle or an enemy army; the only military image ('fall by the sword') lies in Hos.13.16, whose clauses were not supplied as ids. Even on the Berean text, the sword is the instrument of slaughter named against Samaria's inhabitants, not a battle narrated between forces, and the surrounding imagery is wind and drought, not combat. I cannot cite a clause id I was not given.

No supplied clause id carries this: the rebellion ('Samaria will bear her guilt because she has rebelled against her God') and the death clauses are all in Hos.13.16, whose ids were not given; the supplied Hos.13.15 ids (flourish, east wind, spring dried up, treasury plundered) name no sin and no exile. As a characterisation of the section's whole drift—guilt, then slaughter—it is true, so general: true.

The clauses of this section name no idol, image or worship of another god; the demand for a king and the iniquity of Ephraim are not stated as idolatry in these clauses. The stamp may be a theme of the wider book, but no clause here carries it.
The whole section is divine speech delivered through the prophet, but no clause in it names a word, oracle or prophecy as such.
The clauses speak only of ransoming from Sheol and Death in Israel's own horizon; nothing in them names Christ, and the word 'Christ' appears nowhere in the section.

The Berean verse the stamp cites (Hos 14:3) contains the renunciation of idols, but that line is not represented among the supplied clauses: the clause list for Hos.14.3 stops at #cl5 ('that.we.may.pay bulls lips our') and contains no clause glossing 'our gods' or 'the work of our own hands'. On this clause set I cannot pin it; what would settle it is the full Hos.14.3 clause list, which here appears to be Hos.14.1's material (the judgment of Samaria, cl0-cl4) rather than the English Hos 14:3.

Nothing in these clauses is a divine promise: the clauses are either the judgment on Samaria (Hos.14.1#cl0-cl4) or human speech addressed to God (take words, return, say to him, forgive, take good, pay bulls of our lips). The cited verse Hos 14:3 is spoken by the people, not by God, so the oracle-promise character is at most the section's general drift, not carried by any clause.

Wrong for this section: a covenant lawsuit (rib) is accusation and indictment, and Hos 14:4-9 contains no accusation, no summons, no 'therefore' indictment. The section is the reversal of the lawsuit — 'My anger has turned away' (Hos.14.5#cl2) presupposes it but does not perform it. Section is entirely promise and wisdom-saying.

General: the section's drift as a whole is blessing (dew, blossom, root, grain, wine, fruit), but no clause in it is a commissioning or a blessing of a person to a task. 'Blessing' fits the section as atmosphere; 'commission' has no clause at all here.

The 'lovers' (Hos.2.7#cl3, Hos.2.9#cl0, Hos.2.12#cl0) are the unfaithful wife's partners, and the leaders whom the people appoint (Hos.2.2#cl1, 'a leader one') are not characterised as shepherds anywhere in the section; the word shepherd never occurs in this text.

The section is a lawsuit-speech with sentence and a concluding 'declares the LORD' (Hos.2.13#cl0), not a woe-oracle: no clause has a woe form ('Woe to...', hoy). Its tone is the general drift, so no clause in particular carries it.
No clause in the section speaks of a staff, rod or broken support; the staff image is absent from this text altogether.
No sheep, flock, or scattering language occurs; the section's animals are 'the beasts of the field' (Hos.2.12#cl0) devouring the vines, which is devastation of crops, not the scattering of a flock.

No clause names the day of the LORD or any 'day' as a day of the LORD; the only 'day' clauses are 'like the day she was born' (Hos.2.5#cl1) and 'the days of the Baals' (Hos.2.13#cl0), both ordinary uses of the word.

The section speaks throughout of Yahweh wooing, betrothing and marrying Israel, but the role is never named in any clause in Hos.2.14-2.23; it is the drift of the whole unit, not something a particular clause says.

The word 'covenant' in this section (Hos.2.22#cl1, 'in ... covenant.loyalty'; Hos.2.20#cl0) is not a 'new covenant': Hos.2.20#cl0 is a covenant with the beasts, birds and creeping things, and nothing in Hos.2.14-2.23 says the covenant is new or renewed.

The day formulas here ('in that day', Hos.2.18#cl0, Hos.2.20#cl0, Hos.2.23#cl0) introduce betrothal, a covenant with animals and answered harvests; nothing in this section is a day of Yahweh's judgment or wrath, which is what the stamp names.
No clause in Hos.2.14-2.23 uses father language: the roles given are husband (Hos.2.18#cl2-3), Baal (Hos.2.18#cl4-5) and the betrothed people, not a father and child.
No king, throne, reign or royal figure appears in any clause of this section; the only ruler words are 'Baal my' (Hos.2.18#cl5) and the betrothal clauses.
Nothing in this section names a king, a throne, a reign or a kingdom; the betrothal, covenant with animals, and the new names are the subjects, so the stamp has no purchase here.

This section does not mention the temple, the holy place, or an idol set in it; the idolatry language it does have (the Baals, Hos.2.15#cl0-1, Hos.2.19#cl0) is worship of the Baals in the land, never a desolating object in a sanctuary.
Hos.3.5#cl2 has 'in the last days', but that is a general future horizon of restoration with no day-of-Yahweh judgement or visitation language; no clause here carries the stamp.
Hos.4.5 names 'the prophet' only as one who stumbles; nothing in the section calls him false or describes false prophecy.
No staff, rod or broken-support image occurs in this section; Hos.4.16 has a stubborn heifer and Hos.4.12 a divining stick, neither a broken staff of rule.
No clause in Hos 4 names a day of the LORD, darkness, or Yahweh's coming in judgment; the cited verse 19 is a whirlwind and shame, not the day.
The cited verse Hos 4:5 (you will stumble by day / the prophet by night) has 'night' as a time of stumbling, not darkness as an image of judgment; no clause in the section uses darkness symbolically.
No clause in the section mentions fire; Hos 4:19 is a whirlwind (wind), not fire.
No clause speaks of nations being shaken; Hos 4:19 is a whirlwind wrapping Israel, and the section's judgments are on Israel's land and people (Hos 4:3).
No lamp, lampstand or loss of light in the section; the nearest removal is the fish of the sea (Hos 4:3) and the mother destroyed (Hos 4:5).

The clauses are about the wrongness and shame of sacrifices still being offered (Hos 4:13-14, 19), not about sacrifice ceasing. Marked wrong: the stamp's 'no more' is contradicted; the clauses that speak of sacrifice are listed for transparency.

No clause names an altar; the section speaks of sacrificing on mountaintops, hills and under trees (Hos 4:13), not of an altar being profaned. If 'altar' is meant loosely as the place of sacrifice the general idea is present, but no clause carries the altar.
No temple, sanctuary or house of God appears in the section; the desecration clauses concern mountain/hill/tree shrines and cult prostitutes, not the temple.
No clause has an abomination placed in a holy place; Hos 4:17 is idols being joined to, and Hos 4:13 is illegitimate sacrifice, neither of which is the Daniel/Matthew abomination in the sanctuary.
The heifer in Hos 4:16 is Israel itself under a yoke, and no beast kingdom or anti-divine empire appears in the section; the stamp is alien to the text.
No clause mentions the sun or its darkening; the cited verse Hos 4:5 has day and night as times of stumbling, not darkened luminaries.
No stars or falling luminaries in the section; Hos 4:19 is a whirlwind, and Hos 4:3 mentions only beasts, birds and fish.
The section's shaking image is a whirlwind wrapping Israel (Hos 4:19) and land and creatures wasting away (Hos 4:3); no clause speaks of the heavens being shaken.
No heavenly conflict appears anywhere in the section; Hos 4:19 is a wind/whirlwind over Israel, not a war among heavenly beings.
The unit is dominated by accusation and announced disaster, but no clause has the woe/hoy form or a 'woe to' address; 5:1#cl0-cl5 is a summons to hear, not a woe. General drift only.

Nothing here places an idol or the abomination in the sanctuary or holy place; 5:11#cl3 names following a command/idol but no holy place, and the misdeeds named are snares, prostitution and boundary stones.

No staff, rod or broken support appears in the section and no figure of a broken staff (contrast Zech 11:10); Ephraim's reliance on Assyria (5:13#cl2-cl3) is the closest thing, but the text does not say the support was broken, only that the great king cannot heal (5:13#cl4).
No light/darkness language in Hos.5.1-15; the cited verse 5:6 says only that they will not find the LORD and that He has withdrawn (5:6#cl2-cl3), which is absence, not darkness.
6.7 speaks of transgressing a covenant already in force, not of cutting or making one; no clause here enacts a covenant.
No clause names a god, image, or cult object; 7:14's 'grain and new wine' is a fertility-lament without an explicit object of worship, so the stamp is not carried by any clause in particular.

The whole unit is first-person divine speech mediated by the prophet ('I will spread My net', 'I will chastise them', 'I will redeem them'), but no single clause names prophecy or the word of the LORD, so it is the section's general mode rather than a pinned idea.
No clause in the section mentions a holy place, temple, sanctuary, or an idol set up in one; the stamp's cited verse (7:3) concerns flattering the king and princes.
No staff or support-breaking image appears; the closest is the faulty bow of 7:16, which is a different figure.
Sheep, flock and scattering are absent; 7:12's birds are brought down by a net, not scattered.
'The day of our king' in 7:5 is a royal feast day, not the day of the LORD; the section never uses that phrase or its imagery.
No darkness or night-of-judgement symbol; 7:6's night is the time the oven of their plotting smoulders, in the simile of their own anger.
The fire/oven language of 7:4-7 is a simile for the people's lust, anger and plotting, not a theophany or symbol of divine judgement as the stamp is used in the apocalyptic list.
Nothing is set up in opposition to God's presence or temple; 7:13's rebellion is verbal, and the stamp's apocalyptic sense is absent.
No house, dwelling or desolation-of-house image; the cited 7:16 has a faulty bow and leaders falling by the sword, not an abandoned house.

Hos 7:13, the verse cited, is the opposite of a reversal from humiliation to vindication: the woe and devastation stay on the people — Hos.7.13#cl0 "Woe to them", Hos.7.13#cl2 "Destruction to them", Hos.7.13#cl3 "they have rebelled against Me" — while the only saving clause, Hos.7.13#cl4 ("Though I would redeem them"), is immediately cancelled by Hos.7.13#cl5 ("they speak lies against Me"). No clause in the section shows anyone being brought up out of humiliation; every movement is downward (Hos.7.1#cl2 exposure of iniquity, Hos.7.7#cl2 the king's fall, Hos.7.12#cl0-cl2 the net and being brought down, Hos.7.16#cl2 leaders falling by the sword and being ridiculed).
The section does address both Ephraim/Israel and Judah (8:14), but no clause states the division of the kingdom; the cited verse 8:4 is about making kings without God's approval.
No clause in the section speaks of a siege: fire is sent on cities (8:14#cl3-4) but there is no encirclement, siegeworks, or siege language anywhere here.
9:15 cites Gilgal's evil, but nothing in the section puts an idol in the sanctuary/holy place; the house of God at 9:8 is a place of hostility, not an idol.
The section never uses the Hebrew phrase 'day of the LORD' (9:5 is 'day of ... feast', 9:7 'days of punishment'); the symbolic day-of-the-LORD motif is not this section's.
No staff, rod or broken leadership symbol in the section.
The section ends in rejection and wandering (9:17); no return or exaltation follows the exile here.
9:14 and 9:16 reverse the motif: miscarrying wombs and slain children, not conception after barrenness.
Death and bereavement here yield no life; the section proclaims only judgment.
The section names rebellion, iniquity and forsaking, but no idols, images or false gods; Isa.1.4#cl3 speaks of spurning the Holy One, not of worshiping another.
1:23 names rulers/leaders as rebels and companions of thieves; no king is spoken of, and leadership as such is not the stamp
no clause speaks of a watchman, warning, or looking out; 1:23 is about rulers and judges, not watchmen
1:27 speaks of Zion's redemption in justice and righteousness; nothing in the clauses speaks of Christ
no clause in Isa.10.20-34 speaks of a kingdom, throne, or reign; Isa.10.33 gives the divine title 'Lord GOD of Hosts', which is rule/victory imagery, not the kingdom theme
Nothing in this section states a promise or God's faithfulness; the cited verse (Isa 10:12) speaks of finishing His work and punishing Assyria, i.e. judgment, not promise.
Isa 10:17 and its context describe fire burning and devouring Assyria, not mercy or restoration; no clause here restores anyone.
The section announces judgment on Assyria; no clause speaks of rescue or deliverance of a people.

The section's drift is God's dealing with Assyria on behalf of Mount Zion and Jerusalem, but no clause names a people of God as such; Jerusalem appears only as the object of Assyria's intended conquest and of God's completed work.
Isa 10:15 is the axe/saw and rod/staff figure against Assyria's boasting; nothing in this section says the nations are shaken.
Isa 10:16 says the Lord of Hosts sends a wasting disease on Assyria's stout warriors and a fire burns under his pomp — the strong are brought down by God, not by a weak party defeating a strong one.
Isa 10:17 describes fire burning and devouring Assyria's thorns and thistles; nothing in the section says life comes out of death.

No clause in Isaiah 11 names a covenant, David, or covenant language; the section's link to David is the 'stump of Jesse'/'Root of Jesse' (Isa.11.1#cl0, Isa.11.10#cl1), and even those clauses do not state a covenant. The stamp fits the section's drift (Davidic hope) but no clause states it.
The whole section is future-tense promise (all the yiqtol clauses), but no single clause says 'I promise' or names an oracle; the stamp characterises the section's genre, not any particular clause.
Same as covenant_with_david: Isaiah 11 never states a covenant; only the Jesse/David root motif (Isa.11.1#cl0, Isa.11.10#cl1) points to it. General drift, no clause states the covenant.

No clause in Isaiah 11 calls the figure a son (no 'son', 'my son', or 'firstborn'). The citation was 11:1, but 11:1#cl0/#cl1 speak of a shoot/branch from Jesse's roots and name no son. The stamp is an imported title, not something this section says.

The word 'firstborn' does not occur in the section, and nothing in 11:1 (the cited verse) or elsewhere assigns the figure that status; the Davidic sonship language belongs to 2 Sam 7/Ps 89, not Isaiah 11.

No clause gives the figure a priestly role: Isa.11.2#cl0 lists the Spirit of wisdom, understanding, counsel, strength, knowledge and fear of the LORD, a royal-endowment list elsewhere applied to the king (cf. Isa.11.3#cl0 'delight in the fear of the LORD'), not to a priest; nothing here speaks of cult, mediation or sacrifice.
The whole section is prophecy (repeated 'will'), but no single clause names or describes the prophetic word itself.
The section states future fulfilment ('will be') but never grounds it in a divine promise or in God's faithfulness; no clause names either.
The section's gathering of exiles (Isa.11.12) reworks the covenant people, but no clause states a covenant, its making, or its terms.
Nothing here suffers: the Branch judges, strikes and slays (Isa.11.4#cl2, Isa.11.4#cl3) and the section shows his triumph, not his affliction.
No clause speaks of humanity as God's image; the child leading the animals (Isa.11.6#cl3) is not such a statement.
No clause in this section speaks of priests, priestly service, altar or cult.

No clause in Isa 11:1-16 mentions an offering, altar, slaying of a victim for atonement, or priestly act. The nearest thing to killing is Isa.11.4#cl2 'He will strike the earth with the rod of His mouth' and Isa.11.4#cl3 'with the breath of His lips He will put to death the wicked' — these are judicial/military destruction of the wicked, not a sacrifice; and Isa.11.15#cl0 'devote to destruction the gulf of the Sea of Egypt' is divine judgment on waters. The reader cited Isa 11:4, so the stamp appears to rest on 'slay the wicked' read as sacrificial, which the clause does not say.
The speech about "that day" (Isa.12.1#cl0, Isa.12.4#cl0) and the summons "Let this be known in all the earth" (Isa.12.5#cl2) are the section's frame, but no clause presents a prophetic word as such.

Isa.12.6#cl3 says "great in midst your the.holy.one of.Israel" — the Holy One is great in the midst of Zion, but the clause carries no temple or cultic presence (no house, sanctuary, glory or ark language anywhere in the section).
No clause in this section mentions a temple or its destruction; the cited verse Isa 13:19 is about Babylon's overthrow, not the temple.
No clause speaks of a remnant being left; 13:14 speaks of all fleeing, and the cited verse contains no remnant idea.
No individual ruler is portrayed as beastly here; 13:19 is Babylon the city overthrown, and 13:17-18 are the Medes, so the stamp has no clause to rest on.
13:20 has a literal shepherd who will not rest his flock; no shepherd figure is charged with failing his office, so the stamp is not this section's idea.
The cited verse is about scarcity after slaughter, not about anyone bearing witness; no clause in the section speaks of witnessing.

The cited verse — Isa 13:8#cl1 'pangs and labor-pains they will.seize.[them]' and Isa 13:8#cl2 'like.(the) [woman who].gives.birth they will.be.in.anguish' — uses labour as a simile for terror; a bridegroom is nowhere in the section.
Isa 13:8#cl1/#cl2 is a woman in labour as an image of anguish, not the personified Woman Wisdom.
Isa 13:19#cl0 names Babylon 'the beauty of kingdoms, the splendor of the pride of the Chaldeans', a city, not the personified Woman Folly.
Isa 13:14 (cl2 'everyone to people his.own they will.turn', cl3 'everyone to land his.own they will.flee') is flight to one's own people and land — the opposite of the alien resident.
Isa 13:14#cl0-cl3 is fleeing like a hunted gazelle to one's native land, not travel to a holy place.
No guest, host or hospitality in Isa 13:14; the verbs are 'turn', 'flee' (cl2, cl3).
Isa 13:19 records Babylon's overthrow ('like the.overthrow of.God (et) Sodom and (et) Gomorrah', cl1); no builder or building in the section.
Isa 13:20#cl3 'shepherds not they.will.make.lie.down there' is a shepherd, and cl0-cl2 describe emptiness ('not it.will.remain to perpetuity'), not tending vines.
Isa 13:15#cl1 'every (the).[one who.is].captured he.will.fall by the sword' is death in war, not catching fish.
Isa 13:2#cl3 'that.they.may.go [the].doors of.noble.[people]' has 'doors' but no gatekeeper or guarding role; cl0-cl2 command a banner, a shout and a wave, not the keeping of a gate.
Isa 13:3#cl0 '[ones] I.have.commanded to my.consecrated' is a set-apart army ('my warriors', cl1), not priests or cultic service.
Isa 13:3#cl0-#cl1 name no Davidic figure or king; the 'sanctified ones' are warriors for wrath.
Isa 13:3#cl0-#cl1 is a body of commissioned warriors, not Israel reconstituted.
Isa 13:3#cl0-#cl1 has no deliverer-leader figure.
Isa.13.10#cl3 says only 'moon not it.will.make.shine light its' — the moon withholds light; it does not turn to blood.
Isa.13.10#cl0 says 'the.stars of the.heavens and constellations their not they.will.flash.forth light their' — the stars go dark, they do not fall.
No king is named; only 'rule over their oppressors' (cl4) implies a ruling role, and Yahweh acts as lord, so this is at best the section's drift.

The breaking of Assyria and removal of yoke/burden is the background for a victory, but no clause in this section describes a procession or any such ritual; the text states only the defeat and the release.
The section asserts the certainty of God's worldwide purpose, but no clause carries the day-of-the-Lord imagery (darkness, the day coming, cosmic signs) itself.

Nothing in these clauses speaks of a Davidic king, an heir to David's throne, or the restoration of David's dynasty; Isa 14:14 ("I will make myself like the Most High") is the boast of the king of Babylon, the opposite of a new David.
A covenant lawsuit requires indictment of Israel/Judah for breach of covenant; this oracle indicts the king of Babylon with no charge of covenant violation and no lawsuit form.
There is no battle in these clauses: Isa 14:22 is a divine declaration to cut off Babylon's name, offspring and posterity, and there is no combat, mustering of forces or eschatological conflict.
Isa 14:23 speaks only of Babylon made an owl-haunted swamp swept with a broom of destruction, the opposite of new creation.
The section has no beast or eschatological anti-kingdom imagery; what reads as a general counterpart is the king of Babylon's self-deification, but no clause states it. Low confidence.

Isa 14:3 names a day of rest from pain, hard labor and forced service (Isa.14.3#cl1: "the LORD gives you rest from your pain and torment, and from the hard labor into which you were forced"), not a day of the LORD's judgment; no clause of the section carries the day-of-the-LORD idea.

Isa 14:9, the cited verse, speaks of Sheol and the shades rising to meet the king (Isa.14.9#cl3, Isa.14.9#cl4), but no clause in the section names darkness, night or light extinguished; Sheol is the grave/underworld, not darkness as a symbol.
Nothing in the section pronounces a curse; the lion of Isa.15.9#cl2 is added judgement on the escaped remnant, not a curse formula.
The section is unrelieved judgement; nothing in it speaks of mercy or restoration.
Moab's suffering and the speaker's grief (Isa.15.5#cl0) are not a servant who suffers for others.
The Hebrew of Isa 16:7 is an imperative call to lament (wail, moan), not a woe-oracle: there is no 'woe' (הוי) anywhere in the section, so the clauses carry mourning, not a woe pronouncement.

The section is denunciation and ruin throughout — Damascus made a ruin (17:1), cities abandoned (17:2), splendor faded (17:4), the harvest vanished (17:11), the peoples rebuked and scattered (17:13). 17:10 charges Israel with forgetting the God of their salvation; no promise is made and no divine faithfulness is affirmed.

YHWH speaks and is pictured looking on from His dwelling place (Isa.18.4#cl0–cl2), but nothing here narrates a visible divine appearing — no descent, fire, earthquake or glory; it is general drift (divine presence and speech), not a theophany clause.

No clause names Israel/Judah, Zion's people, or 'my people'; the gifts go to YHWH at the place of His name (Isa.18.7#cl0) but the people concerned are the foreign nation, not the covenant people. Stamp does not attach in this section.
The section reads as the LORD's day of reckoning on Egypt, but no clause names a day; the reader cited Isa 19:12, which is about the LORD of Hosts' plan
Isa 19:5, the cited verse, is about the Nile drying up, a single river of Egypt. Isaiah 19 names no sun, moon, stars or sky, and the drought is confined to Egypt's waters; the stamp does not fit
Isa 19:14 names a 'spirit of confusion' and a drunkard's staggering, not darkness; no clause in the section mentions dark, night or blackness
The cited verse Isa.19.23 speaks of a highway from Egypt to Assyria and joint worship, not of Israel returning from exile; no clause in the section mentions return, captivity or exile.
No clause in the section names a covenant at all; Isa.19.25 offers blessing, not a covenant, so this is at best a general echo of the section's peace-and-blessing drift.

The section blesses the three nations but contains no commissioning or sending of a blessing-bearer; Isa.19.24#cl1 'a blessing upon the earth' is the nearest support, but I find no clause stating a commission.
Isa 2:4 speaks of disarmament and the end of war training, not of a new heaven and earth or the renewal of creation; nothing in these clauses says creation is remade
The section speaks of hiding in rocks and dust from terror but nowhere mentions darkness; only the general drift of hiding from divine terror is present.

The section shows exile taken away, but names no sin of Egypt or Cush as its cause and no death; the theme of sin leading to exile and death is the wider prophetic frame, not carried by any clause here.

Nothing in Isa.20.1-6 is a promise or an act of divine faithfulness; the only 'faithfulness' is the misplaced hope of the coastland in Cush and Egypt (Isa.20.6#cl2), which the text goes on to shame rather than to promise anything.
The section is throughout a prophetic oracle ('this is what the Lord says to me', Isa 21:2,6,10) but contains no call or commissioning of the prophet; it is the general frame, not a clause.
Babylon falls and her idols are smashed (Isa 21:9), but nothing cosmic — no sun, moon, stars or heavens — is shaken in the section.
Isa 21:9 has Babylon's images broken to the ground, but no idol is set up in a holy place; the temple and its desecration are absent (contrast Dan 11-12 imagery).
Babylon here is a city destroyed by Elam and Media, not a beast or an eschatological anti-kingdom; the section names no beast and no final kingdom.
All conflict in the section is on earth — chariots, horsemen, a besieged city; no heavenly or angelic warfare appears.
Only Babylon falls; the section does not speak of nations being shaken, and the storm-wind simile of Isa 21:1 describes the invader's sweep, not a shaking of nations.
'My people, crushed on the threshing floor' (Isa 21:10) is threshing imagery, not sheep scattered; no flock or shepherd appears in the section.
The section ends with judgment announced on Babylon and the prophet addressing a crushed people; it narrates no exile and no exaltation or return.
No movement from humiliation to vindication is narrated; the crushed threshing-floor people are addressed but not vindicated in the section.
The destroyers of Babylon (Elam, Media) are not presented as the weak overcoming the strong; the contrast is invader against doomed city.
'The traitor still betrays, and the destroyer still destroys' (Isa 21:2) is treachery and destruction in general, with no insider identified who fails.
No stone, builder or cornerstone imagery occurs anywhere in the section.
Babylon's fall produces no life; the section's outcome is destruction and the end of groaning, not resurrection or renewal.
No scattering and no gathering is narrated; the threshing-floor image of Isa 21:10 is crushing, not dispersion followed by regathering.

No clause in this section names or characterises a prophet. The speaker is the oracle's anonymous caller from Seir and the watchman; the stamp's cited verse (Isa 21:11) contains the watchman, not a prophet, and the Hebrew text of these clauses has no prophetic word or prophet term.

The section's general drift is the burden against Dumah, which is judgment in view, but no clause in particular announces or depicts a judgment: cl0 is only the heading "the.oracle of.Dumah", and the rest is question and answer about night and morning. Hence general.
There is no woe form in these clauses: no "woe" interjection or accusation. The oracle is a summons and a question-and-answer ("what is left of the night?" / "Morning has come").

General drift only: the night-and-morning exchange is read as the night of eschatological crisis giving way to dawn, but no clause in the section says "day of the LORD" or names that day. The clauses speak of "night" (cl3, cl5, 12#cl2) and "morning" (12#cl1) without the phrase.

General drift of the section, not carried by any one clause: nothing here is symbolic diction for the day of the LORD as such; the closest is "night"/"morning" in 12#cl1-2, which are literal in the clause.
The section is announcement of judgment, not a promise; no clause makes a promise, so the stamp at most describes the oracle-speech drift of 21:16-17 generally.

No false god, image or cultic act appears in the section; Isa.22.11 charges Judah with not looking to or considering the One who made and planned it (Isa.22.11#cl1, Isa.22.11#cl2), which is failure to trust the LORD, not idolatry. The later-reading stamps offered for that verse are therefore different: Isa.22.11#cl1-2 are failure to look to God, and I have pinned them to insider_fails, not here.

Isa.22.12 has the Lord calling for weeping, wailing, baldness and sackcloth (Isa.22.12#cl0, cl1), which are the outward signs of mourning and repentance; but the section states they were refused — 'But look, there is joy and gladness' and 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die' (Isa.22.13#cl1, cl6-8), and Isa.22.14#cl1 says the sin 'will never be atoned for'. The only mourning language is the rejected call, so the section is not a case of revival/repentance.

No darkness, night, blindness or light imagery occurs in the section. Isa.22.5, the verse cited for the stamp, names a day of 'tumult and trampling and confusion' and the breaking down of walls (Isa.22.5#cl0-1), which is judgment language, not darkness imagery; 'Valley' and 'burden' are not darkness either.

Isa.22.13, the verse cited, has 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die' (Isa.22.13#cl6, cl7, cl8) — death is the horizon of a death-bound boast, not a source of life, and nothing in the section issues in life.
Isa 22:25 has no witnessing clause: 'Yahweh he has spoken' (Isa.22.25#cl8) is the authentication of the prophetic word, and no clause names a witness, testimony, or someone testifying.
Isa 22:22 gives the key and open/shut power to Eliakim but nothing in the section presents a contest or defeat of a strong by a weak; Yahweh alone acts (Isa.22.17#cl1).

The section's imagery is peg, robe, key, throne; the only possible echo — the peg in a firm place (Isa.22.23#cl0) that gives way (Isa.22.25#cl2) — is the opposite of a rejected stone becoming the head, and no clause concerns a stone or a rejected-then-head figure.
Isa.23.11 speaks of the strongholds of Canaan being destroyed (Isa.23.11#cl3 'destroy strongholds its'), not a temple; the section never mentions a temple or sanctuary.
Isa.23.13 names Assyria allocating the land of the Chaldeans to desert creatures and bringing it to ruin (Isa.23.13#cl4-cl7); no one is taken captive or deported in this section.
Isa.23.9 states the LORD planned to defile Tyre's pride and disgrace the honored of the earth; there is no accusation, summons, or covenant charge against a covenant partner.
Isa.23.12 calls Sidon 'oppressed Virgin Daughter of Sidon', a city epithet with no bride, wedding, or bridegroom imagery.
Isa.23.1 reports that word 'has reached them from the land of Cyprus' (Isa.23.1#cl5), which is news arriving, not a watchman on a wall or a lookout's report.
Isa.23.18 says the profit will go 'to those who live before the LORD', but these are recipients of food and clothing, not servants; no servant language appears.
Isa.23.18 dedicates Tyre's profit to the LORD for food and clothing within the existing order; there is no covenant, no new covenant, and no covenant formula in the section.

No covenant, treaty, or peace is stated anywhere in the section; Isa 23:18 speaks of Tyre's profits being holy to the LORD and going to those who dwell before Him, which is devotion of wealth, not a covenant of peace.

The section's drift is devastation and ruin (Tyre laid waste, no harbor, forgotten seventy years), but no clause names a sin, an exile, or a death; the destruction is stated as the LORD's planned act, not traced to sin or described as exile/death.
Isa 24:23 speaks of the LORD reigning on Mount Zion and the moon and sun being ashamed, not of new heavens and a new earth being created; nothing in this section describes a renewed creation.
Nothing in this section depicts a new creation; Isa 24:23 shows the LORD reigning in Zion with the luminaries abashed, which is a theophany/kingdom scene rather than creation renewed.
The whole chapter is a thanksgiving psalm (v.1) followed by announcements of what God will do; nothing in the clauses performs a promise oracle with the cited verse in view.
Isa.25.2 speaks of a city already made a ruin (no combat, no army, no fighting); the closest thing to a battle, Isa.25.10#cl1 (Moab trampled like straw), is a trampling, not this stamp's cited verse.
Isa.25.8 gives the swallowing of death, wiping of tears and removal of reproach from the earth, but no new heavens or new earth; the renewal of the whole creation is not spoken of here.

Isa.25.4 says God 'has been a refuge ... a shade' — protective, not fighting; the warrior stamp is not carried by the cited clauses, and the subduing in Isa.25.5#cl0 and trampling in Isa.25.10#cl1 are not the cited verse.

Isa.25.9 has 'we have waited for Him, and He has saved us' and 'His people' in v.8, but no clause marks a surviving remainder out of a larger body; 'we' here is the whole waiting community, not a remnant.
Isa.25.8 has death swallowed and tears wiped, a divine victory, but no procession, no march, no entry with spoil or captives in any clause of the section.
Isa.25.8 has no covenant formula, no 'covenant of peace', no oath or treaty language; the closest, 'For the LORD has spoken' (Isa.25.8#cl3), only certifies the act, it does not constitute a covenant.

Isa 25:9 is a community confession ('Surely this is our God... we have waited for Him, and He has saved us'), not testimony given to others; no clause names a witness or act of bearing witness.

No clause mentions a bridegroom, marriage or wedding; the banquet of Isa 25:6 is prepared by the LORD for the peoples, with no marital imagery.
No clause mentions a bride, wedding or marriage; nothing in Isa 25:1-12 carries the role.

No clause in this section speaks of a servant or service; 26:13's 'lords' are rulers, not servants, and 26:12's 'we have accomplished' is not servant language.
The birth imagery in 26:17–18 is maternal (a woman with child, labor, giving birth); no clause presents a father.

26:18's birth imagery has nothing to do with vines; no clause mentions planting, pruning, or a vineyard.

This section contains no speaker called or commissioned as a prophet; Isa.26.8 speaks of waiting on the LORD and His judgments, not a prophetic figure.
No priestly role, mediation, or cultic act appears anywhere in the section, including Isa.26.13.
Isa.26.18's birth imagery ("we gave birth to wind") rests on the Hebrew *bat* nuptial song ("we were with child... we writhed")
Isa.26.17 is a simile of a woman in labor used of the community before the LORD; it does not present a bridegroom.
Isa.26.17's pregnant woman is a simile for 'we' (the people) in the LORD's presence, not a bride.
Isa.26.9 is the speaker's own soul longing for God, not personified Woman Wisdom.

No shepherding imagery or shepherd figure appears in the section; Isa.26.13's 'other lords' are rulers, not shepherds.
Nothing in the section concerns a prophet, true or false; Isa.26.13 names 'other lords', not prophets.
Isa.26.15 (the cited verse) speaks of enlarging the nation and extending the land's borders, but names no deliverer-lawgiver figure; the stamp is not identifiable in this section.
Isa.26.1 mentions a strong city and salvation as walls, but no Davidic king, anointing, or dynastic promise.

Isa.26.20's hidden people under wrath and Isa.26.6's trampled poor do not present a servant who suffers vicariously; the section names no servant figure, so the stamp is absent rather than contradicted.

The only possible pin (Isa.26.21#cl1) is YHWH going forth FROM His place/dwelling (מִמְּקוֹמוֹ) in judgment — a departure from the divine abode, the opposite of a temple-presence/abiding-presence theme. Nothing in the section speaks of God's presence dwelling with or among His people (no 'in the midst of', no sanctuary/Zion dwelling, no 'dwelling with them'); the 'city' of 26:1 is a human stronghold (Isa.26.1#cl1) and its 'walls and ramparts' are salvation (Isa.26.1#cl2), not a temple. The section as a whole is prophetic promise/announcement (vineyard song, restoration, regathering), but no single clause is itself the promise-oracle form. Not the words of Isa 27:2#cl1/cl2, which are the song command and the vineyard itself.

Isa 27:9 speaks of Jacob's iniquity being atoned for and sin removed, but it is not the annual Day of Atonement (Lev 16) — no date, ritual, two goats, scapegoat or high-priest act appear in any clause. The stamp is the wrong category for this section.

Isa 27:10's fortified city is already deserted, overgrown and pastured by calves — a picture of abandonment, not a besieging army or besieged city. No clause in the section shows a siege (no attack, wall, or siege-ramp language).

The clause cited for this stamp (Isa.27.5: "let them lay claim to My protection; let them make peace with Me— yes, let them make peace with Me") rests on Hebrew חסה ('take refuge', Isa.27.5#cl0) and עשה שלום ('make peace', Isa.27.5#cl1, Isa.27.5#cl2). Neither is covenant vocabulary: no ברית ('covenant') appears, and no covenant-making, covenant-ratifying or covenant-formula language is present anywhere in Isa.27.1-13. The verse speaks of refuge and the cessation of hostility, not of a covenant.

The section has no royal figure named or implied as a character in a clause; the crown of Ephraim (28.1#cl1, 28.3#cl0) is a metaphorical object, not a king, and 28.6 has no king mentioned. The stamp may belong to the surrounding oracle but not to any clause here.
No sheep, flock, shepherd or scattering image appears in any clause of the section; 28:13 speaks of the people being broken and captured, not scattered like sheep.
The instruments of judgment in 28:2 are hail, tempest, driving rain and flood (2:2) — water and storm, no fire anywhere in Isa 28:1-13.
The section opens with a summons to hear, not with a hoy/woe; no clause carries a woe formula.
The one-who-believes line is individual trust, not a remnant motif; no clause speaks of a surviving remainder.
Every clause here is judgment: covenant dissolved, scourge, terror, decree of destruction; the stone foundation is promise, not restoration of the judged.
The shaking is of this people (refuge, hiding place, whole land); no clause names the nations.
Verse 19 has 'by day and by night' as ceaseless timing, not darkness as a symbol for judgment.
No staff, rod or broken support image appears in the section.
Sheep imagery is absent; the people are trampled and carried away, not scattered as a flock, and no shepherd is named.
Plowing, harrowing, sowing and planting are agriculture/farming, not creation; no clause speaks of the world being made.
Isa 28:26 speaks of God instructing the farmer, not of a blessing conferred on anyone; no clause carries a blessing.
Threshing sledge, cart wheel and rod are farm implements in a harvest analogy; no clause speaks of judging anyone.
Isa 28:29 closes the unit by grounding the farmer's instruction in the LORD of Hosts - a wisdom conclusion, not a promise stated in any clause.
The section's imagery is farming - plowing, sowing, harrowing, threshing - not creation.
The LORD of Hosts is named in Isa 28:29, but no clause speaks of kingship, a throne, or a kingdom; possibly general drift only.
The section's movement from judgment to the scattering of the besieging nations carries a restorative drift, but no clause states mercy or restoration in particular.

The section's one redemption clause, Isa.29.22#cl1 'who he.redeemed (et) Abraham' ('the LORD who redeemed Abraham'), speaks of the LORD redeeming Abraham, not of Christ; nothing in these eight verses names the Messiah, a servant, or a future redeemer.
rulership is spoken of (Isa.3.4#cl0-#cl1, Isa.3.6#cl2, Isa.3.12#cl2) but no clause names a king; the added 'king' entry is not itself carried by any clause

Isa 3:9's cited clause compares Judah's sin to Sodom (like Sodom), which is a comparison of sin, not a nation acting as a character; no nation other than Israel/Judah appears as an agent in this section
no clause states the weak overcome or defeat the strong; 3:4-5 say boys/young rise and rule, i.e. the reversal of order, not a contest the weak win

The section is shaped as the LORD's accusation and sentence against his people (the 'because' of vv.12–14, the summons and woe form), but no clause in it stages the lawsuit itself — no summons, witnesses, or charge formula naming the covenant.

The section is dominated by the failure of the alliance and by coming judgment; the one saving word (v.15 'you would be saved') is a rejected offer, not a promise kept, and no clause rests on God's fidelity to a promise.
The section's promises to Israel assume the covenant relationship throughout, but no clause states or names a covenant

Cited verse is Isa 30:18, but Isa.30.18 speaks only of the LORD waiting to be gracious, rising to show compassion, being a God of justice, and the blessing of those who wait for Him — no reign, throne, king or dominion. The section's only king language is Isa.30.33#cl1 ('prepared for the king'), which is the Assyrian king and Topheth, not the kingdom theme; so no clause in the section carries this stamp and it is at best the section's general drift (salvation of Zion).
Assyria's fall is by sword and panic, not an attack on a besieged city; no siege works, wall or battering imagery appears in the section
The section presents an ideal reigning king and righteous princes, which may be read as the promised Davidic ruler, but no clause names David, the Davidic line, or a shoot/root of Jesse.
The section describes a righteous ruler and opened eyes and ears, but no clause names Moses, a prophet like Moses, or the exodus deliverance that would identify him.
No clause speaks of a prophet, prophecy, or a messenger speaking for God; Isa.32.3 is about the eyes and ears of the people being opened, not a prophetic figure.
The section's noble man who stands up for worthy causes may be seen as a servant figure, but no clause names a servant, service, or the servant of the LORD.
No clause speaks of testifying, testimony, or bearing witness; Isa.32.4 is about the stammering tongue speaking clearly, not witnessing.
No clause names a nation, peoples, or a corporate body acting as a character; Isa.32.5's fool and scoundrel are individuals.
Folly appears only in the abstract (Isa.32.6: a fool speaks foolishness); no woman, personified or otherwise, is present in the section.
The noble man's honorable plans are wisdom-like, but no woman and no personified Wisdom appears in the section.
No clause speaks of a surviving remainder, escape, or being left; Isa.32.3 concerns the eyes and ears of those who see and hear, not a remnant.
No clause names a foreigner, sojourner, resident alien, or stranger; the hungry and thirsty of Isa.32.6 are not identified as outsiders.
No clause speaks of building, constructing, or a builder; Isa.32.8's noble man plans deeds and stands for them, which is not building.
No clause speaks of hosting, lodging, or receiving guests; shelter and refuge in Isa.32.2 are meteorological images, not hospitality.
No clause names a guest or one received into a house; the hungry and thirsty are deprived, not hosted.
No clause speaks of a journey, road, going up, or pilgrimage; Isa.32.2's shelter and streams are images of protection and provision, not travel.
No clause speaks of a priest, priesthood, altar, or sacrifice; Isa.32.1's king and princes rule with righteousness and justice, which is royal not priestly.
No clause speaks of sonship, a father, or a son; the king of Isa.32.1 is named only as king.
No clause names or implies a father; 32:1 has a king and rulers, and no other clause in the section has a paternal figure.
No clause speaks of a firstborn or of birth order; nothing in 32:1-8 rests on it.
No clause mentions a bridegroom, marriage or wedding.
No clause mentions a bride, marriage or wedding.
No clause names or implies a mother; the only female-ish imagery is the land in 32:2, which is not a mother here.
32:6 names a fool, the hungry and the thirsty, not a slave or bondservant; no clause in the section does.
32:2 has streams of water in a dry land, not a vine or a dresser of vines.
No clause mentions fishing, fish or nets; 32:2 is water in a dry land, not a fisherman's work.
No clause mentions a gate, door or gatekeeper; 32:2's shelter and refuge are not a gate.
32:2 speaks of shelter, refuge, streams and shadow, not of armour or weapons borne by the righteous; 32:7's weapons belong to the scoundrel.
The section has no fruit, no Spirit and no list of virtues; 32:8's honorable plans are a noble man's own, not the Spirit's fruit.
No clause pronounces a blessing ('blessed are...'); 32:8 states what a noble man does, not a blessing on him.
32:4 has understanding and clear speech, but no gift, no Spirit and no giver; nothing in the section names gifts.
32:6 lists folly, iniquity, falsehood and oppression, but no clause speaks of the flesh or of a catalogue of fleshly works.
No clause is a beatitude or a psalm blessing; 32:8 is a contrast statement about a noble man.

No clause names a king, throne, reign or dominion. Justice, righteousness and peace dwelling in the land (Isa.32.16#cl0-cl1; Isa.32.17#cl0-cl1) describe the order of the restored people, which is the section's general drift rather than a kingdom said in any clause; hence general: true.
The section has a prophetic speaker (Isaiah's 'says the LORD' in v10) but no clause names a prophet or prophetic role; the stamp describes the general drift only.

Nothing in Isa 33:1-24 names a priest, priestly office or cultic mediation; the forgiveness of v24 is by Yahweh's own act, not a priestly one. The stamp was cited from Isa 33:24 where there is no priest.

The section never mentions the temple or its destruction; v8's broken treaty and deserted highways are not temple language. The stamp was cited from Isa 33:8 where no temple appears.
No clause speaks of deportation, being carried off, or life in a foreign land. The cited Isa 33:8 gives broken treaties, despised witnesses and disregarded life, not exile.
The section has no journey home or regathering clause; v20's Zion is already looked upon and settled, with no return movement. The stamp was cited from Isa 33:20 where no return is described.
No oath, swearing, or vow appears. The cited Isa 33:8 has 'the treaty has been broken' (berith) and 'witnesses are despised', which is covenant-breaking, not oath-taking.
No clause in Isa 33 mentions anointing, oil, or setting apart; the nearest word is 'the King' (Isa.33.17#cl0), which says nothing about an anointing.
Isa 33:17 names a King but no clause of the section states the Davidic covenant, a Davidic heir, or an eternal throne (contrast Isa 9 / 11 / 2 Sam 7, absent here).
Isa 33:22 calls the LORD judge, lawgiver and king, but the task's cited verse names no mediator, prophet or second Moses; the lawgiver here is the LORD himself, not a new Moses.
As with davidic_covenant: Isa 33:17 shows a King but no clause refers to David or to a covenant with him.
Isa 33:22 says the LORD is lawgiver but the section contains no list of commandments and no clause alludes to the ten words as such.

The section is YHWH's anger poured out on all nations and the dissolving of the host of heaven (Isa.34.2#cl0-cl1; Isa.34.4#cl0-cl2), the drift of a day-of-the-Lord oracle, but no clause names a 'day' or the LORD's coming; the reader cited Isa 34:4, whose clauses say only that the stars rot, the heavens roll up and the host withers.
Same as day_of_the_lord: no clause names the day or the LORD's approach; the cited Isa 34:4 supplies only the dissolving host, rolled-up skies and falling stars.
Isa 34:12 speaks of Edom's nobles and princes ceasing to be, not of a ruler depicted as a beast; no clause here characterizes a ruler as beastly.
Isa 35:8 speaks of the Way of Holiness and who may walk it, not of a covenant; the Hebrew of 35:8 has no covenant word (berith) and no clause here carries covenant-making or covenant-renewal.

Isa 35 describes the transformation of the wilderness and desert (35:1-2, 35:6-7), not the passing away of heaven and earth or a new heavens and new earth; no clause here speaks of the cosmos being remade.

The section speaks of the LORD's ransomed/redeemed returning to Zion (Isa 35:10), with no reference to Christ or to redemption accomplished in him; the stamp is a New Testament identification, not an idea of this text.
Isa 35:10 has the redeemed entering Zion with joy, but no clause mentions the temple, God's dwelling, or his presence in a sanctuary.

The section's challenge to the LORD is spoken on the wall and in the Rabshakeh's mouth; nothing in these clauses places an idol or foreign object in the temple or holy place (the altar of Isa.36.7#cl5 is the LORD's own altar in Jerusalem).
The section speaks from within an Assyrian threat (v.3 distress, v.4 Rabshakeh, v.6-7 Assyria), but no clause states a siege, a besieging army or a city under attack. General, not pinned.

Unsure. 'the sword' in Isa.37.7#cl4 is the only martial word; it describes a death, not a battle, and no clause describes fighting, an army in combat or combatants. Low confidence whether this counts as the stamp here.

Hezekiah's prayer in the temple is royal intercession, not priestly cultic mediation; nothing in the section names a priest, altar, or sacrificial offering. The stamp describes the section's drift at best, so no clause carries it specifically.

No prophet, prophecy, or prophetic messenger appears in the section: Hezekiah receives the letter from messengers and prays in his own voice. The reader's citing of Isa 37:14 points to a royal recipient of a letter, not a prophet.
No idol is set up in a holy place in this section: the gods are cast into the fire and destroyed (Isa.37.19#cl0, #cl3), which is the opposite of an idol installed in the temple.
Judgment falls on Assyria (Isa.37.29#cl3-cl5; 37.33) and restoration on Judah; no sin of the LORD's people, no exile and no death of the people is spoken of in these clauses.

Isa 37:37 describes Sennacherib's retreat after defeat (he broke camp, withdrew, returned to Nineveh, stayed there), not a triumph; the clauses carry departure and staying, nothing processional or victorious. The only cited verse yields no clause for the stamp.
Nothing in Isa 37:38 (or 36-37) presents the ruler as beastly or animal-like: he is worshiping in his temple and then murdered by his sons. The motif is not in this section's clauses.
The section is a message sent to Hezekiah by the Assyrian envoys, not a prophetic word spoken by a prophet of YHWH; nothing here is the prophet's oracle.
No idol and no holy place appears in these verses; the gods of the nations are named only in the Assyrian taunt, and Jerusalem and the temple are not said to be defiled by an idol.
This is a plain historical taunt listing defeated kings (Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena, Ivvah); no beast, apocalyptic kingdom or anti-divine empire figure is present in the text.
Hezekiah prays for himself (Isa.38.2#cl1, Isa.38.3#cl3), not as a priest on behalf of others; no priest, no altar, no mediating role appears in the section.
The text names the Assyrian king as a threat but no fighting, army, weapons or combat occurs in these verses; nothing in the clauses describes a battle.
No clause in this section names a servant; Hezekiah's posture ('I am oppressed; be my security') is the general cast the earlier reader drew on, but nothing in particular states it.
No clause names a priest or priestly act; the only link is 'the house of the LORD' as a place of worship, which is not a priest.

The section's only temple reference is hopeful: 'I will go up to the house of the LORD' (Isa.38.22#cl2) and playing songs 'in the house of the LORD' (Isa.38.20#cl2). Nothing is destroyed; the earlier reader's citation of Isa 38:22 points at the opposite.

The section is a sufferer's psalm with affliction, moaning and recourse to God, but nothing marks Hezekiah as a servant of the LORD or evokes the servant of the LORD elsewhere in Isaiah; the stamp is only general drift.
The unit is shaped as a report of the prophet's speech introduced by a 'hear the word' formulary, but the content of the speech is threat, not promise, so no clause carries the stamp in particular
There is no woe ('hoy') in the section; Isa.39.6 opens with 'here!' plus 'days are coming', the announcement-of-judgment formulary, not a woe pronouncement
Exile is present (Isa.39.6#cl2, Isa.39.7#cl0, Isa.39.7#cl3), but no clause states a sin that caused it nor any death: Hezekiah's death is only implied by 'in my lifetime' (Isa.39.8#cl4)
Isa.39.8#cl1 says the word of the LORD is 'good', not that God is faithful; a judgment oracle is called good, which is not the stamp 'promise/faithfulness'
The section as a whole is future-oriented promise (4:2-6), but no single clause is itself the oracle-form; it is the section's general drift.
