The whole section is prophetic speech, but no clause names a prophet, a word of the LORD, or the act of speaking it; it is the section's general mode.
No clause in Isa.4.1-6 mentions a covenant, covenant-making, or covenant language (berith); the section's themes of cleansing, remnant and divine presence do not require a covenant clause here.

The section speaks of a voice calling to prepare the way (Isa.40.3#cl0-cl2) and of God's mouth having spoken (Isa.40.5#cl2), but no clause names or depicts a prophet; the 'voice' is not identified as a prophet anywhere in these clauses, so the stamp is only the section's general drift.

No clause mentions a king, a throne, a reign or a kingdom; Isa.40.5#cl0-cl1 'the glory of the LORD will be revealed' and 'all humanity together will see it' describe universal revelation of Yahweh's glory, which a reader takes as the general drift of his sovereign rule, but no clause says kingdom.

The section has no temple, house, sanctuary or dwelling; Isa.40.5#cl0 'the glory of the LORD will be revealed' uses glory language that elsewhere attaches to the sanctuary, but here the glory is revealed to all flesh in the open, not in a temple, so this is general drift at most.

No clause mentions a covenant, creation, or an ordinance of heaven and earth; Isa 40:8's clauses are the word of God standing forever, contrasted with withering flesh (Isa.40.8#cl2 against Isa.40.8#cl0-1), which is not a covenant with creation.
No clause speaks of mercy or restoration; Isa.40.8#cl2 affirms only that the word stands forever, and the contrast with flesh's withering is not itself mercy or restoration.
Isa 40:28 speaks of the LORD as Creator of the ends of the earth, not of a covenant with creation; no clause here mentions berith or any covenant with created things.
The section's closing renewal of strength (Isa 40:31) speaks of restored vigor for the weary, not of a new creation; no clause states creation made new.
The servant of Isa 42/49/52-53 is not in view here; Isa 40:11's shepherd tending his flock is the LORD, not a suffering servant.
Nothing in these clauses names Christ or the cross; the section speaks of the LORD coming in might and shepherding His flock, which is not the same as redemption accomplished in Christ.
Isa 40:27 has Israel's complaint that her way is hidden from the LORD; no clause mentions a covenant, its parties, or its terms.
Isa 40:19-20 mocks manufactured idols generally; there is no temple, sanctuary, or holy place in this section where an idol is set.
Isa 40:10 announces the LORD coming with might and reward; it does not describe the day of the LORD's wrath and darkness as in the prophetic day-of-the-LORD passages.
Isa 40:15 says the nations are like a drop in a bucket and a speck of dust, i.e. accounted as nothing; no clause says the nations shake or are shaken.

Isa 40:31 speaks of renewal of strength for those who wait on the LORD (cl0 'they will renew strength', cl2 'they will run', cl4 'they will walk'), but nothing in the section is a death, and no clause says life comes out of death or that death produces anything. The verses contrast the weary/stumbling (Isa.40.30#cl0, cl2) with renewed strength (Isa.40.31#cl0); exhaustion reversed is not death producing life.

Isa 40:27 states the complaint 'My way is hidden from the LORD, and my claim is ignored by my God' (Isa.40.27#cl4, cl5); no clause in this section names exile or a return from it, and no clause names exaltation coming after exile. The nearest ideas are hiddenness/justice passing away (Isa.40.27#cl4-5) and renewed strength (Isa.40.31#cl0), neither of which is exile or exaltation.

Isa.41.21 is outside the given section (only vv.1-20 supplied), so the lawsuit's summons-to-trial clauses are not available; the v.1 court language alone is a general judgement scene, not a covenant lawsuit.
v.19 is a transformed-land planting scene within the present creation, not a new heavens and new earth; nothing in the section speaks of a new cosmos.

Isa 41:14 calls Israel 'worm of Jacob' and 'few men of Israel' and promises help and a Redeemer, but nothing in the section presents a servant who suffers or bears suffering; the humiliation language is Israel's lowliness, not the servant's suffering, and the Servant figure of Isa 42-53 is not in view here.

Isa 41:15 has Israel, the weak party, threshing mountains and hills, but the defeat is accomplished by God's making them a threshing sledge, not by the weak overcoming the strong by their own weakness; the reversal is Israel being empowered, and no clause sets a weak agent against a strong one in victory.

Isa 41:14 addresses Israel as 'worm of Jacob' and 'few men of Israel' and promises help, but nothing in the section states a reversal of rank or order (the last becoming first); being lowly and being helped is not the same as being made first.

Isa 41:18 speaks of rivers, fountains, pools and springs on barren heights, in valleys and the desert, which is barrenness becoming fertility, not death producing life; no clause in the section speaks of death or of life coming out of it.

The word 'prophet' never appears in Isaiah 42:1-9; the Servant is called 'My Servant' and 'My Chosen One' and is given the Spirit to bring justice to the nations, which is a royal/commissioned-figure description, not the term or role 'prophet'.

Isa 42:5 speaks of the Creator who made the heavens and earth and gives breath, but it names no covenant with creation; the covenant language in this section (Isa 42:6 'a covenant for the people') is with people, not with creation.

Isa 42:9 'the former things have happened, and now I declare new things' is about new events announced by God, not a new heavens and earth; the phrase 'new heavens and new earth' appears in Isa 65:17 and 66:22, not here.

Christ is not named anywhere in Isaiah 42:1-9; the section speaks of God's Servant, and 'redemption in Christ' is a later Christian reading of the passage, not an idea carried by any clause of this section.

Isa 42:16 speaks of leading the blind, turning darkness to light and rough places level (cl0-cl5) plus 'I will not forsake them' (cl8) — ethical/spiritual restoration, not the creation of new heavens and a new earth; the phrase and idea are absent from this section.

The whole section is divine speech delivered through the prophet (Isa.42.14#cl0-cl4, Isa.42.15#cl0-cl3, Isa.42.16#cl0-cl8 in the first person), but no clause itself states the idea of a prophetic word; it is the frame the earlier reader cited (Isa 42:13) rather than a content of any clause.
The section has idols only in Isa.42.17#cl1-cl4, and its concern is people trusting and addressing them, not an idol standing in the temple or holy place; the temple does not appear in Isa 42:10-17.
No clause has anyone testifying or bearing witness; the deaf/blind servant is a mere comparison in the rhetorical questions of 42:19, not a witness.
The 'Who among you' questions appeal to the hearers present; nothing marks them as a surviving remnant, and 42:22 says all are plundered with none to rescue.
Nothing here restores or shows mercy: the section ends with anger poured out and the people unknowing (42:25), with no one to rescue them (42:22).
No cultic or intercessory role appears anywhere in the section; Isa.43.3 speaks of Yahweh as deliverer and of Egypt/Cush/Seba given as ransom, not of a priest's office or service.
The section calls Israel sons and daughters (Isa.43.6) and "My servant" (Isa.43.10) but nowhere singles out a firstborn, nor uses firstborn language of Israel, the king or anyone else.
The section's drift is that the called-by-name, created-for-glory people (Isa.43.1, Isa.43.7) are addressed as a restored whole; no single clause names a new Israel.
Waters, rivers and fire (Isa.43.2) describe the people's passage with Yahweh present; there is no figure who leads a deliverance out of Egypt, and the sea is not parted or crossed as in Exod.14.
No royal or Davidic figure, anointing, throne or covenant with David appears anywhere in the section; the only named roles are servant (Isa.43.10) and witnesses (Isa.43.10, Isa.43.12).
Isa.43.5 speaks only of bringing offspring from east and west; the section never mentions peace, an everlasting covenant, or covenant language at all.
Creation is spoken of in Isa.43.1 and Isa.43.7 as forming Jacob/Israel, but with no covenant term, sign or obligation attaching to it.
Isa.43.5 gives the ingathering from east and west without any mention of an oath, or of Abraham, Isaac or Jacob as fathers to whom one was sworn.
Isa.43.8 is a summons ("Bring out a people") with an accusation-like caricature of blind/deaf, but the section pronounces no woe (no הוֹי) and states no coming judgment on the addressee.
Isa 43:2's waters/rivers/fire are images of danger the LORD brings his people through ('they will not overwhelm you'), not a rite of immersion; no clause names a washing, immersion or baptism.

Isa 43:10 contains no call or commissioning of a prophet: no divine initiative to a named individual, no objection, no sign. Being 'My witnesses' and 'My servant whom I have chosen' is the status of the people/servant, not a prophetic call narrative.
Isa 43:8's 'a people who have eyes but are blind, and who have ears but are deaf' is a description of Israel's condition, not a performed action with symbolic meaning.
The cited verse (Isa 43:8) has blind eyes and deaf ears, but nothing is said to be opened, cured or restored; no clause reports healing.
Isa 43:8 states blindness and deafness with no call to repent, no confession and no renewal; the chapter's restoration language (43:5-7) is ingathering, not repentance.
Isa 43:13 speaks of the LORD's eternal being and the irrevocability of his act ('When I act, who can reverse it?'), with no day of the LORD, darkness, trumpet or wrath-of-the-day language.
Nothing in the section describes a battle: nations assemble in 43:9 as witnesses in a legal dispute, not as combatants, and 43:13 is about deliverance out of God's hand.
Isa 43:1's 'I have redeemed you' is the LORD's redemption of Jacob/Israel in the exodus pattern; no clause in the section mentions Christ, his blood, or a new covenant.
Isa 43:10 calls the servant 'whom I have chosen' but says nothing of his suffering, wounding, or bearing sin; the servant's exaltation as witness, not his passion, is in view.
No clause shows a victor's procession, triumph or escort; Isa 43:17 gives the enemy laid low and quenched, not a procession. The stamp does not fit this section.
The section speaks of Yahweh as Israel's Redeemer and of Babylon's fall; no clause speaks of Christ or of redemption in him. Reading the New Testament figure into these clauses is not what they say.
The section never speaks of foreigners, sojourners or resident aliens; those named are Jacob/Israel, the LORD's own servant, and the idol-makers are 'only human' (Isa 44:11) but not called strangers.
The LORD is called King, Redeemer and LORD of Hosts (Isa 44:6), but no clause shows him fighting or waging war; 'LORD of Hosts' is a title, not a battle scene.
No priest, altar or offering appears in the section; the idol-worshippers bow and pray (Isa 44:15, 17), which is the opposite of true priesthood, and 'My blessing' has no priestly actor.
No clause mentions a firstborn or birthright; 'from the womb' (Isa 44:2) is God forming Israel, not a firstborn claim.
Isa 44:12 describes a human blacksmith who hungers, thirsts and grows faint; no beast or bestial ruler appears in the section.

The cited verse (Isa 44:18) speaks of blind eyes and closed hearts; the Hebrew of Isa.44.18#cl0-5 has no woman, no feminine figure, and no folly-personification. The folly depicted here is the idolater's, not a woman.

No clause names Moses, a lawgiver, or a deliverer from Egypt; what the section has is YHWH as Maker/King/Redeemer acting for His servant — the general drift of a new saving act, not any particular clause.

Nothing speaks of a first man or a new humanity; the only 'man' language is Isa.44.11#cl3 ('they are from humankind') and Isa.44.13#cl4 (an idol shaped 'like the form of a man'), neither of which is a new-Adam idea.
Isa.44.10#cl0-1 ask who fashions a god or casts an idol; the figure is a nameless idol-making craftsman, not a lawless man. No clause speaks of lawlessness or of a man of sin.
Isa.44.10 and its neighbours (Isa.44.11-44.17) describe craftsmen and idolaters, not shepherds or leaders of a flock; no shepherd imagery and no flock appear in these clauses.

The cited verse Isa 44:2 has no shepherd, flock, pasture or leading language; its clauses speak of Maker, forming from the womb and help (Isa.44.2#cl0-2). At most the section's general caring-of-Israel drift, not a clause.
Isa.44.5#cl0-5 are declarations of belonging to YHWH, calling on Jacob's name and writing 'The LORD's'; none of them speaks of a wedding, husband or bridegroom.
Same clauses as bridegroom (Isa.44.5#cl0-5): the figures who say 'I belong to the LORD' and take the name Israel are not described as a bride or as being married.

Isa.44.13#cl0-5 describe a woodworker shaping an idol, and Isa.44.13#cl5 says only that it is made 'to dwell a house' (a shrine) — no clause speaks of building. The craftsman is an idol-maker, not a builder.

Isa.44.14#cl0-5 have a man cutting cedars, taking cypress/oak, planting a laurel and rain growing it: tree-felling and planting, not vine-growing. Isa.44.4#cl0 ('they will spring up ... like poplars') is growth imagery too, but nothing in the section names a vine or a vinedresser.
Isa.44.4#cl0 speaks of sprouting 'like poplars at watercourses of water'; there is no fishing, net, hook or catch anywhere in the clauses.
Isa.44.5#cl3 says one 'will write hand his' ('The LORD's'); no gate, door, threshold or keeping of an entrance appears in these clauses.
Isa.44.5#cl0-5 concern public confession of belonging to YHWH; the only eating/drinking in the section is the idolater's own meal (Isa.44.16#cl1-3), which is not hospitality.

The section's idolatry is making and worshipping idols generally (Isa.44.9-44.17); the only shrine is the idol's own 'to dwell a house' (Isa.44.13#cl5), and no clause places an idol in YHWH's holy place or temple.

Isa.44.20#cl0-5 speak of the idolater feeding on ashes, a deceived heart, inability to deliver himself and 'falsehood in my right hand' — the folly of idolatry, not sin leading to exile or death; the section nowhere mentions exile or death.
Isa 44:25-26 name false prophets/diviners who are foiled, and "His servant"/"His messengers" whose word is confirmed; no clause in this section has a prophet speaking or being called a prophet.
The restoration of Jerusalem, the cities of Judah and the temple is the section's drift, but no clause speaks of exiles returning or of exile itself.
Cyrus is named "My shepherd", not king, and no clause here has a king, throne, reign or anointing; kingship is read in from elsewhere.

The section's redemption is the LORD's redemption of Jacob/Israel ("I have redeemed you", "the LORD has redeemed Jacob"); Christ appears nowhere, so this is drift read forward, not a clause's content.
No clause here mentions a king, a throne, a reign or a kingdom; Cyrus is called shepherd, and "the cities of Judah will be rebuilt" is rebuilding, not kingdom.
The section has a universal-judgment, every-knee-bows horizon (Isa.45.23-24) but no clause narrates a day-of-the-Lord event.
Isa.45.17 promises an everlasting salvation to Israel, not a new covenant; no covenant is made, named, or renewed in any clause of the section.
No covenant of peace is stated or implied in the section; Isa.45.17 speaks of salvation, and shalom/peace is never mentioned in these clauses.

Verse 24 speaks of righteousness and strength 'in the LORD', but no clause in this section mentions Christ, Messiah, or a redeemer figure beyond God Himself. Reading 'in the LORD' as 'in Christ' is a New Testament identification (e.g. Phil. 2:10–11 quoting Isa. 45:23) not stated by any clause of Isa. 45. The clauses at 24:cl0–cl1 speak only of Yahweh; the stamp as worded is not carried by this section's text.
Isa 46:5 is a rhetorical incomparability question ('To whom will you liken Me...'), not a manifestation/appearance of God; no clause describes a theophany.
Isa 46:9 is a summons to remember and a declaration 'I am God, and there is none like Me' — not the call/commissioning of a prophet.
Isa 47:12-13 concerns sorceries, spells, astrologers and star-gazing — divination/magic, not worship of images or other gods; no idol or cult-image language appears in the section.
Nothing in the section concerns a temple, sanctuary, or a polluting object set in it; Isa 47:8's 'I am, and there is none besides me' is Babylon's self-deification, not a cult image in a holy place.

Isa 47:13 has astrologers observing the heavens and making known future events; no heavenly body falls, is darkened, or is dissolved, and no creation-order collapse is described anywhere in Isa 47:1-15.

The section is divine speech through the prophet, but no clause narrates the calling or commissioning of a prophet: there is no call, no vision, no 'whom shall I send'. The nearest is the self-description 'I declared / I proclaimed' (48:3, 48:5), which is the content of the speech, not a call narrative.

No clause speaks of a surviving remainder brought through judgment. The 'not cut off' of 48:9 is a possible near-miss, but it is stated as the reason for delaying wrath, not as a remnant as an entity, and the section's addressees are the whole 'house of Jacob' held to account.

The idol mention at 48:5 is a hypothetical claim by the people in their own words ('my idol has done this'), not an idol set up in the sanctuary, and the 'holy city' of 48:2 is the people's self-designation, not a place where an idol stands. Nothing in the section places an idol in a holy place.

The section has no servant: the addressee is the house of Jacob, and the one who is refined and tested is the people (48:10), while the one acting is the LORD. The nearest language is the furnace of affliction in 48:10, and that is the LORD's discipline of Israel, not a servant who suffers on their behalf; 48:11's refusal to yield glory to another confirms the subject is the LORD's own name, not a servant.

The section has an audience summoned to hear (48:12, 48:14, 48:16) and the 48:14 challenge about foretelling, but no clause names a witness, testimony or calling to testify — the audience's role as witness is only the drift of the gathering-and-hearing frame.

No clause of Isa 48:12–22 mentions Christ, his cross or resurrection; the only "redeemer" language is the LORD as Israel's Redeemer (Isa.48.17#cl0) with no Christian referent, so the stamp is not in this section.
The section speaks of a covenant for the people (Isa.49.8#cl4) but nowhere of peace or shalom; covenant_of_peace is too specific for this text.
No clause in the section has a witnessing role or act; the nations seeing kings and the ends of the earth receiving salvation are not witness language.
No priestly role, ritual or mediation appears in the section; a covenant for the people is not a priesthood.
Nothing in the section speaks of the dead being raised; the release of prisoners and return of exiles (Isa.49.9, Isa.49.12) is rescue in this life.
The section has no day of the LORD, judgment of the world, or coming of the LORD in wrath; Isa.49.8 is a day of salvation, which is the opposite.
The section never names David or a Davidic king; the Servant is called Israel (Isa.49.3), and kings bow to him (Isa.49.7, Isa.49.23) rather than being him.
No Mosaic language or role appears; a covenant for the people (Isa.49.8) is not a Moses figure, and the Servant is Israel in Isa.49.3.
No firstborn, inheritance-right of the firstborn, or firstborn language occurs in the section.

Isa 49:12 names places (north, west, land of Aswan/Sinim) and returnees, not a resident alien; the section never speaks of sojourning among foreigners. The reader's citation of 49:12 does not support the stamp.

Nothing in the section has a watchman: no lookout, no warning, no watching over a city. "I will watch over you" (Isa.49.8#cl3) is Yahweh keeping the Servant, not a watchman role; the cited 49:6 has no such figure.
No host in this chapter: no table, no house, no one receiving guests. Isa 49:18 has bride/jewelry imagery of adornment, not hospitality.
Same as host: nothing in the section has anyone received or entertained; 49:18's gathering is return and adornment, not guesthood.
Isa 49:14 (cited) is Zion, a city, speaking abandonment — not a foolish woman. The feminine speaker is personified Zion, not the folly woman of Prov 9.

Isa 49:24 (cited) names a warrior/tyrant holding captives, not a beast or a ruler figured as a beast; no animal imagery attaches to any ruler here. The oppressors of 49:26 eat their own flesh, but that is their punishment, not a beastly portrayal.

Isa 49:7 (cited) has rulers who will bow and a Servant of rulers; nothing marks a shepherd, false or otherwise. Shepherd language appears only in the deliverance imagery of 49:9–10, applied to God, not to a false leader.

This section contains no 'woe' (הוֹי) anywhere; the reader cited Isa 5:7, which is the interpretation of the parable (the vineyard is the house of Israel), not a woe oracle. The woe oracles begin at Isa 5:8.

No clause presents the beloved or the LORD as a king: Isa.5.1#cl1 calls him 'my beloved' with a vineyard, and Isa.5.7#cl0 names 'the LORD of Hosts'. Kingship is not among the ideas any clause here carries.

The only term of endearment is 'my beloved' (Isa.5.1#cl0, #cl1), and Isa 5 nowhere uses bridegroom or marriage language; the beloved/bridegroom reading is imported from Isa 54/Song of Songs, not from a clause here.
The judgment in Isa 5:5-6 is agricultural destruction (removing hedge, breaking wall, trampling, withholding rain) with no warrior, battle, sword or army clause.

The characters named or implied here are 'my beloved', the dwellers of Jerusalem, the men of Judah and the LORD of Hosts (Isa.5.3#cl0, Isa.5.7#cl0); no foreign nation appears as a character, and 'of Hosts' is a divine title, not a nation acting in the section.

Covenant is the assumed backdrop (the LORD's relationship with Israel and Judah, 'the LORD of Hosts' in Isa.5.7#cl0) but no clause here states a covenant, a covenant formula or covenant obligations; the lawsuit framing is only implied by Isa.5.3#cl1 and Isa.5.7#cl2.

The section is entirely accusation and judgment; even the cited Isa 5:4 is a rhetorical reproach ('What more could I have done for My vineyard than I already did for it?', Isa.5.4#cl0), and the favourable deeds in Isa.5.2#cl0-cl4 are past benefits, not mercy or restoration toward Israel here.
The stamp is cited for 5:16, 'the LORD of Hosts will be exalted', but no clause in the section calls the LORD king or depicts a king; only the general divine-sovereignty drift.
The accused are called 'My people' (5:13) and lambs graze in 5:17, but nothing in the section scatters a flock; the stamp's drift only loosely fits the exile.
No clause names a plague: 5:25's striking is warfare and anger, 5:30's darkness an eschatological darkening; the stamp's general drift only.

Nowhere in this section: only the divorce, the sale, the failure of respondents, and the drying up of sea and rivers appear; the one restorative word, 'to redeem'/'to deliver' (Isa.50.2#cl4-cl5), is a question denying inability, not an act or promise of mercy or restoration.

The cited verse 16 has God put his words in 'your' mouth and cover 'you' with the shadow of his hand, and say to Zion 'You are My people' — the addressee is plural-not-servant in framing and the section nowhere names a servant figure; I read no clause that carries an individual servant role.
The section's drift (drunkenness, devastation, famine, sword, subjugation) resembles curse, but no clause names or describes a curse; nothing in it is spoken as a curse formula (cf. Deut 28).
The cited verse (Isa 51:20) has her sons fainting like an antelope in a net and does not depict Yahweh as a warrior fighting; no clause in the section presents a warrior role.
Isa 51:22 speaks of the cup of fury being removed and given to her tormentors; it makes no covenant, no new covenant, and no covenant formula, so the stamp is not supported here.
Isa 51:20 concerns Jerusalem's sons fainting and being full of Yahweh's wrath; there is no servant figure, no vicarious suffering by a servant, and no reference to the Servant of the LORD here.
No clause in the section mentions a covenant, its parties, or covenant language; Isa 51:22 is a promise to remove the cup of wrath, not a covenant statement.
Nothing in this section names a covenant or 'peace' as a covenant; Isa.52.7#cl1 'proclaims peace' is the noun for well-being announced, not a covenant, and no clause here mentions בְּרִית.

No clause in Isa.52.1–12 names a servant; Isa.52.10 speaks of the LORD's own bared arm, and 'servant' belongs to 52:13–53:12, outside this section. If the project intends the servant song's opening as part of this section, this pin is wrong for the clauses supplied.
No clause mentions David, a shoot, or a throne occupant; Isa.52.2#cl1 'arise' and 52.2#cl4 'loosen the fetters' address Daughter Zion, not a Davidic figure.

No clause here names Christ or a messianic agent; the redemption clauses (Isa.52.3#cl2, Isa.52.9#cl4) have the LORD as subject with no mediator named. The Christian reading is a later application, not something a clause of this section says.

No temple, house, or dwelling is named in Isa 52:1–12. Isa.52.8#cl3 says the LORD 'returns to Zion', which is restoration, and the vessels in 52.11#cl6 are temple furniture being carried out of Babylon, not God's presence in a temple.
Isa.52.4 speaks of Israel going down to Egypt and Assyrian oppression; no covenant word, oath, or covenant-making clause occurs there or elsewhere in Isa 52:1–12.

Isa.52.10 names the LORD's bared arm and the nations seeing salvation; nothing in this section describes a servant, his suffering, or his exaltation. That language begins at Isa.52.13, outside the clauses supplied.
Christian reading of the Servant; no clause names Christ or redemption.
The exaltation is stated (Isa.52.13#cl2-4), but no clause speaks of exile.
Vindication/salvation for the nations is implied by 52:15, but no clause states a deliverance.
No clause in Isa.53.1-8 speaks of burial; the grave and 'with the rich in his death' come in Isa.53.9, which is outside this section.

Nothing in the clauses speaks of a covenant, covenant-making, or a covenant people; 'peace' (Isa.53.5#cl2) and 'healed' (Isa.53.5#cl3) are benefits, not covenant language, and the citing reader offered no clause carrying it.
No clause names or depicts a priest, priestly service or mediation in the temple; the servant is the offering, not the officiant, in this section.
The section is prophetic speech but no clause assigns the prophet role to anyone; Isa.53.1#cl0 ('Who has believed our message?') is about the audience's unbelief, not about a prophet's office.
Nothing in these clauses presents kingship, rule or a throne; Isa.53.2#cl1-2 deny 'stately form or majesty' rather than assert royal dignity.
No clause in this section speaks of a surviving or faithful remainder; Isa.53.1#cl0 speaks of general unbelief and Isa.53.6#cl0 of all going astray, the opposite of a remnant.

The scapegoat ritual (Lev 16) is sending the live goat away bearing sin into the wilderness; this section has the guilt offering (a slain offering) and 'I will allot Him a portion' (Isa.53.12#cl0/cl1), not the sending-away of a live animal, and God is not here said to send the servant away.
The whole section is cast in future-oriented divine speech ('I will allot', 'He will see', 'will prosper'), but no clause in it describes a prophetic word or the act of prophesying.
Isa 54:11-12 speaks of rebuilding the city with precious stones; nothing in the section speaks of new heavens and a new earth.
The section's building imagery (stones, foundations, gates) is city restoration, not creation of a new creation.
Redeemer language in Isa.54.5#cl2 is the LORD as Israel's redeemer; nothing in the section mentions Christ.
'king' is not said: the clause has 'witness', 'leader' and 'one who commands' (Isa.55.4#cl1-2). Ruler language is present, royal title is not; the stamp as worded is not carried by any clause here.
No clause in the section names a servant; the figure in Isa.55.3-5 is called a witness, leader and commander, with David named only as the recipient of covenant loyalty in Isa.55.3#cl4.

The whole chapter is a divine speech of promise, but no single clause says 'this is a promise oracle'; the reader cited Isa 55:10, which is the comparison (rain and snow), not the oracle itself. Compare Isa.55.11#cl0-5, which state the efficacy of the spoken word without labelling the genre.
Isa.55.13 speaks of cypress for thornbush and myrtle for brier — transformed vegetation, not new heavens and earth; no clause in this section speaks of a new cosmos.

The section addresses thirsty ones, the wicked and the unrighteous, and speaks of David, a witness, nations and creation; it never calls its addressees 'my people'. 'People of God' is not carried by any clause here.
The section speaks only of “My covenant” (Isa.56.4#cl5, Isa.56.6#cl7); the words “peace” or “covenant of peace” occur nowhere in Isa.56.1–8, so this stamp is not true of this section.

No clause of Isa.56.1–8 names a priest or priestly office: the only cultic clauses are the altar-offerings of Isa.56.7#cl2 and the service of Isa.56.6#cl1–3, which is the “servants” of the foreign nations, not priests.
The section pronounces judgment on the leaders in the prophetic indicting style, but no clause here carries an explicit 'woe'.
Nothing in these clauses speaks of sin, exile or death: the failure is blindness, appetite and self-gain, and no clause mentions exile or death.
The whole section is prophetic speech, but that is its general character rather than something any single clause states.
The clauses speak only of watchmen, shepherds, dogs and revellers; no clause names or addresses the people of God as such.
No clause mentions covenant, and the failure described is the leaders' blindness and greed, not a covenant crisis.
The shepherds are condemned, but no clause speaks of sheep being scattered or the flock abandoned.

No clause in Isa.57.14-21 has any servant figure: the one who is struck and hidden from is 'he' who 'kept turning back to the desires of his heart' (Isa.57.17#cl4), i.e. the wicked addressed in the same passage (Isa.57.20#cl0, Isa.57.21#cl0), and his being struck precedes his being healed in the same person's story, not a vicarious suffering of a servant for others; the cited verse (Isa 57:18) speaks of healing and comfort, not of the servant.

The section addresses the apostate people themselves (sons of a sorceress, adulterers, idolaters, Molech-worshippers); no individual is presented as a prophet speaking falsely, and the cited verse 3 names sorcery and adultery, not false prophecy.

Isa 57:9 is addressed to the same apostate 'you' of the whole oracle, who journeys to 'the king' (Molech) with oil and sends envoys; that is idolatrous diplomacy by the people, not a ruler depicted as a beast.
The whole section is prophetic speech in the first person of YHWH, but no single clause is about the prophetic word as such; 57:13's promise is the closest, yet it is the content, not the stamp.

The section is accusation and indictment against the people, but no clause pronounces 'woe'; closest is the command to declare transgression, so this is general drift rather than any particular clause.
Sin is named (transgression, sins), but there is nothing of exile or death in these clauses; the stamp fits the section only at the level of general indictment.

The fasting of Isa 58:3-5 is a personal affliction (denying oneself, bowing the head, sackcloth and ashes), not a priestly rite; no clause in this section mentions a priest, the temple cult, or mediation.

Nothing in Isa 58:5 speaks of sacrifice; the fast is described as humbling oneself, bowing the head and spreading sackcloth and ashes, and the point of Isa 58:6-7 is precisely that such ritual is not what God chose.
Isa 59:9 ('Therefore justice is far from us...') is first-person confession, not a 'Woe to...' oracle; the section contains no woe formula anywhere.
The figure in 16-17 is the LORD's own arm acting for him, and the passage uses no servant word or title; a reader would hesitate to attach the servant role here.
59:16 has no servant figure and no suffering: the LORD's own arm wins a victory; nothing here speaks of a servant's suffering or vicarious death.
Nothing in the section speaks of peace or shalom; the covenant here concerns the Spirit and words in the mouth (Isa.59.21#cl1, cl3).

The section speaks of a redeemer coming to Zion (Isa.59.20#cl0), which the NT reads Christologically, but no clause of this section mentions Christ or names him; the stamp is an application read into the text, not carried by any clause.

The whole section is a divine promise of future salvation addressed to Zion; no single clause carries the oracle-form itself, so this is general drift rather than a clause-level idea. The clauses listed are the first-person promises that carry it if one must point.

The clauses cited-verse and section speak of the LORD Himself being Zion's everlasting light instead of sun and moon (Isa.60.19#cl0-cl3, 60.20#cl0-cl2), and of perpetual peace and righteousness — this is transformed creation-order imagery, not the creation of new heavens and a new earth. No clause states a new heaven or new earth.

Zion is addressed as mother of sons and daughters (Isa.60.4#cl4-cl5) and as forsaken wife taken back (Isa.60.15#cl0-cl3), but no marriage or bridal imagery is used: 'forsaken and hated' is the closest and it is not bridal. The citation of 60:15 does not support a bride.
Isa.60.13 has the sanctuary being adorned and glorified ('to adorn the place of My sanctuary'), the opposite of destroyed; nothing in the section reports or laments a destroyed temple.

Isa.60.2 does set darkness over the earth and the LORD's rising in glory, which is the day-of-the-LORD pattern, but the section has no judgment-on-Zion's-enemies day, no 'day of the LORD' formula, and the darkness is the backdrop to Zion's light rather than the day itself.
Kings appear only as subjects bringing tribute (Isa.60.3#cl1, 60.10#cl1); no one is crowned or enthroned in this section. The cited verse does not carry a coronation.
Nothing in Isa.60 or its cited verse 60:1 speaks of anointing, oil, or setting apart: Zion is told to arise and shine because her light has come.
The section as a whole is a catalogue of blessing — light, wealth, land, increase — rather than one blessing event; the cited verse 60:17 is one instance among many.

No clause invokes the creation covenant (Gen 9 cosmic order as covenant); Isa 60:19-20 speak of the LORD replacing sun and moon as light, which is the reversal/transcendence of created lights, not the covenant with creation. The cited verse's clauses (Isa.60.19#cl0-cl3) state eschatological unmediated divine light, not a covenant.

Isa 60:22 ('least...a thousand, smallest a mighty nation') is a promise of national multiplication, but no clause names Abraham, seed, or the covenant; kings/nations coming is Abrahamic in echo only, and the clause Isa.60.22#cl1 speaks of the small becoming a mighty nation without covenant vocabulary.

Isa 60:14 ('sons of your oppressors will bow down... call you the City of the LORD') is Zion's vindication, not a Davidic covenant clause; no clause mentions David, an eternal throne, or 2 Sam 7 language.
Isa 60:16 ('you will know that I, the LORD, am your Savior and your Redeemer') is a recognition formula of deliverance, not Sinai covenant making; no clause has covenant, mountain, or law language.
Nothing in the section mentions salt, a perpetual allotment to priests/Levites, or the salt covenant (Num 18:19); Isa 60:16's clauses are about nursing from nations and knowing the LORD.
No clause refers to the oath sworn to the fathers; Isa 60:16 speaks of Israel's deliverer/redeemer, not the patriarchal oath (cf. the land/seed oath language elsewhere).

Isa 60:15 ('forsaken and despised... I will make you an everlasting pride') uses forsaken/despised language that elsewhere evokes the marriage covenant (Isa 54:6; 62:4), but no clause here has husband/wife, betroth, or marriage vocabulary; it is restoration from desolation.
Isa 60:19's sun/moon clauses concern the LORD being everlasting light, not the Noahic covenant sign or its promise; no clause mentions flood, bow, or the Noahic covenant.
Isa 60:21 ('all your people will be righteous; they will possess the land forever') is about righteousness and land possession, not circumcision or its covenant sign.

Isa 60:17 (appointing peace as governor and righteousness as ruler) is about righteous governance, not the Phinehas covenant of an everlasting priesthood (Num 25:12-13); no priestly-covenant clause is present.

Isa 60:16's Redeemer clause (Isa.60.16#cl3) speaks of the LORD as Israel's go'el, but nothing in this section names Christ or the NT accomplishment of redemption; the stamp belongs to the Christian reading, not to these clauses.

Isa 60:21 ('they will possess the land forever; they are the branch of My planting') has land-and-people permanence, but no clause in this section uses covenant (berit) vocabulary or states a covenant; the stamp is an inference from the cited verse, not carried by any clause.
The whole section is a salvation oracle of promise; no single clause states the oracle-form itself, so it is the section's general drift.
The section contains no departure or journey clause; the homecoming is only implied by the road-making and the undoing of the exile names.
Newness, delight and the sworn pledge are the nearest textual footholds, but nothing in the section names a covenant or the covenant formula.
The only 'king' words here are the nations' kings as onlookers who see the glory, not a king as a role or character in this section.
The LORD's 'right hand' and 'mighty arm' at Isa.62.8 are the limbs by which He swears, not warrior's acts; no weapon, battle, foe or combat appears in the section.
The section gives 'the Holy People, the Redeemed of The LORD' and 'Sought Out' as the city's names, with no word for a surviving remnant or a returned few.
No servant word or servant figure appears; the figure who comes is named 'your Savior' (Isa.62.11#cl4), a different role from servant.
Again the only royal word is 'kings' in the plural at Isa.62.2#cl1; the LORD is not named king anywhere in the section.
No David, no Davidic descendant and no royal heir clause occurs; the coming figure on the donkey-less road is called simply the people's Savior.
The renaming of Zion and her land is a corporate national restoration, not a new humanity or a new first man; nothing in the section speaks of Adam.
The section never says 'peace' or 'covenant of peace'; the nearest line is the oath of Isa.62.8#cl0, which is not named as a covenant here.
No David, no dynasty and no covenant formula occurs in the section.

Nothing in Isa 62 names Sinai, Moses, the law, or the giving of the covenant; the reader's cited verse (v.10) is a summons to build up the highway and raise a banner for the nations, which has no Sinai content.

Isa 62:8 swears by the LORD's right hand and mighty arm against giving grain to enemies and foreigners drinking the new wine, but never mentions Noah, the flood, the bow in the clouds, or the covenant with all flesh.
The cited v.8 concerns grain, new wine, enemies and foreigners, not creation or a covenant with all creation; no clause in the section speaks of creation.
Isa 62:9 speaks of those who harvest grain eating it, those who gather grapes drinking the wine in the LORD's holy courts; salt is nowhere mentioned, nor is any enduring covenant of salt.
Isa 62:10 commands going out through the gates, preparing the way, building the highway and raising a banner; it does not name Shechem or recount the covenant assembly there.
Isa 62:9 is about eating harvested grain and drinking wine in the holy courts; it names no Phinehas, no priesthood and no covenant of a perpetual priesthood.
Isa 62:8 speaks of grain, wine and enemies; circumcision is nowhere in the section and no clause speaks of it.
Isa 62:8 has the LORD swearing an oath by His right hand and mighty arm, but the oath is about grain and new wine not going to enemies and foreigners, not an oath to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
Isa 62:5 is a marriage simile ('as a young man marries a young woman... as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride'); it has no Jonathan, no David, and no covenant of friendship.
The cited v.11 announces Zion's Savior coming with His reward and recompense; it names no David, no throne, no descendants, and no everlasting kingdom promise to David.
The speaker here is the conquering warrior stained with his enemies' blood, not the servant who suffers; nothing in the section depicts his suffering.

Isa 63:17 is a lament addressed to God ('Why, O LORD, do You make us stray... Return'), not a lawsuit speech with indictment, accusation and summons of witnesses; no clause of this section carries lawsuit form.
Isa 63:18 speaks of enemies trampling the sanctuary, not of a deportation or life in exile; no clause states exile as an event.
Isa 63:17 names 'Your servants, the tribes of Your heritage', which is all Israel, not a remnant; no clause marks a surviving remainder.

Marked 'general' only because the cited verse (Isa 63:19) gives no clause speaking of prophecy; the whole section is prophetic speech, but the confidence-low clauses cl3-cl5 (torn heavens, coming down, mountains shaking) restate the petition of Isa 64:1 and do not by themselves carry the idea of a prophetic word.

No clause of Isa 63:7-14 names or describes a servant; the cited verse (v.11) speaks of Moses and the shepherds of His flock, and the people's rebellion, not a servant of the LORD. The stamp's cited verse does not carry the idea here.
The section's general drift of the LORD's compassion and love for His people (sons, children) may evoke a father, but no clause says or implies fatherhood.
No clause speaks of a surviving remainder; the people are addressed as the whole ('My people, sons'), and later all rebel (v.10). A remnant idea is not in this section's clauses.

The clauses invoke Moses himself (Isa.63.11#cl1 'Moses people his'; Isa.63.12#cl0 'the right hand of Moses') as the past deliverer, not a new Moses figure. The stamp names a role that this section does not present.
No clause presents a renewed or eschatological Israel; the section describes past and remembered Israel ('the house of Israel', 'His people'). The stamp is not carried by any clause here.
No clause records repentance or renewal; the cited verse (Isa.63.11#cl0 'it.remembered the days of antiquity') is remembrance of the past, and the people's rebellion (v.10) is unrepented here.
No clause speaks of deportation or life in exile; Isa.63.10's 'they rebelled... He became their enemy' is enmity and judgment, not exile. The stamp's cited verse does not carry it.

No clause names or describes a prophet; Isa.63.11 speaks of Moses and the shepherds of His flock, not a prophet figure, and the speaker of v.7 is the people's remembrance, not a prophet role in the clause.
No clause gives the LORD or anyone a royal role; v.11 concerns Moses and shepherds, and vv.12-14 speak of leading, not kingship. The stamp is not carried by these clauses.
No clause mentions priesthood, sacrifice or temple service; Moses in v.11 is deliverer and shepherd, not priest. The stamp is absent from this section's clauses.

No clause presents a judge or judging role; v.11's 'one who brought them up' and the shepherds are deliverers, but the section does not name a judge figure, and 'judge' (shophet) is not in the clauses.
No clause mentions the nations or treats them as an actor; the section concerns Israel, the LORD, Moses and the Spirit. The stamp is absent.
No clause mentions an oath or the fathers; Isa.63.7 speaks of the LORD's loving devotion and goodness to the house of Israel, not an oath sworn to the patriarchs.
No clause names Abraham or the covenant with him; 'the house of Israel' (Isa.63.7#cl3) and 'His covenant loyalties' do not specify the Abrahamic covenant. The stamp is not carried here.
No clause names David or any Davidic promise; the 'covenant loyalty' of Isa.63.7#cl0/cl3 is Yahweh's ḥesed to Israel, not 2 Sam 7.
No clause mentions a new covenant, law written on hearts, or forgiveness of iniquity; Isa.63.7#cl0 is ḥesed, cited only because the reader's keyword list matched 'covenant'.
No clause speaks of peace, an everlasting covenant of peace, or its terms.
No clause refers to creation or a covenant with creation.
No clause mentions Noah, the flood, or the sign of the bow.
No clause mentions circumcision or Abraham.
No clause mentions Phinehas or a priesthood covenant.
No clause refers to Shechem or a covenant made there.
No clause mentions salt or an enduring covenant of salt.
No clause uses marriage language (husband/wife/betrothal); Isa.63.7#cl0's 'covenant loyalty' is not a marriage covenant here.

Isa.63.9#cl0 ('in all their distress, He too was afflicted') is Yahweh, not a servant figure, and the section has no servant, no vicarious suffering, no Servant Songs language; the stamp is a different theme.
Isa.63.9#cl2's 'He redeemed them' is Yahweh's redemption of Israel in the exodus; no clause speaks of Christ or of a redeemer to come.

The section speaks of devastated cities, Zion/Jerusalem laid waste and the temple burned (Isa.64.9-10), but no clause speaks of deportation, being carried off or living in a foreign land; the nearest phrase, 'our iniquities carry us away like the wind' (Isa.64.5#cl3), compares Israel to a leaf carried off, not to exile. The listed desolation is destruction in the land, so an exile event is not present.

Almost no covenant vocabulary in these clauses: no בְּרִית / διαθήκη, no 'I will be your God', and unusually the oath is sworn 'by the God of truth' (Isa.65.16#cl1/#cl3; ַבֵּאלֹהֵי אָמֵן) rather than by the LORD himself as in Jer.31:33 / 32:40. A covenant renewal is at most thematic and is carried by no clause here, so I cannot point to a clause that says it.

Wrong for this section, on two counts. (1) There is no covenant here: no clause in Isa.65.17-25 contains covenant vocabulary (berith) or the covenant formula 'My people / their God' — 22#cl4 has 'my people my' but with no covenant term and no 'their God'. (2) The clause the reader cited, 25#cl4-cl5 (harm and destroy ceased on 'all My holy mountain'), states the end of violence, not the making, granting or naming of a covenant; the peace in 25#cl0 is the wolf and lamb grazing as one. The 'covenant of peace' of Isa.54.10 ('my covenant of peace shall not be removed') is a different passage, and the nearest covenant-of-peace text, Ezek.34.25, is elsewhere; a stamp citing Isa 65:25 for a named covenant cannot be shown from this section. Note also the parallel in Isa.11.6-9, which the text likewise does not call a covenant.

The section contains no 'woe' ('owy/hoy) oracle against anyone. 66:5 does contain a word of the LORD to the trembling ones and a promise that the hostile brothers 'will be put to shame' (Isa.66.5#cl7), but that is a salvation-oracle/assurance, not a woe; the accusation falls on the mockers, not on the addressees.
The section speaks of the LORD's rule, vengeance and gathering of the nations, but no clause names him king or shows a throne, crown or royal court.
No bridal or marriage language appears anywhere in Isa 66:15-24; the drawing-together language is of nations bringing the exiles as an offering, not of a bride.

Nothing in Isa.66.7-14 speaks of new heavens and a new earth. Despite the reader citing Isa 66:12, that clause is about extended peace and the wealth of nations; the explicit new-heavens-and-earth language is in Isa.66.22, outside this section and not quoted in it.

Isa.66.14#cl3/cl4 speak of the LORD's hand being revealed to His servants and His wrath against His enemies; a day of the LORD is not mentioned in this section. If the stamp is meant as judgment-on-the-nations generally, judgment is the stamp that fits; as stated, day_of_the_lord is not in the text.

Isa.66.10 ("rejoice with Jerusalem ... all who love her") is spoken to Zion's lovers, but no bridal or marriage language, no husband, no wedding appears in the section. Childbirth in Isa.66.7-9 is labour, not bridal imagery.
No king, throne or reign is named anywhere in Isa.66.7-14. The LORD speaks as God and as the one who brings to birth (Isa.66.9), which is not a king stamp.

No clause in Isa.66.7-14 names a temple, house, sanctuary, glory or presence. Nursing at Jerusalem's breasts (Isa.66.11) and being carried on her hip (Isa.66.12) are Zion as nursing mother, not temple presence. There is no particular clause to point at, though the section as a whole presupposes the LORD's saving presence with Zion.
The text says the attackers marched up to wage war and “could not overpower the city” (Isa.7.1#cl2–cl3); no siege works, encirclement or blockade is stated in any clause.

Isa.7.5–6 records the plot of Aram, Ephraim and the son of Remaliah and the plan to install the son of Tabeal as king; no clause has anyone claiming to speak for God falsely, which is what a false prophet requires.
The section's drift is that the LORD's word stands: “It will not arise; it will not happen” (Isa.7.7#cl1–cl2). That is the general force of the section, not something any one clause states.
Isa.7.2#cl2 says Aram “has stood,” i.e. is in league, with Ephraim — an alliance between two foreign kingdoms, not a covenant with the LORD or with Israel.
The only judgment stated is Ephraim being “shattered as a people” (Isa.7.8#cl2); no clause here names sin, exile or death.
The only outcome for Ephraim in this section is being “shattered as a people” (Isa.7.8#cl2); no clause speaks of mercy or restoration.
The section presupposes Judah, the house of David and Ephraim as God's people but no clause states the idea; it is background to the whole scene, not asserted in it.
The crisis in Isa.7.2 is “Aram was in league with Ephraim” (cl2) and the resulting trembling (cl3) — a military alliance, not a crisis of covenant.
Isa.7.7 is the LORD's word that the plot “will not arise; it will not happen”; no clause speaks of the day of the LORD.
The section has a promise (7:14) but no clause speaks of the LORD's faithfulness or of a promise being kept; it is at most the general drift of the oracle and its fulfilment in 7:16.

The section names no sin, no exile and no death: Ahaz's refusal in 7:12 is presented as refusal to ask, and 7:16 gives devastation of the land, not exile or death. The three terms are not in the clauses.

Isa 8:4 as worded here is an announcement of coming disaster (the boy's name is a time-limit on the plundering of Damascus and Samaria), not a promise of good; the cited verse carries prediction of judgment, not promise.
Isa 8:9 has no "woe" (הוֹי) and no accusation of the addressee; it is a summons/threat to the nations (an oracle against the nations), not a woe oracle.

Isa 8:7 casts the LORD as the one who brings up the waters and the king of Assyria as the flood/waters, not as a warrior figure fighting; no warrior or warrior-language clause appears in this section.

Isa 8:7 speaks of the LORD bringing the Assyrian flood against Judah in history; no day-of-the-LORD language (יוֹם ליהוה), darkness/trumpet/cosmic signs, or "the day" appears anywhere in this section.

Isa 8:10's "God is with us" is the ground of the thwarting of the nations' plans (Immanuel), not an expression of God's promise-keeping/covenant faithfulness; no clause in this section speaks of God keeping a promise.

"This people" in Isa 8:6 is Judah in its rejection of the LORD, addressed for judgment, not a positive designation of the people who belong to God; the section gives no clause marking a people of God.
No clause in this section names covenant, covenant-making, or covenant language; Isa 8:6's rejection of the waters of Shiloah and trust in Rezin is the background, not a covenant clause.
Isa 8:10's "For God is with us" grounds the failure of the nations' plans against Judah; it says nothing about a kingdom of God or a kingdom as such in this section.

The section has no appearance of God: Isa.8.13 names 'the LORD of Hosts' as the one to regard as holy and Isa.8.18 says he 'dwells on Mount Zion', but nothing in the clauses narrates God appearing, coming or being seen; no clause rests on words describing a divine manifestation.
'among my disciples' (Isa.8.16) presupposes a surviving group, but no clause states that a remnant is left, spared or preserved.

Isa.8.17 is the prophet's own resolve ('I will wait for the LORD... I will put my trust in Him'), not a divine promise spoken to anyone; the clauses rest on 'I will wait' and 'I will put my trust', which are the speaker's words about himself.
the section speaks of victory (shattered yoke, plunder divided) but no clause pictures a procession or triumphant entry
the light/darkness reversal is the section's drift, but no clause names or depicts the day of the LORD
a Christian reading of the section as a whole; no clause in this Hebrew text says anything about Christ or redemption
no clause speaks of creation, a new heaven and earth, or renewal of the world; light in v.2 is rescue from darkness, not creation
the section is rescue and honor throughout (no more gloom, light dawned, yoke shattered); enemy gear is burned, not judged, and no clause pronounces judgment
the child born and son given is enthroned and named Mighty God, Prince of Peace; nothing in these clauses speaks of suffering or servant service
The section is a judgment announcement; it contains no woe (hoy) formula and no clause addresses a woe
The section's general drift is a people's breach of covenant with the LORD who struck them, but no clause names covenant
The section has no warrior figure; Yahweh acts as wrath and fire, and the devouring is done by the people against each other. Nothing in the cited verse names a warrior.
The whole section is prophetic speech (the divine 'His anger is not turned away' refrain), but no clause in the list is itself a report of a prophetic word being given.
No darkness or night appears in any clause; the imagery is fire, smoke (v.18, not in the clause list), scorching and devouring. The earlier chapter's darkness (Isa 8:22; 9:2) is not in this section.
No sheep, flock or scattering language in the section; the people are 'fuel for the fire' and devourers of each other, not scattered sheep.
No woe ('Woe to...', 'Alas') anywhere in this section; the Hebrew woe-form is absent here, and the passage reads as an announcement of judgment, not a woe oracle.
The verse names God, the Lord Jesus Christ and the twelve tribes, but no clause states or presupposes a covenant; any covenant sense is inferred from the addressees, not from words here.
The verse names the Lord Jesus Christ but says nothing of redemption or of anything he does; the stamp is not asserted by any clause here.

No clause names Christ. The nearest candidate, 'the word planted in you, which can save your souls' (Jas.1.21#cl0/cl2/cl3), attributes salvation to the implanted word, not to Christ, and the section contains no redemption language.
The section speaks of 'trials of many kinds' and 'the testing of your faith', never of hostility, opposition or being persecuted by anyone; nothing here names agents or persecution.
No servant figure, no vicarious suffering, no one bearing another's sin appears in these verses.
The section's goal language is maturity and completeness ('mature and complete, not lacking anything') and a crown of life; nothing here speaks of new creation.
Christ is not named anywhere in Jas 1:2-12; the one addressed is God ('ask God', 'from the Lord', 'that God has promised'), so the stamp has no footing in these clauses.

Jas 2:23 quotes Gen 15:6 ('credited to him as righteousness') and calls Abraham 'a friend of God' — that is about the covenant relationship, but no clause of the quoted text states a covenant; it is the general background of the section.

Jas 2:24 ('a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone') is about justification/verdict on a person's works, not a depicted event of divine judgment; no clause here narrates a judgment event.
Not wrong as a description of the section's drift, but no clause in Jas 2:14–26 invokes law, wisdom, or a wisdom saying; the argument is about faith and works.
No clause in the section mentions Christ, and redemption by Christ is the topic of Jas 2:1, not of 2:24; the cited verse is about justification by works.
Jas 2:22 speaks only of faith working with works and being perfected by works; Christ is not named and no union with him is stated anywhere in Jas 2:14–26.

Jas 2:26 uses death only as a negative analogy ('the body without the spirit is dead') — the point is that faith without deeds is dead, not that death yields life. No clause here has life coming out of death.
Jas 3:2's 'we stumble' (Gk ptaiomen) is about stumbling/offending in speech, not temptation to sin (peirasmos); no clause in this section names a temptation.
The general drift of Jas 3:1-2 (strict accounting for teachers, universal stumbling) is judgment, but no clause in the rest of the section carries it in particular.
The section is addressed to the believing community ('my brothers') and its teachers, but no clause states the community's identity as God's people.

Jas 3:17 personifies wisdom only as an abstract quality ('the wisdom from above is ... pure ... peace-loving'); no woman, female figure or feminine personification appears in any clause of the section.
Nothing in this section concerns sin as exile or death; Jas 3:14 speaks of jealousy, selfish ambition, boasting and lying against the truth, not exile or death.
Jas 4:17 speaks of sin as failing to do the good one knows ("is guilty of sin"), not of exile or death; no clause in this section carries exile or death.
The section opposes the devil and calls for resistance, but no clause names a temptation or a tempting; the stamp is the passage's wider setting, not something any clause says.

The section has corruption and death (rotten riches, moth-eaten clothes, corroded gold, flesh eaten like fire, murdered righteous) but no exile, and no statement of sin leading to exile; the stamp's drift of sin-to-death is only generally present. No clause names exile or makes the sin-exile-death chain.

Nothing here uses day-of-the-Lord imagery as a symbol. The nearest temporal phrases are 'in [the] last days' (Jas.5.3#cl3) and 'in [the] day of slaughter' (Jas.5.5#cl2); neither is the day of the Lord, and no clause in the section depends on that symbol.

The section is unrelieved denunciation of the rich; there is no act of mercy, no rescue, no restoration - not even for the defrauded harvesters, whose cry only results in the Lord of Hosts hearing it.

Jas.5.17-18 has Elijah praying, not prophesying: 'with fervent prayer he prayed [for it] - not to rain' (Jas.5.17#cl1) and 'again he prayed' (Jas.5.18#cl0). No clause speaks a word from God; the praying man is the point, so the stamp does not belong to this section (a drought/rain answer to prayer is the theme).

Jas.5.18 gives a past answer to prayer, not a promise or its keeping: 'the heaven rain gave' (Jas.5.18#cl1), 'the earth produced the fruit of it' (Jas.5.18#cl2). The section's own 'promise' language is in the words 'the prayer offered in faith will restore' and 'it will be forgiven him' (Jas.5.15), which are soteriological, not a covenant promise being fulfilled.
Nothing in the section speaks of testimony or bearing witness; the bringing back of a wanderer is not a witness event. (An earlier reader cited Jas 5:19, but no clause there carries the idea.)
No slave/servant, service language, or servant role appears in Jas 5:19-20; the one who brings back a sinner is called 'someone'/'whoever', not a servant.
The section addresses 'my brothers' and one of 'you' (Jas 5:19), so it concerns the community of believers, but no clause states the people of God as an idea; this is the section's general setting.
The stamp names the community addressed (the repeated 'brothers'), but no single clause carries the idea as its content.
The 'suffering servant' is the Servant of the Lord (Isaiah 53); this section speaks of the prophets' affliction and Job's perseverance, not of the Servant.
The section refers to Judah/Jerusalem throughout but names no clause that presents them as God's people in a positive covenant sense.
No clause in the section names a covenant, its making, or its obligations; Jer.1.5 speaks of knowing/setting apart/appointing the prophet, not of covenant. The stamp is not supported here.

The section opens with an address and a command to hear the word; none of the clauses carries a lawsuit: there is no accusation, no summons, no indictment, no plea of the LORD against Israel in this section.
No clause has the woe ('hoy') form or a woe oracle; Jer 10:11 is a command to say that the gods will perish, not a woe, and no other clause pronounces woe.

The idols here are in the nations (cut from a forest, arrayed in silver and gold, carried because they cannot walk); no clause places an idol in the temple or any holy place, so this apocalyptic-crisis stamp has no footing in the section.

Jer 10:24 asks only that correction be in justice, not in anger, 'or You will bring me to nothing' (Jer.10.24#cl3). That is a plea for mitigated judgment, not mercy, restoration or return; nothing here speaks of restoring or gathering back.

Jer 10:21 and 10:17 have scattering and unwilling departure (Jer.10.21#cl3, Jer.10.17#cl0), but no clause in this section speaks of the scattered being gathered back: Jer.10.20#cl4 says only that no one is left to pitch the tent again.

This section has no woe ('oy/'alay) oracle form: Jer 11:11-12 are a divine judgment sentence ('I am about to bring upon them a disaster'), and 11:3 is a curse formula introduced by 'Cursed is', not a woe cry, so the stamp's cited verse does not carry a woe.

The section announces doom, but it is framed as direct divine speech, "Therefore this is what the LORD says" (Jer 11:21) and "So this is what the LORD of Hosts says" (Jer 11:22) — not the 'woe' form. No clause in the section contains a woe cry; at best the stamp describes the drift of the whole oracle.

Nothing here speaks of sin or of exile. The deaths are Yahweh's judgment on the men of Anathoth (sword, famine), and the punishment is confined to the people of Anathoth — there is no exile, no removal from the land, no sin named as the cause. The stamp's verse citation (Jer 11:22) is only the judgment, not this theme.

The people of Anathoth are the subject of the oracle, but the clauses call them "the people of Anathoth" / "the men of Anathoth" as the prophet's opponents, not God's people; no clause marks them as Yahweh's own people. At most this is the section's general setting.
The theme runs through the whole section (the complaint, the plea against the wicked, the withered land); no one clause states 'judgment' in itself.
No clause in the section has a divine saying or 'thus says the LORD'; cl3 is Jeremiah's own speech, not a prophetic word given.
No clause pronounces a curse; v.17 states a conditional judgment by God, and v.16 has an oath formula, not a curse formula.

The section is the prophet's oracle, but no clause names a prophet, a prophetic call, or a prophetic word; the nearest figure is the LORD addressing Israel's brothers (Jer.12.6). It is the section's frame, not a clause content.

Jer.12.8's lion is Israel-as-inheritance roaring against the LORD (it.has.given.forth on me with voice its; I hate.it), and Jer.12.9's beasts are gathered to devour her — no ruler is depicted as a beast.
The whole section is prophetic speech (the LORD speaking through Jeremiah), but no clause is about a word, its reception, or its coming; it is the frame of the section, not a pin.

Nothing in Jer.12.5-13 turns toward restoration: the section ends on 'Bear the shame of your harvest because of the fierce anger of the LORD' (Jer.12.13#cl4), and the only 'return'-like language (12.5#cl3) is falling, not restoring.
No staff, rod, or broken-support image appears anywhere in these clauses; the destruction is by sword, shepherds, beasts and thorns (Jer.12.10-13).
'the.burning of.the.anger' (harôn 'ap) in Jer.12.13#cl4 is wrath kindled, not fire as an image; no flame, burning land, or fire-of-judgment appears in these clauses.
Jer 13:11 is not an unconditional promise but a statement of what Yahweh had made Israel to be, immediately reversed by "But they did not listen", and Jer 13:9-10 are judgment, not promise.
The section speaks of Judeans going after other gods (Jer 13:10) but places no idol in the temple or any holy place.

No clause states sin, exile or death in particular; the section speaks of drunkenness and of being smashed, which a reader may take as the death element of the theme's drift, but no clause names it. Empty list, general.

The section's feminine figure is the adulterous prostitute of 13:27, not a bride; "How long will you remain unclean?" is the opposite of bridal imagery. The reader's citation of 13:27 does not support it.
No bridegroom, husband or wedding language appears anywhere in Jer 13:15-27; Yahweh is the one who strips and scatters, not a bridegroom figure here.
13:19 says "All Judah has been carried into exile, wholly taken captive" — totality, with no remainder; the reader's citation is evidence against a remnant here.
No prophet at all appears in the section (Jeremiah is not named); 13:25's "trusted in falsehood" is the people's false trust, not a false prophet.
The section's female imagery is Jerusalem as adulterous prostitute (13:26-27), an unfaithful wife, not personified Folly; no wisdom figure is present.

13:18 addresses the king and queen mother and 13:21 the close allies, but no clause portrays a ruler as a beast (no horns, teeth, devouring); lustful neighings in 13:27 is sexual imagery, not a beast-ruler.
13:24's chaff and desert wind describe scattering, not a warrior; the agents are the wind and Yahweh, and no battle or fighting clause occurs in the section.
13:19's shut cities are not built or founded in the section; the verb is "have been shut tight", with no building activity and no builder.
13:19's "no one can open them" concerns the shut cities, not a doorkeeper figure; no gatekeeper appears in the section.
13:20 refers to the flock entrusted to Judah, not a host receiving guests, and the section has no meal or hospitality scene.
No guest or hospitality is present; the close allies of 13:21 are trained associates, not guests.
No travel or pilgrimage; 13:19 is deportation (carried into exile), not a journey of worship.
Jer 13:19 speaks of cities shut up, no one to open, and Judah carried into exile; no resident alien, sojourner or foreigner appears anywhere in the section.
Captivity/exile in Jer 13:19 is expressed by גלה (taken into exile), not by slavery or bondservice; no slave, master or purchase language occurs.
Jer 13:22 gives the reason for the exposure ("because of the magnitude of your iniquity"); it names no witness, testimony or evidence given.
"for the LORD has spoken" (Jer 13:15) grounds the summons to hear; it does not present Israel as servant, and no servant role is named in 13:15.
Jer 13:18 addresses the king and queen mother; no father-son relation or sonship is expressed.
Jer 13:18 names king and queen mother; God is not addressed or described as father here.
No firstborn language or firstborn status occurs in Jer 13:18 or elsewhere in the section.
Jer 13:21 speaks of allies being set over them; no judge, tribunal, verdict or judicial role is named.
Jer 13:18 mentions the king and queen mother only; no priest, Levite or cultic office appears.
Jer 13:25 charges Judah with forgetting the LORD and trusting falsehood; no lawless individual or man of lawlessness figure is in view.
Jer 13:19 is wholesale exile of Judah and Jerusalem; nothing of restoration or a renewed Israel is expressed in this section.
Jer 13:18 announces the humbling of the king and the fall of his crown; no future Davidic figure is promised.
Jer 13:15 is the prophet's summons to hear; no new Moses or prophet like Moses is named or implied.
Jer 13:20 asks after the flock entrusted to the rulers, but no staff, rod or broken staff symbol appears anywhere in the section.

The section speaks woe (judgment oracles, weeping over the shattered daughter of my people), but no clause in it has the form of a woe-saying (no 'woe to...' addressed to a party); the stamp describes the drift rather than resting on any clause.

The wounded sufferer here is "the virgin daughter of my people" shattered by a blow (Jer.14.17#cl3), the people lamenting, not the servant of the LORD bearing others' sin; the stamp does not belong to this section.

Jer 14:21's 'do not break covenant your with us' (Jer.14.21#cl3) is a plea not to annul an existing covenant; nothing in the section cuts, ratifies or inaugurates a covenant, and the Hebrew `parar` ('break') means violate, not cut.

Jeremiah's speech as a whole is prophetic, but no clause in Jer.14.19-22 says 'the word of the LORD' or reports a divine utterance; the section is lament and prayer addressed to God, so this is general drift only.

Jer 14:22 speaks of the nations' idols and their powerlessness over rain (Jer.14.22#cl0), but nothing in this section places an idol in the temple or any holy place; the reference to Yahweh's 'glorious throne' (Jer.14.21#cl1) is his own throne, not a profaned sanctuary.
Jer 15:4 speaks of making them 'a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth' because of Manasseh; it names no deportation or exile event. Exile appears only as one of the four fates in 15:2#cl9-cl12.
The section has no woe formula ('Woe to you' / הוי) and no dirge metre; Jer 15:9 is a report of the mother of seven's collapse, not a woe oracle.
Jer 15:9 has no day-of-Yahweh vocabulary: the sun setting while still day is a metaphor for premature death (cl2), not the day of the LORD.
No clause names a servant or servant role; the speaker is a prophet addressed by God, not described as a servant.
Nothing in these clauses presents the speaker as a witness to anything; 'You understand, O LORD' and bearing reproach are appeal and suffering, not testimony.
No clause here speaks of a people belonging to God; 'I bear Your name' is the individual prophet (Jer.15.16#cl3), and the curses of Jer.15.10#cl5 are the land against him, not a people of God.
No covenant, covenant formula, or covenant parties appear in these clauses; 'I bear Your name' is a naming claim, not a covenant statement.

The section has opposition and rescue (fight against you, not overcome you, deliver you), but no servant figure and no suffering borne by him; the stamp's language belongs to Isaiah's servant songs, not here.
The redemption here is Jeremiah's rescue from the wicked (Jer.15.21, 'from the hand of the wicked'), delivered to him in his own lifetime; nothing in the section speaks of Christ.
The section contains no 'woe' cry or woe form; Jer 16:4 is an announcement of death and burial loss, not a woe oracle.
No foreign nation is portrayed: the addressees are Israel/Judah and the Babylonians are not named.

Jer 16:21 speaks of Yahweh making His name and power known to the nations ('I will make them know My power and My might'), not of creation or a new creation; no clause in the section describes created order, new heavens/earth, or renewal of creation.
Blessing is present (Jer.17.7#cl0) but no commission or sending is spoken of in this section.
No clause in Jer.17.1-11 speaks of mercy given or restoration after exile; Jer.17.8 describes the blessed man's condition, not a restoration of the exiled.
The section is a conditional command with blessing and curse (if you listen / if you do not listen) addressed to Judah; no clause mounts a formal lawsuit with indictment, witnesses and summons.
The section commands Sabbath observance and offers the blessing/curse of obedience, a wisdom-like contrast, but it is prophecy given through Jeremiah, not a wisdom saying or a law collection.

The Hebrew carries no 'woe' (הוֹי) in this section; Jer.18.13 has 'Who has ever heard things like these?' plus a strong accusation, which is the surrounding legal/accusatory speech, not a woe oracle with the woe particle.

Jer.18.7 is an announcement of judgment (uproot, tear down, destroy), not a promise of good; the only build-up/planting verse (Jer.18.9) is itself conditional and reversed in Jer.18.10. So the cited verse does not carry a promise.

Jeremiah's persecution, his innocence ('Should good be repaid with evil?') and his intercession for his enemies resemble the servant motif, but no clause in this section speaks of a servant or of suffering borne on others' behalf; it is a general resemblance only, so it is wrong as a stamp pinned to clauses here.

The idolatry is on rooftops, in the Valley of Ben-hinnom and in the city's houses (Jer.19.4#cl3, Jer.19.5#cl0, Jer.19.13#cl1, Jer.19.13#cl2); no clause places an idol in the temple or another holy place.

What is defiled is the city and the houses of Jerusalem and of Judah's kings (Jer.19.13#cl0), made like Topheth; the house of the LORD appears only as the place Jeremiah stands to speak (Jer.19.14#cl3), never as desecrated.

No shepherd, sheep, flock or scattering language occurs anywhere in the section; the dead are given to birds and beasts (Jer.19.7#cl2) and the people fall by the sword, but nothing is scattered as a flock.
No darkness, night or light imagery occurs in this section; Jer.19.6 speaks of the days coming and a renaming, not darkness.

The disaster announced is on this place, this city and its villages (Jer.19.3#cl4, Jer.19.15#cl1); no nations are shaken, and the tingling of ears (Jer.19.3#cl6) is on every hearer of the report, not on the nations.

The shattering of the potter's jar, the unrepairable wreck and the burial-ground with no room speak of destruction and no return, not of a lampstand or a light being taken away; nothing in the section concerns a lampstand or lamp.
No clause in Jer.2.1-13 narrates an exile or deportation; the cited verse (Jer 2:7) speaks of being brought into a fertile land and of defiling it, not of being carried away.
Jer 2:12 is an imperative summons to the heavens to be appalled and shocked ('Be stunned by this, O heavens'), not a woe ('Woe to...') pronounced over anyone; the section contains no woe oracle.
No king is named or addressed anywhere in Jer.2.1-13; the 'leaders' of Jer 2:8 are shepherds/rulers (Jer.2.8#cl3), not a king, and the stamp's cited verse (Jer 2:8) contains no king.

The cited verse (Jer 2:6) describes a land where 'no one travels and no one lives' (Jer.2.6#cl4, Jer.2.6#cl5) — the absence of inhabitants and travellers — and no clause concerns a resident alien or sojourner.

Idols are exchanged for the LORD and prophets prophesy by Baal (Jer 2:8, 11), but no clause places an idol or image in the temple or any holy place; the land is defiled (Jer.2.7#cl3), not the sanctuary.

The clause the reader cited (Jer.2.7#cl0 / Jer.2.7#cl4) is about land and inheritance, not the temple; and no clause in the section names the temple or the LORD's dwelling among His people. If anything the section's presence language runs the other way (Jer.2.8#cl0/cl1 expect the LORD and do not find Him). The stamp fits the book's drift, not this section's clauses.

No clause in the section puts the nations' war strength or staff (Egypt/Assyria) in view; it is a case against Judah for forsaking the LORD, not the breaking of the staff the prophet leans on in Jer 2:1-3. I take the stamp as a wrong fit for this section.

The reader cited Jer 2:7, whose clauses (Jer.2.7#cl0/#cl3/#cl4) accuse the people of defiling the land and inheritance, not of a desolated house; no clause in the section names the temple or its ruin. The stamp can stand only as the section's general drift.
The section has devastation and foreign menace (Jer.2.15#cl2-3, Jer.2.16#cl0, Jer.2.18) but no clause says the people are carried away or deported; no clause in particular carries the exile idea.

No clause pronounces a curse (no 'cursed' formula, invocation or oath); the verse cited (Jer 2:19) states consequences ('will discipline you', 'will reprimand you') which is judgment/punishment, not curse.
The verse cited (Jer 2:22) is the opposite: washing and soap cannot remove the stain of guilt; no clause in the section offers pardon or restoration.
No clause mentions an idol, an image, or the temple/holy place; the high-hill-and-green-tree clause (Jer.2.20#cl4) is illegitimate worship, not an idol set up in the sanctuary.
No clause speaks of a staff, rod or support; the yoke-and-chains of Jer.2.20#cl0-1 are bonds the people broke off themselves, the reverse of a broken staff of reliance.
No clause uses day-of-the-LORD imagery (darkness, a day of the LORD, cosmic signs); Jer 2:19 states inner punishment and the bitterness of forsaking God.
The section is accusation and judgment oracle; no clause pronounces a woe on anyone.
The only bride imagery is a bride's jewelry and wedding sash (Jer.2.32#cl0-1); no bridegroom appears in the section.
Idols are addressed (wood, stone) and made by the people (Jer.2.27#cl0-3, Jer.2.28#cl0), but the section names no holy place or temple defiled by an idol.
The section ends in rejection and shame (Jer.2.37#cl1-3) and contains no offer of mercy, return or restoration.

Jeremiah's own words in this section (20:3-6) are a pronouncement of judgement on Pashhur and on Judah (captivity, sword, death, burial); there is no Servant-figure language of vicarious suffering or exaltation such as Isa 52:13-53:12, only Jeremiah the prophet being beaten and put in the stocks (20:2).
The section speaks of the city being burned (Jer.21.10#cl4), not the temple: 'city' (הָעִיר) is the object, and no clause names the temple or the house of the LORD.
The section's drift is divine covenant loyalty and its breach, but no clause names a covenant, a covenant formula, or covenant obligations; only the epithet 'the God of Israel' touches it. General.

The section has sin (Jer.21.12#cl7; Jer.21.14#cl0) and death-dealing judgment by fire (Jer.21.14#cl2-cl3), but no clause speaks of exile or deportation, so the compound stamp belongs here only as general drift; if it requires exile, it is wrong.

The clause ids carry no 'Jer.22.5#1'; the section has no clause for a judgment event as such — Jer.22.5 states an oath and the house becoming a ruin, which is a consequence, not a depicted judgment scene. I could not map this stamp to any clause carrying it.

The section names no prophet: Jeremiah never appears in these clauses; the only human roles named are king (Shallum son of Josiah, king of Judah) and father (Josiah); the speech is attributed to Yahweh ("thus he says Yahweh"), not to a prophet.

There is no woe form here: no "Woe!" (הוֹי) and no curse; the section is an imperative not to weep plus an announcement of judgment, so the cited verse Jer 22:10 is a prohibition of mourning, not a woe oracle.
