The section's shepherds (Jer.22.22#cl0, 'all your shepherds, a wind will shepherd them') are Judah's failed rulers being carried off, and no clause here presents a shepherd who misleads the flock; the greed and injustice of vv.13-17 are charged to 'him'/'you', not to shepherds as a role. Nothing in this section speaks to the false-shepherd idea.

Every clause in the section is woe, indictment and sentence: the woe (22.13#cl0), the charges (22.13#cl1-cl4, 22.17#cl1), and the judgment (22.19#cl0, 22.22#cl0-cl2, 22.23#cl3). No clause promises mercy, return or restoration. The nearest candidate, 22.15#cl6 'then good belonged to him', describes the good Josiah enjoyed for doing justice, not a promise of restoration.
Only the exile-side is present (Jer.23.39#cl2); no death and no clause names sin as such, so the triad is the section's drift, not any one clause's idea.

The section ends with 'everlasting shame and perpetual humiliation that will never be forgotten' (Jer.23.40#cl0); nothing offers return or mercy — e.g. the total forgetting of Jer.23.39#cl1 runs the other way.

the section pronounces judgement in the form "this is what the LORD says" and "I am against", but contains no woe-form (no הוי / "Woe to…") at any clause: 23:15#cl0 is "thus he says Yahweh of hosts", not a woe
no lookout, warning-cry or watch imagery occurs in the section; the closest clause (Jer.23.18#cl3 "has he listened?") is about heeding the LORD's word, not watching
no surviving or remaining group is spoken of; "My people" at 23:13, 23:22, 23:27 and 23:32 is the whole people being led astray, not a remnant
no torah instruction, wisdom saying or wise/righteous teaching occurs; "stand in the council of the LORD" (Jer.23.18#cl0) is prophetic council imagery, not torah, and I judge it too loose to pin

the section is accusation and judgement throughout; the only forward-looking clause (Jer.23.20#cl3, "In the days to come you will understand this clearly") promises understanding of the judgement, not mercy or restoration
Jer 25:11 speaks of service to Babylon for seventy years; captivity is the stamp exile_ev (Jer.25.14#cl0 enslavement also belongs there). The word 'captivity' does not appear in this section.

Jer 25:8-14 is a judgement announcement with 'therefore this is what the LORD of Hosts says' and accusations, but contains no 'woe' (no הוי) and no woe form; the stamp belongs to this section only as general drift.
The section declares the LORD's judgement through Babylon and its reversal after seventy years, but no clause names the day of the LORD.

Jer 25:12 (seventy years complete, Babylon punished) shows the LORD's word being carried through, but no clause states the theme itself and the section gives no explicit promise of restoration to Judah.
The section has no torah instruction, no wisdom saying and no wise/unwise contrast; Jer 25:6's 'do not follow other gods' belongs to idolatry, not to law/wisdom.
No clause here mentions an idol set in the sanctuary or the holy place; Jer 25:6 speaks only of other gods and the works of their hands.

The section has no darkness imagery: it turns on a cup of wine, drunkenness, sword, storm and unburied corpses (Jer.25.27#cl2-cl6, Jer.25.33#cl4). The reader cited Jer 25:33, which speaks of the slain left like dung, not of darkness.

No fire is spoken anywhere in this section; the cited Jer 25:29 has a sword (Jer.25.29#cl6), and the agents elsewhere are the sword (Jer.25.16#cl3), a storm (Jer.25.32#cl3) and dung (Jer.25.33#cl4). Swapping 'fire' for 'sword' changes the text.

The cited Jer 25:29 speaks of the city that bears God's Name and the sword on all inhabitants (Jer.25.29#cl1, Jer.25.29#cl6), not of covenant breach or covenant curse; the section's 'curse' is the ruin made of Judah among the nations (Jer.25.18#cl1), and the judgement falls on the nations as such (Jer.25.31#cl1).
No sheep, flock or shepherd appears in this section; the cited Jer 25:33 has the slain spread over the ground and left unburied (Jer.25.33#cl0-cl4), a picture of corpses, not of scattered sheep.

The cited Jer 25:29 is entirely judgement: God begins to bring disaster on the city that bears His Name and calls a sword on all the earth (Jer.25.29#cl1, Jer.25.29#cl6). The section contains no promise of restoration or divine deliverance.

The section is the culminating wail of the cup-of-wrath oracle and reads as the day of the LORD's anger, but no clause here names a 'day of the LORD'; the 'days' of Jer.25.34#cl5 are the days of slaughter, not the day of the LORD.

The whole section is Jeremiah's oracle against the shepherds — a word of Yahweh delivered through the prophet — but no clause in it says 'thus says the LORD' or otherwise marks the speech as prophecy; the stamp describes the section's nature, not any clause in it.

The Hebrew here is a conditional sentence with the 'then' apodosis in 26:6 (a 'if you do not... then I will...' threat), not an exclamation beginning with הוֹי ('Woe!'), which is the mark of a woe oracle. The Berean text has no 'Woe' at any point in this section.
The section's drift is the wickedness of Judah's deeds and the disaster threatened because of it (Jer 26:3, 6), but no clause of this section speaks of exile or of death, so nothing is pinned.
The section shows Micah already prophesying and Jeremiah already speaking in the LORD's name; no clause reports a call or commissioning of a prophet.
General: the whole account witnesses to the fate of a prophet who spoke in the LORD's name, but no clause states a witnessing act or role.
The section shows the persecution and death of the prophet Uriah, not a suffering servant figure whose suffering is vicarious; the text says nothing of servant role or atoning suffering.
The section records the execution of Uriah and the sparing of Jeremiah; there is no language of mercy, restoration, forgiveness or return in it.
Only the phrase 'the burial place of the common people' appears, identifying a burial site of the common people, not the covenant people of God as a theme.
the section speaks of the temple vessels being carried away and left in Babylon, not of the temple itself being destroyed
no clause describes a siege; the judgment named is sword, famine and plague (Jer.27.8#cl4, Jer.27.13#cl0), which are not a siege of the city
the section condemns false prophecy and divination, not the worship of other gods; no clause names an idol or false deity
no clause in this section presents Jeremiah as a watchman warning of coming danger; the role is not named or figured here
the section's image of power is the creator's great power and outstretched arm (Jer.27.5#cl0), not a warrior or warfare
no clause indicts Israel for breaking the covenant; the speech addresses the nations and Zedekiah over submission to Babylon, not a covenant charge
The speech to Hananiah is a declarative sentence (removal from the earth, death this year), not the 'woe to ...' form; nothing in this section takes the woe form.
This section contains no indictment with charges and witnesses against Israel; Jer.28.15 (cited here) is Jeremiah's verdict on Hananiah, not a lawsuit speech.
The speech is a divine sentence introduced by 'this is what the LORD says' and reported by messenger formula, not a woe oracle ('Woe to...' / הוי). No clause here carries woe form.

The whole unit is cast as an accusing address to Israel with the LORD as speaker and plaintiff (cl0 utterance-of-Yahweh; the questions of cl6 and cl9; the indictment cl8), i.e. a lawsuit form, but no single clause states the legal charge as such.
No clause id 'Jer.3.4#cl0' exists in this section; the only 'Father' wording is Jer.3.19#cl4
No enemy or adversary appears in the section; the cited verse Jer 3:8 speaks of Israel's adultery, divorce and Judah's lack of fear, not an adversary

'And you will be My people, and I will be your God' (Jer 30:22) is covenant formula language, but nothing in this section speaks of a new covenant, a new act of covenant-making, or the new-covenant promises of Jer 31:31-34; the stamp is Jeremiah 31 material read back a chapter.

Jer 30:11 speaks of not completely destroying Israel and of discipline, and v.10 of Jacob's descendants being saved, but no clause speaks of a remnant as a surviving-portion idea; reading remnant into 'I will not completely destroy you' is an inference the text does not state.
Jer 31:4 addresses Israel as 'O Virgin Israel' — a daughter figure, not a bride; no bride, bridegroom or marriage imagery appears in any clause of this section.
No king, throne, reign or royal figure is named or implied in Jer 31:1–25; 'the LORD of Hosts' in 31:23 is a divine title, not a king role in the section.
The section is spoken as the LORD's own word ('declares the LORD', 'This is what the LORD says'); no prophet is named, commissioned or shown prophesying.
Jer 31:2's wilderness is where the survivors 'found favor' and were given rest — the opposite of wandering; no clause in the section has Israel journeying or wandering in a wilderness.
Jer 31:13 is dancing and rejoicing (maidens, young men and old), not a procession; no clause describes a march, triumph or procession of captives or victors.
The section's tenor is restoration, comfort and security, but no clause states a covenant or 'covenant of peace'.
No clause mentions an oath or the patriarchs; only the general restoration-of-Israel drift could be stretched to it.
Jer 31:22's 'a woman will shelter a man' is a woman, not Woman Wisdom; no wisdom figure, instruction or personified wisdom appears in the section.
No clause in Jer 31:1–25 names David, a Davidic descendant, or a new ruler from David's line.
No clause names Moses or a prophet-like-Moses figure; Jer 31:2's reference to the wilderness is the people's, not a new Moses leading them.
The wounded and vulnerable are carried home ('the blind and the lame'), but no resident alien/sojourner is spoken of anywhere in the section.
Jer 31:1 has only the covenant formula ('I will be the God of all the families of Israel'); no judging, court or verdict language appears in the section.
Jer 31:4 calls Israel 'O Virgin Israel' and speaks of rebuilding and dancing, not of a bridegroom or marriage; Jer 31:22's 'a woman will shelter a man' is cryptic and is not a bridegroom clause.
Jer 31:15 is Rachel weeping for her lost children, and Jer 31:18-19 is Ephraim's discipline and repentance; no figure bears suffering on behalf of others, and nothing here is the servant of Isaiah.
The covenant clauses name the house of Israel and the house of Judah (Jer.31.31#cl3, Jer.31.33#cl1); no clause names David, his throne or his line, so the davidic covenant is not spoken of here.

Jer 31:40 promises the valley and fields will be holy to the LORD and never uprooted again (Jer.31.40#cl0, Jer.31.40#cl1-2), but no clause speaks of new heavens or a new earth; the fixed order of sun, moon and stars is invoked only as a permanence guarantee (Jer.31.35, Jer.31.36).
The text calls Yahweh 'the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel', but no clause states or enacts a covenant; it speaks of a land purchase and its preservation, not of covenant making or covenant terms.

The section speaks of the right of redemption (Heb. ge'ullah) over a family field in Anathoth (Jer.32.7#cl5, Jer.32.8#cl6) and of land being bought again, but nothing in the Hebrew text speaks of Christ or of a messianic redeemer; reading the go'el law as a type of Christ is an inference brought to the text, not carried by any clause here.

The exodus is named, but the clause says nothing of crossing the sea/Reed Sea: Jer.32.21#cl0 mentions only signs, wonders, strong hand, outstretched arm, great terror. No water-crossing clause exists in this section.
The section states the siege and the fall of the city into Babylonian hands, not the deportation of people from the land. No clause speaks of being carried away/exiled.
The section deals with God's sovereign rule over nations (Jer.32.19's great counsel and mighty deeds, the fall of the city), but no clause names a kingdom, king, throne or reign as such.

The temple's destruction is not stated: Jer 32:29 names the city and the houses of the people ("set it on fire, and burn it, along with the houses"), and Jer 32:34 says the house bearing God's Name was defiled ("defiled it"), not destroyed.

Nothing here is pronounced woe upon anyone: Jer 32:26-35 is a word of accusation and a sentence of judgment ("I am about to deliver this city", "I will remove it from My presence"), with no "woe" (hoy/ouai) form or address of lament.
No deportation or removal of people from the land is said: Jer 32:28 speaks only of the city being delivered and captured ("into the hands of the Chaldeans ... who will capture it").

Jer 32:27 predicates power of God ("I am the LORD, the God of all flesh. Is anything too difficult for Me?"), not a promise kept; this section's movement to the city is accusation and wrath (Jer.32.31#cl0), with no promise or act of faithfulness in it.

The words 'covenant'/'new covenant' do not appear in this section; Jer 33:8 speaks of cleansing, forgiving and reconciliation ('I will cleanse them from all the iniquity ... and will forgive all their sins'), which is forgiveness of sin, not a covenant-making statement.

Jer 33:6 says only 'I will reveal to them the abundance of peace and truth' — no word for 'covenant' and no covenant-making clause in the section; calling this the covenant of peace reads a label in from elsewhere.

Jer 33:9 has the nations hearing, trembling and seeing God's goodness, but no clause in the section has anyone testifying, testifying to, or serving as a witness; the idea is at most the drift of the verse.
No clause speaks of a remnant: Jer 33:7 says God will restore 'Judah and Israel from captivity', naming the whole house, not a surviving remainder.

Jer 33:9 promises the city renown and prosperity before the nations, not a renewal or remaking of creation; nothing in the section speaks of creation being made new (the 'made the earth' clause of v.2 is God as maker, not new creation).

Jer 33:24 speaks of rejected 'two families' and despised 'My people', not a remnant; no clause in this section carries a remaining-remnant idea. The cited verse's content (clans chosen then rejected, people spurned) is the opposite of the stamp.

The section names David's sprouting Branch, Judah's salvation and restored captives, but no clause states redemption in Christ or identifies the Branch as Christ; that reading is imported from outside the text (within this section 'The LORD Our Righteousness' is the name given to Jerusalem, Jer 33:16).

The nearest fits are the dirge formula 'Alas, O master!' (Jer.34.5#cl3) and the judgement speech of v.2, but the former is a lament over a dead king, not a woe on the addressee, and the latter is plain announcement, not a 'woe' form; I could not pin this stamp to clauses.
The burning named is of 'this city' (Jer.34.2#cl7), with no mention of the temple anywhere in the section.

No restoration is spoken: the section announces the city given over and burned (Jer.34.2#cl5, cl7) and the king taken to Babylon (Jer.34.3#cl1, cl2, cl5). 'You will die in peace' (Jer.34.5#cl0) is a mitigation for Zedekiah, not mercy/restoration of the people or city.

No oath or swearing appears in this section; the covenant is described as made before the LORD (Jer.34.15#cl3, Jer.34.18#cl3) and passed between cut pieces (Jer.34.18#cl4-5), which is covenant-cutting, not an oath formula.

Jer.34.22 speaks of this city being burned and the cities of Judah made desolate; the temple (the house that bears My Name, Jer.34.15#cl3-4) is not said to be destroyed, and the cited verse concerns the city, not the temple.
No clause in Jer 35:1–11 speaks of mercy or restoration: the passage ends with the Rechabites sheltering in Jerusalem under military threat (Jer.35.11#cl5). The theme is absent, not merely general.
Jer 35:13-17 announces disaster ('I will bring ... all the disaster I have pronounced against them'), but there is no woe-form (הוי / 'Woe to you') anywhere in the section.

'stand before Me' in Jer 35:19 is cultic service language that can suggest a priestly or temple role, but the section names no priest and the promise is to a Rechabite man, so no clause plainly carries the role.
Judah and Jerusalem as the addressed community is the section's assumed frame rather than something a clause asserts; no clause in particular makes the community idea its point.
The section's own note is disaster brought on Judah and Jerusalem (Jer 35:17) with no restoration of Israel in view; Jer 35:19 is blessing on the Rechabites, not restoration of those under judgment.

This section has Jeremiah dictate a scroll and Baruch read it aloud; nothing here speaks of a watchman (Ezek 3/33 imagery), no warning-or-blood-guilt language. The stamp may be true of Jeremiah elsewhere but no clause here carries it.
Sin is named ('their wicked way', 'iniquity and their sin'), but exile and death are not in this section; the stamp's full pattern is not carried by any clause here.

No covenant word or formula ('cut a covenant', 'my covenant', covenant lawsuit) appears in this section; the closest is the forgiveness promise at Jer.36.3#cl4, and even that names iniquity and sin, not covenant. The reader's citation of Jer 36:2 supplies no covenant clause.

Nothing in Jer 36:11-19 presents Jeremiah as the suffering servant: he never appears, is not afflicted, and the only clause that concerns him (Jer.36.19#cl2) is advice to hide, which is prudence, not servant suffering.

The reader cited Jer 36:23, but the king's cutting and burning of the scroll is a literal act of destroying a document, not an action performed to signify something else; no clause in the section presents it as symbolic, so the stamp does not belong here.

The section's divine speech is entirely judgment: no son to sit on David's throne (Jer.36.30#cl1) and calamity brought on Judah (Jer.36.31#cl1); the restoration of the scroll (Jer.36.32#cl2, Jer.36.32#cl4) preserves the prophet's words, not a divine promise.

This section carries only a word of doom (Jer.37.8 'they will capture it and burn it down'; Jer.37.7 'the army of Pharaoh... is about to return to its own land'), with no promise or act of divine faithfulness to Israel; cf. The section has no shepherd, sheep or flock imagery; Jer 8:3 says the remnant 'will choose death over life' and Jer 8:7 uses birds, not sheep.
The section's drift of doom and hoped-for peace that turns to terror matches the day-of-the-Lord frame, but no clause names the day, the LORD's coming, or a day of visitation.
The section begins with a question ("Why are we just sitting here?") and a summons to flee; none of the clauses is a woe (הוֹי / "Woe to...") pronounced over anyone.
No clause presents the LORD as a warrior or describes a warrior's equipment, fighting, or victory; the LORD appears only as the one who doomed and poisoned his people (Jer.8.14#cl4, #cl5).
The whole section is prophetic speech, but no clause speaks of a word being spoken or received; it is the section's general mode, not a pinned idea.
Nothing in these clauses identifies the speaker with the servant of Isaiah; the mourner here is the prophet/people over the daughter of my people, not a servant bearing sin.
The section mentions carved images only as what provoked the LORD (Jer.8.19#cl4); no clause places an idol in the temple or any holy place.

The whole section is first-person prophetic speech and narrative about the prophet (9:1-5, 9:10, 9:16-22), and the prophet speaks in the LORD's name throughout, but no clause in this section names him or describes his role, so the stamp is the section's general drift rather than pinned to a clause.

The watchman topos (a figure set to warn of coming danger, e.g. Jer 6:17; Ezek 3:17; Hab 2:1) is not present here: 9:1 shows the prophet weeping over the slain, and 9:12 asks who can explain the ruin, but nothing commissions or pictures a watchman.

Nothing in this section restores or shows mercy; the cited verse (9:24) in fact ends 'Behold, the days are coming ... when I will punish all who are circumcised yet uncircumcised' in the next verse. 9:24 declares the LORD's character and delight, but no act of mercy or restoration to the people is stated here.

The apocalyptic topos of an idol set up in the sanctuary is not in this section. The cited verse (9:14) names going after the Baals, but no holy place, temple or sanctuary is mentioned, and the desolation of Jerusalem (9:11) has no idol-in-the-temple element.
The section concerns one man and his household, not a people; nothing in it names or addresses a people of God.
The heavenly wager of Job 1:6-12 is not narrated here; this section is the disasters and Job's response, so the stamp describes the drift of the section rather than any clause in it.
Job 1:16 is the fire of God burning sheep and servants, not a sacrifice; the Hebrew has no offering word here (the burnt offerings are Job 1:5, outside this section).
No clause of the section curses anything; the opposite is stated at Job.1.21#cl5 and Job.1.22#cl0-cl1.
The Sabeans (Job.1.15) and Chaldeans (Job.1.17) are human raiders; the adversary who instigates the attacks (Job 1:6-12) does not appear in any clause of this section.
Same as for Job.1.15: the Chaldeans are human raiders, and no adversary figure is present in these clauses.
Job 1:13 names only 'their oldest brother'; no clause states Job's fatherhood or any father's act toward his children (the oxen report evokes Job's holdings, not his fatherhood).
Yahweh is named in Job.1.21#cl3-cl5 but no clause calls him king or speaks of kingship; the verb is 'gave/taken' and 'blessed'.
Job's tearing his robe, shaving his head and falling to the ground (Job.1.20#cl0-cl3) are mourning and submission, not priestly acts, and no priest appears in the section.
Job speaks in 1:21, but nothing in the clause marks him as a prophet or relays a prophetic word; the speech is a lament and blessing, not a prophetic oracle.
1:22 says Job did not sin or charge God with wrongdoing, which is a verdict about Job's own conduct, not Job acting as a judge over anyone.
In 1:19 the wind collapses the house on the young people, described as Job's sons and daughters (1:18); the clause itself names no servants.
The Sabeans in 1:15 are foreign raiders who take the oxen and donkeys; they are not resident strangers or sojourners.
The Chaldeans in 1:17 are raiders who form three bands and take the camels; nothing presents them as sojourners.
1:13 presents the sons and daughters eating and drinking in their oldest brother's house; the clause gives no host–guest relation or act of hosting.
The clause names eating and drinking in the brother's house, not anyone received as a guest.
1:21 speaks of coming naked from the womb and returning naked, i.e. birth and death, not pilgrimage or journeying.
In 1:15 the one survivor is a lone messenger who escaped to report, not a remnant of a people preserved by God.
1:21 is Job's own lament and blessing; the suffering-servant theme concerns the servant of the LORD, and Job is not cast in that role here.
1:21 states the LORD gives and takes away; no clause in the section speaks of mercy or restoration.
No promise or divine faithfulness is stated; 1:21 affirms the LORD's giving and taking and blesses his name.
1:20 shows Job rising, tearing his robe, shaving his head and bowing down; it names no people of God.
No covenant, covenant-making or covenant language appears in the section.
1:21 blesses the name of the LORD but does not speak of kingship, rule or a kingdom.
1:22 reports that Job did not sin or charge God with wrongdoing; it states no law, instruction or wisdom saying.
1:14 is a messenger's report of the oxen and donkeys, not a prophetic utterance.
The only creation-adjacent language ('the fire of God fell from heaven', Job.1.16#cl3) is a reported disaster, not an act or account of creating; no clause speaks of creation.
No clause mentions likeness, image, or human nature as such; Job.1.22#cl0/cl1 speak only of not sinning or charging God with wrongdoing.
No offering, altar, or victim appears; Job.1.20#cl1 'tore his robe' and #cl2 'shaved his head' are mourning gestures, and the word 'sacrifice' is not in the text.
No priest, mediation, or cultic duty is spoken of; Job's acts in Job.1.20#cl0-#cl4 are mourning and worship by the household head, not priestly service.
No temple, sanctuary, or divine dwelling is named; Job.1.21#cl5 blesses the name of the LORD without any place of presence.
Nothing in the section speaks of Christ, rescue from sin, or redemption; Job.1.21#cl4 'The LORD has taken away' is the opposite of a redemption statement.
No clause speaks of renewal, restoration, or a new creation; the section ends in loss and in Job not sinning (Job.1.22#cl0).
No clause mentions Christ or any 'in him' relation; Job's stance in Job.1.21#cl1-#cl5 is his own speech to God, not union with Christ.
This section speaks of a wager over Job's loyalty, loss of property and a curse, but no clause states sin, exile or death; the threatened harm stops short of the man himself (Job.1.12#cl4).

Job is called My servant and is blameless and upright (Job.1.8#cl1-2), but no clause in this section has him suffering: the losses are only proposed and permitted (Job.1.11#cl1, Job.1.12#cl2), and he is expressly not to be touched (Job.1.12#cl4). The suffering is later in the book, not here.
Job 10:18-19 wishes only for death ('Oh, that I had died'; 'If only I had never come to be'); no clause here speaks of life coming out of death.

Job 11:2 is Zophar challenging Job's 'stream of words' and asking whether a man of lips will be acquitted; no prophet, prophetic role, or prophetic speech is named or implied in the clause. The stamp is for the role of prophet, which this section does not contain.

Job's hope is voiced for himself only (Job.13.15#cl2, Job.13.16#cl0); no petition for mercy or restoration is made anywhere in this section — the section's drift is accusation and demand for a hearing.

The phrase belongs to Isaiah's Servant (Isa 52-53): an innocent figure suffering vicariously for others. Nothing in these clauses says that; Job asserts his own knowledge (Job.13.2), his innocence (Job.13.18), and his willingness to argue with God (Job.13.3).
No clause presents Job as speaking God's word on God's behalf; the speech of Job.13.7-10 condemns the friends for speaking falsely 'on God's behalf', the opposite of a prophetic word.

No covenant term or idea appears: God is addressed as Almighty and as an adversary in a legal dispute (Job.13.3, Job.13.24), not as covenant partner; no covenant, oath, or obligation is named in any of these clauses.
The clause names the three friends ('you are all worthless physicians', Job.13.4#cl1) as Job's opponents, not as God's people Israel; no collective people of God is in view in this section.
Eliphaz addresses no 'woe to you' over the wicked; 15:20-35 is third-person description of the wicked man's fate, not a woe oracle.

Job.16.7 speaks of ruin (weariness, family devastated) but no clause names sin, exile, or death. The reader's citation is likely to the long-running Job debate, not to this verse's wording. General drift at best.
Job 17:9 has no mercy or restoration: the righteous simply holds his way and the clean-handed man grows stronger; the section closes on Sheol and the dust. The stamp is read into the section.

No clause in the section carries law or wisdom teaching; the reader cited Job 18:21, but cl0/cl1/cl2 state the wicked's ruin and his not knowing God, which is judgment language, not law or wisdom instruction. If the stamp is intended as the general theme of the book (wisdom), it applies only as background drift, so empty and general.
Job 19:23-24 is about recording/inscribing Job's words (a written record), not about a witness who testifies; no clause in the section presents a witness.
Job 19:9 ('removed the crown from my head') is about lost honor, not a king; no king or reign appears in the section.
Job 19:17 ('my own family', literally 'sons of my womb') names the family/household but no father as such.
Same: the verse points to Job's wife and born-family, not to a mother.
No firstborn is mentioned; at most 'my brothers' (19:13) is kin language, which is not the firstborn role.
Job 19:15 mentions maidservants and 19:16 a servant, and the digests' glosses use 'servant' for both, but nothing marks them as slaves/bondservants.
The guest/host relation is only half present: 19:15 names guests and maidservants of Job's house, but no clause presents Job acting as host/hosting.
No nation or people-group appears; Job 19:29 speaks of the sword, wrath and judgment, not of nations.

Job 19:25-26 speaks of the living Redeemer standing and Job seeing God from his flesh, but nothing says the dead rise or that Job is raised/resurrected; that is an inference, not a clause in the text.
Job 19:21 ('Have pity on me, my friends') is a plea for pity, not a woe-pronouncement against anyone.
Job 19:25 ('I know that my Redeemer lives, and in the end He will stand upon the earth') is Job's own assurance, not a divine promise spoken with a formula; the section is a speech, not an oracle.
Job 19:20 ('my skin and flesh cling to my bones; I have escaped by the skin of my teeth') describes affliction and survival, not healing or cure.
Job 19:14 ('my kinsmen have failed me, and my friends have forgotten me') states abandonment, not a curse or cursing speech.
Tearing down is of Job himself ('He tears me down on every side until I am gone', v.10); no building, let alone the temple, is in view.
v.13-14 is about brothers, kinsmen and friends withdrawing from Job, not about anyone being taken captive.
v.23 is Job wishing his own words were recorded; there is no call, commission or divine speech to a prophet.
v.24 is a wish that his words be engraved with an iron stylus on lead or in rock, not a performed gesture standing for something else.
v.9 has stripping and removal ('He has stripped me of my honor and removed the crown from my head'), the opposite of anointing; no oil is mentioned.
v.12 is an advance to besiege Job, not a triumph or procession of a victor; captives and celebration are absent.
There is no David, no dynasty and no covenant promise in v.25; Job's living Redeemer is not a covenant with David.
v.4 says 'if I have truly gone astray, my error concerns me alone' - a general moral error, with no idol or false worship named.
v.13-14 concerns Job's personal relationships ('He has removed my brothers from me'), not a divided kingdom.
v.4 is Job conceding a possible error, not a call to or account of national repentance and revival.
The suffering servant is an innocent figure bearing others' sin (Isaiah 53); Job here protests his innocence and seeks his own vindication (19.25), and his suffering is not vicarious.
This section gives Job's own go'el ('my Redeemer lives', v.25); applied to Christ it is later Christian reading, not something any clause here carries.
The clause is the inflicting of sickness, not healing; no clause in the section speaks of healing.
Job's holding fast (2:3, 2:9) is integrity under trial, not a divine promise or covenant faithfulness; no clause states a promise.
No clause speaks of the Spirit or a spirit being; the adversary is a personage, not a spirit mentioned as such.
No covenant, treaty or its language appears in this section.
No king, rule or kingdom language in the section; God is not spoken of as ruling here.
The three friends come to sympathize and comfort, not as enemies or adversaries; the adversary of the section is not in these clauses.
The seven days of silence sitting on the ground is mourning, not fasting; no clause mentions abstaining from food.
The period named is seven days and seven nights, not forty.
"the day of calamity" / "the day of wrath" (Job.21.30) is the personal doom of the wicked man, not the eschatological day of the Lord; no clause in the section speaks of that.
Job.21.20 asks that the wicked man see his own destruction and drink God's wrath; there is no cursing, curse-formula, or imprecation vocabulary (no "curse" word and no invoking of a curse on anyone).

Job.21:6 ("terror takes hold, and my body trembles in horror") is Job's personal dread at the fate of the wicked, not the suffering of a servant of the Lord who bears others' sin; no clause here presents a servant figure.

Job.21:30 states what happens to the evil man ("the evil man is spared from the day of calamity") as reported observation/common knowledge, not a divine word spoken through a prophet; no clause claims prophetic utterance.
Job.21:19 asks God to repay the man himself ("Let God repay the man himself, so he will know it") — retribution, not mercy or restoration; the section has no restoration or forgiveness clause.
No clause in the section names a covenant, a lawsuit, or a charge laid in court. Job 22:5-9 are accusations Eliphaz speaks about Job, addressed to Job, without any courtroom or covenant framing.

Job 22:24 tells Job to consign gold and Ophir gold to the dust, which is a call to renounce trust in wealth, not an act or charge of worshiping an idol. Nothing in the section mentions a god, an image, or worship of anything but the Almighty; Job.22.24#cl0-#cl1 are generosity/renunciation in the restoration sequence.

Job 22:19 has the righteous see and the innocent mock; there is no witnessing or testifying in a legal sense, no one called to witness, no testimony. Job.22.19#cl0-2 are observation and mockery, not witness.

The section is Eliphaz's speech of accusation and counsel; no clause presents a word from God, a prophet speaking 'thus says the LORD', or a prophetic utterance. Job.22.22#cl0-1 are instruction and words God gives, but not a prophetic word spoken here.
No clause presents anyone as a witness: Job.23.10 speaks of God knowing/testing, not of testimony given by a witness; the Hebrew behind 'he knows the way with me' is knowledge, not witness testimony.
Job.23.15 speaks of terror at God's presence, not of a divine appearing; and Job.23.8-9 deny that God can be found or seen, which is the opposite of theophany.

No clause casts Job as a servant bearing suffering for others; Job.23.13-16 describes God's arbitrary power and Job's terror, and Job.23.10-12 asserts Job's own righteousness, not vicarious suffering.
Job.23.6 offers only that God 'would certainly take note of me' — no mercy or restoration is stated; the section's remaining clauses (23.13-17) stress terror, not restoration.
Job.23.10 states God knows the way and tests Job, but there is no promise and no divine faithfulness claimed; Job.23.13-14 in fact stresses God's unchangeable arbitrary decree against him.
Job.23.14 speaks of God's 'decree' and 'plans' being executed against Job, not of a prophetic word spoken through Job or to him.
Job 24:22 depicts God dragging off the mighty unjustly — an image of divine violence against the wicked, not a final eschatological battle of nations/armies.
Job 24:25 is Job's legal-warrant challenge ('who can prove me a liar?' calling his words to nothing) — no book, record of deeds, or opened book appears in the clause(s).

Job 26:12's 'stirred the sea' / 'shattered Rahab' is a cosmic combat image (sea stirred by power, Rahab shattered), not the crossing of a sea by a people; no clause here speaks of crossing or of Israel passing through water.
God acts throughout with sovereign authority, but no clause names Him king, throne (26:9#cl0 is 'surface of the throne', a covering, not a reign), or rule.
No clause speaks of a kingdom, a reign, or rule over a people; the section's theme is God's cosmic power.
The clauses are Job's sarcasm to Bildad — he credits Bildad with help and salvation, not God; nothing here speaks of God's mercy or of restoration.

Job 27:5 has Job refusing to concede ('I will never say that you are right'), i.e. an assertion of his own integrity, not testimony, witness, or a witness-role; no clause in this section names a witness or witnessing.

Job 27:4 speaks of lips not speaking wickedness and tongue not uttering deceit (Job.27.4#cl0, Job.27.4#cl2) — an ethical resolve, not law or wisdom as a theme; the reader's cited verse does not carry the stamp.

Wisdom in Job 28 is a sought, hidden, personified-but-unfemale thing ('where can wisdom be found'), never figured as a woman; no clause here presents wisdom as a woman or female figure. The stamp's role does not occur in this section.

Job 28:13 speaks only of wisdom's value and its not being found 'in the land of the living', which is a statement about wisdom's inaccessibility, not about sin, exile or death as such; the only death-word in the section is 'Abaddon and Death' at 28:22, and there it is a witness to ignorance of wisdom, not a theme of sin-exile-death.
No clause gives a commission to bless or an Abrahamic blessing-to-the-nations; v6's cream and oil are prosperity imagery only.
Job 29 speaks of Job, his household and the townsmen (young men, elders, princes, nobles, mourners), never of Israel or a people belonging to God; the stamp's covenant-people sense is not present.
The section is Job's lament over his birth and his longing for death (Job 3:11-22); there is no sin, no exile, and no statement that sin brings death.
The 'rest' in Job 3:17-19 is the rest of Sheol, the grave Job longs for (Job 3:13-16, 21-22), not God's mercy or restoration; the section has no act of mercy or restoring.
The stillborn child in Job 3:16 is cited as a death Job wishes had been his, alongside the grave he longs for (Job 3:21-22); nothing in the text makes death yield life.

Nothing in the section speaks of slavery or bondage: the men are outcaste squatters driven from the community (Job.30.5#cl0, Job.30.8#cl2), not slaves or bondservants, and no clause uses servant/slave language.
No clause speaks of a surviving remainder; Job.30.5 and Job.30.8 describe the whole outcaste brood being driven off, not a remnant preserved.
The section concerns one outcaste band ('A senseless and nameless brood', Job.30.8#cl0); no clause speaks of nations or peoples as a character.

Nothing in this section presents a ruler or ruler who behaves as a beast; the mockers are a nameless brood without rule, and the beast-like behaviour in Job.30.7#cl0 is the outcaste' own braying, not a ruler's.
The only shepherding word is Job.30.1#cl2 ('with my sheep dogs'), which is about Job's own dogs, not about a shepherd who fails or exploits; no clause describes a false shepherd.
General only: the mockers arise 'at my right' and Job has his bow unstrung and his path torn up, the drift of a great man brought down, but no clause in this section says king, throne, reign or rule.
No clause names a servant or slave role; the mockers are 'men younger than I am' and an outcaste brood (Job.30.1#cl0, Job.30.8#cl0), not servants of anyone.
No clause speaks of a firstborn, birthright or pre-eminence; the sons language in Job.30.8#cl0 is a term of worthlessness, not of firstborn status.
Nothing in the section speaks of a bridegroom or of marriage; the mockery of Job.30.9 is public taunt, not a wedding setting.
No clause in this section mentions a bride or marriage.
No clause in this section mentions a mother.

Low confidence and general only: the section's drift is of a crowd sheltering on Job's land and then assaulting him, but no clause speaks of entertaining or receiving guests, which is what a host role would require.

Nothing in Job 30:1-14 presents anyone as a guest or sojourner received into a house; the men of 30:1-8 are mockers, outcasts and raiders, and the only hospitality word is Job's own 'my flock/flock dogs' (30:1), which is about what he would not entrust, not about welcoming a guest.
No clause speaks of a journey to a holy place or a pilgrim; 30:3-7 describes destitute outcasts gnawing dry ground and living in wadi slopes and rock holes, which is homelessness, not pilgrimage.
No one here stands watch, warns, or keeps guard; 30:1's 'my sheep dogs' is the closest word, and it is Job's livestock, used as a measure of the fathers' worthlessness, not a watchman role.

The building vocabulary in this section is the enemies' work against Job - 'they lay snares', 'build siege ramps' (30:12), 'they tear up my path' (30:13), 'as through a wide breach' (30:14) - all destruction of Job's way, not building.
No vine, vineyard, pruning or harvest work appears; 'they plucked mallow among the shrubs, and the roots of the broom tree were their food' (30:4) is foraging for wild food, not cultivation.
No water, boat, net or fish in the section; the snares of 30:12 ('they lay snares for my feet') are foot-traps on land, not fishing nets.

No gate is kept by anyone; 'they were banished from among men, shouted down like thieves' (30:5) and 'driven off the land' (30:8) put these men outside the gate, and no clause gives anyone the role of guarding an entrance.
Job speaks no oracle from God in these verses; the only speech is the mockers' song (30:9) and Job's own complaint of mockery and affliction (30:1, 9-10), so nothing marks prophetic speech.
No altar, sacrifice, offering or priestly duty occurs in Job 30:1-14; the section has mockery (30:1, 9), destitution (30:3-7) and hostility (30:11-14) and no cultic act.
No female figure speaks or is personified here; the men of 30:1-14 are mockers and raiders, and 'a senseless and nameless brood' (30:8) is a description of men, not of Wisdom.
There is no personified woman, and 'A senseless and nameless brood' (30:8) is a plural description of these outcast men, not the figure of Folly.
No one in the section claims to speak for God; the mockers only sing taunts (30:9) and spit (30:10), so there is no false prophetic claim to identify.
The section has violent wrong done to Job by a rabble (30:12-14) but no single 'man of lawlessness' figure and no man who sets himself above God; the enemies are a collective crowd.
Job in this section is the humiliated sufferer (30:1, 9-10, 11-14), not a second Adam, and no clause in it speaks of a new head of humanity or of undoing Adam's state.

No deliverer, lawgiver or exodus imagery appears; Job's complaint is that God 'has unstrung my bow and afflicted me' (30:11) and that he is besieged (30:12-14), which is the opposite of a Moses-like deliverance.

The section gives only the humiliation pole - mockery of the once-honoured man (30:1, 9-10), God's affliction (30:11) and the enemies' onslaught (30:12-14); no clause in Job 30:1-14 states a turning to vindication, so the stamp fits the section's drift but no particular clause carries it.

The exile note is present in the drift - the men are 'banished from among men' (30:5), 'driven off the land' (30:8), living in the wadis (30:6) - but the section itself gives no statement of sin or of death, and no clause inside Job 30:1-14 carries the full theme, so I set it as general rather than pinning the exile clauses.

God's action here is discipline of Job - 'Because God has unstrung my bow and afflicted me' (30:11) - and the rabble's raids (30:12-14) are the outward execution of it, but the section names no verdict, verdict-declaration or judgment scene, so it is the drift and not a particular clause.

Job suffers mockery (30:1, 9-10), spitting (30:10), divine affliction (30:11) and siege by a rabble (30:12-14), which matches the suffering-servant pattern in its general shape, but no clause in the section assigns Job the servant role or interprets his suffering as vicarious, so no clause can be pinned.

The cited verse's clauses (Job.30.20#cl0 'I cry for help to you', cl1 'not you answer me', cl3 'you have considered carefully (in) me') present God as an unresponsive, watching party, not as one who hears, tries or pronounces; no clause in the section names a judge, a bench, a verdict or a sentence.

Job.30.24 (the cited verse) says the opposite of a servant relation: 'no one stretches out his hand to a ruined man when he cries for help in his distress' — no master, no service, no obedience anywhere in these clauses.

Job.30.19 (cited: 'he has thrown me to the mud', 'I have become like dust and ashes') gives humiliation and nearness to death, but no clause in the section speaks of sin or of exile; the closest to death, Job.30.23, is stated as appointed for all the living, not as judgment for sin.
Job.30.24 (cited) reports the absence of mercy — 'no one stretches out his hand to a ruined man when he cries for help' — and no clause in the section shows mercy given or anything restored.
cl0 is a self-imposed resolve (a covenant with my eyes), not the swearing of an oath by God or a curse-formula; no oath-taking act is expressed in the section.
Job 31:37 'like a prince' is a royal image of approach to God, not a priest; no clause of this section speaks of priesthood or priestly office.
The section's drift—Job's plea for God to weigh him honestly and clear him (31:6)—is a plea for vindication rather than a statement of mercy or restoration; no clause carries the idea in particular.
Job 31:15 speaks of God as maker of master and servant alike; no clause of this section speaks of a people belonging to God, covenant community or Israel.
Verses 6-7 contrast youth with age ('you are old', 'days should speak'); nothing in the section speaks of fatherhood, and no clause names a father.
Verse 13 contains no woe; it is an instruction not to claim 'We have found wisdom', and no clause in the section pronounces woe on anyone.
The speakers are Israel's forebears, but no clause marks them as a people or congregation of God; the section concerns four individuals arguing.
Verse 2 has Job justifying himself, but that is his act of self-vindication and no clause describes him being humiliated and then restored; nor does Elihu describe such a reversal.
The section speaks of sin (Job.35.6), suffering under oppression (Job.35.9) and unanswered cries (Job.35.12-13), but has no exile, banishment or death; the theme's full triad is absent.

Job.35.16 is Elihu's verdict on Job's words, not a prophetic utterance; Elihu is nowhere called a prophet and no 'thus says the LORD' or oracle formula appears — the stamp describes the passage's general form (a speech correcting Job) but no clause carries it.

Job 36:5 says God is mighty in strength of understanding — the strength is of heart/understanding, not of arms; no clause in this section speaks of fighting, enemies or battle, so warrior is not present.
Nothing in the section names God as father or the relation of fatherhood; 'I will ascribe justice to my Maker' (36:3#cl1) is Creator, not father.
36:6 speaks of 'the afflicted' and 'the wicked', not of the stranger or sojourner; no clause in the section names the foreigner.

Nothing in Job 37:1-24 speaks of God as father: no begetting, no fatherly care, no son; God appears only as thunderer, cloud-master and just ruler (cf. Elihu's mediating role, which is not fatherhood).
No clause in Job 37:1-24 mentions sin, exile or death; the section's darkness (Job.37.19#cl2) is the obscurity of man's case before God, not sin or exile.
Job 38:28 asks who fathered rain and dew; nothing in it or the section speaks of a firstborn or of primogeniture, so the citation rides on 'begotten' alone
Job 38:2 is God rebuking Job for darkening counsel with words without knowledge; a prophet is one who carries the divine counsel, not one charged with obscuring it, so the citation is backwards
Job 38:13 shakes the wicked out of the earth, and the wicked here are individuals, not a nation acting as a character; the section names no nation
Job 38:15 has light withheld from the wicked and their arm broken; it names no surviving remainder, and no clause in the section speaks of one
The raven's young are not guests; they are fed by God. Nothing in the section speaks of a guest or hospitality received.
Job 38:27 has God causing vegetation to sprout on wasteland, not a vinedresser tending vines; no vine, vineyard or dressing appears.
Job 38:35 is about lightning obeying God; no priest, altar, offering or mediation appears.
Job 38:12 is about commanding the dawn, not about a lawgiver or deliverer like Moses.
Job 38:33 speaks of the heavens' rule, with no king, throne or covenant of David in view.
Fatherhood/begetting of rain and dew in Job 38:28 is meteorological, not marital imagery.
Womb and birth in Job 38:29 belong to ice and frost, not to a bride.

Nothing in 23:1-3 names Sinai, a covenant, or covenant-making; the paragraph is a speech formula plus regulations about appointed feasts and the Sabbath, so the stamp has no foothold in this section.

These verses give commands (keep the Sabbath, proclaim the feasts) with no reflection on wisdom, understanding, or the fear of the LORD, which is what the stamp would require; it is at best a general biblical theme, not something these clauses say.
The verses speak of sacred assemblies and a Sabbath to the LORD, but never of a sanctuary, temple, dwelling place of God or his presence; the stamp is not carried by any clause in this section.
The section is cultic calendar/ritual instruction (a day of rest, a sacred assembly, a fire offering); no clause here speaks of wisdom, understanding, insight or skill.
The section is legislation delivered through Moses, but no clause states or depicts an act of law-giving; 23:26 only introduces the speech.

Lev 23:28, the verse cited, speaks only of atonement being made and of doing no work; the section's one offering clause is 23:27 ('present an offering made by fire'), so the stamps citing 23:28 for sacrifice do not hold for that verse.
Lev 23:31 cites a statute/decree of perpetuity, which is legal instruction, not wisdom; nothing in the section speaks of wisdom or wise dealing.
Lev 23:43 mentions the exodus from Egypt, not the Sinai covenant; no clause in this section speaks of covenant-making at Sinai.
The section is prescriptive ritual law (feasts, assemblies, offerings); no clause carries wisdom instruction, and the reader's cited verse (Lev 23:34) is a festival calendar command.

No priestly figure, function or ordination is named anywhere in this section; note this is an empty pin but I do not call the stamp wrong, since offering presentation implicitly assumes a cultic institution.

The section has the people dwelling in booths and rejoicing "before the LORD" (Lev 23:40), but no temple, sanctuary, dwelling place of God or divine presence in a place; the reader's cited verse concerns branches and rejoicing only.
The section is a calendar of appointed feasts and their regulations; there is no accusation, indictment, summons or lawsuit language anywhere in these clauses (cf. Lev.23.4#cl0-8#cl2).
The chapter is instruction/torah in form, but no clause here makes a wisdom claim (no 'fear of the LORD', no contrast of wise and foolish); the stamp describes the section's general drift only.

The whole section addresses Israel's communal observance ('you are to proclaim', 'you must eat', 'you are to hold', 'you must not do'), but no clause names the people or states their identity as God's people.

The sacred assemblies of Lev.23.7#cl0 and the fire offering of Lev.23.8#cl0 are assigned to the whole congregation ('to you'), and no priest, Aaronide, or priestly duty is mentioned in any clause of Lev.23.4-8.
The section speaks of appointed feasts, sacred assemblies and an offering 'to the LORD' (Lev.23.8#cl0), but never of a sanctuary, dwelling, or the LORD's presence among his people.
The section is about firstfruits (reshit) of the harvest, offered as a sheaf; no firstborn (bekhor) human or animal is in view, so the firstborn idea is not what this section speaks of.
The section is instruction and statute for the firstfruits offering; it contains no accusation, indictment, summons or divine lawsuit against Israel, so a covenant lawsuit is not present.

Nothing here is framed as wisdom; the section is a cultic command about oil and lamps, with no wisdom teaching, sage, or "hear/instruction" language. The nearest content (Lev 24:2 'Command the Israelites') is law-giving, not wisdom.
The section is casuistic law carrying no wisdom saying or motive clause of the wisdom kind; only the general drift of law.
The section gives a perpetually binding ordinance, but no clause names the making of the covenant at Sinai; only the standing obligation is in view.
This section is a priestly cultic regulation about bread, incense and the priests' portion; no clause has the character of law-teaching or wisdom. I can see no clause that speaks to it.
General drift only: the section is instruction, but no clause speaks of wisdom, understanding or discerning.
General: Yahweh's giving of the land (Lev.25.2#cl2-3) presupposes covenant, but no clause names a covenant or its making.

The Hebrew behind "neighbor" in Lev 25:14 is a fellow citizen/kinsman (cl0 'to your.fellow citizen', cl1 'from the.hand your.fellow.citizen your'), not a foreigner or sojourner; no clause in this section mentions a stranger, sojourner, resident alien or foreigner.

No clause speaks of judging, a judge, a court, or legal arbitration; Lev 25:15 (cl0, cl1) regulates the price of a sale by the number of years, and Lev 25:17 (cl0-cl2) forbids maltreating a fellow citizen and grounds it in fear of God, not in a judge.
Lev 25:17 speaks only of not wronging one another and fearing God ("I am the LORD your God"); there is no mention of peace, a covenant of peace, or shalom anywhere in these clauses.
The section speaks to the Sinai covenant only by being part of it; no clause names or enacts the covenant.
No clause in this section commissions anyone; the blessing here is divine provision, not a charge given to a person.
The provision answers a worry about food, but no clause speaks of mercy or of restoring what was lost.

Lev 25:23 states Yahweh's ownership of the land and Israel's tenant status; it contains no accusation, indictment, summons or covenant charge against Israel, which is what a covenant lawsuit (rîb) requires. The nearest thing to a claim in the cited verse is 'the land is Mine', which asserts title, not a grievance.
Lev 25:25 speaks of a brother becoming impoverished and selling his property, and of a kinsman-redeemer; no clause in this section speaks of slavery, bondage, servitude or a bondservant.

Lev 25:32 concerns the Levites' right of redemption over their houses; no clause mentions priests, the priesthood, or priestly service. The Levites here appear as a land-holding tribe among the Israelites, not as priests.
Lev 25:32 names the Levites and their cities; nothing in the section speaks of a king, kingship, monarchy or royal authority.
Lev 25:28 speaks only of a sale remaining with the buyer until Jubilee and of the property being released; nothing in the section states or recalls a divine promise or Yahweh's covenant faithfulness.

The section speaks only of the redemption of land and houses through a kinsman-redeemer, the price reckoning and the Year of Jubilee; nothing in these clauses names Christ, the new covenant, or any fulfilment, so the stamp is not a reading of this section in the text itself.
No clause speaks of a slave or bondservant; the man is a destitute brother who is to be strengthened, and the words 'sojourner' and 'resident alien' are the only role terms used.
Lev.25.38#cl0/#cl1 speak of the exodus from Egypt and the gift of Canaan, not of a covenant made at Sinai; no clause names Sinai or a covenant-making there.

no clause names a covenant or its making; only the exodus redemption motive and brotherhood within Israel are stated

The verses are imperative commands to Israel (count, sound, consecrate, do not sow); no clause states a promise or God's faithfulness, so this is the section's general covenant context rather than any particular clause.

The only sacrificial reference is the name of a day, 'the Day of Atonement' (Lev.25.9#cl1); this section commands a horn blast on that day, not a sacrifice. No clause here performs or commands a sacrifice. Cites Lev 25:9 for sacrifice, which I could not confirm as belonging in this section.

No clause in this section mentions a priest, Aaron, the sons of Aaron, or priestly duty. The horn blast is commanded of the addressee ('you'), and no priestly actor or office appears. I judge the stamp not present in this section.
Lev 26:9 says only 'I will establish My covenant with you' - no mention of Sinai, Horeb, the mountain, or the covenant being made/given there in this section.
Lev 26:3 speaks of Israel keeping/walking in statutes and commandments already given, not of God giving law; no clause in the section has God giving statutes.

Lev 26:11 speaks of God putting His dwelling place among them, not of a visible manifestation/appearance of God; the section clothes no appearance of God in fire, cloud, smoke or glory.
Lev 26:13 mentions only being brought out of the land of Egypt and out of slavery; no sea, water, or crossing appears in the section.

The section opens with commands to keep statutes/Sabbaths and promises fruitfulness to the obedient, but no clause states that law is wisdom or that keeping it makes one wise - only Israel's walking in the statutes is in view (Lev.26.3#cl0-cl1).

The whole 'If you follow My statutes ... I will ...' structure and the repeated 'I am the LORD your God' speak of God standing by His undertakings, but no single clause says He is faithful or keeps His word.

No clause in the section speaks of a king, a throne, or a kingdom; at most Lev.26.5#cl3, Lev.26.6#cl0 and Lev.26.11#cl0 describe security and God's presence in the land, which is not kingship language.

Lev 26:33 speaks of being scattered among the nations while a sword follows, and the land becoming desolate - dispersion outside the land, not Israel's wilderness wandering (which is never mentioned in this section).
A woe pronouncement is a prophetic 'woe to...' cry; this section is divine first-person threat and curse, with none of that form, and no clause rests on 'woe'.

Lev 26:34-35 (the cited verse) says the land will enjoy and rest in its Sabbaths while desolate - that is the land recovering sabbath rest, not mercy shown, restoration, or return. The section Lev.26.14-39 ends in wasting away and perishing (vv.38-39); no clause here promises mercy or restoration.
The stamp is the section's general frame - 'My covenant' presupposes a covenant people addressed as 'you'; no single clause in this section speaks of the people's identity as such.
Nothing in Lev.26.14-39 has the day-of-the-Lord imagery (day of darkness, coming day of the LORD); Lev 26:16 is ordinary covenant-curse threat.
Lev 26:19 says 'I will make your sky like iron and your land like bronze' - hard, unyielding heaven and earth, not darkness; no clause in the section mentions darkness or light failing.
The verse has idols thrown down and covered with corpses, the opposite of an idol enthroned/ruling; nothing in Lev 26:14-39 enthrones an idol.

Lev 26:26 gives famine (bread cut off, eaten but not satisfied) but no clause in Lev 26:14-39 moves from famine to provision; the section only worsens. The stamp matches the section's drift as a contrast with covenant blessing, not any clause.
Exile is plainly here (scattered among the nations, perishing among them), but nothing in the section raises the exiles up; there is no return or exaltation clause. General drift only.

The section ends in humiliation — survivors wasting away and decaying in their iniquity and their fathers' sins (Lev 26:39) — with no vindication anywhere in Lev 26:14-39. The stamp names a pairing whose second half is absent.
No clause names David or a Davidic covenant; the covenants named are Jacob, Isaac, Abraham, and the fathers.
No covenant-cutting rite (sacrifice, oath ceremony, cutting) appears; the section only recalls and remembers covenants.
The section lists statutes and penalties but nowhere connects keeping them with wisdom or understanding; law is present, wisdom is not.
No clause here accuses, indicts or brings a case; the section is legislation spoken by Yahweh to Moses, with no plaintiff, charge or covenant lawsuit.
No clause mentions a stranger, sojourner, foreigner or resident alien; the valuation lists only age and sex of the Israelite addressed.

The whole section is legislation delivered to Moses at Sinai and so presupposes that covenant, but no clause names Sinai, the covenant or its making.
This section is about guilt, confession and sacrificial atonement; no clause speaks of exile or death, and sin is dealt with by offering and forgiveness, not banishment or death.
The section speaks of guilt, restitution and atonement, not of sin leading to exile or death; no clause in the supplied clause list carries that idea.
The section as a whole is a block of grain-offering/sin-offering regulations, so the stamp is true in a general sense; no single clause states the system itself.

Atonement is named in Lev.7.7#cl2-3 but the section never speaks of mercy, forgiveness or restoration; the guilt offering here is a demand of the law and the priest's perquisite, so the stamp as an idea of mercy/restoration is not carried by this text.
No indictment, accusation or summons; the section is instruction plus penalty, not a covenant lawsuit (no 'because/witness/charge' language).
No priest appears: the addressees are the Israelites ('Speak to the Israelites'), and no priestly role or action is named in these verses.
Moses is addressed as the mediator of the instruction; nothing in the clauses presents Moses as a prophet (only 'he spoke Yahweh to Moses' / 'speak to the people').

The section is set within the covenant commands at Sinai (Lev 7:38), but no clause states a covenant, covenant-making, or covenant parties.

This is the ordination of Aaron and his sons with a sin offering for the altar (Lev 8), not the Day of Atonement ritual of Lev 16: there is no scapegoat, no entry into the Most Holy Place, and no year-day framework in these clauses. The mention of 'atonement' (Lev.8.15#cl5-#cl6) is the general verb, not the festival.
No clause in Lev 8:18-21 mentions oil, anointing or pouring on Aaron; the section is the burnt offering of the ram, not the anointing.

The section is entirely the ordination of Aaron and his sons (Lev 8:22-36). No covenant is made, named or referred to in these clauses; 'covenant' is not present in the text, and the Hebrew of Lev 8:33/8:34 is about filling the hand and making atonement, not covenant.

The section is introduced on the eighth day of the ordination-and-consecration sequence, but no clause here mentions anointing, oil poured on Aaron, or the anointing of priests: the only oil words are 'a grain offering mixed with oil' (Lev 9:4). The anointing itself is Lev 8, not Lev 9.

Lev 9:4 cites the ox and ram for a peace offering, but a covenant meal is eating the shared sacrifice in the LORD's presence; no clause in this section has anyone eating, and the peace offering here is slaughtered, sprinkled and burned (vv. 18-21), so the stamp is not present in this section.

Nothing here presents a prophetic word or its fulfilment: 'the word' in 1:2 is the apostolic message handed down by eyewitnesses, and the things 'accomplished among us' (Luk.1.1#cl3) are events, not a prophetic utterance. The stamp belongs to a different theme, so no clause carries it.

The section's 'us'/'we' (things accomplished among us, handed down to us) presupposes a community but no clause names the people of God as such; it is the general drift of the addressees, not a particular clause.

This is an announcement to Mary, not a call commissioning a prophet: no call, commission or sending of Mary appears. Elizabeth's conception (Luk.1.36#cl1) is cited by proximity to the cited verse, not by idea.

The oath to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob is not named or alluded to in this section; only the Davidic throne (Luk.1.32#cl2), which belongs to the separate Davidic covenant stamp. General drift of Luke's fulfilment theme, no clause carries it.
Verse 35 contains no witness: angel, Mary and the Spirit are the parties; no one testifies or attests to another in these clauses.
No word of redemption, deliverance or salvation is spoken in this section; the clauses give conception, birth and rule. The idea is the wider drift of Luke's narrative, not carried by these clauses.
No clause here speaks of rescue or deliverance; the nearest, the reign over Jacob (Luk.1.33#cl0), is rule, not deliverance. General drift only.

No clause in this section uses 'son' or any sonship word: the child is called 'fruit of your womb' (Luk.1.42#cl4) and 'the baby' (Luk.1.41#cl2, Luk.1.44#cl0) and 'the Lord' (Luk.1.43#cl1) -- never 'son'.

The v.45 clauses say only that the things spoken to her from the Lord will be fulfilled; they do not say she testifies to anything. Elizabeth's own speech (Luk.1.42#cl1, Luk.1.44#cl0) is declaration and recognition, not witness-bearing.
This section has no 'mercy', 'remember', 'raise up' or restoration language; it can only be read as an instance of God's favour, which is the section's general drift, not any single clause.
Two believing women of Israel and the child in the womb are the people of God here, but no clause speaks of a people, a nation or a community; the stamp is atmosphere, not text.
The section has no redemption, salvation, ransom or deliverance word, and the title 'my Lord' (Luk.1.43#cl1) is not by itself redemption language.
The section contains blessing (Luk.1.42, Luk.1.45) but no sending, charge, or commission: no clause tells anyone to do anything. Only the idea of blessing attaches, generally.

Both clauses in view are about Mary's pregnancy (Luk.1.41#cl2 'leaped the baby in the womb of her'; Luk.1.44#cl0 'leaped in exultation the baby in the womb of me'), and the section never says Elizabeth was barren or that she conceived; that belongs to the preceding chapter, not to Luke 1:39-45.
Elizabeth's 'why am I so honored' (Luk.1.43#cl0) is astonishment at honour, not a reversal from humiliation, and the section states no prior lowliness being overturned.
No clause in the section ranks or reverses anyone's position; 'the mother of my Lord ... to me' (Luk.1.43#cl1) names the Lord's superiority, which is the opposite of a first/last reversal.
The clause cited (Luk.1.45#cl0, 'Blessed is she who has believed') concerns Mary, who is not an outsider in the section; no clause marks anyone as outside and believing.
Rulers/thrones imply kingship but a king is not named; covenant_with_abraham (the 'fathers'/patriarchal promise of descendants) likewise fits only in essence, so both are marked general.
Abraham is named, but the word 'covenant' never occurs; the clause gives the promise, not a covenant as such.
Kingship vocabulary ('rulers', 'thrones') marks the reversal, but no reign or kingdom is asserted in this section.
The promise to the fathers is the covenant setting, but the word 'covenant' and any covenant-making are absent from the section's text.

nothing in Luke 1:5-25 is healed. The barrenness of Luke 1:7#cl1 is ended by conception (Luk.1.24#cl0), not by healing, and Zechariah's muteness (Luk.1.20#cl2) is neither cured nor lifted within this section. No clause carries the idea.

The question "What then will this child become?" asks what the child will be, and the Lord's hand is with him, but no clause names him prophet or speaks of prophetic office; the stamp is the section's drift, not a clause's content.
Luke 1:57 reports the birth, not a conception, and the text here says nothing of Elizabeth being barren; the clause support would have to be read in from Luke 1:7/1:36, which are not this section.

No clause in Luke 1:57-66 names the Spirit or the Holy Spirit; Zechariah's speech is attributed in the clauses to his opened mouth and released tongue (Luk.1.64#cl0, cl1), and "praising God" (Luk.1.64#cl3) names God, not the Spirit.
No clause mentions the temple, the sanctuary, or God's presence in a place; Luk.1.66#cl4 says the Lord's hand was with him, which is favour on a person, not temple presence.
Luke 1:72 speaks of God remembering His holy covenant and the oath to Abraham (the old covenant), not of a new covenant; nothing in the section is a new-covenant statement.
Luke 1:76 addresses John as 'child', not as son; no sonship relation is stated in this section.

No clause speaks of a kingdom, king, throne or reign. The cited verse's only relevant clause, Luk.1.69#cl0 ("has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David of the servant of Him"), is dynastic/Messianic language (a horn raised up in David's house), a royal heir rather than a kingdom or its rule; nothing in the section says God or the Messiah reigns. If the stamp means only "Davidic royal hope", Luk.1.69#cl0 would be the clause, but as stated ('kingdom') no clause carries it.

The section has no suffering servant: the only servant named is David (Luk.1.68#cl1 / Luk.1.69#cl0, "David of the servant of Him"), who does not suffer here, and the servant's task in Luk.1.76#cl0-1 is to prepare the way, not to suffer. The cited verse's clauses (Luk.1.79#cl0, Luk.1.79#cl1) speak of those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death being shone upon, which is the condition of the people, not a suffering servant. The nearest ideas are mercy to the fathers (Luk.1.72#cl0) and salvation from enemies (Luk.1.71#cl0), neither of which is a suffering servant.
The section's addressees (the seventy-two, the 'man of peace', the welcoming town) presuppose a people of God, but no clause names or depicts that people as such.

Nothing in 10:1-12 speaks of the Servant or of his suffering; the only hardship is the messengers being 'lambs among wolves' (Luk.10.3#cl2), which is the fate of the sent, not the Servant's suffering.
No clause in 10:1-12 mentions the Spirit or any act of the Spirit.
The section has a triumph (demons subject, Satan fallen), but no clause describes a procession or any triumphal march; only the general drift of victory is present.
New creation turns on the renewal of the world/heavens and earth; nothing here speaks of it. 'written in heaven' is an enrolment register, not new creation, and Satan's fall is judgment, not renewal.

No clause in this section carries the idea of the kingdom: God is called 'Lord of heaven and earth' (Luk.10.21#cl2) and the Father's delivering of all things to the Son (Luk.10.22#cl0) speaks of authority and knowledge, not of a kingdom; the word does not occur in the section.
Nothing in the section speaks of redemption or of being bought back; the Son's work here is knowledge and revelation (Luk.10.22#cl1 through Luk.10.22#cl7), not redemption.

No clause speaks of the believer's union with Christ; the relation described is the mutual knowledge of Father and Son and the Son's revealing of the Father to whom He chooses (Luk.10.22#cl2 through Luk.10.22#cl7).

The text has no witness/testimony act; the lawyer answers a question and Jesus commands action ('Go and do likewise'), which is not bearing witness. The cited verse 10:37 yields only 'compassion' and a command, not witness.

The section's drift is that the one who has chosen the good portion will not have it taken away, which a reader may call a restoring/keeping mercy; no clause states mercy or restoration as such. If pinned, the nearest wording is 'it will not be taken away from her' (Luk.10.42#cl3/cl2) and 'Mary has chosen the good portion' (Luk.10.42#cl2).

No clause here speaks of a kingdom, a king, rule or reign. The section concerns hospitality, service and sitting at the Lord's feet; the word 'Lord' (Luk.10.39#cl3, Luk.10.40#cl3) is a form of address, not a statement about the kingdom.

No clause reverses rank or order: no first/last, greater/lesser, exaltation or humbling. Martha's demand that Mary be told to help her (Luk.10.40#cl6, Luk.10.40#cl7) is not granted, and Mary's portion is commended (Luk.10.42#cl2), but the text never states a reversal of first and last.

The 'testing' here is the crowd demanding a sign from heaven (Luk.11.16#cl0) — an attempt to test Jesus, not the wilderness temptation narrative the stamp names. The event it invokes does not occur in this section.

There is a victory — overpowering, stripping the armor, dividing plunder (Luk.11.22#cl0–cl4) — but no procession: nothing in these clauses has anyone marching, leading captives or parading. The stamp adds a component the text lacks.
The parable reverses the stamp: the strong man is defeated by 'someone stronger' (Luk.11.22#cl0), so the stronger wins, not the weak. Nothing in the section has the weak overcoming the strong.
The only 'scatters' is Luk.11.23#cl2, where the one not gathering with Jesus scatters — no sheep, flock or shepherd imagery appears in the section.

No clause speaks of sin, exile or death: the passage concerns an unclean spirit leaving and returning with seven worse spirits, and a worsened plight. 'Exile' could be stretched to the spirit's wandering in waterless places (Luk.11.24#cl1), but that is the spirit's roaming, not exile as judgment, and no clause names sin or death.

Luke 11:32 names the Ninevites' repentance only as the ground of their condemning this generation; no clause of the section speaks of mercy or restoration to the repentant or to anyone else, so the stamp is not true of this section.

The section declares that the Queen of the South and the men of Nineveh will condemn this generation (11:31, 11:32); no clause states that the last are first or the first last, and neither Luke 11:31 nor 11:32 uses that reversal formula.

Luke 11:34 speaks of the eye as the lamp of the body and of the body being full of light or dark, not of law or wisdom instruction; the clauses (Luk.11.34#cl0-cl4) carry a light/eye metaphor, not law or wisdom themes. The stamp does not fit this section.

Luke 11:36 speaks of the whole body being full of light and radiant as when a lamp shines, but no clause mentions spirit, Spirit, or anything spiritual; Luk.11.36#cl0-cl3 concern the body, light, and darkness only, so the stamp is not evidenced here.
The section names prophets and apostles who are killed and persecuted (Luk.11.49#cl2), but no clause speaks of a servant of the Lord who suffers; the stamp's idea is absent.
The section speaks of blood charged to this generation (Luk.11.50#cl0) and of tombs of the prophets (Luk.11.47#cl1), not of a covenant made, kept or broken; no clause carries the idea.

The section's drift is generous giving to the needy and to those who ask, but no clause names mercy or restoration; the giving is of loaves, of 'as much as he needs', of good gifts and of the Holy Spirit.
The section is addressed to disciples and speaks of 'your Father in heaven' and those who ask Him, so it concerns God's people as a whole, but no clause names a people, a nation or a community.

Luke 12:1-3 speaks of hypocrisy, hiddenness and disclosure, not of sin as exile or death; the only candidate is the leaven of the Pharisees named hypocrisy (Luk.12.1#cl4-5), which is a warning against a teaching/disposition, not exile or death. No clause carries sin_exile_death.
Nothing in Luke 12:13-21 presents Jesus or anyone as a prophet; the cited verse 12:14 names only 'judge or executor'.
No king or royal figure appears in the section; 12:14 names 'judge or executor', not a king.
No servant/master role is named in the section (the rich man's workers are not mentioned, only his own reasoning).
No father is named; the only family relation is 'my brother' (12:13), which is a brother, not a father.
No witnessing role or testimony appears in the section.
The rich man feasts only with his own soul in 12:19 ('Eat, drink, and be merry'); no host receiving guests is named.
No guest is named; 12:19 addresses only 'my soul'.
The section ends in the rich man's death and the warning 'This is how it will be'; no mercy or restoration is spoken of.
no servant, slave or master is spoken of; the disciples are addressed as a 'little flock' with God as Father, not as servants
the promise of the kingdom is given to the little flock; covenant-making and its parties are not spoken of here
'do not be afraid' is comfort, not a covenant of peace being made
no one is appointed or sent to a task; selling possessions and giving alms is almsgiving, not commissioning
selling possessions and giving alms is not a sacrifice offered to God; no victim, altar or cultic act appears
'treasure in heaven' is a store laid up with God, not a new heavens and new earth
the passage speaks of an unfailing treasure in heaven, not of creation renewed; no clause carries the idea
the cited verse (12:34) is about where treasure and heart are; nothing in the section speaks of redemption or of Christ redeeming
No bridegroom appears in Luke 12:35-48: 12:36 has a master returning from wedding feasts (γάμοι), not a νυμφίος, and nothing in the clauses describes a bridegroom role.
The cited verse 12:42 calls the man κύριος and οἰκονόμος with servants under him; no king or kingship is spoken of in these clauses.

12:40 speaks of the Son of Man coming in judgment at an unexpected hour; nothing in these clauses speaks of ransom, redemption or Christ's saving work - the servants are rewarded or beaten according to their conduct.
The cited verse 12:37 speaks of the master serving his watching servants; no clause in the section speaks of new creation, resurrection or renewal of the world.

Luke 12:6 names God only as the one by whom the sparrows are 'not forgotten' (Luk.12.6#cl1); the Berean text of this section never uses father language or any paternal role word, so no clause carries the stamp.

Luke 12:49 speaks of casting fire on the earth and wishing it were kindled, not of a judgment event; the section's fire is real fire imagery of division (12:51-53), and no clause here names or depicts a judgment.
No clause here presents Jesus as a warrior; the fire of 12:49 is cast on the earth and the conflict of 12:52-53 is within households, with no military role, arms or battle attributed to him.
The section speaks of households and family division, not of a people of God; nothing in these verses characterises the community of God, so the idea is at most the section's general background.
No clause names or addresses a prophet; the crowd is addressed about reading weather signs and the time, not about prophets or prophecy.
The section's drift is Jesus' authoritative word about discerning the time, but no clause itself speaks of a prophetic word.
The addressees are disciples ('you', 'everyone who confesses Me'), but no clause in this section names or describes them as God's people; it is the section's general setting, not a stated idea.
The section speaks of death (the tower killed them) and of sin, but there is no exile: no clause carries removal from the land. The stamp bundles sin, exile and death, and exile is absent here.

Nothing in the section offers mercy or restoration. The only clauses about the fate of the hearers are the two warnings that unless they repent they will all perish (Luk.13.3#cl1-2, Luk.13.5#cl0-1); the passage names no mercy, forgiveness, or restoration.
Nothing in the section presents the woman as a wisdom figure or teacher; her only named role is 'daughter of Abraham' (13:16), a covenant, not a wisdom, designation. The stamp misreads the character.
The section's sufferer is the woman, and the figure who acts is Jesus as healer and Sabbath-debater; no servant of the Lord bearing suffering is in view. The stamp does not belong to this section.

No clause names a kingdom, a king, or a reign; the section shows Jesus' authority over illness and the Sabbath, which a reader might take as kingdom drift, but no clause speaks it. General, not wrong.
