No clause names or implies a king: Jesus asks what the kingdom is like and compares it to a mustard seed (Luk.13.18#cl1, Luk.13.19#cl0); no human or divine king appears in the section.
No clause mentions a prophet or prophetic speech; the section is Jesus' own comparison of the kingdom to a mustard seed (Luk.13.18#cl1, Luk.13.19#cl0), with no prophet named or implied.

The only kingship language here is 'the kingdom of God' (Luk.13.20#cl0/#cl1), i.e. the kingdom, not a king; no clause names or implies a human or divine king figure, so the role 'king' is not carried by this section.

Nothing in this section is divided or split: the kingdom of God is the thing being likened (Luk.13.20#cl0/#cl1) and the leaven is hidden in the meal until all is leavened (Luk.13.21#cl1-#cl3). Division is the image of the earlier kingdom parables (cf. Luke 11:17), not of this pair.

The section's leaven-permeating-the-meal image (Luk.13.21#cl1-#cl3) is read by many as a picture of the kingdom's pervasive growth, which is the general drift this theme claims, but no clause in the section says new creation, creation, or renewal; the stamp rests on the section as a whole, not on any particular clause.

The section does describe insiders shut out and outsiders brought in (a divided outcome), but no clause speaks of a kingdom or house itself divided; the stamp in its proper sense is not carried by any clause.
The only ruler named is Herod, and he is called 'that fox' (Luk.13.32#cl1), not a king; the quoted 'Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord' (Luk.13.35#cl5) names no king.
The coming in the name of the Lord (Luk.13.35#cl5, citing Ps 118) is Jesus' own coming, and the house left desolate (Luk.13.35#cl0) is a judgment on Jerusalem; neither is the day of the Lord.
The section has a killing threat (Luk.13.31#cl3-4), a prophet perishing (Luk.13.33#cl4) and a refusal (Luk.13.34#cl7) followed by desolation (Luk.13.35#cl0) — no clause makes death the means of life.
The fruit here is literal fruit sought on a fig tree (Luk.13.6#cl3-4, Luk.13.7#cl2-4); no clause speaks of the Spirit or of character.
The tree here is alive and being cultivated, not withered (Luk.13.8#cl2-4); nothing in this section mentions withering.
No clause treats Jesus as a servant who suffers: he is host, healer and questioner here; no suffering, servanthood or Isaiah-servant language appears in this section.

No clause mentions a kingdom, reign or king; 14:5 speaks of a son or an ox in a pit, not of God's rule. A ruler of the Pharisees (Luk.14.1#cl1, 'one of the rulers of the Pharisees') is human, not the kingdom.
No servant or slave appears anywhere in the section; the roles named are father, mother, wife, children, brothers, sisters, king, builder, and the disciples themselves.
A bride is not mentioned or implied; the only marital term is 'wife' in Luke 14:26, and wife is a distinct role from bride.
No bridegroom or wedding appears; the nearest wedding language elsewhere in Luke 14 (the parable's supper) is not in this section.
Nothing in the section is sworn, vowed, or sealed by an oath; the peace delegation in Luke 14:32 asks terms rather than swearing anything.
The word 'kingdom' never occurs in Luke 14:25-33; 'king' in 14:31 is a parable figure, and the section's drift is about the cost of discipleship rather than the kingdom itself.

No clause states redemption, atonement, or purchase; the section's demands (hating family, carrying the cross, giving up possessions) presuppose discipleship to Christ but do not themselves speak of redemption.
The crowds travelling with Jesus in Luke 14:25 and the disciples addressed are the only candidate referents, but no clause speaks of a people belonging to God as such.
Nothing is judged, condemned, or sentenced in the section; the ridicule in Luke 14:29-30 is human mockery, not divine judgment, and the king's reckoning in 14:31 is military calculation.

The section's drift is total allegiance to Jesus, and Luke 14:33 states it ("give up everything he has"), but 'promise_faithfulness' names promise/covenant-keeping, which no clause here carries: there is no promise made, received or kept, only the demand of renunciation in Luk.14.25#cl1 / Luk.14.26#cl0 ("does not hate his father and mother..."), Luk.14.27#cl0 ("does not carry his cross and follow Me"), and Luk.14.33#cl0 ("does not give up everything he has"). The closest content is discipleship renunciation, not faithfulness to a promise.

Nothing in Luke 14:25-33 speaks of new creation: no clause mentions creation, renewal, resurrection or a new order. The clauses are about the conditions of discipleship (Luk.14.25#cl1, Luk.14.26#cl0, Luk.14.27#cl0, Luk.14.33#cl0) and two parables about counting the cost (Luk.14.28#cl1, Luk.14.31#cl0, Luk.14.32#cl3). The mention of "his own life" (Luk.14.26#cl2) is self-renunciation, not creation, and the temple-kind/creation reading would need a clause this section does not contain.
No clause in the section names or depicts a king; the father is a landowner who divides his estate (Luk.15.12#cl3), hires servants and kills a calf, but kingship is nowhere said.

The cited verse (15:9) speaks of the woman's friends and neighbors, and 15:10 of angels, not of a covenant people; the stamp describes the parable's wider drift (the community that rejoices) but no clause here names God's people.
Nothing in the section has anyone testifying, bearing witness, or serving as a witness; 16:8 is about the master commending the manager for shrewdness, not about witness.
No father (pater) is named or implied anywhere in 16:1-13; 16:13 has masters, servant, God and money, not a father.
'Sons of light', 'eternal dwellings' and serving God touch kingdom imagery in the background of 16:8-9 and 16:13, but no clause states a kingdom, a king, or rule.
The section shows no mercy and no restoration: the manager is dismissed (16:2), commended for shrewdness (16:8), and the following sayings are about faithfulness, not restoration.

16:1 is addressed 'to His disciples', but the section says nothing about a people belonging to God; the actors are a rich man, his manager, his debtors and 'the sons of this age/light'. A named addressee is not the same as the theme.

No sin, exile or death is spoken of in these clauses; the closest is 'dishonest/unrighteous' (16:8, 10, 11) used adjectivally of the manager and of wealth, which is not the theme of sin, exile and death.
The section has no redemption, no ransom, and no Christ: 'true riches' (16:11) and 'eternal dwellings' (16:9) are not redemption language, and Jesus speaks here as teacher, not as redeemer.
Luke 16:16 speaks of the Law and the Prophets being proclaimed until John, i.e. the end of the law-prophets period, not of the giving of the Law at Sinai; no clause narrates law-giving.

No clause mentions a covenant, its making, or its parties; the only covenant-adjacent clause is Luk.16.16#cl0 'The law and the prophets [were] until John', which marks the close of the old order, not the institution of a new covenant.
The section's only king-language is the kingdom of God in Luk.16.16#cl1/2, which names God's reign and never a human king as a character; no clause in this section presents a king.

The rich man's sonship is only implied by the address 'Father Abraham' (Luk.16.24#cl2, Luk.16.27#cl2, Luk.16.30#cl1); no clause names him as son or states the relation. General to the passage's Abraham-as-father framing.
Lazarus is a beggar (Gk ptochos) lying at the rich man's gate (Luk.16.20#cl0), not a stranger or sojourner (paroikos/proselytos); no clause speaks of sojourning or foreignness.
No clause in the section speaks of a slave or bondservant; Lazarus is not called a servant (Gk doulos) anywhere in these verses.
No clause presents anyone as a servant; Lazarus is asked to be sent as a messenger (Luk.16.24#cl4, Luk.16.27#cl2) but is never called or described as a servant.
The section has no corporate or national character; all parties are named individuals (a rich man, Lazarus, Abraham).

No clause shows the man humiliated and then vindicated: Luk.17.16#0 is a voluntary act of thanksgiving, not humiliation, and the lepers' physical cleansing (Luk.17.14#6) is not vindication of a humiliated person; the stamp reads a pattern into the passage that no clause states.
No clause in this section speaks of a covenant, its institution, or its blood; v.25 speaks only of the Son of Man's suffering and rejection.
The 'marrying and being given in marriage' of v.27 is ordinary life in Noah's day, not a bridegroom figure; no bridegroom language appears in the section.
The section concerns the unseen coming of the kingdom and the day of the Son of Man; no clause has anyone testifying or bearing witness.
Sodom's destruction in v.29 is judgment on a city, not a collective character of the nations acting in the narrative.
No clause draws a Moses parallel; v.25's suffering and rejection does not evoke Moses in this section.
No Davidic language or David parallel appears; the Son of Man in v.24 is not presented as a new David here.
No clause speaks of Israel reconstituted or restored; the section addresses the kingdom's coming and the day of the Son of Man.
The Noah comparison in v.26 is about the days being like Noah's, not about Adam or a new Adam.
No servant figure or servant language; v.25 states suffering and rejection without servant imagery.
The day of the Son of Man (v.24, v.30) carries judgment in the Noah and Lot comparisons, but no clause names the Son of Man as judge or depicts a judgment seat.
v.21's 'in your midst' speaks of the kingdom's presence, not of a kingdom divided against itself.
No clause mentions rising from the dead; the section moves from suffering (v.25) to the day of the Son of Man (v.24, v.30) without resurrection language.
No clause speaks of ascending or being taken up to heaven.
No books, records, or opening of books appear; v.34's 'taken and left' is a separation, not a book judgment.

The only marital words in the section are the ordinary daily-life activity of Noah's contemporaries ('marrying and being given in marriage', Luk.17.27#cl3/#cl4), which is cited as the very thing people were doing when judgment fell — not a messianic marriage supper or wedding feast.
Nothing here is divided into or counted by sevens; Luk.17.24 speaks of lightning shining across the whole sky, not of a schema of sevens.
Luk.17.25 speaks of the Son of Man suffering and being rejected; there is no atonement ritual, high priest, or Day-of-Atonement imagery anywhere in the section.
Luk.17.25 says He must suffer and be rejected; the clause speaks of rejection and suffering, not of a sacrifice offered.
No Passover lamb, meal, or festival appears; Luk.17.25 is a passion-and-rejection logion, not Passover material.
Luk.17.29 describes fire and sulfur rained from heaven on Sodom, not deportation of a people from their land. I could not determine any clause in this section that speaks of exile.
No clause here speaks of captivity or of people taken into captivity; Luk.17.29 is destruction, not captivity.
The section never mentions the temple, its destruction, or its stones; Luk.17.29 concerns Sodom.
No besieging army, encirclement, or city under siege is in view; the destruction in Luk.17.29 comes from heaven, not from besiegers.
There is no 'woe' (ouai) and no denunciation addressed to a party in this section; Luk.17.25 states necessity ('must suffer'), not woe.
No indictment, summons, or lawsuit speech form is present; Luk.17.25 is a statement of what must happen to the Son of Man.
Nothing in Luk.17.22 or the section speaks of return to the land or of exiles coming back; the clause is about longing to see a day and not seeing it.

No clause in this section is itself a prophetic oracle introduced as the word of the LORD; the whole speech is prophetic teaching about the days of the Son of Man and the coming day of revelation, which is why no particular clause can be pointed at.
Luk.17.24 gives the lightning as the model for the Son of Man's day; there is no renewal or making-new of the world, sky, or creation anywhere in the section.

Luk.17.33 speaks of losing one's life and so preserving it, which is a paradox of surrender and preservation rather than an act of mercy restoring the lost; I am not sure the stamp is wrong, but I cannot name a clause that carries mercy or restoration.
The addressees are the Pharisees and then the disciples (Luk.17.20#cl1, Luk.17.22#cl0), but no clause in this section describes a people belonging to God, being gathered, or being named as His.
The Noah and Lot comparisons (Luk.17.26#cl0, Luk.17.28#cl0) presuppose that what God announced then happened exactly so, but no clause in this section states God's promise or His faithfulness to it.
Nothing in 17:5-10 speaks of the kingdom; the passage concerns faith, a servant's duty and unworthiness, with no clause naming or implying God's reign.
The addressees are the apostles/disciples, but no clause itself states the idea of God's people.
No clause in this section speaks of mercy or restoration; the servant is not shown mercy but simply does his duty, and the mulberry tree's uprooting is not restoration.
The section addresses the Lord and speaks of faith and service but never of being united with Christ; no clause carries the idea.

The section's stated theme is persistent prayer and God's justice, not mercy or restoration: the judge acts not from mercy but 'because this widow keeps pestering me' (18:5), and the outcome is 'avenge/execute justice,' not restoration. The only near-miss is 8:2-3, but 'will He find faith' is about faith at the coming, not restoration. No clause carries mercy_restoration.

The word 'kingdom' appears (Luk.18.16#cl5, Luk.18.17#cl3) and God is its possessor, but no clause presents God as a king acting or being addressed; 'kingdom' is the only footing and it is not read as a character role here.

No clause calls Jesus a prophet or has him speak a prophet's oracle; the nearest is Luk.18.16#cl1/Luk.18.17#cl0 where he speaks, but that is a command/declaration about the kingdom, not prophetic role.
No clause in the section speaks of a servant or service.
No clause speaks of sonship; 'children' in Luk.18.16#cl3 and 'child' in Luk.18.17#cl4 are children of the people, not sonship language.
God appears only as possessor of the kingdom (Luk.18.16#cl5, Luk.18.17#cl3), never as father, and no clause has anyone addressing or being addressed as father.
No clause mentions nations, gentiles or peoples as an agent; the agents here are people bringing infants (Luk.18.15#cl0), the disciples (Luk.18.15#cl2) and Jesus (Luk.18.16#cl0).
'Blessed are ...' This section has no beatitude: Jesus commands (Luk.18.16#cl2, Luk.18.16#cl4) and declares (Luk.18.17#cl0, Luk.18.17#cl3), with no blessing formula.
The kingdom appears (Luk.18.16#cl5, Luk.18.17#cl3), but nothing is divided or split; 'do not hinder them' (Luk.18.16#cl4) is not a division of a kingdom.

No covenant is made, named or referred to in any clause; the kingdom is spoken of as belonging to such as these (Luk.18.16#cl5) and as something to receive/enter (Luk.18.17#cl3), without covenant language.
No clause mentions creation or a covenant with it.

The people brought the infants 'for Him to place His hands on them' (Luk.18.15#cl1, 'them He might touch'), but the text of the clause says touch, not bless, and no clause words a blessing or blessed condition. If blessing is read into the touch it is inference, not what the clause says.
The purpose clause Luk.18.15#cl1 says only 'them He might touch', with no sickness, cure or healing in any clause; the action is a touch on infants.
Jesus permits the children to come and forbids hindering them (Luk.18.16#cl2, Luk.18.16#cl4); he gives no task, office or charge to anyone, and no one is sent out.
No one is sent in any clause; 'come to Me' (Luk.18.16#cl3) is movement toward Jesus, not a sending.
No clause mentions baptism or nations.

There is speech of the kingdom belonging to such as these (Luk.18.16#cl5) and of entering it (Luk.18.17#cl0), but no clause gives a divine promise or 'I will' oracle; the clauses are an imperative and a condition.
'Truly I tell you' (Luk.18.17#cl0, Luk.18.17#cl1) is an asseveration, but no clause swears an oath, invokes a witness, or uses curse/self-imprecation.
No clause has any covenant-making action; the only physical action is a touch (Luk.18.15#cl1).
No clause mentions food, eating or a table; the setting is people bringing infants (Luk.18.15#cl0).
No clause brings an accusation, charge or suit; the rebuke in Luk.18.15#cl2 is the disciples silencing the parents and is immediately overruled (Luk.18.16#cl4), not a lawsuit speech.

There is no 'woe' and no clause pronouncing judgment on anyone; the negative clauses are a prohibition ('not do forbid them', Luk.18.16#cl4) and a condition ('whoever not shall receive', Luk.18.17#cl3).
Luk.18.17#cl0/'#cl3 states a condition for not entering the kingdom, but no clause depicts a judgment: no judge, verdict, accused or sentence.
No clause has a contest, dispute or trial proceeding; the only conflict is the disciples rebuking (Luk.18.15#cl2), resolved by Jesus' command in Luk.18.16#cl4.

Luk.18.15#cl2 ('the disciples were rebuking them') is a rebuke of those bringing the infants, not persecution; no clause has hostility, harm or suffering for faith, and Jesus stops the rebuke (Luk.18.16#cl4).
No clause has a council, assembly in deliberation, or a process of discerning a matter; the disciples' rebuke in Luk.18.15#cl2 is not deliberation and no decision procedure appears.

No clause here concerns bearing testimony or being a witness; the section is about bringing infants, rebuking, and receiving the kingdom like a child. The disciples 'seeing' (Luk.18.15#cl2/cl3) is not witness-bearing.
No clause speaks of watching over or warning on a wall or watch; the disciples' rebuke (Luk.18.15#cl2) is not a watchman's vigilance over a city.
No clause has battle, weapon or warfare language.
No clause speaks of building, foundation, house or construction.
No clause mentions a vineyard, vine or its tending.
No clause mentions fishing, nets, boats or fish.
Only 'enter' in Luk.18.17#cl2/cl3 ('shall enter into it'), which is entering the kingdom, not a gatekeeper's office of opening or guarding a gate.
No clause has a table, meal, banquet or welcoming-a-guest scene.
The children are 'brought' (Luk.18.15#cl0) and 'come' (Luk.18.16#cl0/cl2/cl3), but no clause casts anyone as a guest at a table or feast.
No clause speaks of journey, road, Jerusalem pilgrimage or sojourning; 'bring/come' here is to Jesus, not a pilgrim route.
No clause speaks of a surviving remainder of Israel; 'the such' (Luk.18.16#cl5) is a class of people (the childlike), and 'whoever' (Luk.18.17#cl3) is universal, not a remnant.
No clause presents a woman figure personifying wisdom; 'the little children' (Luk.18.16#cl2) are literal children.
No clause presents a woman figure personifying folly.
No clause depicts a ruler as a beast or in Daniel's beast imagery.
The section exalts the little children over the rebuking disciples, but no single clause states a reversal of first and last; it is only the drift of the passage.
The passage has a 'ruler' (Luke 18:18) but no clause carries kingship; 'kingdom of God' in Luk.18.24#cl2 is God's reign, not the ruler's role.
No clause names or describes a prophet; Jesus is addressed as 'Good Teacher' (Luk.18.18#cl2) and nothing in the section speaks of prophecy.
No clause speaks of servanthood or a servant; the ruler is 'a certain ruler' (Luk.18.18#cl0) and Peter's leaving all (Luk.18.28#cl1-2) is not service language.
Nothing about a divided kingdom; the kingdom language is 'enter the kingdom of God' (Luk.18.24#cl2, Luk.18.25#cl2), which is entry, not division.
No clause speaks of judging or a judge; the question 'Who then can be saved?' (Luk.18.26#cl2) is about salvation, not judgment.
No clause mentions a covenant, new or old; Luk.18.29#cl4 is 'for the sake of the kingdom of God', which is not covenant language.
No clause speaks of reversal of first and last; the rich/ruler failing (Luk.18.23#cl0, Luk.18.24#cl2) is a warning, not the last-becoming-first idea.

The section never calls anyone a servant; Luke 18:32 speaks of the Son of Man being delivered to the Gentiles, mocked, insulted and spit upon, with no servant wording or servant figure anywhere in the clauses.
The sequence kill then rise again (Luk.18.33#cl0 then cl2) is the section's drift, but no single clause states that the death produces the life.
Luke 18:34 says only that the disciples did not understand; no clause in this section speaks of sin or of exile.
Nothing in the section speaks of the Servant's suffering, vicarious bearing, or Isaiah 53 language; the healing is by Jesus' word and the man's faith (Luk.18.42), not by Jesus' suffering.
Deliverance here is physical sight for one man; no purchase, ransom, sin or cross language appears in the section, and 'Christ' is never named.
The cited verse, Luke 18:39, is the crowd rebuking the blind man and his louder cry; no reversal of rank or order is stated or implied there or elsewhere in the section.
No contest, conflict or defeat occurs; a helpless man is healed and a crowd praises God, which is not weakness overcoming strength.
There is no death in the section; the movement is blindness to sight, not death to life, and the healing is not framed as issuing from a death.

No judge appears in the section: the two men are a Pharisee and a tax collector, and God is addressed in prayer ('God, I thank You', 'God, have mercy on me') but never as judge; the cited verse Luke 18:9 speaks only of those 'who trusted in their own righteousness and viewed others with contempt'.
The cited verse names only 'a Pharisee and the other a tax collector'; no priest is mentioned anywhere in the section, and going up to the temple to pray does not make either man a priest.

No sacrifice is offered or described; the tax collector's act is 'he beat his breast' with the plea 'God, have mercy on me, a sinner' (Luk.18.13#cl3, #cl5), and the Pharisee's acts in the temple are prayer, fasting and tithing, not sacrifice.
The only sin language is the tax collector's self-designation 'a sinner' in his plea for mercy; there is no exile, no death and no curse in the section.

The section describes the Son of Man coming to seek and save (Luk.19.10#cl0-1), which is service in the general sense, but no clause names a servant or servant role; Jesus is named as Son of Man, not as servant. General drift only, unless the stamp means the servant-Saviour theme rather than a servant role, which I cannot settle from the stamp alone.

I could not determine a clause that carries this. Jesus is a guest received into a house (Luk.19.5#cl5-6; Luk.19.6#cl2), not a stranger or sojourner, and the crowd's complaint is over his lodging with a sinner, not over his being an outsider; there is no language of sojourning anywhere in the section. If the stamp is meant to cover the guest-as-outsider idea, Luk.19.7#cl3 would be the nearest clause, but a guest is not a sojourner, so I mark it unsure rather than pinning it.

No one is sick and no one is healed in this section. The cited verse (19:9) speaks of salvation coming to the house and sonship of Abraham, which is not healing; the only lack named in the section is blind-stature in the crowd (Luk.19.3#cl3), not a sickness. If the stamp is meant only loosely for salvation as restoration, it is still not healing.

I could not determine a clause that carries this. The cited verse (19:5) has Jesus claiming the right to stay at a house; nothing in it or in the section says kingdom, king, reign or rule, and the section does not, unlike the parable that follows it, mention the kingdom. If the stamp is read as the kingdom arriving with Jesus' presence the drift might cover the whole section, but then no clause in particular is the pin.

The promise to Abraham lies behind "son of Abraham" (Luk.19.9#cl2) and God's seeking of the lost is faithful action (Luk.19.10#cl1), but no clause in this section states a promise or God's faithfulness, so this is the section's general drift and not any clause in particular.

The section's drift — rejected would-be king becomes the returning king who settles accounts and puts enemies down — fits this reversal, but no clause in particular stages humiliation followed by vindication; Luke 19:12 and 19:15 name the nobleman's departure to receive kingship and his return with the kingdom, not a suffering-then-vindication sequence.
No exile: the nobleman leaves voluntarily to a distant country to receive a kingdom (Luk.19.12#cl1), and the enslaved-forced-away-and-restored pattern this stamp names is not present.
Nothing here speaks of death producing life; the cited verse (19:16) is about a mina earning ten more minas, i.e. profit through trading, and no clause mentions death or life.
The only candidate words are the Pharisees' address 'Teacher'; nothing in the section presents Jesus as a prophet speaking God's word.
The acclamation bears on the section's drift, but no clause states redemption or names Christ as redeemer.
Luke 19:39 is an objection to the disciples' praise, not a judgment; no clause speaks of judgment.
The peace-and-glory acclamation fits the section's tone generally, but no clause carries mercy or restoration.
No temple, and no divine presence language in the clauses; the stamp rests only on general drift.
A deliverance reading of the King's coming is an inference; no clause states rescue or deliverance.
The King is hailed in triumph; no clause here speaks of suffering or servant service.
The stones here cry out if the disciples are silent; nothing speaks of a rejected stone becoming the cornerstone.
The King's public welcome reads as vindication, but no clause here names humiliation or its reversal.
No reversal of rank or order in this section; the royal acclamation is not that reversal.
No clause identifies Jesus as a prophet; he speaks of the visitation of God, but no clause names the role.
The section pronounces coming destruction and hidden peace; no clause offers mercy or restoration.

The temple is entered (Luk.19.45#cl1) and called a house of prayer made into a den of robbers (Luk.19.46#cl2, Luk.19.46#cl3), but no clause speaks of its destruction; the cited verse 19:45 has nothing about the temple being destroyed.
Jesus is shown teaching (Luk.19.47#cl0) and quoting scripture (Luk.19.46#cl1), but no clause names or describes a prophet; the cited verse 19:47 speaks only of teaching and of the plot to kill Him.
The section shows sin in the temple trade (Luk.19.45#cl2) and a death plot (Luk.19.47#cl1), but sin-exile-death as a theme is not stated by any clause in particular.
The plot to destroy Him (Luk.19.47#cl1) is opposition to Jesus, not the servant who suffers; no clause carries the servant-of-the-Lord idea.
The cited verse 19:48 says the people hung on His words (Luk.19.48#cl2); nothing in the section speaks of mercy or restoration.

An annunciation is an announcement of a birth to come (as in Luke 1:26-38); in 2:1-7 no angel or messenger announces anything - the only proclamation is Caesar's census decree, and the birth itself happens without announcement.
No clause contains a prophetic utterance; the section's fulfilment-of-Scripture drift is carried by the whole narrative, not by any clause in particular.
Nothing in the clauses names a promise or its keeping; only the general shape of the Davidic birth in Bethlehem can be read that way.
No rescue, release or salvation is spoken of; the section reports a census and a birth.
No clause speaks of mercy, pity, or restoring what was lost.
No temple, sanctuary, or divine presence appears in these clauses.
The child is wrapped and laid in a manger, but nothing here speaks of suffering, bearing sin, or servant service.
No purchase, ransom, or redemption language; the census 'registration' is Roman, not redemptive.
Nothing in the clauses speaks of creation, new birth, or renewal.
No reversal of rank or order is stated; the clauses give no 'first' and 'last' at all.
No conflict and no defeat; the infant's weakness is described, but nothing is overcome by it.
No death is spoken of; the clause set is a birth without any death on which to pattern it.
No famine, hunger, or provision of food; the manger holds the child, not food.
No priest appears in this section; the actors are the child's parents and the angel, and the offerings are made by the parents, not a priest.
The section involves purification and presentation by the parents, with no priestly figure or priestly office named.
No clause presents Simeon as a priest: no priesthood, no offering or cultic act by him; he only takes the child in his arms and blesses God (Luk.2.28).

The consolidation/restoration of Israel is the drift of the section (consolation of Israel, falling and rising up in Israel), but no clause states a reconstituted people; it is carried only by words inside larger clauses.
No clause presents the Servant of Isaiah as suffering; the only sword pierces Mary's soul (Luk.2.35#cl0), which is her own grief and not the child's or a servant's suffering.
Anna is called a prophetess, not a priest; the temple clause describes her worship ('serving night and day'), not priestly office, and no priest is named in the section.
The section shows an old woman faithful in temple worship awaiting redemption, but no clause states a promise or God's faithfulness; the stamp fits only the drift.

Nothing in this section speaks of the Son taking flesh or being born; the birth is past and unmentioned. The clauses concern the family's return to Nazareth and the Child's growth. The reader's citation of Luke 2:39 looks misplaced (incarnation is narrated in Luke 2:1-20).
The stamp is a general reading of the section's place in Luke's narrative (Jesus recapitulating Israel's story); no clause in particular says it.
No clause in this section mentions the Spirit. 'Filled with wisdom' (Luk.2.40#cl2) is wisdom, not the Spirit; the Spirit's filling of Jesus belongs to Luke 3:22 and 4:1.
No clause here speaks of rule, throne or kingdom; the section narrates a return to Nazareth and the Child's growth only.

Nothing in the section names Moses, the law, or an Exodus/legislator typology; the temple scene of 2:46 ("sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions") shows Jesus as a twelve-year-old pupil/participant in the teachers' discussion, which does not itself carry the idea.

The section's general portent is that this boy is extraordinary ("all who heard Him were astounded at His understanding and His answers"), but no clause here presents Him as a prophet speaking God's word.

The cited verse, Luke 2:51 ("He went down to Nazareth with them and was obedient to them"), describes subjection and obedience, the opposite of kingship; no clause in the section gives Him royal role or rule.
The temple appears in 2:46 only as the place where the boy is found among the teachers ("they found Him in the temple courts"); no clause speaks of its destruction, ruin or loss.

The cited verse, 2:49 ("Why were you looking for Me? ... I had to be in My Father's house?"), is Jesus' own statement about himself, not a prophetic oracle or the fulfilment of one; the section contains no prophecy or scripture citation.

The section's drift (the boy sought and found in the temple, then growing in wisdom and favour) fits a low-to-high arc, but no clause states a humiliation followed by vindication; note 2:51 moves downward to Nazareth and subjection.
Nothing in this section speaks of a new creation; Luke 2:14 gives glory and peace, not creation language.
No clause names the kingdom, a king, or rule; the question of authority is the section's subject but that is not the stamp's idea.
No clause states or implies a judgment: stoning is a threatened mob action (Luk.20.6#cl0), not divine judgment, and unbelief is lamented, not adjudicated.

The only kingship language is Caesar as the emperor to whom tax is owed; no clause has Jesus or anyone else as king: the word used is Caesar/denarius, not king. Luke 20:21's cited clause speaks of Jesus as 'Teacher', not king.

No clause calls or treats Jesus as a prophet speaking God's word; the spies' flattery names Him 'Teacher' and says 'You speak and teach correctly' (Luk.20.21#cl4), which is teacher language, not prophet.
No clause here has anyone bearing testimony or being a witness; the section's business is a trap question, not testimony.
There is no sentencing or act of judging here; the only judgment-adjacent thing is Caesar's 'rule and authority of the governor' (Luk.20.20#cl5), a threat of handing over, not a judgment event.
No people or nation is presented as an acting character; 'the people' (Luk.20.19#cl2; Luk.20.26#cl0) are the crowd whose fear restrains the leaders, and Caesar is a ruler, not a nation.
No clause has a prophetic utterance; the quoted speech is the spies' flattery and question (Luk.20.21, 20.22) and Jesus' teaching answer (Luk.20.25), not prophecy or fulfilment.
Nothing here speaks of sin, exile or death; the section is a controversy over tax and authority.
No clause shows mercy or restoration; the opponents' amazement and silence (Luk.20.26#cl2) is not restoration.
No clause speaks of Christ redeeming anything; the cited verse's clause is a command about tribute and God's due, not redemption.
No clause mentions Christ's redemptive work; the passage concerns resurrection, marriage and the God of the living.
Nothing in these clauses speaks of union with Christ; being 'sons of God' in v.36 is grounded in resurrection, not in Christ-mysticism.

The Davidic covenant is never named or alluded to in this section; the text only quotes Ps 110 to argue the Christ is David's Lord, not David's son, and no covenant, oath or promise to David is stated or cited.

Nothing in Luke 20:41-44 speaks of a rejected stone or a cornerstone; the cited verse is Ps 110:1 about sitting at the right hand, and 'footstool' is subjection of enemies, not a stone becoming the head.

A woe pronouncement is a first- or second-person denunciation with an explicit 'woe' (Greek ouai); here Jesus addresses His disciples with 'Beware' (Luke 20:45-46) and speaks of the scribes in the third person. No clause contains a woe.
The section presupposes an audience of disciples and 'all the people' (Luke 20:45) but no clause states anything about the people of God as such.
the section's dying is killing by tenants and the owner's judgment (Luk.20.14-16), not sin-exile-death as a theme; no clause speaks of sin, exile or death as the stamp means them
no clause in this section states redemption; the son's death (Luk.20.15) is narrated as an act of the tenants, not as redemptive in the clauses themselves
Nothing here is law or wisdom instruction: the passage is a narrative of Jesus watching and then a pronouncement about proportional giving. No clause states or teaches a maxim about Torah or wisdom.

The section's whole subject is gifts cast into the treasury (cl0, cl2, Luk.21.4#cl0), a freewill/charity offering rather than a sacrifice proper — no animal, altar, priest or atoning rite is mentioned, so no single clause names a sacrifice; the stamp is the drift of a giving section.
No death or dying and no life coming from it: the widow gives 'all she had to live on' (Luk.21.4#cl2), which is loss of livelihood, not death yielding life.

The section's suffering is that of the disciples (seized, persecuted, betrayed, hated, put to death) and of the general populace (famines, pestilences, earthquakes); it never speaks of the Servant of Isaiah 53. The only near-match is the collective hated-by-all clause (Luke 21:17), which describes the disciples, not a singular servant.
The section's promise is "I will give you speech and wisdom" (Luke 21:15); no clause mentions the Spirit or the Spirit's agency. The Spirit is absent from Luke 21:10-19 in this text.

Nothing in the four verses is a battle: the conflict is cosmic and inward (nations bewildered, men fainting from fear), with no combatants, armies or warfare language, and the one who acts is the powers of the heavens being shaken.
No rising of the dead is spoken of: verse 28 speaks of the disciples' redemption drawing near, not of resurrection, and no clause mentions resurrection or the dead.

This section never says the sun is darkened; the sun appears only as the location of signs ('signs in the sun', Luk.21.25#cl1). The darkening belongs to the parallel material in Luke 21:29-31's synoptic counterpart (cf. Luke 23:45; the Mk/Mt parallels), not to these verses.
The stars are named only as the location of signs ('signs in the sun and moon and stars', Luk.21.25#cl1); no clause says the stars fall.

The only redemption language is 'draws near the redemption of you' (Luk.21.28#cl5), which names the disciples' redemption without naming Christ; the Son appears in verse 27 only as the coming Son of Man. Calling it redemption in Christ imports a link the clauses do not state — at most a possible implication, not something a clause here says.

The section speaks of 'these things coming to pass' and the nearness of the kingdom of God (Luk.21.31), but no clause names or depicts the day of the Lord — no coming of the Lord, no day, no judgment; it is a parable about reading signs (the fig tree) and about the kingdom's nearness.
Luke 21:33 mentions 'Heaven and earth will pass away' only as a contrast to the permanence of Jesus' words; it does not speak of new heavens and a new earth being made.
Luke 21:33 contrasts the passing away of heaven and earth with the permanence of Jesus' words; nothing speaks of a new creation.
The temple clauses (Luk.21.37#cl0, Luk.21.38#cl1) describe Jesus teaching and the people coming to hear him, not any priest or priestly act; temple setting alone is not the priest role.

Jesus speaks prophetically here (21:6, 21:8, 21:9 are all his predictions), but no clause in this section names, gives or describes the role of prophet; the disciples address him as 'Teacher' (Luk.21.7#cl2), not 'prophet'. So the stamp is the section's drift, carried by no particular clause.

The section has the temple's stones thrown down (Luk.21.6#cl2, cl3) but no clause speaks of the temple being defiled, profaned or desecrated. Destruction is not desecration, and the listing of 'consecrated gifts' (Luk.21.5#cl1) is praise of its adornment, not defilement.

No clause in this section mentions sun, moon, stars, heavens or earth shaking; the only collapse is of the temple's stones (Luk.21.6#cl2, cl3), which is not cosmic. The cosmic signs in this discourse come later in the chapter, outside the section.
No clause here reports a prophetic word spoken or fulfilled: the Feast's approach and the leaders' plot are narrated, not presented as prophecy.
The verses name no sin, exile or death as an idea, only a plot to kill; the stamp's complex of themes is not carried by any clause.
Nothing here judges anyone; the leaders' intention to kill is not a judgment, and no clause states an act of judgment.
No clause in the section carries a servant figure or servant language; the cited verse (Luk.22.22) speaks of the Son of Man and the betrayer, not a servant. The idea is imported from Isaiah.
Nothing in these clauses names David, a son of David, or a Davidic figure; the kingdom is given by the Father, with no Davidic language.
No covenant is made, cited or mentioned; 22:29 speaks only of bestowing/appointing a kingdom, not of a covenant with David.
The money in Luke 22:5 is a price paid to Judas for the betrayal; no clause in the section speaks of a slave, of serving, or of being owned, and the stamp is not carried by this text.
The cup here is the cup of suffering that Jesus asks to be taken from Him (Luk.22.42#cl1), not the covenant cup of Luke 22:20; nothing in this section names a covenant.
No servant language or figure appears; 'the will of Me but of You be done' (Luk.22.42#cl4) is obedience, not a servant stamp the text states.
The angel appears to strengthen Him (Luk.22.43#cl1), not to testify; no witnessing or testimony is expressed.
There is no battle, weapon, or fighting; the struggle is prayer and agony (Luk.22.44#cl0).
No sacrifice is performed or described; the sweat like drops of blood (Luk.22.44#cl2) is agony, not an offering.
No Passover meal, lamb, or festival reference occurs in these verses.
No scapegoat or sending-away of a victim; the cup is asked to be taken away from Him (Luk.22.42#cl1), which is not a scapegoat rite.
The crucifixion is not narrated here; the blood-like sweat (Luk.22.44#cl2) is not a crucifixion.
No ascent to heaven; the angel comes down from heaven (Luk.22.43#cl0) but Jesus does not ascend.
No persecutors act in this section; the disciples merely sleep (Luk.22.45#cl3).
No mountain, shining face, or heavenly glory; the Mount of Olives (Luk.22.39#cl0) is not the mount of transfiguration.
No water, baptism, or Spirit descent occurs here.

The section is Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane (agony, sweat, sleeping disciples, watchfulness); no clause speaks of a people turning back to God or of repentance, which is what the stamp names. The reader cited Luke 22:44, but 22:44 is anguish and sweat, not repentance.
Nothing in the section speaks of rebuilding anything (a wall, city or house); 22:44, the cited verse, is prayer in agony and sweat like blood.
No clause mentions exile, return, or a scattered people being brought back; the section is confined to the Mount of Olives and the disciples asleep.
No oracle of promise is uttered here; Jesus' words are a prayer to the Father (22:42) and a rebuke to the disciples (22:46), not a divine promise-speech.
"Why are you sleeping?" (22:46) is a rebuke/question, not a "woe" oracle of judgment; no clause pronounces woe on anyone.
No indictment, accusation or covenant charge is brought against a party; the prayer and the rebuke contain no legal complaint.

The actions here (withdrawing, kneeling, praying, sleeping) are literal narrative, not performed signs carrying a further meaning; Jesus' withdrawal is even a literal distancing "about a stone's throw".
No call of a prophet, commissioning or vocational summons occurs in the section.
No clause speaks of captivity, imprisonment or being taken away; the section ends with the disciples still free on the Mount of Olives.
The temple is not mentioned or alluded to in any clause; the cited verse 22:44 is about sweat like drops of blood.
No besieging army, wall or encirclement appears; "about a stone's throw" (22:41) is a distance measure for Jesus' withdrawal, not a siege.
No kingdom, division or rival rule is spoken of; the only divided wills in the section are "not My will, but Yours be done" (22:42), which is submission, not division.
No idol, image or worship of a false god appears in any clause.

No clause names mercy or restoration; the section's only motion toward restoration is the angel strengthening Him (22:43) and the call to pray (22:46), which are acts to keep the disciples from falling rather than restoration of the lost. General drift only.

The Spirit is not mentioned in the section. The reader cited Luke 22:43, but the clause there is about an angel appearing and strengthening Him (Luk.22.43#cl0, cl1); the Berean text has no "Spirit". The nearest thing to spirit is Jesus' own submission of will (22:42) and His earnest prayer (22:44), which are not the Spirit.

Where the section shows weakness it shows weakness being helped, not overcoming: the angel strengthens Him (22:43) and the disciples, exhausted from sorrow, are rebuked (22:45-46). "not My will, but Yours be done" (22:42) is surrender, not a reversal of strong by weak.
No death and no life-giving result is stated. "take this cup from Me" (22:42) and "sweat became like drops of blood" (22:44) point toward suffering and death but no clause says death yields life.

Judas is named 'one of the Twelve' and shown betraying by a kiss (Luk.22.47#cl4/cl5/cl6, Luk.22.48#cl1), but nothing in these clauses speaks of a shepherd, flock or false teaching; the stamp is not carried by this section.
No clause here speaks of testifying, testimony or being a witness; the scene is an arrest and its aftermath. The stamp is not carried by this section.
The section names leaders (chief priests, temple officers, elders) and a crowd, but no clause speaks of God's people as a body; the stamp is not carried here.
No clause in this section speaks of redemption, ransom or purchase; the betrayal (Luk.22.48#cl1) is the act itself, not the redemption it may elsewhere lead to.
Nothing in these clauses speaks of covenant, its making or its breaking; the closest is betrayal by one of the Twelve (Luk.22.48#cl1), which is not a covenant clause.
The section's drift is a hearing/interrogation scene (high priest's house, accusations), but no clause stages a formal trial or contest.
No clause in this section identifies Jesus or anyone as a prophet; the cited verse has the Lord's prediction, not a prophet role.
No clause shows anyone judging or pronouncing judgment; the high priest's house is mentioned only as the place Jesus is taken.
No clause mentions crucifixion, cross, or death by execution; the section ends with Peter weeping, not Jesus being crucified.
Nothing in this section describes the Servant's suffering; Jesus is seized and looked at, but the section's focus is Peter's denial, not the servant's affliction.
The section's drift involves the covenant community's leaders and Peter as one of the disciples, but no clause speaks of the people of God as such.

The section supplies only the humiliation half of the reversal (mockery, beating, blindfolding, blasphemy); no clause here states or implies the vindication side, so the stamp cannot be pinned to a clause.
No clause in Luke 22:63-65 speaks of sin, exile, or death; the section is mockery, beating, blindfolding and blasphemy. The stamp's themes are not present in these clauses.

Nothing in the section speaks of the servant's suffering, vicarious death or bearing of sin; the cited verse (67) is only the question 'If You are the Christ, tell us' and Jesus' refusal to answer, and even the Son of Man saying (69) is exaltation, not suffering.
No clause here speaks of redemption, ransom, blood or deliverance; the section is a trial scene ending in the council's charge, with no saving act or its interpretation present.
Jesus is called 'the Teacher' (Luk.22.11#cl1) or 'the master of the house' (Luk.22.11#cl0), not a prophet; no clause gives anyone the role or words of a prophet.
The section's general drift belongs to the Passover of Israel and Jesus' disciples, but no clause here names a people, a nation or the church as God's own.
The upper room of Luk.22.12#cl0 is a furnished guest room in a house, not the temple, and no clause here speaks of the temple or of God's presence.
No clause in this section quotes or fulfils scripture or contains any prophetic utterance; the speech is accusation, interrogation and verdict.

The section has a prisoner released and a prisoner handed over, but no clause sends anyone out into the wilderness or lays guilt on a scapegoat; the ritual pattern (Lev 16) is not carried by any clause here — the handing over to 'their will' is a legal surrender to a crowd, not a sending-away of guilt.

Pilate acts throughout as the Roman prefect who examines, sentences and releases (cl0 of 23.13, 23.14#cl3, 23.24#cl0), which is the authority of a ruler; but no clause in this section names or addresses anyone as king. The stamp is the section's general drift, carried by the framing figure rather than by a clause.
No clause here describes anyone as a servant, slave or serving; Jesus is the handed-over prisoner, not a servant figure in the wording of this section.

The clauses contain a beating only as Pilate's proposed chastisement ('I will punish Him', 23.16#cl0/#cl1, 23.22#cl4) and the handing over (23.25#cl4); no clause answers the Isaianic servant language (no servant, no bearing of sin, no 'for us'), so the stamp is not carried by a clause in this section.

Nothing in the wording speaks of buying back, ransoming or rescue through Christ; Jesus is the one handed over (23.25#cl4) and Barabbas is the one released (23.18#cl3, 23.25#cl0), which is not redemption language in these clauses.

No clause in this section quotes or cites scripture as fulfilled (contrast the passion narrative's citation formulas elsewhere); the fate of the innocent one at the crowd's demand is scriptural in drift only, so this is general, with nothing specific to point at.

The cited verse (Luke 23:34) is Jesus' prayer of forgiveness and the dividing of His garments; nothing in this section presents Jesus as a servant (no doulos/diakonos language, no servant role or servant song allusion). The stamp is not carried by this section.
The cited verse (Luke 23:43) is the promise of Paradise; the section (Luke 23:26-43) contains no burial, tomb, or interment. No clause speaks to it.

The section narrates the death of Jesus, which Christian reading takes as sacrificial, but no clause here says sacrifice, offering, blood, lamb, or sin-bearing; it is the section's general drift, not carried by any particular clause.

Nothing in the section desecrates the temple: the veil is torn from top to bottom with no human agent, no defiling act, no pollution or profanation. Treating the rending as desecration is a wrong fit.

The section narrates the death of Jesus, and the life that comes from it in Christian reading, but no clause states any production of life; the reversal is the section's drift, not a clause's content.
No clause here says redemption, ransom, or purchase; the death of Jesus is the general ground of the theme but no clause carries it.

Nothing in the section shows mercy granted or restoration: the centurion's words are a verdict on Jesus, the crowd goes home in grief, and the acquaintances stand at a distance. No clause carries the idea.
No clause in the section speaks of sin, exile, or death as the consequence of sin: death appears only as Jesus breathing his last and darkness over the land. The stamp does not fit these clauses.

Nothing in this section speaks of a kingdom or house divided against itself; the cited verse (23:51) is about Joseph waiting for the kingdom of God and not consenting, which is the opposite of division.

This section is the burial preparation, not a sacrifice; Joseph's asking for the body of Jesus (23:52) is a request for a corpse, not an act of sacrifice. No sacrifice is described or offered in these clauses.
Joseph is called a Council member (bouleutes), which is not a priest; nothing in the section identifies him or any figure as a priest, and no priestly act is performed.

The general drift of the section — the dead Jesus treated with care by a sympathetic councillor — resonates with the servant theme, but no clause here states or describes the servant's suffering; it presupposes a death that occurred off-stage.
No clause in this section speaks of life coming from the death; the section is a burial and preparation for rest, with no reversal to life stated or implied.

The women from Galilee who followed Jesus are plausibly the people of God, but no clause names them as such or speaks of a people belonging to God; the stamp names a group the section presupposes rather than asserts.
The burial of Jesus is a step in the redemption story, but no clause in this section states redemption or speaks of it being in Christ; it is background to the section's events.
The section has accusation by the chief priests and scribes, but no clause presents anyone as a witness testifying: the only clause is their 'vehemently accusing Him'.
No clause in this section describes anyone as a servant or in service; the 'troops' and the robe-bearing action are soldiers and mockery, not service.
This section contains the humiliation (mocking, splendid robe) but no vindication clause; the reversal is completed outside this section, so nothing here states the reversal.
union with Christ is not stated by any clause here; Christ's risen life is proclaimed but no clause speaks of believers' union with him
The section only reports the empty tomb ('they did not find His body', Luk.24.23#cl0); no clause in this section depicts a burial.
No healing occurs or is reported anywhere in Luke 24:13-35; the cited verse (v. 23) speaks of angels saying Jesus is alive.
Nothing in this section appoints or sends anyone to a task; v. 33 only reports the disciples returning to Jerusalem.
No servant role or service is spoken of in this section; v. 19 describes Jesus as a prophet 'mighty in deed and word', not as a servant.
No father-son relation appears in Luke 24:13-35; v. 19 mentions Jesus of Nazareth but no sonship.
God is called 'God' in v. 19; no father role or fatherhood language occurs in this section.
No bridegroom imagery or marriage language is present in this section.
No bride imagery or marriage language is present in this section.
Nothing in this section speaks of a firstborn.
No warfare or fighting occurs in this section; 'mighty in deed' (v. 19) is not military.

Nothing here presents anyone as a builder; 'builder' in 24:19 could only be extrapolated from tekton/trade language the text does not use (Jesus is called 'a prophet, mighty in deed and word'), and no clause names a building trade or its practitioner.
No vine, vineyard or gardening language anywhere in the section; 24:19 says 'prophet, powerful in speech and action', not vinedresser.
No fishing, fish, boat or net in the section; 'Jesus of Nazareth' in 24:19 supplies no fishing role.
No gate, door or entry-guarding language; the entry in this section is Jesus going in to stay (24:29) and vanishing from sight (24:31), not a gatekeeper standing at a door.

No gentile or nation appears as an actor here; the actors are the two disciples, Jesus, the chief priests and rulers of Israel (24:20), the women, the Eleven and Simon. Jerusalem's visitors (24:18) are not nations.
The women of 24:22–24 are witnesses ('told us they had seen a vision of angels, who said that Jesus was alive'), not personified Wisdom; no wisdom speech or role is attributed to them.
Nothing in the section treats the women as folly: their report is factual and is then confirmed by the men who went to the tomb (24:24).

Jesus is here called 'a prophet, powerful in speech and action before God and all the people' (24:19) — a true prophet, honoured, not a false one; and the leaders in 24:20 are not accused of false prophecy.

No lawless man is described: the deed of 24:20 is done by 'our chief priests and rulers' of Israel, and the section's own verdict on the events is that the Christ 'had to suffer these things' (24:26), not that lawlessness is personified.
No Adam, first-man or second-man language; 24:19 presents Jesus as 'a prophet, mighty in deed and word', and 24:34 as the risen Lord, neither of which is the Adam typology.

No temple, sanctuary or divine-presence-in-a-place language in the section; the risen Jesus is present on the road and at table (24:15, 24:30, 24:31) and then vanishes from sight, but nothing says he is present as the temple.
The section's general drift includes an inward, spiritual burning of heart, but no clause names or refers to the Spirit; the cited verse Luke 24:32 speaks of the heart burning, not the Spirit.

the Spirit is not named in this section: Luk.24.49#cl0/cl2 speak of 'the promise of My Father' and 'power from on high', which a reader hears as the Spirit, but no clause says 'the Spirit' (contrast Luk.24.37#cl3, where 'spirit' is the disciples' mistaken fear). The stamp holds only as the section's drift.
The disciples are present and worship, but no clause in this section has them testifying or bearing witness to anything.
No clause here speaks of redemption, purchase, or its accomplishment; the section is departure, blessing and worship.
The worshiping group could be read as the community of God's people, but no clause states it as such.
There is a blessing here, but no commission: no clause sends, authorises or assigns the disciples any task.
The kingdom is not named or implied in these clauses; heaven is the place He is carried into, not a kingdom saying.
Nothing in the clauses speaks of creation renewed or made new.

No clause in Luke 3:1-20 narrates Jesus being baptized; 3:16#cl2/cl3 (and 3:16#cl6) speak of John's water baptism and the Coming One's baptism with Spirit and fire, which is John's prediction, not Jesus' baptism, and he is never named here.
No servant figure or servant language appears in these clauses; 3:16#cl4/cl5 (untying the sandals) marks John's unworthiness before a mightier one, not a servant role.
Nothing in 3:16 or elsewhere in the section speaks of a covenant, old or new; 'baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire' is the nearest words, and they name the Spirit, not a covenant.
The fruit in 3:8#cl0 and 3:9#cl1/cl2 is the fruit of repentance and good deeds required by John, not the Pauline fruit of the Spirit; the Spirit is not the source named in these clauses.
'You brood of vipers' (3:7#cl3) rebukes the crowds for their presumption (3:8#cl1) and coming wrath, not for a list of fleshly works; the phrase 'works of the flesh' belongs to Paul, not Luke 3.
Nothing in Luke 3:1-20 speaks of the servant who suffers; John's imprisonment (Luk.3.20#cl0) is John, not the servant, and the reader's citation of 3:20 does not match the stamp.

The section speaks of the mightier One, the Spirit and fire, and the threshing floor, but no clause names a kingdom or reign of God; the stamp describes the section's drift rather than sitting in any one clause.
Abraham as father (Luk.3.8#cl3) and the Lord's way (Luk.3.4#cl3) are covenant material in the section's background, but no clause states a covenant.

Incarnation is the Son's taking of human flesh (conception/birth); no clause here speaks of it. The nearest text (Son, bodily form) asserts sonship and the Spirit's visible descent, not a taking of flesh.
No clause mentions the temple, nor a dwelling place of God's presence. The opened heaven and descending Spirit are a theophany, not a temple presence; the theme is not carried by any clause here.
Nothing in the section speaks of redeeming, saving, sin-bearing or purchase. 'In You I am well pleased' (cl3) is divine favour, not redemption; the stamp is not carried by any clause here.
No clause here names creation or a creation covenant; only 'of Adam' and 'of God'.
General drift of a genealogy, but no clause here states promise or faithfulness.
The genealogy as a whole is Israel's line, but no clause names a people or God's people.
No clause speaks of redemption; only Jesus being about thirty and beginning.
temptation by the devil and the hunger of the forty days are the section's drift toward sin; no single clause names sin, exile or death.
the section has an idolatrous offer (Luk.4.7#cl1) and a temple setting (Luk.4.9#cl1), but no clause places an idol in the holy place.
no clause here speaks of the servant's suffering; the section's hunger (Luk.4.2#cl3) and the devil's departure (Luk.4.13#cl0) are not that.
the devil merely leaves until an opportune time (Luk.4.13#cl0); nothing in the section is a redemption or victory over the devil in Christ.
Nothing in 4:14-15 says rule, throne, kingdom or royal authority; 'in the power of the Spirit' and 'glorified by everyone' are not kingship language in this text.
No slave/service language occurs in either clause of the section.
Jesus' move to Galilee in the Spirit is movement back into his mission field, but no clause states a sending or commissioning act.
No clause records anyone being appointed or charged to a task.
No deed of power is narrated in 4:14-15; the power named is the Spirit's upon him, and the acts named are returning and teaching.
No repentance, turning, or renewal of the people is described; the section reports teaching and acclaim, which is compatible with either.
The word 'kingdom' does not occur in the section, and teaching in synagogues does not in itself assert it here.
No language of the servant's suffering, vicarious bearing or abuse appears in this section; the crowd's violence (Luk.4.29) is an attempt on Jesus by his own townspeople, not the servant's suffering.
Nothing here describes the servant's suffering; the only harm in view is harm to the demon-possessed man that does not happen (Luk.4.35#cl6), and Jesus is not said to suffer.

No clause of this section speaks of the kingdom; the demons' confession 'You are the Son of God' / 'the Christ' (Luk.4.41#cl3, cl7-8) is a messianic title, not a kingdom statement, and nothing here mentions a reign, a king, or the kingdom of God.
The title 'the Christ' (Luk.4.41#cl8) names Jesus but no clause here speaks of redemption, purchase, ransom, forgiveness or salvation; the section's events are healings and exorcisms.

The suffering in this section is the affliction of others (Luk.4.38#cl2, Luk.4.40#cl3), not the Servant's own suffering; Jesus here rebukes fever and demons and heals, and no clause speaks of him being wounded, bearing, or suffering. The 'serve' of Luk.4.39#cl3 is Simon's mother-in-law serving, not the Servant.
The section says 'the kingdom of God' but nowhere names Jesus as king or kingly rule; kingdom_of_God as a theme is present, the character role 'king' is not.

No clause names Israel, the people or a gathered people; the crowds seek Him (4.42#cl3) and the synagogues of Judea (4.44#cl0) imply hearers, but neither clause itself states people_of_god. Distinctly the stamp is only the section's background.

Preaching the kingdom and being sent do not by themselves state redemption, deliverance or a saving act; nothing here speaks of ransoming or salvation. The stamp is read into the section, not said by it.

Luke 5:6 is a catch of fish; nothing in the clause list speaks of rescue or release from anything — no enemy, danger, bondage or death from which anyone is delivered. The stamp is read into the passage, not said by it.
Nothing in the section speaks of purchase, ransom, blood or sin-bearing; 5:10 is an appointment to catch men. The stamp is not in the clauses.

Luk.5.16#cl0 has Jesus withdraw to the wilderness (eremos) to pray; there is no wandering, journey or sojourn in the wilderness in this section, only a place of retreat. The stamp names the Exodus wandering, not the wilderness as such.
No clause in this section mentions not eating; Luk.5.16#cl0 and #cl1 say only that He withdrew and was praying. Fasting is not stated.
Nothing here presents Jesus as the Servant who bears suffering; He is the one who heals another's suffering (Luk.5.13#cl5). The stamp's idea does not appear in this section.
Luk.5.15#cl0 and #cl1 speak of the report spreading and crowds coming to hear and be healed; no reign, king or kingdom is named in this section.

No clause of this section names the Spirit; Luk.5.16#cl1 speaks only of Jesus praying. If the stamp means the Holy Spirit it is wrong here, so I leave the list empty rather than guess the reader's intent.
The section speaks of the Son of Man's authority on earth to forgive sins, not of God's reign or kingdom; no clause names or implies the kingdom.
Nothing in the passage speaks of the servant's suffering or vicarious bearing of sin; the paralytic's healing is in view.
Not directly stated; the closest clauses (Luk.5.32#cl1-2) voice calling and repentance rather than mercy or restoration, so no clause carries the idea as such.
The section names tax collectors and sinners as those Jesus calls and eats with; it does not speak of a people of God, so nothing pins.
The section has Jesus calling sinners to repentance, but no clause states redemption or anything 'in Christ'; unclear whether it belongs.
No clause states or reverses rank/order: 5:32 says 'not ... the righteous, but sinners', which concerns who is called, not first and last.

'the bridegroom will be taken from them' in Luk.5.35#cl2 is the only possible hook, but the text says taken away from them, not that he suffers, is struck, or bears anything; nothing in these clauses carries the suffering-servant idea itself.
The section contains no law, commandment, Torah citation, or wisdom saying; it reports fasting practice and gives a bridegroom saying, so the stamp is not this passage's idea.
Nothing here speaks of mercy, forgiveness, healing or restoration; the nearest note (the bridegroom present) is stated as a reason the guests cannot fast, not as an act of mercy or restoring.
No clause speaks of creation or renewal as such; 'new wine ... new wineskins' is a parable about the new thing Jesus brings, not a clause about new creation.

The imagery of old and new garments may be read as old and new communities, but no clause in the section names a people, a covenant people, or a community; the stamp is inferred from the drift, not stated.

Nothing in these clauses speaks of redemption, deliverance, Christ's work, or its purchase; the section is a parable about old and new wineskins and garments. Reading redemption in requires the wider context, not this text.

No clause speaks of sin, exile or death. The bursting skins and spilled wine (Luk.5.37#cl2-cl4) are an image of ruin for a garment/wineskin, not a statement about sin, exile or death; treating them as such would be reading the image as the thing.
David is mentioned (Luk.6.3#cl3), but no clause here speaks of a covenant, an oath, or a promise to David; the mention is of David's hunger and the bread, not of the covenant.

No clause here speaks of redemption, rescue, or salvation; 'Lord of the Sabbath' (Luk.6.5#cl1) is authority language, not redemption. If the stamp is meant as the section's general drift it is too broad; if meant specifically it has no clause.
The only clause touching this (Luk.6.16#cl0, 'who became a traitor') names Judas's betrayal, the opposite of redemption; no clause in the section speaks of redemption.

no clause in 6:17-19 speaks of a kingdom, reign, or kingship; the section is a healing scene on a level place, and the reader's citation of 6:19 points only to power going out to heal, not to the kingdom

The section's suffering is that of the disciples (hated, excluded, insulted) and of the prophets; nothing here speaks of a servant who suffers, and the Servant theme's Isaianic marks (vicarious bearing, the Servant himself) are absent. The nearest phrase, 'because of the Son of Man' (Luk.6.22#cl4), names the Son of Man as the reason for persecution, not as one suffering.

The reversal promises ('you will be filled', 'you will laugh') could be read as the section's general drift toward renewal, but no clause in the section says creation, newness, or renewal; if the stamp is meant as new creation it is not stated in these clauses.

The section as a whole is Jesus' teaching on love of enemies, addressed 'to those of you who will listen' (Luk.6.27#cl0); the stamp names the section's general drift, and no single clause is a beatitude ('blessed are...').

The cited verse (6:39) is the blind-leading-the-blind parable; the only speech-act is 'He spoke also a parable to them' (cl0), which does not make Jesus or anyone a prophet, and no clause names a prophet.
The cited verse (6:40) contrasts disciple and teacher; 'disciple' (cl0) is not 'servant', and no clause speaks of serving or a servant.
The cited verse (6:41) concerns looking at a splinter versus a beam; seeing faults is not bearing witness, and no clause names a witness.
The cited verse (6:42) addresses a 'brother' and calls him 'hypocrite'; brother and hypocrite are not enemy/adversary, and no clause names an enemy.
Cited at Luke 6:43, but no clause of this section speaks of sin, exile or death; at most 'bad tree / bad fruit' is a general negative image. Empty list, general.
Nothing in the section speaks of mercy or restoration; it divides good from evil and names evil fruit, with no note of pardon or repair.
Calling Him 'Lord, Lord' and doing or not doing what He says implies authority, but no clause judges, accuses, or passes sentence on anyone.
No clause names kingship, a kingdom, or a royal act; 'Lord, Lord' is address, not a royal title in this text.
Neither the address nor the two hearers is described as a servant or slave anywhere in these clauses.
No clause speaks of a son, fatherhood, or sonship; the figure is a man building a house.
No clause has anyone testify, attest, or bear witness to anything.
The flood is a natural onslaught on a house, not a legal contest or trial; no clause stages an accusation, defence, or verdict proceeding.
No clause presents an enticement to sin or a testing of desire; the flood is not described as tempting anyone.
The falling and ruin is stated as consequence of the house's footing, not as a curse pronounced by anyone; no clause has cursing.
No clause speaks of deportation, captivity, or removal from a land; the house's collapse is not exile.
No clause calls anyone a prophet or describes prophetic speaking; 'what I say' is not marked as prophecy here.
No priestly role, sacrifice, or temple service appears in any clause.
No sheep, flock, or shepherding language occurs in the clauses.
No father, child, or parental relation is named in any clause.
No bridegroom, bride, or wedding language occurs in the clauses.
No clause mentions a firstborn, birthright, or first offspring.
No clause depicts fighting, arms, or a warrior; the flood bursting on a house is not warfare in this text.
No clause has anyone keep watch, warn, or stand guard.
No clause has a host receiving, entertaining, or providing hospitality.
No clause places anyone as a guest at a table or in a house so received.
No clause describes a journey to a shrine or festival; coming to Jesus (47#cl1) is not a pilgrimage here.
Nothing in 6:46-49 marks out a surviving remnant; the faithful-hearer contrast is discipleship/obedience, not remnant language.
No Gentile nations or corporate foreign peoples appear in this section; only individual hearers.
Wisdom is not personified as a woman here; the builder is simply 'a man'.
Folly is not personified as a woman here; the foolish builder is 'a man'.
No beast imagery or ruler figure in the parable or its frame.
No shepherd or flock imagery; no leader misusing a flock is in view.
The disobedient hearer is not called or depicted as a prophet; the contrast is doing vs. not doing Jesus' words.
No Adam typology: rock, house, flood and doing the words do not evoke Adam.
No Davidic or royal imagery, and no David typology is signalled in these verses.
No stranger, sojourner or alien appears; nothing in the section concerns resident foreigners.
No enemy or adversary stands in view; the contrast is between two kinds of hearer, not between foes.

No clause speaks of mercy or restoration; the section's content is obedience, firmness under flood, and ruin. The first house's survival is endurance, not mercy, and the reader cited 6:48, which says the house 'could not shake it, because it was well built.'

Nothing in these clauses presents Jesus as the suffering servant: He teaches, heals a withered hand and rebukes His opponents, and His own suffering is not in view here (the hostility of 6:11 is against Him but is not His vicarious suffering).
The synagogue crowd and the scribes and Pharisees are the setting throughout, but no clause states an idea of the covenant people as such.
No clause pronounces or depicts judgment; 6:11 shows the opponents' rage and plot, which is hostility, not judgment.
The clauses speak of healing and of doing good or evil, but nothing about sin, exile, or death is said or implied in this section.

The only prophetic figure named is John the Baptist (Luk.7.20#cl2, 'John the Baptist has sent us'), but no clause here calls anyone a prophet: John is identified only by name and as sender, and 'the coming [One]' (Luk.7.19#cl1, Luk.7.20#cl4) is a messianic designation, not the role-word 'prophet'. The stamp is the drift of the passage (John's disciples act as a prophet's messengers), but no clause carries the role.

This is the sending of John's disciples to ask whether Jesus is 'the coming [One]' and Jesus' answer listing his works (Luk.7.19#cl1, Luk.7.22#cl5-cl10). Nothing in the section speaks of a servant who suffers: no clause has suffering, Servant, Isaian quotation, or vicarious death. The nearest note, 'does not fall away on account of Me' (Luk.7.23#cl0), is about stumbling over Jesus, not about his suffering.

The word 'kingdom' (basileia) does not occur anywhere in Luke 7:18-23, and no clause speaks of a reign, king, or kingdom: the section is about John's question, Jesus' healings and his reply. 'The good news is preached to the poor' (Luk.7.22#cl10) and 'the coming [One]' (Luk.7.19#cl1) are read by some as kingdom-adjacent, but the section itself names no kingdom.

The section is built on the question whether Jesus is 'the coming [One]' (Luk.7.19#cl1, Luk.7.19#cl3, Luk.7.20#cl4, Luk.7.20#cl6) and on Jesus answering with works done (Luk.7.21#cl0, Luk.7.21#cl1, Luk.7.22#cl5-cl10). That is the general drift of promised expectation and its fulfilment, but no clause here asserts a promise or God's faithfulness to one; John's question (Luk.7.19#cl3 'another are we to look for') and Jesus' 'blessed is the one who does not fall away' (Luk.7.23#cl0) presuppose it without stating it.
No clause in this section speaks of a servant or of serving; the woman's acts are anointing, weeping and kissing, and the household roles named are host, guest and teacher.
No clause here presents anyone as a witness to an event; the Pharisee's seeing (Luk.7.39#cl1) is private judgement within himself, and the others merely murmur at the table (Luk.7.49#cl2).
The section's vocabulary is sin, forgiveness, faith and peace (Luk.7.47#cl0, Luk.7.48#cl1, Luk.7.50#cl1); exile and death do not appear, and the woman is not sent away but saved.
No clause here speaks of death or of life coming from it; the sequence is sin, forgiveness, love, faith and peace (Luk.7.47#cl0, Luk.7.48#cl1, Luk.7.50#cl1).
This clause names a role, 'household manager', not a servant, and no clause speaks of any of these people serving in a servant role.

The section's own clauses at 8:18 are the opposite: 'whoever does not have, even what he thinks he has will be taken away from him' (Luk.8.18#cl4, cl5, cl6). Nothing in 8:16-18 speaks of mercy or restoration; the giving in Luk.8.18#cl3 is given to the one who already has, not to the destitute.
No clause in the section carries the idea "son": the relatives are named (mother, brothers), but no one is called or described as a son, and no father-son relation is stated.
The stamp could only rest on the report or on "to see You", but in Luke those verbs mean physical sight of Jesus, not witnessing/testimony to an event; no clause has a witnessing role.
No one is sick or cured in this section; the act is a rebuke of wind and water, not a healing of a person.
No act of creating is narrated; the clauses describe stilling an existing storm, not bringing something into being.
There is no combat, enemy or armed conflict; the wind and water are stilled by a word, with no fighting narrated.
No procession, entry or triumphal march appears in these verses.
Jesus is never presented as a fighter; the section shows him asleep, rebuking wind, and teaching about faith.
A teacher who speaks with authority to disciples and to nature is the section's general drift, but no clause names or depicts a prophet.
No father-son relation is stated or implied anywhere in the section.
Nothing in these verses invokes David or a Davidic figure.
No corporate Israel imagery, exodus or covenant people is named in the section.
The scene is a lake crossing on a boat, not a journey through wilderness.
No fishing, nets or fishing trade is mentioned in the section.
No period of forty days or years is mentioned; the temporal note is "One day".
No fasting or abstinence from food appears; Jesus is asleep, not fasting.
Nothing solicits Jesus or the disciples to sin; the storm is a danger, not a temptation.
The threat comes from wind and water, not from people opposing or oppressing them.
No judicial sentence or judgment scene is narrated; the rebuke of the storm is not a verdict on persons.
No cursing or cursed state is spoken; the sea is calmed, not cursed.
No flood here: the water is a lake (Luk.8.22#cl3/cl4) and the windstorm on it; the great flood of Genesis is a different event, and the stilling of the storm is not an image of it.
Nothing covenantal in the section; the disciples' wonder at His command of wind and water (Luk.8.25#cl5-7) is amazement, not a covenant with creation.
No Noah, no ark, no covenant sign; the storm on the lake and its calming are not the Noahic covenant.
The calm after the rebuke ('there was a calm', Luk.8.24#cl7) is a stilled storm, not a covenant of peace being made.
No oath, vow or swearing anywhere in the section; the disciples' question 'Who is this?' (Luk.8.25#cl5) is not an oath.
No oath and no reference to the fathers or to Abraham's descendants.
Nothing about Abraham, his seed or the promises made to him; the section is a lake-crossing and a storm.
No David, no throne, no dynasty language; the disciples' question about Jesus' identity is not the Davidic covenant.
No covenant language, no blood, no meal; nothing in the section institutes or evokes the new covenant.
No Sinai, no law-giving, no mountain; the storm is natural, not a theophany of covenant-making.
No cutting of animals or covenant rite; 'He rebuked the wind and the raging waters' (Luk.8.24#cl4) is a rebuke, not covenant-cutting.
No meal, table or eating in the section.
The Gerasenes are a local Gentile region, not a nation acting as a character; no clause personifies a people or nation.
No beast or anti-kingdom figure appears; "Legion" is a name for many demons, and the pigs are an ordinary herd, not a symbolic beast.
The Abyss is named only as the place the demons beg not to be sent into (Luk.8.31#cl2); no clause has the Abyss being opened.
The pericope has no clause about a people belonging to God; the Gerasenes send Jesus away and the healed man is sent home alone.
No clause in Luke 8:4-15 names or portrays a prophet; the cited verse (8:4) is only the crowd gathering and Jesus beginning the parable. Nothing here carries the role.
The 'fruit' here is a crop/harvest produced by hearing and persevering (Luk.8.8#cl1, Luk.8.15#cl3); nothing in the section speaks of the Spirit's fruit (Gal 5:22), which is a different idea.
Nothing here shows the Servant suffering: the woman suffers (8:43) and Jesus' power goes out (8:46), but his own suffering is not in this section.

The section shows Jesus' authority over sickness and death, which is the kingdom's drift, but no clause names reign, kingdom or kingship; Jairus' 'synagogue ruler' (8:41) is a local office, not the kingdom.
The mocking of 8:53 is met by the raising, but no clause speaks of rank, order, or first and last.
No contest is in view: the bleeding woman is healed and the dead child raised without any opposing strong power being defeated.
There is no conception or birth: the woman's bleeding is stopped (8:44) and a child is raised (8:55).
The Spirit is not named or referred to in any clause of Luke 9:1-6; the power given is simply 'power and authority over all demons, and power to cure diseases' (Luk.9.1#cl0), not the Spirit.
Luke 9:11 has only 'the kingdom of God' (Luk.9.11#cl2); no clause divides a kingdom, names a ruler or a house against itself.
