'host' is not a stock character role in this scene; the host is Jesus, identified only by pronoun in Luk.9.14#cl1 ('He said to the disciples of Him'), so no clause supplies the role, and the crowds are the guests, not the host.
No clause has two parties in conflict or any defeat; 9:13 says only that there is not enough food, and the reader's 'weak defeats strong' does not appear.

The concept of witness in the sense of testifying to Jesus is present only in the sense that Peter answers and the disciples report; no clause states testimony as a category. The section's general drift includes reporting what others say and Peter's confession, but no clause carries the idea of witness specifically.
No clause in this section mentions "Son" or any sonship language; the text calls Jesus "the Christ of God" (Luk.9.20#cl5), not Son. The stamp is incorrect for this section.
The section concerns Jesus and His disciples and the crowds' opinions, but no clause names or describes the people of God as a category.

The section contains Peter's confession "The Christ of God" (Luk.9.20#cl5), which points to Messiah, but the section does not speak of redemption as such; the stamp describes the broader drift rather than any clause here.
Son of Man as rejected prophet is implied by the rejection and suffering, but no clause names a prophet role; general drift only.
Servant is a theological reading of the suffering Son of Man; no clause says 'servant'.
No clause states redemption or its purpose; the death is reported without a redemptive interpretation.
The section addresses 'anyone' who follows Jesus, not a servant figure; no clause carries a role of servant.
No clause describes anyone bearing witness; the reference to those standing here seeing the kingdom does not make them witnesses in the stamp's sense.
Luke 9:27 speaks of some not tasting death before seeing the kingdom; it does not speak of a resurrection as the clauses have it.
The cross belongs to the disciple who takes it up, not to a servant who suffers for others; no clause here portrays the suffering servant.
The section speaks of saving and losing one's life, not of redemption or of any price paid; no clause states redemption in Christ.
Luke 9:24 is losing and saving one's life, not a reversal of first and last order; no clause states that reversal.
The section names Moses as a figure present and speaking with Jesus (cl1 of 9.30), but no clause makes Jesus a new Moses; the stamp is Luke's literary drift, not something a clause states.
The presence of Moses and Elijah with the Messiah may be read as the promise kept, but no clause states a promise or its fulfilment.
Nothing in the section speaks of believers' union with Christ; the disciples' presence is companionship, not union. The stamp seems wrong for this section.
No clause in Luke 9:28-36 mentions the Spirit; the cloud and voice are the Father's, and the Spirit is not named. A Trinitarian reading is possible but no clause here says it.

No clause names or personifies nations or peoples; only the kingdom of God (4.26#cl1), a man, the earth, seed and grain appear.
No clause mentions a woman or personified wisdom, and the only human figure is 'a man' (4.26#cl2).
No clause mentions a woman or personified folly; the one human figure is explicitly a man (4.26#cl2).
No clause portrays a ruler as a beast or an oppressive empire; the section has no ruler and no beast imagery.
No clause mentions sheep, flock or shepherding, true or false; the man sows seed, he does not tend animals.
No clause mentions prophecy, a prophet, or deceptive speech; the section has no speaking figure other than the narrator and the unknowing sower.
No clause mentions lawlessness, transgression, or a rebel figure; the man acts innocently (sows, sleeps, reaps).
No clause alludes to Adam, Eden, a first or last man, or the fall; the section speaks only of seed, growth, and harvest.
No clause alludes to Moses, the exodus, or covenant mediation; nothing in the section points to a deliverer figure.
No clause alludes to David, a throne, an anointed king, or the Davidic promise; the kingdom is mentioned only as a simile (4.26#cl1).
No clause alludes to Israel, a restored people, or a new covenant community; the section's only corporate term is 'the kingdom of God' in the simile line (4.26#cl1).
No sheep, flock or herding language anywhere in the section; the actor is a sower/harvester, not a shepherd.
No cultic, altar, offering or priestly language; the only 'offering' is the earth offering its fruit (Mrk.4.29#cl1), which is not a priestly act.
Nothing legal or judicial occurs; the man neither judges nor is judged.
No father/son relation is named or implied in the clause text.
No marriage imagery; the man is identified only as one who scatters seed.
No bride or wedding imagery in the section.
No parenting or fatherhood language.
No mothering language; the earth 'brings forth fruit' but is never called a mother.
'first' in Mrk.4.28#cl1 orders the stages of the crop, not a firstborn child.
No foreigner, sojourner or resident-alien idea appears.
The man is a free sower; no servant or slave is named.
No opponent, opposition or hostile act; the seed grows without hindrance.
No creating or making event: the earth's bringing forth fruit (Mrk.4.28#cl0) is growth from seed already sown, not creation.
Nothing is named; the comparison with the kingdom is a likeness, not a naming act.
No breath, wind or spirit language in the section.
Nothing dies in this section; the seed is sown and grows, and no burial or death of the seed is mentioned.
The section speaks of the kingdom of God but names no human king; the idea belongs to the section's general drift (the reign of God) rather than to any clause.
No clause identifies anyone as a prophet; Jesus is presented as the speaker of parables, which is the general drift of the cited verse rather than a clause in particular.
The clause about the birds is a simile within the parable of the mustard seed; no clause says or implies nations acting, and the Berean text names only 'the birds of the air'.
The section is about the kingdom of God without naming its members; the only plural figures named in the cited verse are 'the birds of the air', which are not said to be people.
No procession, entry or triumph over enemies appears; the boat is not a triumphal march and no crowd escorts anyone, so the stamp does not belong in this section.
The crowd's astonished question implies an authority that commands even wind and sea, but no clause of this section names, addresses or depicts Him as king.
Jesus here commands wind and sea and is addressed as Teacher; nothing in the section presents Him as a servant or in servile role.
No clause speaks of sonship, of God as Father, or of Jesus as Son; the question 'Who is this' remains unanswered in the section.
The disciples in the boat with Jesus could be read as the people of God in transition, but no clause speaks of Israel as a body or of a new people.
No clause of this section speaks of a kingdom, of rule, or of God's reign; the question 'Who is this' concerns His identity, not a kingdom.
The implied carrying-through of Jesus' 'Let us cross to the other side' is a general drift of the passage; no clause states a promise or God's faithfulness.
A windstorm on the lake is not the shaking of the cosmos in the apocalyptic sense; no clause speaks of stars, hosts, or the ordering of creation coming apart.
No clause touches the heavens; the storm is in the wind and the waves over the boat, not above.
No clause has the day-of-the-Lord markers (darkness, trumpet, theophany coming); the sea-storm is a real boat emergency, not the day itself.
Nothing in the section says the sky went dark; the darkness stamp has no clause to rest on here.
The rebuke of the wind in 4:39 is a stilling of a storm, not a judgment executed by God against the wicked; no clause describes judgment.
The disciples' cry 'don't You care that we are perishing' (4:38#cl4-#cl6) questions His care; it does not attack His presence, which the narrative keeps asserting (4:36#cl2, 4:38#cl0).
There is no outsider in the section and no coming to faith; the disciples' question is 'Who is this?', and 4:40 says they still have no faith.
4:38#cl6 ('we perish') names the feared death, but the section shows no death yielding life; the calm of 4:39 is not portrayed as life out of death.
Dismissing the crowd in 4:36#cl1 may look like scattering, but no clause shows a gathering resulting from it; the boat crossing just leaves the crowd behind.

This section's suffering is the demoniac's self-harm and the pigs' drowning; Jesus himself is active as exorcist and is begged to leave, and no clause speaks of the Servant bearing suffering or Isaiah's Servant motif.

No servant appears in this section; Mrk.5.35#cl0's messengers are from Jairus's house, not servants of the healed girl, and the cited verse 41 has no servant role (only Jesus, the child, and her parents).
The woman's twelve years of suffering (Mrk.5.25#cl0-cl1, Mrk.5.26) is her own affliction, not a servant who suffers on others' behalf; verse 29 has no servant figure.
No clause in this section names or depicts the kingdom; it is at most the general drift of Jesus' healing and restoring activity (including the cited Mrk.5.43#cl2), not something a clause says.
Nothing in this section states or enacts a reversal of rank or order — a child is raised, but no last/first, least/greatest claim is made; verse 41 has no such idea.

Mark 6:3 names Jesus' family and the offense taken at Him, but the section has no servant, no bearing of sin or suffering for others — the rejection here is the crowd's unbelief, not vicarious suffering. The stamp is not what this section says.

Jesus teaches in the synagogue and travels teaching, which is kingdom proclamation in the larger scope of the Gospel, but no clause in 6:1-6 says 'kingdom' or names a reign; it is the section's general drift only.
Herod is a king/ruler, not a shepherd over a flock; no clause in this section speaks of rule as shepherding or of a shepherd who fails.
No clause attributes beast-imagery or beast-like character to Herod; he acts as a fearful, oath-bound king (6:26), not as a beast.
The only military men are Herod's guests ('military commanders', Mrk.6.21#cl1) who hold no combat role; no clause has fighting or a warrior.
The one sent is an executioner ordered to bring John's head (Mrk.6.27#cl0-2, Mrk.6.28#cl0-2); the clauses speak of an execution, not of service or a servant.
The clauses present John as a righteous prophet and the one beheaded, with no servant-language, no vicarious suffering and no exaltation; the stamp's frame does not fit here.

Wrong for this section. Mark 6:37 ('You give them something to eat') is about the disciples' inability and Jesus' provision, not about any reversal of rank or order; no clause here sets one person above or below another.

Wrong for this section. Nothing in Mark 6:30-44 speaks of death; the loaves are broken and distributed, not killed, and the crowd is fed, not raised. The bread-being-broken reading of Mark 6:41 is not warranted by any clause here.
No sickness, demon, or cure appears anywhere in 6:45-52; v.51 reports Jesus climbing into the boat and the wind ceasing (Mrk.6.51#cl0, Mrk.6.51#cl1), not a healing.
Nothing in this section speaks of temple, sanctuary, or divine presence dwelling in a place; the boat, the sea, and the mountain (Mrk.6.46#cl0) are not temple language.
The section has no servant, no suffering, no rejection or vicarious death; the disciples' fear (Mrk.6.50#cl1) is not the Servant's suffering.
deliverance is the section's drift, but no clause names it: 'healed' is the only rescue word.
Isaiah's Servant suffers for others; here Jesus heals others and suffers nothing — Mark 6:56 has no servant, no bearing, no suffering.
Nowhere in the section is the rule or reign of God mentioned; healing crowds are not the kingdom.
No clause of the section speaks of the kingdom; the Berean text has no 'kingdom' word in Mark 6:7-13, and the nearest words (authority, preach, repent) do not name it.

The clauses accuse the Pharisees of hypocrisy (lips honour, heart far off) and of teaching human precepts as doctrine; no clause speaks of them as prophets or of false prophecy. The prophet named (Isaiah, Mrk.7.6#cl1) is a true prophet.
No clause describes a sacrifice or sacrificial rite. Corban is a gift devoted to God (Mrk.7.11#cl4), i.e. a vow/dedication of property, not an offering being sacrificed.

The speech is a rebuke of the Pharisees and scribes, but no clause in this section frames it as a formal lawsuit with indictment, witnesses and verdict, nor invokes the covenant as the charge; the quoted Isaiah text (Mrk.7.6#cl3, Mrk.7.6#cl4) is accusation, not lawsuit.
No clause pronounces a woe; the nearest elements are "hypocrites" (Mrk.7.6#cl1) and the Isaiah quotation, and the Hebrew/Greek here has no woe form.

No clause narrates a judgment event. The only judgment language is the Mosaic penalty quoted in Mrk.7.10#cl2 ("must be put to death"), which is a citation of the law Moses said, not a judgment happening in this section.
Defiled hands and unwashed eating (Mrk.7.2#cl1, Mrk.7.2#cl2) are ritual purity, not sin, exile or death; the only death in the section is the Mosaic penalty for cursing parents (Mrk.7.10#cl2).

The section's drift is criticism of the tradition-keepers, but no clause states a judgment; the closest is the quoted penalty in Mrk.7.10#cl2, which is part of the quoted law rather than the section's own judgment.
Nothing in the section concerns mercy or restoration; the command quoted (Mrk.7.10#cl1) is about honouring parents, and the section's thrust is accusation (Mrk.7.8#cl0, Mrk.7.9#cl1, Mrk.7.13#cl0).
No clause speaks of an idol, a temple/holy place, or an abomination; teaching human precepts as doctrine (Mrk.7.7#cl1) is not an idol in the holy place.

General drift only: the section does speak of sin and defilement (evil thoughts, murder, adultery, etc., Mrk.7.21#cl1), but no clause speaks of exile or death, and no clause ties defilement to mortality. Nothing in these clauses carries the stamp as a particular.

No clause in the section speaks of mercy or restoration. 'Thus all foods are clean' (Mrk.7.19#cl3) declares food clean but names no restoration of persons, and nothing here is said of forgiveness or healing.
No clause names Christ as redeemer, and nothing is said of redemption or rescue. The pronouncement that what defiles comes from within (Mrk.7.20#cl1, Mrk.7.23#cl1) diagnoses, it does not redeem.

The woman at 7:25 is a suppliant who falls at Jesus' feet; the only hostile force is the unclean spirit afflicting her child, which the stamp's 'adversary' role is not about. Nothing here is an enemy of Jesus or of the woman.
No one serves or is called a servant; the cited 7:28 speaks of dogs eating the children's crumbs, and the woman asks a favour rather than serving. The stamp is not present in this section.

No clause speaks of the servant who suffers or bears sin: the section is a healing (ears opened, tongue released, Mrk.7.35#cl0-cl2) plus the crowd's astonishment (Mrk.7.37#cl0-cl5); the 'deaf hear / mute speak' words are the crowd's praise, not Isaiah's servant language, and nothing here describes suffering, rejection or vicarious bearing.
No clause in the section mentions the kingdom, a king, or rule/authority; Mark 7:31-37 has no kingdom saying at all, so the stamp would rest on nothing but general inference from the pericope.
The crowd's identity as God's people is nowhere said by a clause; the text speaks only of "the crowd" and "four thousand men".
No clause in Mark 8:1-10 mentions the kingdom, reign, or kingship; the passage is a feeding narrative only.

Whoever cited Mark 8:8 seems to read the leftover basketfuls as a promise kept, but no clause here speaks of a promise or of faithfulness; the clauses say only that the people ate, were satisfied and that broken pieces were picked up.
The word 'prophet' never appears; the stamp fits only the section's general drift of a heavenly sign demanded and refused, not any clause that names or describes a prophet.
The Pharisees are Israel's religious insiders who fail by demanding a sign, which is the section's general drift, but no clause states the failure as such.
The section's rebuke is about dullness of heart and failure to understand, not sin, exile or death.
Mark 8:21 is a rebuke ('Do you still not understand?'), which does not speak of mercy or restoration.
Mark 8:22–26 never calls anyone 'son' — neither the blind man nor Jesus as Son; nothing in these clauses carries the idea.
The section is a healing of blindness, not a rescue from an oppressor or danger; no clause speaks of deliverance.
The Servant's suffering (Isaiah 53) is not present: Jesus acts with power here and no clause speaks of his suffering.

Nothing in this section speaks of redemption, the cross, or saving work; Peter's 'You are the Christ' is a title/confession only, and the section's theme (Messianic identity and silence) is not redemption.
The section concerns Jesus, the disciples and the crowds' opinions; 'disciples' is the nearest thing to a people of God, but no clause states the idea.
No clause mentions suffering, death, or servant; the section is the confession at Caesarea Philippi, before the passion predictions.
No clause speaks of a promise, covenant, or God's faithfulness; the section is questioning and confession.
No clause calls Jesus a prophet or describes prophetic activity; the teaching is present but the stamp is not locatable in a clause.
No clause speaks of ransom, sin-bearing or redemption; the death and rising are stated without redemptive force or purpose.
The section names suffering, rejection, killing and rising, but nothing of sin or exile, and the death is not presented as the consequence of sin; the stamp does not fit here.
No kingdom, king or reign is named anywhere in the section; 'the things of God' is the only possible echo but does not itself speak of the kingdom.
No clause speaks of testifying or bearing witness; the nearest material is being ashamed of Jesus and his words, which is not witness.
The section's drift is self-denial and cross-bearing, but the servant of Isaiah who suffers for others is nowhere in these clauses; the cross is the disciple's, not the Servant's.
The reversal here is loss and gain of one's own life, not the overturning of rank or order; no clause makes a last person first or a first person last.
Six days and three named companions on the mountain evoke Israel at Sinai, but no clause states a new Israel; the stamp is the section's general drift.
No clause in the section mentions the Spirit; the cloud and voice are the Father's, not the Spirit named.
Nothing in the section speaks of the Servant's own suffering; the boy's affliction and Jesus' rebuke are not that idea.
The section never speaks of the kingdom; the exorcism and rebuke are not the kingdom idea.
The section's only speech-role is 'The Son of Man' (Mrk.9.31#cl1); no clause names or depicts a prophet, and the predicted death/resurrection is not framed as a prophet's fate here.
No clause in the section states purpose, benefit or ransom; the saying is bare prediction of death and rising, so the redemption idea is at best the section's general drift.
Mark 9:38 uses 'we saw' (Mrk.9.38#cl2-3), which is bare seeing, not testimony about God or the gospel; there is no witness/testimony clause in this section.

Nothing here is suffering inflicted on believers: the only hostile acts are forbidding the exorcist (Mrk.9.38#cl5) and being unable to speak evil of Jesus (Mrk.9.39#cl4-5). Opposition to Christ's name is not persecution of his people in this text.

The section speaks of the Twelve (Mrk.9.35#cl0) and of 'us' against outsiders (Mrk.9.38#cl4, Mrk.9.40#cl1), but it nowhere names or characterises a people belonging to God; 'in My name' in vv.37-41 identifies Christ, not a body of the redeemed.
Mark 9:37 contains no act of mercy or restoration: receiving a child is said to be receiving Jesus and the One who sent him. A welcoming clause is not a mercy-restoration clause.

The section's subject is greatness and service among the Twelve (v.35), which is kingdom discourse, but no clause names the kingdom, a king, or reigning; the stamp is the section's drift, not any particular clause.
Mark 9:41 promises a reward for a cup of water given to those who bear Christ's name; no clause speaks of purchase, ransom, or being redeemed.
Mark 9:48 speaks of the worm that never dies and the fire that is never quenched; no clause of this section states a curse, and 'never dies / never quenched' is unending destruction, not cursing.

The section's only 'salt' language is the salting-with-fire saying (Mrk.9.49#cl0) and the salt-sayings of 9:50; nothing here invokes, names or alludes to the covenant of salt of Lev 2:13 / Num 18:19 (a covenant with Aaron's priesthood), so the stamp is not present in this section.

The section addresses 'everyone' (Mrk.9.49#cl0) and the community of disciples ('among yourselves', 'one another' in Mrk.9.50#cl3 / #cl4), so the stamp fits the address of the whole passage, but no clause states the idea of a people belonging to God.

No clause says Jesus is a new or second David; the section only names David in the genealogy (Mat.1.1#cl0 'son of David', Mat.1.6#cl0, Mat.1.17#cl0). The stamp is a reading of the section's drift, not something any clause states.
No clause mentions a covenant, oath, or promise; David appears only as an ancestor (Mat.1.1#cl0, Mat.1.6#cl0, Mat.1.17#cl0). General drift only.
Abraham appears only as an ancestor in the genealogy (Mat.1.1#cl0 'son of Abraham', Mat.1.2#cl0, Mat.1.17#cl0); no covenant is spoken of in any clause.
No clause contains an oath or a promise to the fathers; the section is a genealogy plus a summary of its fourteen-generation divisions.
No clause states a promise or God's faithfulness; Mat.1.17#cl1 and Mat.1.17#cl2 only count the generations 'from David to the exile to Babylon' and 'from the exile to the Christ'. General drift only.

No clause says anyone believed. The four women named in descent clauses — Tamar (Mat.1.3#cl0), Rahab and Ruth (Mat.1.5#cl0, Mat.1.5#cl1), Uriah's wife (Mat.1.6#cl1) — are introduced only as the mother of a child ('out of Tamar', 'out of Rahab', 'out of Ruth', 'out of the [wife] of Uriah'), not as outsiders who believed. This belongs to the section's drift, if at all.
No clause quotes or cites a prophet; Mat.1.17#cl2 names 'the Christ' but says nothing prophetic being fulfilled. General drift only.

Nothing in the section names or describes a covenant, new or otherwise; 'He will save His people from their sins' is salvation, not covenant language, and no covenant word or concept appears in any clause.

Saving from sins may be read as mercy, but the section states the act without the category; no clause says mercy or restoration, so this is the section's drift rather than a clause that carries the idea.
As with new_covenant: no clause in the section speaks of a covenant, and 'God with us' is a name, not a covenant statement.
No clause mentions a kingdom, a king, or rule; 'son of David' (Mat.1.20#cl3) is the nearest thing and is a bare address, so the stamp is not supported by any clause.

No clause in this section says Jesus sends the twelve out: the only clause acts (cl0) are his summoning them to himself, his giving them authority, and the purpose clauses casting out and healing (cl2, cl3). The actual sending comes later (Matt 10:5). The stamp matches the drift of the section as the start of the mission charge, and the reader cited Matt 10:2, where no clause says it.

The only clause that could carry it, Mat.10.4#cl0 'also having betrayed Him', names Judas's betrayal of Jesus; that is the opposite of redemption, and no clause in this section speaks of being bought, ransomed or saved through Christ.

No clause in this section names a shepherd, sheep-keeping, or anyone tending or gathering the sheep; the sheep of v.16 appear only as those sent out among wolves (Mat.10.16#cl0/cl1), which is the sending image, not a shepherd image.

The section presupposes the disciples and Israel as God's people throughout, but no single clause states the idea of a people belonging to God; it is the general backdrop rather than something a clause says. Clauses about Israel's towns (Mat.10.23#cl3) and the Father (Mat.10.20#cl2) are near it but do not themselves carry it.

The suffering in this section belongs to the disciples who are handed over, flogged, hated and killed (Mat.10.17#cl1-2, Mat.10.21#cl0/cl3, Mat.10.22#cl0), not to the Servant of Isaiah; the section has no servant figure who suffers for others, and 'servant' here (Mat.10.24#cl1, Mat.10.25#cl2) is a household slave in a comparison of status.
Matt 10:27 concerns the disciples' own proclamation of what Jesus tells them in the dark, not the words of a prophet or the prophetic word as such; no clause here carries a prophetic-word idea.
Matt 10:28 speaks of those who kill the body and of the One able to destroy soul and body; it says nothing of the Servant's own suffering or vicarious death, so the stamp does not fit this section.

The section's closing reassurance (Matt 10:31, 'you are worth more than many sparrows') expresses God's care, but no clause states mercy or restoration as such; the stamp describes the section's drift rather than any particular clause.
No clause here speaks of redemption, ransom, blood, cross or rescue; the text is about confession/denial and its consequence, not about being redeemed.

The section concerns the confessing/denying individual and the Father, not a collective people of God; it is at most a background assumption that those who confess belong to God, so no clause in particular carries it.
The only military image is the bare noun 'sword' (Mat.10.34#cl5), a figure for division within households; no warrior, soldier or fighting is present in this section.
The section speaks of division within households and cross-bearing, not of persecution as such; the cited verse 39 names no persecutor.
No clause mentions a kingdom, king or reign; the verse cited (10:34) has 'earth' only.
No clause names a people, a community or God's own; 10:35 speaks only of a household split apart.
Worthiness and losing one's life imply a reckoning, but no clause states a judgment; the cited verse 34 says only 'a sword'.
‘For My sake’ (Mat.10.39#cl3) is the nearest phrase, but no clause speaks of ransom, purchase or rescue; the idea is the section's background, not its wording.

No clause of Matt 10:40-42 names a servant or service. Matt 10:42 speaks of 'one of these little ones' and 'a disciple' (Mat.10.42#cl0), which is not the same idea; the stamp must rest on wording that is not here.

The section is about receiving Christ's messengers and their reward; no clause says anything about bearing witness or testimony. The cited verse (10:40) has 'receives' (Mat.10.40#cl0, cl2), not witness.

No clause says anything about a word, message or prophecy being spoken; the prophet appears only as a person to be received (Mat.10.41#cl0-cl1). The idea of a prophetic word is not carried by any clause here.

Nothing in Matt.10.5-15 concerns priests or priestly service. The reader's cited verse, Matt 10:11, is about finding a worthy host to stay with ('inquire who in it worthy is', Mat.10.11#cl3); 'worthy' there describes a hospitable household, not a priest, and no clause names a priest, temple, altar or cultic act.

The commission is present as the section's frame (Mat.10.5#cl0-cl2), but blessing is not stated in any clause: the imperatives are prohibitions, healings, preaching and peace. I could not find a clause that itself carries 'blessing'; what would settle it is whether the peace saying (Mat.10.13#cl0, Mat.10.13#cl2, 'let your peace rest on it') is to count as the blessing.

Nothing in this section speaks of the servant's suffering; John's imprisonment (Mat.11.2#cl0/cl1) is John's, not the servant's, and Mat.11.5 lists acts of healing and good news, not suffering or rejection.

The section is about the works of Christ (Mat.11.2#cl1, 'the works of the Christ') and the good news (Mat.11.5#cl5), but no clause states redemption, atonement or purchase; this is the drift of the passage rather than a claim any clause makes.

No clause here names a kingdom or a king. The nearest is the preaching of good news to the poor, which in Matthew is kingdom preaching, but the clause itself says only 'good news'; the stamp is the passage's general drift, not a clause's content.
Nothing here offers mercy or restoration: the section is a denunciation, the repentance is counterfactual and the only movement named is being brought down to Hades.
No clause here calls or portrays Jesus as a servant; Mat.11.29#cl0/#cl1 speak of taking his yoke and learning from him, which is discipleship, not servanthood.
Nothing in 11:25-30 speaks of a covenant, its making, its parties or its terms; the cited verse 11:28 is an invitation to the weary to come and be given rest, with no covenant word in the text.
No suffering, wounding, or bearing of others' sin is spoken of; 11:28-30 describes the disciples' weariness and the lightness of Jesus' yoke, not Jesus' own suffering.
Nothing in Matt 11:7-19 speaks of a kingdom or house divided against itself (that is Matt 12:25-26); 11:12 speaks of violence done to the kingdom, not division.
Matt 11:13 speaks of the Prophets and the Law prophesying until John, not of a new covenant; no covenant language appears in the section.
Matt 11:14 identifies John as Elijah, not as a Moses figure; the section has no Mosaic typology.
Matt 11:16-17 is the parable of the children in the marketplaces about 'this generation', not a figure of a new Israel.
No bridegroom or wedding imagery occurs in Matt 11:7-19; 11:19 mentions eating and drinking, which is not bridegroom language.
The section speaks of the crowds, Israel's prophets, the kingdom and 'this generation', but no clause names or describes the people of God as such.
Matt 11:16-19 pronounces on 'this generation' and the violent, and John's accusers, but no clause states a judgment; it is the drift rather than a specific statement.
The counterpart of 11:18 in 11:19 is not an outsider believing but the Son of Man being slandered and wisdom being vindicated; nothing in the section shows an outsider coming to faith.

Matt 12:6 asserts the temple's inferiority to what is 'here' ('something greater than the temple is here'), which presupposes the temple standing; nothing in these clauses speaks of the temple being destroyed.

The section's gathered people are the nations hoping in His name and the crowds who follow and are healed; but the clauses speak of 'the nations' and of crowds, never of a people belonging to God, so no single clause carries the stamp.
Nothing in the section depicts a triumph or procession; the nearest figures are healing (12:22), driving out demons (12:24,27,28) and a housebreaking image (12:29).

Satan's kingdom divided against itself (12:26) is the opposite figure: an anti-kingdom at war with itself, more than it plausibly carries an apocalyptic beast motif. Unsure whether the stamp means that.
The strong man is bound by a stronger one (12:29); nothing here says the weak defeat the strong.

No clause narrates a judgment event: the section only states the forgiveness or non-forgiveness of sin and blasphemy; 'will not be forgiven' (Mat.12.31#cl2, Mat.12.32#cl3) is a pronouncement about forgiveness, not a judgment scene or act.

'Sin' is explicit (Mat.12.31#cl1, 'every sin and blasphemy'), and unforgiven sin implies remaining under judgment, which is the drift of the theme; but no clause in this section speaks of exile or of death, so no clause in particular carries the whole theme.

The section's 'fruit' and 'good things' are the good a person's own heart store produces; nothing here is the Spirit's fruit (Gal 5:22) — the Spirit is not mentioned, and the contrast is good vs evil persons, not spirit vs flesh.
Nothing in the section offers mercy or restoration; the section's own alternative to condemnation is acquittal by one's words (Mat.12.37#cl0), which is the opposite of mercy shown to the guilty.
Solomon is named only for his 'wisdom' (Mat.12.42#3); no clause of this section presents anyone as king.
Matt 12:40 speaks of the Son of Man being three days and three nights in the heart of the earth, which is burial/death, not resurrection; no clause says he is raised.
Matt 12:40 states the three days and nights in the heart of the earth but says nothing of life coming out of it; the reversal is not stated in this section.
The one humiliation clause (Mat.12.40) has no vindication counterpart in this section; the Son of Man's exaltation is not stated.

Nothing in Matt.12.43-45 solicits, entices or tests anyone: the unclean spirit returns on its own initiative (Mat.12.44#cl0/cl1) and brings seven worse spirits (Mat.12.45#cl1). The re-entry is an affliction, not a temptation.
The section has no human or national adversary, and no word for enemy; the unclean spirit and its seven companions are the man's affliction (Mat.12.45#cl4), not an enemy role in the text.
No clause of this section names Jesus as son or uses the word 'son'; the family terms are mother, brothers, sister, father. Jesus is called 'My brother' (Mat.12.50#cl1), not son.

The section is instruction/regulation about sanctuary and priesthood duties (Num 18:1-7), which is the general drift of law material, but no clause states a law/wisdom idea itself; the stamp is too broad to pin to particular clauses.

The section has no divine promise and no appeal to a prior promise: Israel's vow in Num.21.2#cl2 is conditional and stated by Israel, and the LORD's response in 21:3 is a granting of that vow, not the keeping of a promise He made. The only clause the cited verse offers is Num.21.14#cl0, the quotation formula 'it.is.said in the.book of.the.wars of.Yahweh (et) Waheb in Suphah and (et) the wadis Arnon' — a citation of a source book and a list of place names (Waheb, Suphah, the wadis of Arnon). No fighting, enemy, weapon or defeat is spoken of anywhere in the section; 'Book of the Wars of the LORD' names a book, not an event here.

The water in this section comes from a well dug by the princes (Num.21.18#cl0, Num.21.18#cl1, Num.21.18#cl2, Num.21.17#cl2 'O well'), and Num.21.16#cl4 is the LORD's promise 'so that I may give them water' — there is no rock, no striking, and no Moses-strikes-the-rock language (contrast Num.20.8-11, not in this section).

Num.21.14 cites 'the Book of the Wars of the LORD', which names a book, not a promise kept; nothing in the section states or recalls a divine promise. General drift at most.

Nothing in the section speaks of a sanctuary, tabernacle, dwelling of God or divine presence — Beer, the well, Mattanah, Nahaliel, Bamoth and Pisgah are travel stations and a viewpoint (Num.21.16#cl0, Num.21.18#cl3 through Num.21.20#cl3), and the 'dwelling of Ar' in Num.21.15#cl1 is a Moabite town.
No procession is described anywhere in the section; Num.21.24 reports a rout and land seizure ("put him to the sword", "took possession of his land"), not a victory march or parade.

Num 21:35 speaks of defeat, total destruction and taking possession of land; there is no procession, no triumphal march, no entry rite anywhere in the section.

Num 24:8 speaks of defeated foes (devouring nations, broken bones, arrows), but no clause in this section depicts a procession or triumphal march.

As with sacrifice_ev: Num.25.13's 'made atonement' (kipper) is expiation, and the section contains no sacrifice, no offering and no altar.

If Claude judges the stamp requires an explicit promise statement, mark it wrong for this section.
The section is a clan/registration list within the census of the tribes; nothing in it states or recalls a promise or divine faithfulness.

Nothing in the section speaks of promise or faithfulness; it is a registration list.

Section is a census/clan list of Zebulun; no clause says these are God's people, only that they are Zebulun's descendants by clan.
No clause mentions a promise, oath, or God acting; a numbering of 60,500 is census data, not a statement of promise-keeping.

Nothing in these clauses states or alludes to a promise or its fulfilment; the census of Ephraim's clans (Num 26:35-37) presupposes the ancestral promise but no clause here speaks to it. General drift only.

Nothing in this section states or alludes to a promise or to God's faithfulness; the census of Naphtali and of Israel is the general setting in which the stamp is being read, not something any clause here carries.

I am unsure whether the stamp belongs here at all; I would read it as the section's general drift (general: true) rather than as carried by a particular clause, and no clause in particular puts it in words.

The section is addressed to Israel ('you will bring near'), and no clause names a priest or priestly act; the priestly mediation of these offerings is presupposed by the cultic setting, not stated in any clause here.

Nothing in Num 28:16-25 names a priest or the sons of Aaron; the commands are addressed to the people/assembly ('you will bring near', 'Present to the LORD', 'you shall hold a sacred assembly'). The atonement clause (Num 28:22) states the purpose, not a priestly actor.

The section speaks of offerings brought near 'to Yahweh' (Num 28:19 cl0) and a pleasing aroma, but never of the sanctuary, the tent of meeting, the ark or any divine dwelling/place. The 'sacred assembly' is a convocation of the people, not a locus of God's presence.

No priest, Aaron or sons of Aaron appears anywhere in the clauses; the addressee is the congregation ('you', 'for you') and the actor is not specified.

No clause describes an offering or sacrifice; Num.3.4#cl1 is 'they brought.near fire strange', the bringing of unauthorized fire, not the slaughter or offering of a sacrifice.
The section's news is the loss of two sons and the survival of the Aaronic line through Eleazar and Ithamar, not a promise made or kept; no clause speaks of a divine promise.

No clause in Num.3.21-26 names a priest or priestly role. The cited verse Phil 4:13 speaks of Christ strengthening Paul; no clause in the section mentions the Spirit (ruach/pneuma).
Phil 4:20 is a doxology: glory to our God and Father forever. No clause mentions a kingdom or rule of God.

No clause here speaks of testifying or bearing witness; Phm.1.1#cl0 names Paul, Timothy, Philemon, Apphia, Archippus and the house church, and Phm.1.3#cl0 gives a greeting — nothing about witness.

Phm.1.3#cl0 speaks only of 'Grace and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ'; there is no word of redemption, ransom, purchase or blood in this section. (Redemption language appears in Phlm 1:18-19, outside this section.)

No reign, king, kingdom or royal rule is mentioned in the section. 'in the Lord' (Phm.1.20#cl0) is a sphere of Christian relation, not kingship language.

The stamp is wrongly applied to this section.

The section warns and describes ruin (Pro.1.16#cl0-1, Pro.1.18, Pro.1.19); no clause shows mercy, rescue or restoration.

The verse sets the fool's self-assurance against a wise man hearing advice; there is no contest, courtroom or trial in the clause.

The stamp is cited to Ps 107:20, outside this section, and no clause here speaks of healing.

Ps 111:3 'Splendid and majestic is His work' describes the character of God's work, not a visible appearing of God; the section records no manifestation, descent, fire, storm or voice.
Ps 111:6 'by giving them the inheritance of the nations' reports the gift of the land, not a triumphal march or procession; no clause depicts God or His people processing in victory.

Ps 111:3 'Splendid and majestic is His work' is about the greatness of God's deeds, not kingship or rule; the section has no king, throne, reign or dominion language (the 'inheritance of the nations' in v.6 is land given, not a kingdom established).

No clause names a king or royal figure; the man is 'a person fearing Yahweh' (Psa.112.1#cl1) and 'a.righteous.[person]' (Psa.112.6#cl1), and 'mighty in the land' (Psa.112.2#cl0) is about offspring, not a king.
No clause has a servant or service role; Psa.112.5#cl0 has 'a.person [who].shows.favor and.[who] lends', a generous lender, not a servant.
Psa.112.5#cl1 says '[who].he.maintains affairs his with justice' — the man's own affairs are guided by justice, not that he judges others.
Psa.112.10 speaks of 'a.wicked.[person]' (cl0) and '[the].desire of.wicked.[people]' (cl4) — individuals, no nation or peoples anywhere in the section.

A beatitude pronounces a person blessed ('blessed is...'); Ps 113:7 'He raises the poor from the dust' is a statement of what God does, with no blessing formula and no 'blessed' in the Hebrew or the Berean text. The only 'Blessed' in this psalm is Ps 113:2, which blesses the divine name, not a person, and is not the cited verse.
Ps 113:8 'to seat them with nobles' gives the poor an exalted seat but pronounces no blessing; no 'blessed' anywhere in the verse.

Ps 113:9 'a joyful mother to her children' is declared about the woman, not to her as a blessing formula; no 'blessed' in the Hebrew or in the Berean text, and the section's only 'Blessed' is Ps 113:2, applied to the name of the LORD.

The cited verse is 113:6, 'He humbles Himself to behold the heavens and the earth', which is about God's condescending to look down, not a person first humbled then vindicated; the reversal to vindication appears in 113:7-8, but that is not the verse cited and the clauses there rest on 'raises the poor from the dust', not on 'humbles Himself'.
The sea, Jordan and mountains that respond to God are part of the created order, but no clause in this section speaks of creating anything.
No clause names a covenant, its parties or its making; 'the God of Jacob' in Psa.114.7#cl2 names a god, not a covenant.
The section is about departure from Egypt, nature trembling and water from rock; no clause speaks of mercy, forgiveness or restoration.

No clause in the section has testimony, evidence, or witnessing; the nations' question in v.2 is a taunt, not their witness, and Israel's trust is not framed as testimony. The stamp as cited rests on the wrong idea in 115:2.
The idols of v.4 are the nations' own idols, made by human hands, not an image set up in God's temple or holy place; nothing in the section places an idol in a sanctuary.
No beast, empire, or anti-kingdom figure occurs; the nations merely ask a mocking question in 115:2 and are not described as hostile power here.
115:16 speaks of the heavens as the LORD's and the earth given to mankind; there is no temple, sanctuary, or dwelling-presence clause in this section.
115:18 is a general vow of praise 'now and forevermore'; the section ends in praise rather than in a statement of renewal or new creation, so no clause in particular carries it.
Ps 116:8 speaks of rescue from death, tears and stumbling, not of healing sickness or wounds; no clause here names healing, and the psalm's verb is 'delivered/rescued' (Psa.116.8#cl0), not 'healed'.

Ps 116:15 says the death of His saints is precious in the LORD's sight; it does not say death produces life. The reversal in this psalm runs the other way — death is escaped and life is walked in the land of the living (Psa.116.8#cl0, Psa.116.9#cl0).

No clause speaks of a covenant with creation or with any non-human creature; Ps.117.2#cl0 has 'loyalty his.covenant' (loving devotion toward us) and Psa.117.2#cl1 has Yahweh's faithfulness forever, i.e. covenant loyalty to his people, not creation.

The section speaks of Yahweh's enduring covenant loyalty (hesed) and of a day the LORD has made, but nothing here names a new covenant or covenant renewal; 'new_covenant' is not the idea carried by Ps.118.24.
Ps.118.26 calls the coming one 'blessed' and speaks of his coming in the LORD's name, but no clause of this section gives him a royal title or royal act; 'king' is read into the verse from outside.
No clause of this section describes the coming one of v.26 as a servant or assigns him service; 'servant' is not carried by 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD'.
Ps.118.19-20 ask that the gates of righteousness be opened and call this 'the gate of the LORD'; no clause assigns a gatekeeper, and a gate is not a gatekeeper.
Nothing in the section names or addresses a guest; at most a worshipper enters the gates (v.19#cl1, v.20#cl1), which is not the guest role.
Ps.118.28 says 'You are my God', which is a personal covenant confession, not a father relation; no clause of this section calls God father or anyone a son.
Nothing in the section names a prophet or prophetic speech; Ps.118.26's blessing on the one who comes in the LORD's name does not carry the prophet role.
No clause of this section speaks of shepherding or of the LORD as shepherd; Ps.118.27 is about light and a festal sacrifice.
No clause of this section uses sonship language; Ps.118.26 names the coming one merely 'he who comes'.
No marriage or bridegroom language occurs in the section; the 'tents of the righteous' (v.15#cl0) are not a wedding image in the text.
No marriage or bride language occurs in the section; the addressed groups (Israel, house of Aaron, those who fear the LORD) are not called a bride.
The stone/builder clause is about a rejected stone becoming the cornerstone, not a firstborn, and 'firstborn' appears nowhere in the section.
The clause cited ('let those who fear the LORD say...') speaks of the God-fearers, not strangers or sojourners; nothing in the section mentions a foreigner or resident alien.
'from the distress I called out to Yahweh' concerns the psalmist's distress and prayer, not slavery or bondservice.
'Open to me the gates of righteousness' has the speaker asking entry through gates, not a watchman standing guard.
The altar clause binds a festal sacrifice to the horns of the altar; no vine, vineyard or vinedresser is present.
The nations 'surrounded me' / 'cut them off' clause uses warfare imagery, not fishing.
The verse cited (stone rejected by the builders) does not personify wisdom as a woman; no woman-wisdom figure appears in the section.
'They were extinguished like burning thorns' is about enemies burnt up, not a personified Woman Folly.
'than to trust in princes' contrasts refuge in the LORD with trust in nobles; it is not a beastly ruler motif.
The nations surrounding/cut off clause is not shepherd imagery, and no shepherding figure is mentioned in the section.
The surrounding nations clause concerns hostile nations, not false prophets.
The surrounding nations clause names hostile nations, not a 'man of lawlessness' figure.
The rejected-stone clause is about a stone becoming the cornerstone, not about a new Adam.
'The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation' is a confession of Yahweh as savior, not a new-Moses role.
No clause names a servant; the speaker's distress, discipline and near-death remain first-person speech about the psalmist.
'This is the day that the LORD has made' speaks of a day of deliverance, not of a new creation; no clause in the section does.

The psalm refers to the whole of the LORD's statutes, precepts and laws collectively—never to the specific Decalogue or 'ten words'. The cited v.6 ('commandments') is a general term, not the ten commandments.
Rulers/kings at v.46 are individuals, not nations. The psalm never speaks of the nations (gôyîm) as a character or collective actor.

The psalm's only oath is the psalmist's own (v.106), and the 'word to Your servant' (v.49) is God's promise to the individual psalmist, not the ancestral oath of the patriarchs. The cited verse does not carry the stamp.
Ps 119:67 speaks of affliction and going astray, not a contest; no clause in this section stages a trial or contest.
Ps 119:135 asks God's face to shine on His servant, which is favour/light, not anointing; no clause anoints anyone.
Ps 119:46 has speaking before kings, not crowning one; no clause in this section makes a king.
Ps 119:95 has the wicked waiting to destroy the speaker, which is threat, not battle; no clause describes combat.
Ps 119:45 has walking in freedom/a broad place, which is liberty, not a procession; no clause shows a triumph march.
Ps 119:37 turns the eyes from 'worthless things', which is not stated to be idols; no clause mentions worship of another god.
Ps 119:21 is a report that God rebukes the arrogant, not a 'woe to ...' speech; no clause pronounces woe.
Ps 119:126 says it is time for the LORD to act because they have broken His law, which complains of law-breaking but stages no lawsuit; the section has no accusation and verdict form.
Ps 119:48 is lifting up the hands to the commandments, which the clause itself presents as prayer/pledge, not as a sign-act; no clause performs a symbolic deed.
Ps 119:33 asks to be taught; the section commissions no one to a task.
Ps 119:101 restrains the feet from every evil path, which resists temptation but no clause shows a tempting.

Psalm 119 contains no temple, sanctuary, Zion, house-of-God or divine-presence-in-a-place language; the cited verse Ps 119:151 is 'You are near, O LORD', which concerns the LORD's nearness to the psalmist, not a temple presence. No clause in the section carries the stamp.

The clause built on the cited verse, Psa.119.18#cl0 'uncover eyes my', is an illumination/enlightenment request addressed to God; the Hebrew has no word for spirit (no ruaḥ) and the verse is about seeing wonders in the law, not the Holy Spirit or a spirit.

The clauses built on the cited verse, Psa.119.50#cl0 'this comfort [is].my in affliction my' and Psa.119.50#cl1 'word your it has.preserved.me.alive', speak of preservation/reviving by God's word; they carry no creation, new-creation, new-heavens-and-earth or cosmic-renewal idea.

Ps 12 contains no beatitude ('blessed is...' / 'ashrei') anywhere; the section opens with a plea for help (Psa.12.2#cl0 'save ה'), not a blessing formula. The stamp belongs to wisdom/thanksgiving psalms, not this lament.
The antagonists here are 'the wicked' and 'men' within the psalm's own society ('from among men', 'among men'), not nations or foreign peoples. No gentile/nation character appears in Ps 12.
Nothing in the section has the speaker testifying or bearing witness before anyone; Ps 120:7 has him speaking for peace, not witnessing.

The section has no sin, no exile and no death: the threat is lying speech (120:2-4), and dwelling in Meshech/Kedar is voluntary sojourning, not exile; the word "soul" (nephesh) in 120:2 means the self, not death.
The section has no servant figure, no vicarious suffering and no servant-of-Yahweh language; the speaker suffers hostility but is not portrayed as a servant bearing it for others.
No clause states mercy or restoration; 120:6 states only the long duration of hostile dwelling and 120:1's "He answered me" is deliverance, not restoration.
The section speaks of the LORD as protector but never as king; no clause carries kingship.
No clause in this section depicts the LORD as a warrior or fighting on behalf of anyone; conflict and battle are absent.
The section names the LORD and relies on his relation to his people, but no clause states a covenant, its making, or its terms.

The psalm blesses Jerusalem and its lovers (vv.6-7) and the speaker undertakes to speak peace and seek the city's good (vv.8-9), but no single clause commissions anyone to bless; it is the section's drift.
No clause in the section names a covenant, a covenant partner, or covenant-making; v.4 speaks of 'a testimony for Israel' and the tribes' ascent, not a covenant. The stamp is misplaced here.

Nothing in the section names or describes a king; Ps 123:1 calls God 'the One enthroned in heaven', a heavenly enthronement, not a human (or explicitly royal) king. The clause 'sit in the heavens' speaks of God's throne in heaven, not kingship, and the reader's citation of Ps 123:1 supplies no king words.

Ps 123:3 speaks of 'we', not a servant: 'we have endured much contempt'. The servant/slave image in Ps 123:2 is a simile for the praying community's dependence on God, and no clause attributes suffering to a servant figure.
Ps 123:4 states humiliation only ('We have endured much scorn ... much contempt'); the section contains no clause of vindication or reversal, and the cited verse gives no such turn.

Nothing in Ps 124 is a procession: no going up, no entry, no shrine, no escorting of God or people. Psa.124.1#cl0 'the song of the ascents' is a genre note, not an event, and Ps 124:6-8 is thanksgiving and confession of help, not movement.

No clause in Ps 125:1-5 names a king or royal figure; the cited verse (Ps 125:1) speaks only of 'those who trust in the LORD' and Mount Zion ('the song of the ascents', 'trust in Yahweh', 'like the mountain of Zion'). Yahweh is named but never as king here.

Ps 125:2 ('mountains [are].around (to) it', 'Yahweh [is].around (to) people his from now and until perpetuity') speaks of the LORD surrounding His people as the mountains surround Jerusalem — protective divine presence, not the temple. No clause names the temple or its presence, so the stamp fits only the section's general drift.

The title שִׁיר הַמַּעֲלוֹת is rendered in the clause as "the.song of the.ascents" (Psa.126.1#cl0) and is not a clause about a pilgrim; no clause in this section speaks of a pilgrim or of pilgrimage travel.

The section reports what the LORD has done (great things, restoration of Zion) but no clause names a promise, a word spoken by God, or חֶסֶד; the stamp is the section's drift, not any clause's content.

The reversal in the section is sowing in tears and reaping in joy (Psa.126.5#cl0); no clause speaks of death, of dying or of life coming from a death, and seed committed to the ground is not said to die. The stamp is the later reading of the verse, not what the clauses say.

The gate in Psa.127.5#cl3 is only the place where enemies are confronted; no one who keeps or guards a gate appears in the clause, and the only guarding figure in the section (Psa.127.1#cl3–cl4) is the watchman of the city, which is the 'watchman' stamp, not a gatekeeper.

The section's house, city, watchmen and gate (Psa.127.1, Psa.127.5) evoke a settled realm, but no clause speaks of a king, a throne, rule or dominion; the stamp is general drift, not carried by any clause.
'Fruitful' here is literal agricultural fruitfulness of vine and olive shoots, i.e. wife and children, not the New Testament fruit of the Spirit; nothing in the section speaks of the Spirit.
The woman in v.3 is called 'your wife' (Hebrew 'ishtecha), wife of the blessed man, not a bride; no wedding or betrothal language appears in the section.
The man is the husband/householder of v.3 and the blessed fearer of the LORD in v.1; nothing speaks of a bridegroom or a wedding.
Zion in v.5 is the LORD's holy hill, the place from which he blesses, not a king or royal figure; no king is spoken of.
The blessing 'from Zion' in v.5 is the LORD blessing from his sanctuary-city, not a priest or priestly act.
No prophetic figure or prophetic speech appears; v.5 is a blessing wish, not a prophet.
Nothing in the section speaks of judging or a judge; Zion in v.5 is the city, not a judge.
No servant or service language; 'fear the LORD' (v.1) is devotion, not servitude, and no 'servant' is named.
Nothing in the section speaks of bearing witness; walking in the LORD's ways (v.1) is not witness.
No watchman, wall or keeping-watch language appears; v.5's 'all the days of your life' is duration of blessing, not a watch.
No battle, weapon or warrior language; the section is domestic and peaceful.
The house of v.3 is a dwelling where the wife flourishes, not building work; no builder is spoken of (contrast Ps 127:1, which is a different psalm).
No water, fishing or fish language anywhere in the section.
No gate, door or keeping language; 'your house' (v.3) is a dwelling, not a gate or gate-keeper's post.
'around your table' (v.3) is the family's own table, not a host receiving guests; no hospitality to outsiders is spoken of.
The sons around the table (v.3) are members of the household, not guests; no guest or stranger is named.
v.6 blesses 'Israel' as the whole people with 'Peace be upon Israel'; nothing speaks of a surviving remnant.
No nations or gentiles are spoken of; 'Israel' in v.6 is the covenant people, and 'Zion'/'Jerusalem' in v.5 are Israel's own city.

The wife in Psa.128.3#cl0 is a blessing to the man (fruitful vine), not a figure of wisdom; wisdom in the OT is personified as a woman elsewhere, but nothing in this clause presents her as wisdom, and the Hebrew of Ps 128:3 is an ordinary domestic blessing.
Nothing in Psa.128.3#cl0 or the section portrays the wife as folly; she is the man's blessing, the opposite of the folly-woman of Proverbs.
Nothing in Ps 128:5 (Psa.128.5#cl0/cl1) or the section describes a ruler as a beast; the LORD blessing from Zion is a blessing, not a beastly ruler.
No shepherd or ruler imagery at all in Ps 128:5; the cited verse has the LORD blessing from Zion (Psa.128.5#cl0).
No prophet or prophecy is mentioned in Ps 128:5 or anywhere in the section.
No figure of lawlessness appears in Ps 128:5; the only actor is the LORD blessing (Psa.128.5#cl0).
No second/new Adam figure; Ps 128:1 blesses the God-fearer (Psa.128.1#cl1), which is a generic pious man, not Adam.
No Mosaic figure; Ps 128:1 has no reference to Moses, lawgiving, or exodus.
No Davidic figure or royal language in Ps 128:1 (Psa.128.1#cl1/cl2); the man who fears the LORD is not presented as David.
Ps 128:6 names Israel only in the closing blessing 'Peace be upon Israel' (Psa.128.6#cl1); that is a wish for Israel's peace, not a claim about a new Israel.
Ps 128:5 (Psa.128.5#cl0/cl1) mentions Zion and Jerusalem as places of blessing, with no mention of David or a covenant with him.
No ancestral oath or patriarchal promise is invoked in Ps 128:5; the blessing comes from Zion (Psa.128.5#cl0).
Ps 128 is a wisdom/torah psalm; no clause states or assumes a covenant, though the phrase 'fear the LORD' (Psa.128.1#cl1) belongs to covenant piety generally.
The section is entirely a statement of blessing on the God-fearer (Psa.128.1#cl1, Psa.128.4#cl1), but no clause names a promise, an oath, or God's faithfulness.

The psalm asks for the haters of Zion to be like withered roof grass (Ps 129:6-8), but the Hebrew makes it a wish/declaration with no curse formula (no 'cursed be', no qalal/arur); the word 'curse' never appears in the section.

Ps 129:5 asks for the haters to be turned back in shame, which a reader may take as divine judgment, but no clause states an act of judging, verdict or sentence; it is blessing-and-shame language, not a judgment scene.
Same content as judgment_ev: the wish in Ps 129:5 (turned back in shame) plus the withering in 129:6-7 is the section's judgment-like drift, but no clause names a judging, a judge, or a sentence.

The section does end in blessing (Ps 129:8), but that blessing is withheld from Zion's enemies, not granted to the speaker; no clause promises restoration or mercy to Israel, so only the general blessing tone fits.
The heading names David and the text addresses Yahweh as God and LORD; no clause of this psalm calls anyone king. Ps 13:1's cited verse contains only lament questions.

The enemy is said to be exalted over the psalmist and to prevail over him, but no clause depicts anyone as a warrior, fighting, arming or waging war; 'wrestle in my soul' is inner struggle, not combat imagery.
Ps 13:4 has the enemy's taunt and the foes' rejoicing, and the enemy is said to be 'exalted over me' - a triumph, but no procession, entry, march or parade anywhere in the section.
Ps 13:5 has 'But I have trusted in Your loving devotion' - trust, not an oath; no clause swears, vows, or calls a witness.

This section has a sufferer, but nothing marks him as a servant: no 'servant', no commissioning, no bearing of others' sin, no silence before accusers. The stamp belongs to the Servant songs (Isa 42-53), not to Ps 13's first-person lament. Note this is a judgement about the stamp's fit here, not about later Christian reading of the psalm.
Psa.130.8#cl0 speaks of redeeming Israel from all its iniquities, not of a covenant, a new covenant, or its mediated blessings; nothing in the section mentions a covenant being made or renewed.
The section's redemption language (Psa.130.7#cl3, Psa.130.8#cl0) names the LORD and Israel only; no clause mentions Christ, the Messiah, or any anointed mediator.
Psa.130.1#cl1 has the speaker crying from the depths, but the speaker is the psalmist in first person, not a servant figure, and no clause describes a servant's suffering, vicarious or otherwise.

The section names David only in the superscription ('the.song of the.ascents of David', Psa.131.1#cl0) and addresses Yahweh; no clause says or implies kingship, throne, reign or rule. The stamp is read onto the section from the cited verse's Davidic attribution, not from anything the clauses say.

The only foothold is 'the.song of the.ascents' (Psa.131.1#cl0), a genre label, not a clause that speaks of journeying or pilgrimage; no clause mentions going up, road, or festival. General drift of the collection, not of this section's clauses.

Nothing in Ps 131:2 is a beatitude: Psa.131.2#cl0 ('not I.have.made.still and I.have.made.quiet self my') and Psa.131.2#cl1/#cl2 (the weaned child) are a self-description and simile, with no 'blessed'/'happy' form or declaration of blessing. The stamp's citation of the verse does not match its clauses.
No clause in this section speaks of a coronation or of installing a king; the crown appears only in the antithesis of the final verse (Psa.132.18#cl1), with no crowning act.

No clause speaks of a pilgrim, journey or ascent; 'brothers dwelling together' (Psa.133.1#cl2) is settled cohabitation, and the superscription 'song of ascents' (Psa.133.1#cl0) is a title, not a clause about pilgrims.
Nothing here commissions anyone: Psa.133.3#cl2 has the LORD himself commanding the blessing, with no mediator, recipient or charge to act.
Ps 135:11 names defeated kings (Sihon, Og, the kings of Canaan) in a list of conquests; there is no procession, no entry, no triumphant march in the section, and no clause carries that image.

Ps 135:4 speaks of the LORD choosing Jacob and taking Israel as His treasured possession; the clause has no Abraham, no seed, no land and no covenant formula, and the section never names Abraham, so this named covenant is not spoken of here.
Ps 135:13 speaks of the LORD's enduring name and renown, not of David, his house, or an everlasting throne; no Davidic clause or word appears in the section.

Psalm 136:25 praises God for giving food to all flesh; it does not speak of a covenant made with creation (the clause is 'He gives food to every creature', Psa.136.25#cl0). No clause in the section mentions a covenant with creation, so the stamp has nothing to rest on here.
No clause shows a besieging army or a city invested.
The city is the object of destruction; no clause refers to the temple.
No ruler is named or characterised; only nations and undefined captors/mockers.
There is no אוֹי / “woe” here — the Babylon line is a blessing formula (אַשְׁרֵי), not a woe.
The day named is “the day Jerusalem fell”, a past day of Jerusalem's ruin, not the day of Yahweh.
No eschatological battle is depicted; the clauses are vengeance against Babylon, and v.9 is addressed to “the one who seizes”, not an end-time war.
No act of mercy or restoration is spoken; the section asks Yahweh to remember Edom's cruelty and blesses Babylon's destruction.
The section's drift as a psalm; no clause carries a prophetic utterance from within the section.
the psalm's 'I' is David (Psa.138.1#cl0) and speaks as a dependant of Yahweh, but no clause names a servant role
Ps 139:7 speaks of God's Spirit only as the one from whom the psalmist cannot flee, not as breath, wind or a life-giving spirit; the idea does not attach to any clause here.

Ps 139:23 is God examining the psalmist, the reverse of a witness testifying; no clause here has anyone bearing testimony or being a witness, and the deceitful speech of Ps 139:20 is the enemies' blasphemy, not testimony.
No clause in this section calls anyone servant, slave or attendant; the Hebrew word for servant does not appear. 'Of David' (Psa.139.1#cl1) is an author notice, not a servant role.

There is no image, likeness, or 'in our image' language anywhere in this section, and no echoes of Gen 1:26-27; the wonderful making of Ps 139:14 is God's craftsmanship, which is creation, not image-bearing.
Ps 139:7 concerns God's omnipresence, not a temple or sanctuary; no clause mentions a house, temple, dwelling place or cultic presence. Vv. 8-12 locate God in heaven and Sheol, not in a temple.

Ps 139:16 asserts God's prior writing/ordaining of the psalmist's days, not a promise made and kept; the section contains no covenant, oath, or faithfulness vocabulary, and the cited verse speaks of a book of days, not a promise.
Ps 139:21-22 draws a line between the psalmist and God's enemies, but no clause speaks of a people, nation, congregation or community belonging to God; it is an individual's loyalty, not a people.
The denial 'There is no God' is practical atheism/foolishness, not the worship of another god; no clause names an idol or a rival deity.
The section speaks of 'all' being corrupt with 'not even one' righteous, so no surviving remnant group is named in any clause.
No clause in this section presents a speaker delivering a divine oracle of rebuke or prediction; Ps 14:7 is a wish/prayer for salvation, not a prophetic utterance.

'the day of battle' in Ps 140:7 is the setting in which God shields the psalmist's head; no clause of this section portrays anyone as a warrior or describes warrior activity (arming, fighting, warfare). The stamp is a character role, and no character in these clauses is cast as a warrior.
No clause of this section names or addresses a king; Ps 140:10 speaks only of burning coals, fire and pits for the enemies. Kingship is not spoken of here.

The psalmist is a victim of the wicked and appeals to God, but no clause presents him as a servant of God, and none speaks of vicarious or redemptive suffering; the stamp (a servant who suffers for others) has no clause here.

David is named only in the superscription 'a.psalm of David' (Psa.141.1#cl0); no clause in this section speaks of him as king, and David's kingship is nowhere asserted or presupposed by the text here.
The clauses cited (Psa.141.5#cl0, #cl2, #cl6) are the righteous man's blow and rebuke and the psalmist's prayer against the wicked; none speaks of testimony or witnessing.
Psa.141.10 speaks of the wicked falling into their own nets and the psalmist passing by, with no warfare, arms, or fighting.

The heading calls David 'a.poem of David' with the cave setting (Psa.142.1#cl0-cl2); nothing in the section names or addresses a king, and the speaker's own role is petitioner, not king. The stamp as a character role present here is not carried by any clause.
No clause speaks of prophecy, a prophetic word, or a prophet's role; the heading (Psa.142.1#cl0) names David and a prayer only.

The petitioner never calls himself a servant of the LORD in this section; Psa.142.6#cl0-cl1 address God directly ('I.cry.out to you / O.Yahweh') without a servant term, and no other clause supplies one.

Ps 142:4's 'no one attends to me / no one cares for my soul' (Psa.142.5#cl2, cl5) speaks of the absence of anyone who regards the speaker, i.e. the opposite of a witness; no clause presents a witness or witnessing.
Nothing in the section speaks of a stranger or sojourner. Psa.142.6#cl4 'portion my in the.land of the.living' concerns the LORD as the speaker's portion, not alien status.
No clause portrays the speaker or God as a warrior; Ps 142:6 (Psa.142.7#cl2, cl3) has the speaker as the one pursued and overpowered, not fighting.
Conflict language is present (enemies, deliverance), but no clause in this section describes anyone as a warrior or depicts combat.
Nothing in Ps 143:1 or the section involves a priest, cult, temple or mediation; the cited verse is a plea for a hearing.

No clause in this section mentions a stone, a builder, a cornerstone or a rejection; the stamp's image is absent from Ps 16 entirely.
