No creation-wide covenant, cosmic order or Noahic covenant language; 34:10's young lions and seekers are creatures in want, not a covenant with creation.
No legal contest, lawsuit or courtroom exchange anywhere in the section; the troubles and cries are physical danger and affliction, not litigation.
The assembly of Psa.34.4 is a call to magnify the LORD, with no procession, march or triumph over enemies described.
No oil, pouring, or setting apart of a person appears in the section.
No king is installed, crowned or enthroned; Psa.34.4#cl1 exalts the LORD's name, not a ruler's accession.
The angel encamping and the delivering are rescue of the weak (Psa.34.8#cl0–cl1), with no combat, weapons or armies; no war language is used.
No human judge, deliverer or ruler is raised up; the LORD alone delivers, and the wicked are condemned (Psa.34.22#cl1).
Taste and see (Psa.34.9#cl0–cl1) is a metaphor for experiencing the LORD's goodness; no bread, meal, table or breaking of food appears.
No individual servant figure bears suffering on behalf of others; Psa.34.20–21 speaks of the righteous collectively, though Christian usage applies it to Christ.
The section has no temple, sanctuary, house or dwelling place; the angel encamping (Psa.34.8#cl0) is protection, not temple presence.

No clause names or addresses God as king; the divine titles used are LORD, Lord, my God (e.g. Psa.35.23#cl1, Psa.35.23#cl2, Psa.35.24#cl1), and 'of David' (Psa.35.1#cl0) names the psalm's author, not a king role in the section.

The psalm's sufferer and the 'servant' of 35:27 are not joined in any clause here: the sufferer speaks as 'I/my soul' in the first person (Psa.35.13#cl1, Psa.35.13#cl3, Psa.35.12#cl1) with no clause calling him God's servant, and the 'servant' appears only in the phrase His servant's well-being (Psa.35.27#cl3) with no suffering. The title is a reading across the psalm, not something a clause states.
No clause of Ps 36 names or addresses David as king; the Hebrew title word is 'servant' (Psa.36.1#cl1) only.
This psalm contains no beatitude; the blessed formula as a class does not occur in the clauses here.
No clause of this psalm names, addresses or depicts a king; the cited verse 37:1 concerns fretting over evildoers, not a king.
The psalm's contrast between the cut-off wicked and the preserved righteous (37:9-11, 28) is remnant-shaped in drift, but no clause marks a surviving remnant as such.
No nation, people-group or 'goi' appears in the section; the cited verse 37:12 concerns an individual wicked man scheming.
No clause mentions David, an oath, or an everlasting covenant; 37:29 is a general promise of the land to the righteous, not the Davidic covenant.
37:15 is a private reversal on the wicked (their own swords pierce them), not a climactic eschatological battle; no battle of the nations appears.
No heavenly book, record or opening of books is spoken of; 37:33 is the LORD preventing condemnation in judgment, not a books-opened scene.
The section speaks only of the righteous inheriting and dwelling in 'the land' forever; nothing concerns new heavens, a new earth, or a recreated cosmos.
No one is called servant, and 37:30 (the righteous man's mouth uttering wisdom) is the wise man, not a servant of the LORD.
The section never calls the LORD father or depicts fatherhood as a role; 37:25 speaks only of the righteous man's children.
No clause shows anyone receiving, feeding or sheltering a guest; 37:19 promises the righteous will be satisfied in famine, which is the LORD's provision, not hospitality.
No one is received or hosted in this section; 37:19's 'they will be satisfied' is blessing from the LORD, not a guest at a table.
There is no journey, road or pilgrimage in the section; the 'dwell/inherit the land' hope (37:3, 9, 11, 29) is settled land-possession rather than pilgrimage, so at most the stamp is general drift.
Wisdom in 37:30 is what a righteous man's mouth utters; wisdom is nowhere personified as a woman in this section.
Ps 37:30 speaks of the mouth of the righteous man uttering wisdom, which is the opposite of a false prophet; nothing in the section describes a false prophet.
Ps 37:37 speaks of the blameless and upright man and the man of peace, not of a new Adam or a representative head of a new humanity.
Ps 37:31 has the law of God in the heart of the ordinary righteous man, not a new Moses who gives or mediates the law.
Ps 37:39 calls the LORD their stronghold, but the section has no armour, no armour items and no command to put armour on.
No clause here states any of the ten commandments; the law of God in the heart of Ps 37:31 is a statement about the law being internal, not a list of commandments.
Ps 37:29 and 37:11 promise the inheritance of the land, not a new creation; nothing in the section speaks of a new heaven, new earth or renewed creation.
Ps 37:20 says the wicked perish and fade away like smoke; no clause in the section has death producing life.
No clause in this section has a servant, service, or slave—the psalmist is a sufferer and suppliant (Psa.38.16#cl0 'for you I have waited'), not described as anyone's servant.
The prayers in this section are for the psalmist himself ('do not forsake me ... come quickly to help me'), not intercession on behalf of others, and no priest or sacrificial mediator appears.
No oath, vow, or swearing formula occurs in this section; the psalm's speech is petition and confession, not oath-taking.

No plaintiff, indictment, covenant summons or formal accusation by God appears; the enemies' words against him (Psa.38.13) are not a lawsuit and God is addressed as healer/savior, not as prosecuting party.
There is no 'woe to...' oracle against anyone; the only 'woe'-like speech is the psalmist's own complaint about his suffering.
No divine promise is spoken or reported; Psa.38.16#cl2 'You will answer' is the psalmist's confidence, not an oracle from God.
No anointing, oil, or anointed figure is mentioned anywhere in the section.
No crowning, throne, or acclamation of a king occurs; the psalm is a sick man's lament, and its heading names only David.
No reference to God's covenant with David, his dynasty or throne appears in these verses.
There is no battle scene, army or fighting; the enemies lay snares and speak (Psa.38.13), and the arrows/hand of Psa.38.3 are God's discipline, not combat.
No procession, triumph or celebration; the section ends with a plea for rescue, not a victory march.
Fasting is nowhere mentioned or implied in these verses; the mourning of Psa.38.7#cl2 is lament, not a fast.
No challenge, contest, or wager is framed; the psalmist makes no defense of a case but appeals for mercy and help.
No sacrifice, offering, altar or cultic act appears; the psalm's remedy is confession (Psa.38.19#cl0) and divine help, not sacrifice.

Nothing in the section speaks of the Passover: no lamb, blood, unleavened bread, or passing over; Ps 38:17 ('I am ready to fall, and my pain is ever with me', Psa.38.18#cl0-cl1) is lament, not the night of Exodus.
The confession in Ps 38:18 ('I confess my iniquity; I am troubled by my sin', Psa.38.19#cl0-cl1) is personal confession, with no priest, altar, blood, fast, or two goats as in Lev 16.
Ps 38:4's 'my iniquities have overwhelmed me; they are a burden too heavy to bear' (Psa.38.5#cl0-cl1) is a burden image, but nothing is laid on a goat or sent into the wilderness.
Ps 38:6's 'I am bent and brought low; all day long I go about mourning' (Psa.38.7#cl0-cl2) is the psalmist's own bowed mourning, not Israel's journey or camp in the desert.
No numeral or period of forty appears anywhere in the section; 'all day long' (Psa.38.7#cl2) and 'continually' (Psa.38.18#cl1) are open-ended, not forty.
Ps 38:5's wounds festering 'because of my sinful folly' (Psa.38.6#cl1) and Ps 38:18's confession name sin already committed, not an enticement to sin.
Ps 38:1's superscription 'A psalm of David. To bring remembrance' (Psa.38.1#cl0-cl1) is a title, not a call or sending; no one is appointed to a task here.
Ps 38:20's 'Those who repay my good with evil attack me for pursuing the good' (Psa.38.21#cl0-cl2) is persecution, not a blessing given or received.
Ps 38:1 'A psalm of David. To bring remembrance' (Psa.38.1#cl0-cl1) attaches a name but no one is named, renamed, or given a name in this section.
Ps 38:9's 'O Lord, my every desire is before You; my groaning is not hidden from You' (Psa.38.10#cl0-cl2) is prayer about the psalmist's inner state, with no creating, making or forming.

Ps 38:10's 'My heart pounds, my strength fails, and even the light of my eyes has faded' (Psa.38.11#cl0-cl3) describes failing vitality, but no word for breath, wind or spirit occurs, and none is called God's spirit.
Ps 38:1's superscription (Psa.38.1#cl0-cl1) is a psalm title; no commandments, covenant, mountain, or mediator, and no law is given.
David is named only in the superscription (Psa.39.1#cl2 'a.psalm of David'); no clause of the psalm's body presents him as king, and the Davidic superscription is not itself a clause about kingship.
No clause speaks of prophecy, a prophet, or prophetic speech; Psa.39.4#cl2 'I.spoke with tongue my' is the psalmist's own speech, not prophecy.
The section moves from silenced suffering to appeal for deliverance, but no clause states a reversal from humiliation to vindication; it is the psalm's drift, not a formulated idea in any clause.
No clause in Ps 4 states a blessing formula (no 'blessed/happy' equivalent); the stamp is a category label for the whole psalm.
No clause presents a priest, a priestly act, or intercession on behalf of others: Psa.4.2#cl0-5 are David's own plea for himself, and nothing in the section names a priest or a mediating role.
No clause mentions a covenant, Davidic promise, eternal throne or seed; Psa.4.1#cl2 'a psalm of David' only names authorship, not a covenant.
No clause ascribes kingship to anyone; the section has no 'king/melek', no throne and no royal act. Psa.4.1#cl2 names David, but the clause says 'a psalm of David', not 'the king'.
No clause speaks of a prophet, prophecy or a prophetic word; nothing here names or describes a prophetic role.
No clause has battle, weapon, army or martial language.
No clause uses 'servant/ebed' or describes service to a master.
No clause has testimony, witness or legal-testimony language.
No clause has watching, keeping watch, or a watchman's report; Psa.4.5#cl2-3 ('on your bed ... be still') is self-examination and silence, not watchman duty.
No clause pronounces or describes judgment/legal arbitration; the psalm addresses the wicked and asks God for help, but no judging role or act appears.
No clause has shepherd, flock or pasture imagery; Psa.4.8#cl0 names grain and new wine, not pasture or sheep.
No clause calls God 'father' or names a father-son relation (cf. Psa.4.3#cl0 'O sons of man' is 'sons' of men, not of God).
No clause describes a son role; Psa.4.3#cl0 'O sons of man' names men addressed as mortals, not a son of God or of David.
No clause has firstborn language or imagery.
No clause presents a new/coming David or applies Davidic promise language to anyone in the psalm.
No clause mentions Moses, exodus, law-giving or a mediator like him.

No clause speaks of Israel, its restoration, or a renewed people; Psa.4.4#cl0-1 and Psa.4.3#cl0 could bear on a faithful/godly group, but the clauses name 'the faithful/godly' and 'sons of man', not Israel.
No clause has Adam, creation or new-creation language.
No clause names a remnant or a surviving/delivered group; Psa.4.4#cl0-1 sets apart 'the faithful/godly', but the text says nothing of survival, a residue, or remnant-of-Israel.
Psa.4.3#cl0 addresses 'O sons of man' (men, not nations/goyim); no clause names the nations or treats them as a character.
Vanity and lies in Psa.4.3#cl2-3 are the opponents' general falsehood, not a prophet or prophetic claim.
No clause has shepherding or leadership-of-a-flock imagery that the opponents abuse.
No clause names a lawless man/antichrist figure; Psa.4.5#cl1 'do not sin' is an exhortation to the hearers, not a character.
Ps 4:2 addresses human 'sons of man' who love vanity and falsehood; no beast, beast-king or ruler imagery appears in the section.
No woman and no personified Folly is spoken of anywhere in Ps 4; the addressees are 'O men / sons of man'.
No woman and no personified Wisdom appears in the section.
Nothing in Ps 4 speaks of a bride or marriage.
Nothing in Ps 4 speaks of a bridegroom or wedding.
No guest, table or hospitality setting occurs in the section.
No host or hospitality setting occurs in the section.
No journey, road or pilgrimage is spoken of in Ps 4.
No gate, door or gatekeeper appears in the section.
No fishing or fisherman imagery occurs in Ps 4.
No vineyard or vine-tending is spoken of; 'new wine' in v.7 is a harvest blessing, not vine-dressing.
No building, house or construction imagery occurs in the section.
No slave, servant or bondage language appears in Ps 4.
No stranger or sojourner is spoken of; 'dwell in safety' (v.8) is about secure dwelling, not alien status.
No mother, childbirth or maternal image occurs in the section.
The section asks God for the light of His face and invokes the LORD, but no clause speaks of God's rule, king or reign.
Nothing in Ps 40:8 ('Your law is within my heart', Psa.40.9#cl3) names or implies a covenant, let alone a new one; 'new covenant' is read into the verse by Hebrews 10:16, not present here.
David the king is named only in the superscription 'of David a psalm' (Psa.40.1#cl1), which names the author, not a clause speaking of kingship; no clause in the section ascribes a royal role or act.
No clause in Ps 41 mentions a journey, a feast, or going up to the house of the LORD; the cited reference (Ps 42:4) is outside this section.
No clause here reports testimony or bearing witness; the cited reference (Ps 42:10) is outside this section.
The doxology names the God of Israel, the community's God, but no clause speaks of the people as a body; I read this stamp as the section's general frame rather than a pinned idea.
No clause in the section mentions a covenant, its oath, its parties or its signs; 'my integrity' and 'Your presence' are personal, not covenant formulary.
No clause in Ps 41 mentions the Spirit or God's Spirit; the cited reference (Ps 42:8) is outside this section.
Nothing in Ps 41 mentions Christ, the cross or redemption; the cited reference (Ps 42:11) is outside this section, and any Christian reading is external to these clauses.
No clause in the section speaks of a king, kingship, or royal rule; Psa.43.4#cl0 (altar of God) is priestly/temple language, not royal, and the only cited verse (Ps 43:4) contains no king.
Nothing in the section speaks of testifying, witnessing or bearing witness; Ps 43:3 asks that light and truth be sent to lead the speaker, which is guidance, not witness.
The section speaks of God's holy mountain and dwelling place as the destination the speaker longs to reach (Psa.43.3#cl2), not as destroyed; no clause mentions destruction.
No clause speaks of deportation, captivity or being carried away from the land; the enemy's oppression (Psa.43.2#cl2) and unjust men (Psa.43.1#cl4) are named, but not exile.

The section pleads for the survival of the whole people and never speaks of a surviving remnant; the closest phrase, 'we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered', describes being killed, not preserved.

The Leviticus 16 scapegoat is sent away bearing sin; here - 'You have given us up as sheep to be devoured', 'You sell Your people for nothing', 'we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered' - the sheep imagery is of slaughter and sale, with no sending away and no bearing of guilt.
Israel as God's people/servants is the assumed backdrop, but no clause here speaks of serving; 'we face death all day long' is suffering for God's sake, not service.
No clause in this section names or addresses a bridegroom; the bride is led to 'the king' (Psa.45.15#cl0), and the stamp rests on that picture rather than on any particular clause.

No clause depicts God as a warrior: the weapons in Psa.46.10#cl1-cl3 are broken and burned (note the English "He breaks the bow and shatters the spear" corresponds to Hebrew 'bows he breaks' and 'spears he cuts in two' — 'he cuts' is the verb of Psa.46.10#cl2), not wielded, and the only divine speech-act is Psa.46.7#cl2 'he.gave.forth with voice his'. Israel's army is the subject of no clause here.

The section has de-creation (Psa.46.3#cl1 'changes [the].earth', Psa.46.4#cl2, Psa.46.7#cl3 'it.melted [the].earth') but no clause of a new heaven and earth; that is the stamp 'cosmic_collapse', not this one. Stamped from Ps 46:2, which in the clause division is Psa.46.3#cl0.
David is never named and no clause carries Davidic covenant language; the closest is the title "the God of Jacob" in Psa.46.8#cl1, which is Jacob/Israel, not David.

Genesis 8:22 / covenant-with-creation language is about the ordering of creation continuing; here creation is undone (Psa.46.3#cl0, Psa.46.4#cl2, Psa.46.7#cl3) and no covenant with creation is asserted. Stamped from Ps 46:2 = Psa.46.3#cl1 'changes [the].earth', which is the opposite.

The section's reused refrain ('The LORD of Hosts is with us', Psa.46.8#cl0-cl1) and God's help 'when morning dawns' (Psa.46.6#cl2) carry the general assurance, but no clause makes a promise or names faithfulness.
The section's king is God/the LORD himself (Psa.47.8#cl0 'God is King of all the earth'); no Davidic figure, or anyone standing in for David, is named or described anywhere in the clauses.
The only Abrahamic material is the name in Psa.47.9#cl2, 'the people of the God of Abraham'; nothing in the clauses speaks of a covenant, its making, its promises or its sign.
The section attests God's favour to Jacob/Abraham but nowhere states a promise or its keeping; no clause carries the idea itself.
The section has Zion, God as king and eternal establishment, but no clause speaks of David or of the covenant with him.
Nothing in the section speaks of creation renewed; Zion's establishment forever is not the same idea.

The verse cited (49:5) is the psalmist's own fear of wicked usurpers surrounding him; no clause in the section depicts an act of judgment — the closest, Psa.49.15#cl1 'death it will.shepherd.them', describes death's shepherding, not a divine judgment event.

Psa.49.16#cl0 'surely God he.will.redeem life my from the.hand of.Sheol' and cl1 'he will.take.me' speak of rescue from Sheol, not of a rising/resurrection event; nothing in the section describes the dead being raised.
No clause in the section names Christ or refers to him; Psa.49.16#cl0's 'God will redeem my life' is the psalmist's own redemption and Psa.49.8#cl0 denies that any man can pay a ransom.
Ps 5:9 speaks of the enemies' untrustworthy speech, open graves and deceitful tongues, not of anyone bearing witness or giving testimony.
Duplicate of the earlier oath_swearing pin; if a single entry is wanted, keep the one with clause Psa.50.14#cl1.

The section is a first-person plea for personal cleansing; no priest, no intercession on another's behalf, and no cultic ritual act is performed or named. Washing/purification (Psa.51.9) is petitioned, not enacted by a priest.
The section speaks of renewal of heart and spirit, which a reader may take as the drift of new-covenant promise, but no clause itself names or describes a covenant.
Zion/Jerusalem building (Psa.51.18) may evoke David's throne-city, but no clause states a covenant with David.
The section has the speaker confessing and God as the offended party; no witness is named or called.
Pleading language is present but no clause names the speaker or anyone as servant.
The speaker is David, but no clause says son or describes a father-son relation.
God is addressed, but never as father in this section.
No enemy is named; the opposition in the section is the speaker's own sin.
No watchman figure or watchkeeping act appears.
No warfare or warrior appears in the section.
No host or hospitality appears; Psa.51.17's 'You will not despise' is not hosting.
Zion/Jerusalem is named but no remnant is spoken of.
No nation or peoples appear; 'transgressors' and 'sinners' are individuals, not nations.
Wisdom is taught by God (Psa.51.8), not personified as a woman.
No folly figure appears; the section's sin is the speaker's own, not a woman.
The speaker is David himself, not a new David.
Zion/Jerusalem is named (Psa.51.18) but nothing marks a new Israel.
Nothing in this section presents David as a new Moses; the only figure named is David the psalmist (Psa.51.1#cl1, Psa.51.2#cl0-cl2), and no clause sets him over against Moses or in a Moses-like role.
No rock, wilderness, or water-from-rock imagery occurs in this section; the washing of Ps 51:7 rests on hyssop and snow, not on water struck from a rock.
The hyssop of Ps 51:7 has no passover features here; no lamb, blood, doorpost or passing-over is spoken of, so the hyssop need not carry the passover image.
No atonement day elements are named — no scapegoat, no blood manipulation, no high priest, no holy place; cleansing by hyssop is not by itself the day's rite.
Ps 51:9 asks God to hide His face from my sins and blot out my iniquities; there is no sending away, no goat, no wilderness, no bearer of sin.

Ps 51:7 has hyssop and washing, but no priest, no altar, no offering rite performed by a priest — the cleansing is asked of God directly; the sacrificial and priestly material of the psalm is elsewhere and is about its cessation.

Nothing in Ps 51 is prophetic speech: the section is David's first-person prayer of confession, petition and vow (Psa.51.1#cl1 'a psalm of David'; Psa.51.2#cl0 names Nathan the prophet only as the one who came to him, not as a word spoken through him). No clause reports a divine word coming to or through a prophet, and no clause is introduced as prophecy; the reader's citation of Ps 51:1 points only at the superscription, which supplies no such idea.

No clause names a king or royal office; 'O mighty man' (Psa.52.3#cl1) is a description of the adversary, and the superscription (Psa.52.2#cl0–cl4) concerns Doeg, not a king. The stamp fits only as the general drift of a psalm addressed to a powerful man.

I could not determine a clause id for this line from the list supplied. The clause list jumps from Psa.53.6#cl4 to the end of the section with no clauses given for Ps 53:6 (English) — 'Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come from Zion! When God restores His captive people...'. The only wording in this section that speaks of captivity ('His captive people') is in that missing line, so no listed clause carries the stamp and I cannot pin it.

Same gap as captivity: 'restores His captive people' is the only clause that could carry return_from_exile, and it falls in the unlisted final verse of the section. Nothing in Psa.53.1#cl0–Psa.53.6#cl4 speaks of a return.

Nothing in this section speaks of a new David or of a Davidic figure to come. 'A poem of David' (Psa.53.1#cl2) names the author of the psalm, not a new David; the heading is a superscription, not the psalm's content.
No clause names a king or a royal figure. Israel is named only in the closing wish for salvation (unlisted in the clause list), and no kingship language appears anywhere in Psa.53.1#cl0–Psa.53.6#cl4.

The restoration and the joy of Jacob/Israel are the section's closing wish, which sits in the final verse that has no clause ids in the list given. No listed clause carries mercy or restoration, so this is marked general, but the stamp is right for the section as a whole.

The only deliverance wording in this section is 'the salvation of Israel... from Zion', which is in the final verse with no clause ids supplied. Psa.53.6#cl2–cl4 describe God's judgment on the enemies, not Israel's deliverance, so no listed clause carries the stamp.

The people of God are named only in the unlisted final verse (Israel, Jacob, His captive people). The nearest listed clause is Psa.53.5#cl1, 'they devour my people like bread' in the English text, but in the clause list that line is given as '[those.who].devour people (of).my they.eat bread' at Psa.53.5#cl1 — I judge it wrong to pin people_of_god there because the clause describes the wicked devouring the people, not the people of God as such, and I am not certain the 'my people' of the Hebrew corresponds to the Berean 'my people' in this versification. Flagging the versification problem rather than guessing.

Nothing in the section presents God or David as king; the cited verse Ps 54:1 ('Save me, O God, by Your name') has only the vocative 'O God' (Psa.54.3#cl0) and a plea for salvation/vindication (Psa.54.3#cl1-2). David is named only as 'a.poem of David' in the superscription (Psa.54.1#cl2), which is a title, not a royal role. No clause carries kingship.

The clauses describe hostile men rising up and seeking the speaker's life, but nothing presents anyone carrying the role 'warrior' — no arms, battle, or combatant language; the clause is a statement of threat, not a warrior character. If the stamp is meant to be the enemies as fighters it is stretched; as a role present in the section there is no clause that carries it.

The cited verse Ps 54:4 names God as 'my helper' and 'the sustainer of my soul' (Psa.54.6#cl1-3, cf. Psa.54.6#cl0 'here!'), i.e. God as helper, not the speaker as servant. No clause uses 'servant' or servant language of the psalmist.

The cited verse Ps 54:6 ('Freely I will sacrifice to You; I will praise Your name') concerns a vow of sacrifice and praise, not testimony. No clause in the section speaks of witnessing, testimony, or a witness.

No clause pictures a procession, entry, or celebratory march. The cited verse Ps 54:7 ('He has delivered me from every trouble, and my eyes have stared down my foes') has no clause id in the supplied list at all — the last clauses given are Psa.54.7#cl0-1, which are the imprecation, not a procession. The section's deliverance is stated, not enacted as a procession.

The cited verse Ps 54:6 ('Freely I will sacrifice to You; I will praise Your name, O LORD, for it is good') is the individual speaker's vow, with no clause naming a people, congregation, Israel, or community. The 'strangers'/'ruthless men' in Psa.54.5 are the enemies, not God's people.
The psalmist's stance as one who calls on God and trusts in Him runs through the section, but no clause states a servant role.
Psa.55.21#cl1 says he violates his covenant, the breach of an existing covenant, not the cutting of one; nothing in the section describes covenant-cutting.
No oath, vow or swearing appears in the section; 'covenant' in Psa.55.21#cl1 is not an oath.
The wish to fly away and lodge in the wilderness (Psa.55.7, Psa.55.8, Psa.55.9) is flight and dwelling, not deportation into exile.

Psa.55.19#cl0 ('He redeems my soul in peace') and Psa.55.23#cl1-2 ('He will sustain you') are restoration, not healing of sickness; no clause names healing. Not marked wrong because a broad reading could include it.
Psa.55.16#cl1 wishes the wicked to go down to Sheol alive; that is the opposite of resurrection, and no raising of the dead appears in the section.
God's enthronement and coming judgment of the wicked (Psa.55.20, Psa.55.23) is the section's drift, but no clause speaks of the day of the LORD.
The battle of Psa.55.19#cl0 is the psalmist's present conflict, not an eschatological final battle; nothing in the section is final or cosmic.
No books, records or opening of books appear anywhere in the section.
No new creation, new heavens or new earth is spoken of; the psalm asks for judgment on the wicked and the psalmist's own deliverance.
No shepherd in any sense is named: Psa.55.19#cl0 says 'He redeems my soul in peace from the battle waged against me', not that He shepherds. (I found no shepherd-language clause in this section.)
Walking into the house of God with the crowd (Psa.55.15#cl2) is worship attendance, not priestly service, and no priest or priestly act appears.
No prophet, prophetic speech or oracle appears in the section.
No clause in this section names or implies a son: Ps 55:13's clause Psa.55.14#cl0 speaks of David's close friend ('friend my.close'), not a son, and nothing else in the section carries the role.

The cited verse (Ps 55:14) has only Psa.55.15#cl0/cl1 'we.made.sweet counsel' and Psa.55.15#cl2 'in the.house of.God we.walked.about in a.crowd' — shared fellowship and worship, no bridegroom, wedding or marriage language anywhere in the section.
Same cited verse Ps 55:14 contains no bridal figure or marriage imagery; the clauses describe David and his companion as companions in worship.

Ps 55:19 (Psa.55.20#cl0 'he.will.hear God and [he.is].sitting antiquity' … Psa.55.20#cl6 'not they.fear God') speaks of God as the eternal enthroned one, not as a father, and no clause in the section calls anyone father.

Ps 55:15 (Psa.55.16#cl0 'may.it.deceive death on them', Psa.55.16#cl1 'may.they.go.down Sheol alive', Psa.55.16#cl2 'evil.deeds [are].in sojourning-place their') has no firstborn or birthright language.

The section speaks throughout in God's own first-person voice (I relieved, I rescued, I answered, I tested, I gave them up) and never sets up a later mediator like Moses; 'I tested you at the waters of Meribah' names the event but not a new Moses. General drift of the psalm's divine speech only.
The psalm is 'of Asaph' (Psa.81.1#cl2) and never names David or a royal successor; the human leader mentioned is Joseph (Psa.81.6#cl0). No clause carries the idea.

No Israel, exodus, wilderness or covenant-people language in the section.

Ps 91:16 is "With long life I will satisfy him and show him My salvation" — long life is length of days in this life, not raising from the dead; no death or raising language anywhere in the section.

Ps 91:13 is "You will tread on the lion and cobra; you will trample the young lion and serpent" — victory over beasts, with no king, throne, reign or dominion in the section.

Ps 91:16 is "With long life I will satisfy him and show him My salvation" — long life and salvation to an individual, with no renewal of creation, new heavens or new earth in the section.

This section shows only the book's apocalyptic opening (revelation, angel, soon-coming events); nothing in it uses seven or any series of seven.

No priest, no priestly act, no temple service in this section. The stamper's citation (22:9) concerns fellow servants and prophets, not priests.
No nations appear in this section; 22:15 lists types of persons (dogs, sorcerers, etc.), not nations.
No curse is pronounced or removed in this section; being outside the city (22:15) is exclusion, not a curse. Rev.22:3's 'no longer any curse' lies outside this section.
No raising of the dead in this section; 22:12's coming-and-reward is not a resurrection statement.
No procession, entry-in-triumph image; 22:14's entering the city by the gates is the blessed ones' admission, not Christ's victory procession.
No crowning or enthronement in this section. The Alpha/Omega and First/Last (22:13) and the morning star (22:16) are titles, not a coronation.
No covenant, no peace, no covenant formula in this section.
No oath, no swearing, no sworn formula. Rev.22.6's 'These words are faithful and true' is an assertion of reliability, not an oath; the stamper's citation of 22:6 does not support the stamp.

Rev 22:15 'But outside are the dogs, the sorcerers...' is a flat declarative list of who is excluded, not a woe ('woe to...') pronounced over them; the section contains no woe formula anywhere (cf. Rev 8:13; 11:14; 12:12).

Rev 22:13 'I am the Alpha and the Omega...' is a self-identification formula spoken in first person, with no appearance, no sight of the divine glory and no human reaction of awe or fear, which is what a theophany clause would carry.
Rev 22:17 is the Spirit, the bride and the hearer inviting the thirsty to come; nothing in the section speaks of the Spirit being poured out or given, of tongues, or of the events of Acts 2.
Rev 22:17 promises 'the water of life' to the one who desires it, which is salvation/life given, not a distribution of charismata (Rom 12; 1 Cor 12) to believers.
No clause lists character qualities produced by the Spirit (contrast Gal 5:22-23); Rev 22:17 is an invitation, not a description of the Spirit's fruit in a life.
Rev 22:6 reads 'the God of the spirits of the prophets', which is God's relation to the prophets' spirits, not the sevenfold Spirit of Rev 1:4; 3:1; 4:5; 5:6.
Rev 22:16 says 'to give you this testimony for the churches' (plural, undifferentiated); no seven named churches appear in this section.
Rev 22:12 speaks of reward 'to give to each one according to what he has done', not of books being opened (contrast Rev 20:12); no book is opened or read in this section.

No clause in this section states a covenant, covenant-making, or covenant formula; the cited Rev 3:3 speaks of remembering and keeping what was received, which is not the covenant idea itself. I judge the stamp wrong for this section.
The section is addressed to one church only (Rev.3.7#cl0); the seven-church frame is the drift of the letters as a whole, not said in any clause here.
The only temple language here is positive — the overcomer made a pillar in God's temple (Rev.3.12#cl2); nothing in the section speaks of a temple destroyed.
Rev 4:1 opens the vision sequence, but no clause in this section carries the idea of sevens.
Jasper, carnelian and emerald describe the appearance of the One on the throne and the rainbow; nothing in these clauses speaks of new creation.

No clause in this section names a priest, priesthood, sacrifice or temple service. The elders' falling down and casting crowns is homage, not priestly action; 'Holy, Holy, Holy' and 'Worthy are You' do not entail it. Nothing here carries the idea.

The section shows God's reign — the throne, the elders' homage, the acclamation of the Lord God Almighty — but no clause says 'kingdom', 'reign', 'king' or 'rule'. The stamp is the section's general drift, not carried by a particular clause.

Nothing in this section speaks of renewal, new heavens/new earth, resurrection or the passing of the old order. The glassy sea (4.6#cl0) and the four living creatures are not new-creation language, and 4.11 speaks of the original creation ('You created all things'), not of new creation.
No clause in Rev 5:1-10 carries testimony or witnessing; the nearest thing is the elders' song (Rev.5.9#cl0, Rev.5.9#cl1), which is praise, not witness.
The section's blood and purchased-for-God language (Rev.5.9#cl6) is redemption imagery; no clause here speaks of a covenant, new or old.
Nothing in this section is prophecy as spoken word; the elder's speech (Rev.5.5#cl2) is an announcement of what has already happened ('has triumphed'), and the song is praise.
Rev 5:3 (Rev.5.3#cl0) states no one was able, not that anyone is judged; no clause of this section pronounces or describes judgment.

The clause the stamp's verse could rest on, Rev.5.9#cl6 ('You purchased - to God by the blood of You out of every tribe and tongue and people and nation'), speaks of purchase/ransom by blood, not of believers being 'in' Christ or joined to him; nowhere in Rev.5.1-5.10 does any clause express incorporation into Christ, and the Berean text has no 'in Christ', 'in Him' or equivalent wording.

The stamp's cited verse (Rev 5:10) speaks of being made 'a kingdom and priests' and reigning on the earth, which is kingship/priesthood language, not image-of-God language; no clause in Rev.5.10#cl0 or #cl1, and no clause elsewhere in the section, mentions image, likeness, or being made in God's image.

The cited verse Rev 5:9 contains purchase and the list of tribes/tongues/peoples/nations, but no blessing and no commission to a person or people; the only commissioning-like note (the seven Spirits 'sent out into all the earth', Rev.5.6#cl5) is a sending of the Spirits, not a blessing given to anyone in this section.

No clause in Rev 5:11-14 names a priest, a priestly act, or mediation; the cited verse (5:12) says only that the Lamb was slain — sacrificial victim, not priest. The elders' falling down (Rev.5.14#cl1) is worship, not priestly service.

No clause in this section carries the numbered sevenfold pattern; 5:12 lists seven items, but the Greek text the gloss preserves (power, riches, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, blessing) is not marked as a seven in the clause and 5:13's and 5:14's groups are four (living creatures, elders) and four (praise terms). The list is a feature of the whole-book structure, not of any clause here.
No clause in 5:11-14 speaks of a people, the redeemed community, or its members; the groups named are angels, living creatures and elders. The nearest clause (5:9) is outside the section.
Nothing in 5:11-14 judges anyone; the scene is unbroken praise. "Worthy" in 5:12 is an ascription of worth, not a verdict rendered on others.
No clause mentions mercy, forgiveness, or restoration; the section is praise for the Lamb's worthiness, and the ground of mercy (ransom, 5:9) lies outside it.
No promise, oath, or fulfillment language appears in these clauses; the aorist participles (having been slain) and present praises carry no promise-faithfulness statement.
As with priest: the elders' prostration (Rev.5.14#cl1) and worship (cl2) are acts of homage in a throne room, not priestly ministry; no clause names priests or priestly service.
The Spirit (the seven spirits of 5:6) is not mentioned in any clause of 5:11-14; the plural "myriads of myriads" and the sevenfold list in 5:12 are not the Spirit.
No clause states believers' being in Christ, or any identity between the worshippers and the Lamb; the creatures and elders praise him from outside, they are not said to be in him.

No clause here is a prophecy, a "thus says the Lord", or a report of a prophetic utterance; the words spoken are doxologies of praise, not prophetic speech. The framing "I looked, and I heard" (5:11) is visionary reportage, not prophecy delivered.
No clause mentions image, likeness, or humanity as God's image-bearers; "every creature" in 5:13 is creation in general, not the imago Dei.
The blessing named in 5:12-13 is blessing ascribed to God and the Lamb in worship, not a blessing given to humans, nor any commission to be fruitful or to go.
No covenant, oath, or covenant formula appears in these clauses; "to the ages of the ages" (Rev.5.13#cl0) is an eternal-duration phrase in doxology, not a covenant statement.

The only clause naming wisdom is Rev.5.12#cl0 (with cl1/cl3 nested in it), where 'wisdom' is simply one item in a doxological list of seven things the Lamb is worthy to receive ('power and riches and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing'). That is the Lamb's worthiness to receive praise, not law, Torah, or wisdom as a theme; nothing in the section speaks of law or of wisdom as an idea. The stamp is a topical label attached to a verse that only happens to contain the English word.

The reader cited Rev 5:12, and the only death-related words there are 'having been slain' (Rev.5.12#cl2, inside cl1/cl0). A slain Lamb is a violent death that redeems, not the theme 'sin_exile_death' (sin, exile and death as the human condition/curse), and nothing in the section mentions sin or exile. The one clause that could be stretched toward 'death' is being used for the Lamb's past slaughter, not for the theme.
The section opens the seals whose judgments follow (6:3-17); the Lamb's opening of the seal is the trigger but no clause here states judgment.
A conquering rider with a bow and crown can be read as an anti-kingdom figure, but no clause names a beast or an opposing kingdom; the clauses instead give victory.

No warrior or fighting man appears in this clause: the list is 'kings ... nobles ... commanders ... rich ... mighty ... every slave and free man', who 'hid in the caves'. 'Mighty' (cl0) is a strength adjective, not a warrior; the one who fights is the Lamb in his wrath (Rev.6.16#cl2), and the kings do not fight but hide.
Nothing in this section speaks of a beast or an anti-kingdom; the rider is one of the four horsemen, not the beast, and no kingdom opposes God here.

The rider of Rev.6.5 is not a beast or a ruler figure: he is 'its rider held in his hand a pair of scales' (Rev.6.5#cl7), an emblem of weighing and famine. The beastly-ruler stamp belongs to the beast from the sea/earth and the rider of Rev.6.2 who is given a crown, not to the third seal.

Nothing here is a battle: no armies, no combatants, no conflict between opposed forces. Death and Hades are given authority to kill by sword, famine, plague and beasts - a plague-like judgment on the earth, not the final battle.
No killing is presented as an offering here; the souls under the altar were slain by persecutors, not sacrificed.
The plea for judgment on the earth's dwellers fits the day-of-the-Lord horizon, but no clause in this section states a coming day of the Lord.
Rev 6:11 speaks of rest, white robes and further killings, not of anyone being raised.
The slain here are a corporate multitude of servants, not the one servant of Isaiah who suffers for others.
The altar is present, but nothing in these clauses is offered as a sacrifice; the deaths are executions by persecutors.
No blood, ransom or purchase by Christ appears in this section; the blood mentioned is the martyrs' own, to be avenged.
The section ends with further killing and waiting, not with the renewal of creation.
Rev 7:1 names only the earth, sea and trees as the spheres of harm, not the nations or peoples as a character; no clause here speaks of nations.

Nothing in the section states a promise or God's faithfulness; the closest is the sealing itself, which the reader cited at Rev 7:5 but which the text does not expound as promise. General drift at most.
The section speaks of the temple as a place of service ('serve Him day and night in His temple', 7:15) and of God's tabernacle spread over the redeemed; it says nothing of a temple being destroyed.

No clause in this section has anyone testifying or bearing witness; the crowd's cry ascribes salvation to God and the Lamb, which is praise, not witness. The nearest candidate, Rev.7.10#cl2, does not say it.
Nothing in this section depicts the day of the Lord; the multitude stands before the throne in the great tribulation's aftermath, and no clause speaks of the Lord coming or of that day.

The Lamb is not depicted as the servant who suffers here; this section has the Lamb enthroned, shepherding and wiping tears. The suffering belongs to the great tribulation crowd, not to the Lamb, and the stamp concerns the servant of Isaiah, not present in this section.

The clauses of Rev 7:16-17 promise an end to hunger, thirst, scorching heat and tears, and springs of living water; there is no clause in this section about a new heaven and new earth, or creation renewed.
The blood of the Lamb appears at Rev.7.14#cl6, but as the means of washing and making white, not as a sacrifice being offered or depicted; no clause in this section presents a sacrifice as an event.
This section has no verdict, no judgment scene and no condemnation: the crowd has come out of the great tribulation, God spreads His tabernacle over them, and no clause speaks of judging anyone.
The only physical upheaval here is the earthquake and the fire cast to the earth (Rev.8.5#cl2, Rev.8.5#cl3).
Heaven here is silent and then noisy with thunder and lightning (Rev.8.5#cl3), but no heavenly body is shaken.
No nation is mentioned or shaken; the earthquake of Rev.8.5#cl3 is in the heavenly/earthly scene, not a shaking of nations.

The stamp names a whole day-of-the-Lord scenario rather than one locution, so it is marked 'general' and pinned to the clauses where the portents occur; the eagle's "Woe" of v.13 is not itself such a portent, which is why the reader's cited verse is not among them.
This section contains only trumpet blasts; no seals or seal-openings occur anywhere in Rev.8.6-8.13, so the stamp is wrong for this section.
The section is trumpet-plague judgment that still leaves men unrepentant, which fits the day's drift; no clause names the day, its coming or its fire.
The idols named here are gold, silver, bronze, stone and wood worshiped by men on earth (Rev.9.20#cl2); no clause in this section places an idol in the temple, the holy place or any sacred site.
The cited verse names fire, sapphire and sulfur on the riders' breastplates (Rev.9.17#cl1) and smoke from the horses' mouths (Rev.9.17#cl4); the section never mentions darkness.
The trumpet judgment, the altar voice, the vast host and the unrepentant men are day-of-the-Lord material, but no clause says the day or its signs.
Rom 1:6 speaks of being "called to belong to Jesus Christ" — the recipients' calling, not any witness/testimony (martyria) given by them; no clause here says anyone testifies or bears witness.

The section's addressees are "called to belong to Jesus Christ" / "called to be saints", but no clause states or describes a people of God as such; the idea is the section's drift rather than any one clause.
Rom 1:7 is a greeting of "Grace and peace" from God; mercy and restoration are not spoken of in this section.

The section's idolatry is images of men, birds, animals and reptiles (1:23) and serving the creature (1:25); there is no 'abomination of desolation' standing in a holy place, which is what this apocalyptic crisis stamp denotes.
Nothing in the section speaks of mercy or restoration; it moves only through wrath, being given over, and vice, and the closest final note is approval of evildoers.

1:16 speaks of the gospel as God's power for salvation to everyone who believes; the section names no covenant, no covenant partner and no covenant-making, so a new covenant is not spoken of in any clause.
The only group terms in the section are 'Jew'/'Greek', 'Greeks and non-Greeks', 'wise and foolish', 'the other Gentiles' (1:13-16); no clause reconstitutes or names Israel as a people.

No clause in 11:11-24 speaks of a remnant; the root/branches and the 'some of them' saved (11:14#cl1) are not a remnant idea, and the reader cited 11:17 where the branches are Israel as a tree, not a remnant.
Nothing in the section establishes a 'new Israel' entity; the grafting language in 11:17-24 concerns Gentile believers grafted into Israel's olive tree, not a replacement people.
No enemy or adversary appears in the section; 11:20 contrasts unbelief and faith, not enmity.

The section speaks of salvation, reconciliation and life from the dead (11:11#cl4, 11:15#cl1-2) but never names Christ or his redeeming work; the idea is the drift of the wider argument, not any clause here.

No clause here speaks of rule, reign, throne, or kingdom; 11:36 asserts God as source and goal of all things, not kingship, and the only possible anchor would be the doxology to Him be the glory, which is praise, not kingdom.
The verse cited (11:33) praises the depth of God's riches, wisdom, knowledge, judgments and ways; it names no mercy, compassion, forgiveness, or restoration, and nothing in 11:33-36 does either.
No clause mentions Christ, the Messiah, cross, blood, sin-bearing or purchase; 11:36 is about God as source and goal of all things, without naming Christ.
No clause speaks of renewal, making new, resurrection or a new order; the language is God's unsearchable judgments and all things being from, through and to Him.

Unsure: the Spirit is not named anywhere in clause set or Berean text of Rom 12:1-8; 'spiritual service of worship' (Rom 12:1) and 'renewing of your mind' (Rom 12:2) are the only candidates, and the Greek logike ('reasonable/spiritual') need not mean the Holy Spirit. I cannot pin a clause that carries the Spirit as such.
the section's addresses to the community ("one another", "everyone") presuppose a people of God throughout, but no clause names or characterises that people
the section speaks of evil done and suffered (Rom.12.17#cl0, Rom.12.21#cl0/#cl1) but never names sin, exile or death; the stamp's themes are not present in these clauses

Nothing here is framed as law, commandment, statute or wisdom instruction: the clauses are imperative exhortations to dispositions (love, zeal, hope), with no appeal to Torah, wisdom sayings or 'the wise'. The idea is imported from elsewhere, not spoken by any clause here.
No clause names a king, reign, kingdom or rule. 'the Lord' (Rom.12.11#cl2) is a title of the one served, not a kingdom statement, and 'hope' (Rom.12.12#cl0) is not here identified as kingdom hope.
Nothing in the section speaks of bearing witness or testimony; Rom.13.5 speaks of conscience and punishment, not witness.
The section addresses 'everyone' and the governing authorities; it does not single out God's people as a group.
The section is about submission, punishment and retribution; no clause speaks of mercy or restoration.
The section speaks of waking, casting off darkness and putting on light/Christ; it never speaks of creation, a new creation, or being made new, so no clause carries the idea.

This section lists commandments and demands love, but there is no accusation, indictment, summons or charge brought against anyone; Paul quotes the law's prohibitions only to sum them up in love, so the lawsuit motif is not spoken of here. The reader's verse (Rom 13:9) contains the imperative commandments and a summarizing citation, no legal charge or covenant dispute.

Nothing here speaks of Christ, his death, grace, or any act of redemption; Rom 13:10 speaks only of love fulfilling the law. The stamp names a theme the section does not state, so the reader's citation of Rom 13:10 does not make it true here.

No clause of Rom.14.1-12 speaks of sonship; 'brother' (14.10) and God as 'Lord'/'master' (14.4, 14.8) are the relations named, and the clause of 14.12 cited rests on 'account ... to God', not sonship.
No clause here shows a covenant meal; 14.6 and 14.3 speak only of eating and abstaining and giving thanks to God, with no covenant or meal-of-covenant language.
The only kingship language in the section is the noun 'kingdom' (Rom 14:17), not a king figure. No clause names or implies a king; basileia is God's reign, not a king as character role.
'son' language would require huios; Rom 14:15 speaks of 'your brother' (adelphos), which the digest tradition does not treat as son. No clause names a son.

No covenant (diathēkē) word or covenant-making language appears in the section; 'in the Lord Jesus' (Rom 14:14) and 'in the Holy Spirit' (Rom 14:17) are not covenant formulae. The citation rests on 'kingdom of God', which is not a covenant phrase.
The cited verse Rom 15:3 speaks of Christ enduring reproach, not of anyone as a servant; no clause here names a servant role (Hebrews/Greek doulos/pais absent from these clauses).
Cited Rom 15:5 speaks of endurance, encouragement, harmony and Christ Jesus; no clause here mentions covenant, new covenant, or covenant-making.
Cited Rom 15:6 speaks of glorifying God with one accord and one mouth; no clause speaks of bearing witness or testimony.
The section's drift is comfort and hope for the weak (Rom 15:4-5), but no clause names mercy, restoration, or a restoring act.

The section's drift is Paul's apostolic mission, not redemption in Christ; the cited verse (15:19) concerns proclaiming the gospel, and no clause in this section states Christ's redemptive work. Clauses like 15:16#cl2 speak of sanctification and offering, but not redemption.
The section's drift is material generosity to the poor among the saints, but no clause speaks of mercy or restoration as such.
Christ is named only as the one in whose blessing Paul comes and by whom he urges the brothers; no clause speaks of redemption, atonement or being bought back.
Nothing in the section speaks of redemption, ransom or being bought back; no relevant Hebrew or Greek word underlies any clause here.
No clause in Rom 16:1-16 speaks of testimony or bearing witness; the holy kiss in Rom.16.16#cl0 is a greeting, not witness.
No bridal or marriage language anywhere in the section; the kiss of Rom.16.16#cl0 is a greeting, not a wedding image.
None of the section's clauses speak of redemption or of being bought back, and Rom 16:7 (the cited verse) concerns apostleship and being in Christ before Paul.
No language of mercy or restoration; Rom 16:2 speaks of Phoebe receiving and being assisted and of her having been a patroness.
The Spirit is not mentioned in Rom 16:1-16; Rom 16:16's holy kiss is a greeting with no reference to the Spirit.

The one 'serving' word here (Rom.16.18#cl0 'not serving our Lord Christ') is negated of the opponents and means being devoted to Christ; the clause contrasts it with serving 'their own appetites', so it is not the slave/bondservant role in this section.
The section's closing peace and the wish that the readers be wise to good and innocent to evil reflect this drift, but no clause speaks of mercy or restoration in particular.

The Greek participle in this clause (cl0) is συνεργός, 'fellow worker' (the gloss's 'fellow worker'), not μάρτυς, 'witness'; nothing in any clause of 16:21-23 speaks of bearing witness or testimony. The stamp appears to be generated from the English word 'worker' and has no footing in the text here.
Rom.16.22#cl0-1 rest on 'ὁ γράψας' / 'who wrote down this letter' — writing, not building; nothing in 16:21-23 speaks of building or construction.

No clause in 16:21-23 speaks of redemption, blood, or being bought; the nearest is 'in [the] Lord' (Rom.16.22#cl1/cl0), a locative formula in a greeting, which does not state redemption. If the stamp is read as the general Christian frame of the letter it is general drift only.

16:23 is a greeting from Gaius/Erastus/Quartus; the only candidate words are 'all the church' (Rom.16.23#cl0) and 'in [the] Lord' (Rom.16.22), neither of which speaks of temple, sanctuary, or divine presence. The reader's citation of 16:23 does not support it.

Rom 16:27 as quoted here is doxology only — 'to the only wise God be glory forever through Jesus Christ! Amen' — with no creation, renewal, new-Adam or new-creation vocabulary; the clause list for this section contains no such words ('to the ages of the ages' is duration, not new creation).

The one day named in the section is "the day of wrath" (2:5) and "the day when God will judge" (2:16), i.e. a day of judgment for every person; nothing speaks of a day of the Lord's coming/deliverance as the stamp means.
"books_opened" rests on the heavenly record books of Rev 20:12/Dan 7:10; Rom 2:16 has God judging "men's secrets", with no book, scroll or opening anywhere in the section.
Christ Jesus is named only as the agent of judgment (2:16, "through Christ Jesus"); the section says nothing of redemption, and the other clause you cited, 2:5, has no reference to Christ at all.

The section is a sustained indictment of the Jew who has the law (Rom.2.17 through Rom.2.24) and closes with the charge that God's name is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you; that is the drift a lawsuit image names, but no clause states an accusation, summons or covenant suit, so it is general.

The section names transgression of the law (Rom.2.23, Rom.2.25, Rom.2.27) and the resulting blasphemy of God's name among the Gentiles (Rom.2.24), which is the drift this theme names, but no clause speaks of exile or death, so it is general.

No clause in the section speaks of witnessing or of anyone as a witness. Rom 3:4 clause cl3 ('it has been written That - You may be justified in the words of You and will prevail in - being judged Your') is Scripture quoted about God being proved right in his words and prevailing when judged—'justified/prevail' is a legal verdict, not testimony given by a witness. Nothing in the section presents a witness, testimony, or bearing witness.
No covenant is named, made or renewed anywhere in the section; Rom.3.24#cl0 speaks of 'the redemption that is in Christ Jesus', not of a covenant. The word 'covenant' does not occur in these verses.

'Judgment' in this section is the declared verdict of justification ('to be Him just and justifying'), not an event of judging or a day of judgment; no clause narrates a judgment event. The stamp cites Rom 3:26, which shows God's righteousness, not a judgment.

No promise is made or recalled, and God's faithfulness to a promise is not asserted; what is asserted is His righteousness revealed apart from law and attested by the Law and the Prophets (Rom.3.21#cl0-1), which is a different idea.
The section names no sacrifice, altar, offering, blood of atonement or priestly act; verse 20 speaks only of works of the law and knowledge of sin. The stamp is not true of this section.
Only as the presupposed frame of the argument (Rom 3:21-26 follows); no clause in 3:9-20 names Christ, redemption, blood or propitiation.

The clause of Rom 4:1 (#cl1) names Abraham only as 'the father of us according to [the] flesh' and asks what he 'discovered'; no clause here mentions a covenant, its making, or its terms. The passage's subject is how righteousness was credited (4:3, 4:5, 4:9-12), not the Abrahamic covenant.

The word 'covenant' never occurs in the section and no clause states a covenant; what the section does is argue how Abraham, the covenant partner, was reckoned righteous. General drift of the Abraham material, not a clause in particular.

Nothing in Rom 4:1-12 mentions Christ, the cross, or redemption; the section argues from Abraham, David, faith and crediting. The link to Christ's redeeming work is made elsewhere in Romans, not in these clauses.

Nothing in Rom 4:13-25 speaks of a new covenant; the covenant terms here are the Abrahamic promise (4:13, 4:16-18, 4:22-24). The verse cited (4:24) concerns righteousness credited to those who believe in the One who raised Jesus, not a covenant.

No clause in the section speaks of believers being in Christ, joined to him, or sharing his death and resurrection; the clauses speak of crediting, believing and Christ's death and raising for us, not of union with him.

Nothing in Rom 5:1-5 (or its clauses) speaks of a covenant, its parties, or its inauguration; "the love of God has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit" (Rom.5.5#cl0/cl1) is the Spirit's gift of love, not covenant language.
The section's "tribulations" (Rom.5.3#cl1, cl3) are the believers' own afflictions, and no Servant figure, vicarious suffering or Isaianic echo appears in the clauses or the Beresn text.

The section has the representative/one-and-many structure (Rom.5.15#cl3, Rom.5.17#cl0, Rom.5.19#cl0) but never says believers are in Christ, are baptized into him, or share his death and life; no clause states union.

No clause in 5:12-21 speaks of a promise, an oath, or God's faithfulness to it; the section's contrasts are trespass/gift, condemnation/justification, sin/grace. The stamp belongs elsewhere in Romans, not here.
No covenant language (no 'covenant', no institution, no blood of a covenant); 'reconciliation' and 'justified by His blood' are not a covenant

Rom 6:23 ('the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus') speaks of grace, justification and eternal life, not of a covenant, its parties, its promises, or its institution; the section contains no covenant-language clause (no 'covenant', 'testament', 'mediator', 'blood of the covenant').

This section's metaphor is slavery/freedom and fruit, not death and resurrection with Christ: Rom 6:18 says 'set free from sin and become slaves to righteousness', with no clause speaking of being buried, dying, or raised with him.
Rom 6:23 names 'the gift of God' as eternal life, not a gift/spiritual enablement of the Spirit; no clause mentions the Spirit or any spiritual gift.
The section's whole argument is a corporate address to believers ('you' throughout) about whose slaves they are, with no clause naming God's people, Israel, a remnant, or their gathering.

"fruit of the Spirit" is the Spirit's fruit (cf. Gal 5:22); Rom 7:6 speaks only of serving "in newness of Spirit", and the section's only "fruit" clauses (Rom.7.4#cl3, Rom.7.5#cl2) are fruit to God / fruit to death, not the Spirit's fruit. The stamp is not true of this section.
No covenant language anywhere in Rom 7:13-25; the cited verse (25) names 'Jesus Christ our Lord' but says nothing of a covenant, old or new.
v.12 pronounces the law holy, righteous and good; it says nothing of mercy, forgiveness or restoration, and the section ends under death (v.11) with no reversal.

Paul's πνεῦμα here is the Spirit of God/life as a person and power, not breath as a natural image; nothing in the clause speaks of breath/wind, and the digest warns against building on an English word the Greek does not carry. If the stamp means 'spirit as breath/ruach imagery', this section gives it no footing.

Rom.8.1's 'no condemnation ... in Christ Jesus' is covenant-blessing language of life under the new order, but no clause in this section names or describes the making of a covenant (no διαθήκη, no covenant formula, no 'I will be your God'). It is the section's drift, not a clause.
The section speaks of sons/children and heirs, but nothing of a firstborn or pre-eminence: no clause says any of these is the firstborn (Rom.8.17#cl3, #cl4 give heirs and co-heirs, not firstborn).
No clause here mentions a covenant, its making, or covenant language; Rom.8.15#cl1/#cl2 speak of adoption and crying "Abba! Father!" without any covenant term. The stamp is not carried by any clause.

The only suffering clause, Rom.8.17#cl5 ("we suffer with Him"), is the suffering of believers with Christ, not the Servant of Isaiah who suffers for others; nothing in the section presents Christ as the suffering servant.

The covenant of salt (Numbers 18:19; 2 Chronicles 13:5) is nowhere in Ruth 2; no salt, no priestly or royal grant.

The covenant of Jonathan and David (1 Samuel 18, 20) is a different book and different persons; nothing in Ruth 2 concerns it.

The oath sworn to the patriarchs (Genesis 22:16-18; Deuteronomy 7:8) is not referred to in this section. Being 'from the clan of Elimelech' (Rut.2.1#cl1, Rut.2.3#cl3) is a family detail, not the patriarchal oath.

Boaz's words in 3:10 speak of Ruth's kindness and the blessing on her, not of any witness or testimony; the clause that does report common knowledge (Rut.3.11#cl4) is a statement about her reputation, not a witness being called or giving testimony. Ruth is the Moabite outsider, but no clause here presents her coming to faith or believing: her line in 3:9 is the request for redemption (Rut.3.9#cl4, cl5), and Boaz's word in 3:10 blesses her loyalty (Rut.3.10#cl3). Ruth 4:12 speaks of offspring the LORD will give and of Perez, Tamar's son -- but no clause here is about a firstborn as such, nor about firstborn status or rights. Perez is not named as firstborn.

No clause in this section names a king or the exercise of kingship, including the verse cited (vs 6).
No clause shows a visible manifestation of God; only a messenger figure stands by.
No clause mentions the Day of Atonement or any of its rites; the iniquity is removed by a bare divine declaration (Zec.3.9#cl7), not by the atonement ritual.
No clause states a covenant, its parties, or its terms; Zec.3.10#cl2 is an invitation to peaceful rest, not a covenant formula.
No clause in the section names a sacrifice, an altar, an offering or a victim; iniquity is removed without one.
The clause names the servant but says nothing of suffering, wounding or rejection; the stamp is imported from Isaiah, not read off this text.
No clause in the section mentions Christ or names him as the one who redeems; it is a Christian re-reading of Zec.3.9, not an idea the clauses state.
No clause speaks of creation, a new heaven and earth, or making all things new; Zec.3.10#cl2 promises security under vine and fig tree.
The speaker is the interpreting angel and Zechariah is the one roused and shown a vision; no clause in this section names or presents a prophet or prophetic call.
The section speaks of founding and completing the house, never of its destruction or ruin; nothing here asserts a destroyed temple.
Zerubbabel's work presupposes the return, but no clause in the section states a return or an exile.
Yahweh speaks but no clause in the section describes an appearing, glory or manifestation of God.
Zerubbabel is commissioned to do the work, but the section never uses the servant role or language of him.
Zerubbabel is a governor of Davidic descent and is promised the capstone, but no clause calls him king or describes kingship.
No clause names a priest, and the 'anointed ones' of v.14 are not called priests here.
No clause speaks of a kingdom, a throne, a reign or a king; the mountain, capstone and shouts are temple-rebuilding imagery, not kingdom language.
The priests (Joshua and the anointed ones) belong to the section's context but no clause in it speaks of priesthood or priestly service.
The restoration of the community's temple is assumed throughout, but the section names only Zerubbabel, the angel and the two anointed ones, not the people as such.
Zech 5:4 has only the prophetic formula "declares the LORD of Hosts" (Zec.5.4#cl1); no appearance, glory or visible divine manifestation is narrated in these verses.
The section names theft and false swearing by the divine name, but states no covenant breach, exile or restoration crisis; the stamp would be a general, imported reading.
No day-of-the-Lord language (darkness, coming day, visitation) occurs; the judgment here is the curse cutting off individuals' houses, with no eschatological day named.
Nothing in this section places an idol in a holy place; the basket goes to Shinar, not to the temple or sanctuary.
The section speaks of Wickedness being removed to Shinar, the opposite of an abomination bringing desolation to a holy place.
A vision of heavenly agents going out to patrol the earth is the section's general drift; no clause states a day of the Lord.

Zech.6.6 names destinations (north, west, south) and Zech.6.8 says the north horses have given rest to My Spirit; rest, not judgment, is the outcome stated here. The horses going out is unexplained by any clause in this section.
Chariots and horses are present, but no clause presents a warrior; the four are called 'the four spirits of heaven' (Zec.6.5#cl2) and their task is patrol, not battle.
Zech.6.8 states the outcome for the north as giving rest to the LORD's Spirit; no clause in this section states judgment.

The section speaks of building the temple, not of its destruction. Destruction of the temple is presupposed, not asserted: nothing here states the temple was destroyed. Closest clauses (Zec.6.12#cl8, Zec.6.13#cl0, Zec.6.15#cl1) say the opposite, that it will be built.
The section calls the figure 'a man' whose name is 'the Branch' and a priest on his throne; no clause gives him the role of servant (Hebrew עבד) nor anything a reader would point to for it.
Zech 7:2 mentions 'the people of Bethel' and 7:14 'behind them', but no clause says a remnant survived or returned.
The covenant formula in Zec 8:8 is covenant language, but no clause in this section states a new covenant; the stamp restates the section's general drift and I cannot pin it to particular clauses.
Zech 8:4-5 describes restored peaceful city life, not a new creation; no clause here speaks of creation renewed.
The section is delivered as an oracle of Yahweh, but no clause names or portrays a prophet; the speaker stands behind the text, not in it.
The whole section is future-tense divine promise, but no single clause states 'promise' itself.
Prophetic speech-form of the whole oracle, not carried by any one clause.
Nothing in the section speaks of creation or renewal of the world; the imagery is battle, deliverance, and agricultural abundance within the land.
the section presents a coming king of Zion but never names David or any dynastic heir; the stamp is the section's general drift, not carried by any clause
the whole section is first-person divine speech of what God will do, but no single clause states that it is a promise oracle
The section is universal-judgment speech by the LORD against earth, Judah and Jerusalem, the stuff the day of the LORD is made of, but no clause here names 'the day of the LORD'. General, not pinned.
Nothing in these clauses pronounces woe (no hoy/woe form); the speech is first-person divine action, 'I will sweep away / cut off', not a woe oracle.
No lawsuit form appears: no summons, no accusation-indictment, no rib. The section is a first-person judgment speech; covenant language (Baal, the LORD) is present but the lawsuit genre is not.
the whole passage is prophetic speech, but no clause in it names or describes the word of the LORD itself

Nothing in the section presents a ruler, man or beast: the only agents are the LORD (Zep.2.13#cl0–cl1), the city personified as a boasting woman (Zep.2.15#cl2), and animals that merely lie down and roost (Zep.2.14#cl0–cl1). The reader cited Zeph 2:15, but that verse gives a ruined city as a resting place for beasts, not a beast-like ruler.

The section has no besieging army, siegeworks, ramps, walls attacked or starvation; Nineveh's fall is described only as the LORD stretching out His hand and making it a dry waste (Zep.2.13#cl0–cl3). Wanton words “desolation” (Zep.2.14#cl3) and “ruin” (Zep.2.15#cl5) describe the aftermath, not a siege.

Zeph 2:14 is about Nineveh's palaces: the Hebrew behind “pillars” (Zep.2.14#cl1) is capitals, and “beams of cedar” (Zep.2.14#cl4) is cedar panelling of a palace laid bare, not a temple. Nothing in the section names a temple or sanctuary.

No deportation, captivity, forced march or return is stated: the doomed peoples are slain (Zep.2.12#cl2) and their cities left as ruins inhabited by animals (Zep.2.14#cl0, Zep.2.15#cl5), not carried away.

The section never uses the phrase or names a day of the LORD; it announces the LORD's judgment on Cush and Assyria (Zep.2.12#cl2, Zep.2.13#cl0–cl1) without dating it as that day. This is the section's drift in the book's frame, not something a clause says.

The section is an oracle of Yahweh's judgment on the nations and the exaltation of Yahweh over the gods, which is the drift of the day of the LORD, but no clause here says 'day' or names that day; the reader's cited verse (2:11) carries the theme only in this general way.

Nothing in these clauses is mercy or restoration: they are reproach received, destruction of Moab and Ammon like Sodom and Gomorrah, and the remnant plundering them. The nations bowing in worship to Yahweh (2:11) is the nations' submission, and Yahweh starving the gods of the earth is judgment on the gods, not mercy or restoration; the reader's cited verse does not carry the stamp.
The clause names 'officials/princes' (roaring lions), not a king; no king is spoken of in this section (Zep.3.3#cl1 'judges' likewise is not a king).
The whole oracle concerns the city/Jerusalem and its rulers (princes, judges, prophets, priests) — the body politic — but no clause names a kingdom, king or royal rule.
Zeph.3.1–3.5 is entirely accusation and judgment (woe, no correction, unfaithful leaders, no shame); no clause speaks of mercy or restoration in this section.
The peace of 3:15 and 3:17 is announced and enjoyed, but no clause here states a covenant or its making; it is the drift of the section, not any clause in particular.
The clauses of 3:18 speak of the grieved and the reproached, and 3:19 of the lame and the scattered; the word 'remnant' and the idea of a surviving remainder do not appear.
The section has restoration of people and city, not the making of a new heaven and earth or a new creation; no clause carries the idea.
No woe ('woe to...') form appears; the section is first-person divine speech of past devastation and future gathering for judgment, not a 'woe' oracle.
No clause in Zep.3.9-13 speaks of creation, a new heaven and earth, or cosmic renewal; resting securely (Zep.3.13#cl3-5) is peace, not new creation.
